#3015. The 17 Best Cocktail Bars in Milan, Where Aperitivo Is Just the Beginning

One common misconception about cocktail bars in Milan is that the city’s drinking culture begins and ends with the aperitivo. Yes, the pre-dinner ritual still defines much of the city’s social culture, but the bar scene in Milan has evolved significantly over the past few years, thanks to a brigade of hospitality-minded, boundary-pushing talent.

While the Spritz and the Negroni Sbagliato aren’t going anywhere anytime soon, a new wave of mixologists has elaborated on the customary red-orange palette, pouring an array of jewel-toned beverages layered with technique, seasonality and innovation. Some of these cocktail bars in Milan are part of larger operations with restaurants; others distinguish themselves independently. From the classic to the new, here are 18 of the best cocktail bars in Milan where even teetotalers will drink exceptionally well. Reservations are recommended whenever possible.

Like its equally multi-faceted sibling Moebius (named after the French cartoonist), Lubna claims a namesake: a radical Italian comic book heroine of the 1970s. It arrived on the scene in December 2024 inside a former tram depot in the district dubbed SouPra (“South of Prada”—the Foundation, that is). The vast, faintly industrial open warehouse incorporates concrete and wood surfaces, and glass walls frame views of the al fresco crowd in the courtyard. The layout splits between a restaurant and a cocktail bar, with a listening lounge tucked into the back corner, whose walls come alive with flickering anime cartoons. The cocktails echo executive chef Enrico Croatti’s flame-driven cooking, incorporating ingredients grilled or charred over open fire. The Strawberry and Roasted Capsicum is a smoky riff on a Negroni, built from mezcal and diluted juice from a roasted pepper, while a spin on the tequila-based Toreador adds yoghurt and house-made “black oil” infused with fiery charcoal ember.

Rita, Edoardo Nono and Chiara Buzzi’s modern classic opened in 2002 along the Naviglio Grande—well before the banks of the canal-crossed district evolved into the bar-loaded hotbed it is today. Nono and his team pioneered practices now considered commonplace, such as house-made infusions and juices and buffet-free quality aperitivo eats served at the table. Sit at the U-shaped Larchwood bar backed by a bottle rack displaying over 500 premium labels that stretch to the ceiling, or plop yourself on one of the red banquettes edging the walls. Among the ever-changing, inventive cocktails is one retro throwback: the Gin Zen, a 90s-style hodgepodge of crushed ice, gin, muddled fresh ginger, lime, and soda that Nono’s been mixing since day one. Just across the street is Rita’s Tiki Room, which opened in 2019.

This epic institution evokes the charm of a bygone era while still setting the benchmark for cool. Avail yourself of a Negroni Sbagliato, or the “Mistaken Negroni” swapping prosecco for gin, created in 1972 by late owner Mirko Stocchetto. Better yet, ask for “uno Sbagliato grande” which swims among clinking ice cubes in a glass goblet bigger than your head. If you’re not in the mood for bitter, Bar Basso’s plentiful cocktail list runs 500 long and counting. The clientele represents all walks of life: young and old, regulars and newbies, locals and travellers. Stocchetto’s son Maurizio, the current owner, marked the 50th anniversary with a light refurbishment but one that kept the vintage backbone intact, from the brocades and mirrors to the marble floor and dark wood panels. The crowds can spill onto the sidewalk any given evening (especially during Design Week), so make sure to book in advance for prime-time imbibing.

Bob The Other Side is the newest venture from Luca and Michele Hu, the twin brothers behind the Chinese Box Group and longtime stalwarts of Milan’s mixology scene. The name is literal: the bar is just beside Bob Milano, their cult Isola cocktail spot, hidden behind an unassuming teal door that recalls the entryways of old Milanese tenements. Step inside, though, and the mood shifts entirely. The design plays with geometry, reflection and depth—think warm wood panelling, bronzed mirrors, walnut tables, brass accents and luminous geometric details, including a striking hexagonal counter. Cesar Araujo, who also leads the cocktail program at Bob, crafts the drinks, which include the Hidden Love with gin, tomato–pomegranate cordial, and Timut pepper; Ray of Illusions, blending pisco, sherry, black sesame and apple-flavoured matcha; and Holy Water, a lush mix of Woodford Bourbon, spiced honey, citrus and coconut milk infused with Lapsang.

Don’t be alarmed by Camparino’s proximity to the Duomo—there’s nothing tourist-trappy about this 110-year-old mainstay. At the ground-floor Bar di Passo, sip Campari classics at the counter, surrounded by an exquisite Art Deco backdrop that has captivated patrons since its opening. In the upstairs Sala Spiritello, Tommaso Cecca and his bar team push boundaries with creative cocktail pairings. The current menu, crafted in honour of Camparino’s 110th anniversary, traces Camparino’s history through 12 drinks, starting in 1915, then marking the start of each subsequent decade through 2025. Among them: Italian Blood (1935), with Campari, tomato water and aromatic herbs; Lacto Garibaldi (1975), which combines Campari with lacto-fermented orange juice; and the Breeze (1995), a vibrant blend of Campari, vodka, pomegranate juice, zallotti blossom, and pink grapefruit soda. At the intimate, reservations-only Sala Gaspare, named for Campari’s founder, the drinks reimagine the aromas and ingredients that make up his iconic bitter.

Occupying a 700-square-metre former textile warehouse, Moebius juggles multiple concepts, one of which is a cocktail bar that currently ranks seventh on the World’s 50 Best Bars list. Bar manager Giovanni Allario weaves unexpected twists into classics, like the Pesto Martini with vodka, white balsamic vinegar, and homemade pesto and a Gremolada Negroni with notes of lemon and parsley. The decor juxtaposes its iron-flecked industrial skeleton with warm and natural accents like a 700-year-old Andalusian olive tree. A backlit concrete bottle rack extends three metres high from behind a light wood counter that seats seven, while wood tables and couches and chairs in earthy grey, brown, and blue hues speckle the boundless venue.

Don’t let the name fool you – Dario Comini’s trailblazing molecular mixology mecca is about as far from a British sports pub as it gets. The elaborate, experiential drinks are presented on trays or pedestals alongside clever fixings. The French Kiss rests beside illuminated lips, clutching an aphrodisiac flower, and patrons put the finishing touches on the signature C.S.I. cocktail with syringes and test tubes. A dark wood bar salvaged from New York’s Knickerbocker Hotel anchors the room from its post in front of shelves crammed with over 1800 bottles. Dozens of eclectic objects, like stone buddhas and African masks, that Comini procured from his travels, complete the treasure trove look. No reservations, no exceptions. Ever. There’s always a line, but it’s worth the wait. If you get there around 10-15 minutes before it opens, you should be able to get seated during the first turn.

Named after a former Futurist magazine, Lacerba opened in 1999 and strikes the perfect balance between nostalgic and zany: vintage ads and abstract art adorn the walls, dozens of empty bottles dangle from the ceiling, an illuminated cutout of Milan’s Duomo twinkles beside shelves stocked with analogue clocks and travel books – an ambience that can dub as an icebreaker if you’re struggling for conversation on, say, a first date. Though, Lacerba’s always a blast with friends and loved ones. Of owner Angelo Trapasso’s 51 cocktails, five change monthly – a sure bet year round is the Discorso aritmetico alla fidanzata (Arithmetic Speech to the Girlfriend), a riff on the classic Americano. Lacerba’s famous Bloody Mary menu features ten recipes ranging from classic to playful, like the flowery Saint Mary in Love with dry sherry and elderflower liqueur.

Luca Marcellin’s 26-seat cocktail bar couples the conviviality of a neighborhood place with the intrigue of a speakeasy. You ring a bell to enter, but the mystery isn’t so much what’s inside as the windowed facade reveals a lively, chatty crowd, but rather in the curiously clever cocktails, like the Negroni all’avocado, which incorporates their own avocado oil distillate or the Sazerac Fire, mixed with Cognac, cocoa beans and chilli pepper, and hazelnut bitter. Gin and tonic lovers can choose from five versions. Drinc.different, which Marcellin co-owns with Desiree Brunet, is just five minutes from its sibling. The narrow, 18-seat nook feels equally inviting but more discreet with low tables and chairs and dim lighting—perfect for date night. The equally curious drinks include N’Doritos with Doritos-infused Pisco, red vermouth, and chocolate bitter, and the refreshing Fra’Paloma with tequila, cinnamon, citric, grapefruit soda, and a house-infused strawberry and vanilla mezcal.

Niccolò Caramiello and Stefano Rollo’s bar in Lambrate evokes “Old Milan” with its sleek green Guatemalan marble bar top and custom-made furnishings procured from recycled materials, lived-in walls, and dark wood floors. Absinthe is the star of the glass here, with 11 Italian, Swiss, and French labels on offer, appearing in reworked classics like the Absinthe Marini, Absinthe Rita, Absinthe Mule, and Absinthe Julep. For an alternative to the anise-flavoured liqueur, try the Million Dollar Hotel made with vodka, port, mastiha, beets, and a hint of wasabi. Provisions include tinned Spanish and Portuguese fish and French oysters—it’s not unusual for the latter to appear in a martini. Earlier this year, the team opened Cactus Joe, a cocktail bar focused on agave distillates. Who’s Norah? Accounts may vary, but the one consistency is that she’s a figment of the owners’ imagination.

An anagram for “Casual Ristorante Cocktails”, Carico also means “powered” in Italian, a fitting pun to a concept packing punchiness and prowess. Domenico Carella oversees a selection of cutting-edge drinks, like the Capsicum Funky, with tequila, white chocolate, jalapeño, and citrus; Arantius Siesta, a mix of mezcal, sherry, orange, and sesame; and the Chipotloni, a negroni kicked up with Chipotle. Can’t decide? Opt for the mini cocktail route: four half-portions for 30€, or stick to reliable staples like a gin and tonic—with over two dozen types of gin to choose from. The kitchen delivers playful, elevated small plates, such as a croque monsieur with mortadella and Parmigiano fonduta, and pulled pork tacos, among others. Every so often, the seven-seat Negroni Room pops up for an experiential, all-sensory food-and-drink experience dedicated to its namesake legend—book your spot in advance. Carella is also one of the forces behind Ultra, a pizzeria and cocktail bar that opened last year.

The Bulgari Hotel’s swanky bar area centres around a glossy, oval black resin island that seats 20 and rests beside a glass wall looking out at the garden. Bar manager Patrick Greco and his team update the menu twice a year, and on the list today are a half-dozen evocatively named creations. The Polaris dazzles with tequila, mezcal, blackberry syrup, and a touch of citrus air foam, while the Hydra balances gin, mastiha, carrot, celery, and a bright, zesty twist of lime. For a deeper dive, the Belvedere Martini Experience presents two scaled-down Belvedere-based martinis side by side to illustrate the subtle contrasts in flavour, aroma, and texture. When the weather cooperates, book an al fresco table among the pagoda trees and boxwoods of the lush garden that feels light years away from the city.

The eighth floor of Casa Brera, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Milan, houses one of the city’s most stunning rooftop venues: Etereo, a sky bar and restaurant whose spectacular 360-degree panorama of the city encompasses the Duomo, Galleria, Castello Sforzesco and the Porta Nuova skyscrapers. The space feels both vintage and contemporary, decorated in shades of cherry red, brown sugar and desert sand, with windowed walls, cane-backed chairs and lacquered tables, all anchored around a red arabesque marble bar. The “Art of the Aperitivo” cocktail list features 13 signature drinks, each paying tribute to a different Milanese neighbourhood. The Bell’Art Martini, an ode to the Brera, combines vodka, gin and white penja and is finished with a spritz of black pepper, while the Heritage draws inspiration from Castello Sforzesco and Corso Sempione, mixing tequila, mezcal, mastiha, tonic, angostura bitters, Champagne, passion fruit, and a touch of green mandarin.

The first cocktail bar in Milan from Flavio Angiolillo’s now epic Farmily Group, MAG Cafe, opened in the heart of the Navigli in 2011. The cocktail current roster, named “World Comes to Milan”, features a selection of cleverly crafted cocktails, each named after a different country, in honour of the 2026 Winter Olympics. China combines ginseng rum, litchi liqueur, rice-and-peach cordial, sapsang souchong tea and lime, while France mixes Cognac Martell VS, prickly pear distillate, Ratatrip (a proprietary take on French ratafia), ratatouille water, wine-tomato reduction and lemon. The boho-vintage interior ups the charm factor: an Argentine pharmacy counter, dangling bicycle wheels affixed with lights resembling the spokes of a ship helm, and ever-changing paintings and ornaments. The group’s other establishments include La Pusterla, MAG’s sibling; 1930, the elusive invite-only speakeasy; Backdoor 43, the world’s smallest bar; Iter, a cocktail bar equipped with a proper kitchen; and two outposts of Tripstillery, Italy’s first cocktail bar with a distillery onsite.

In Milanese dialect, “Tusa” means “girl”, the inspiration for owner Norma Galdamez’s cocktails, all named after 20th-century female trailblazers. The Sissi combines rum, lime and chestnut honey, with notes of coffee and mint, for a tipple as intense, sweet and unpredictable as its namesake princess. Gin, cardamom, Lapsang, Verjus and pink grapefruit soda channel the vivacious spirit of the late Raffaella Carra, an iconic, boundary-breaking Italian entertainer, while the Ella Fitzgerald, with Jameson Black Barrel, toasted sesame, Shochu, toasted hazelnut and rakomelo reduction, is warm, velvety and elegant–just like her voice. The inviting, feels-like-home ambience is enhanced with low velvet sofas in shades of green, blue, and yellow, marble and wood tables, and quirky gold-framed artwork and portraits on the sapphire walls.

At the Mandarin Oriental, Milan's chic retreat, beloved local barman Guglielmo Miriello has crafted a cocktail menu inspired by far-off lands like the Majorelle with eucalyptus-infused vodka, Acqua Bianca liqueur, blue spirulina, Moroccan lemon cordial, and mint bitters, and the Port Elizabeth, with almond-infused cognac, rooibos and honeybush shrub, hibiscus water, and sherry. Sit indoors among the sleek black and white marble interiors or, weather permitting, head outside to the garden nestled into the courtyard outfitted with pastel armchairs and sofas among the climbing ivy and leafy potted plants.

Gesto’s dining room, brightened by Michela Picchi’s pop art, carries a hint of speakeasy intrigue, with a short passage leading to the listening bar, or Sala Malinconia (Melancholy Room), concealed behind a mustard-yellow curtain. In Italian, malinconia evokes a softer, more nostalgic feeling than pure sadness, an appropriate descriptor as the room evokes the good days of the analogue era. Emerald-green walls display framed vintage prints, while guests gather around candlelit dark-wood mid-century-style furnishings. At the front, a turntable rests in a wooden wall unit lined with more than a thousand vinyls, its central mirror tilted down to reflect the DJ’s hands at work. The cocktail list gives new life to classics, like the Boogie Mary with butter-and-sage-infused Grey Goose; the San Carlo, a Negroni spiced with pink pepper; and the Matcha Amor, a gimlet-style blend of mezcal, coconut cream, lime, matcha and white chocolate. A tapas menu lets you easily turn your evening of cocktails into a fully-fledged dinner.

#3016. The Best Morning Routine for Digestion & a Bloat-Free Start to Your Day

Starting your day with a healthy morning routine can set the tone for the rest of your day. If you often struggle with bloating or digestive issues, incorporating a few simple habits into your morning can make a big difference in how you feel throughout the day.

Hydrate First Thing

After a night of sleep, your body is dehydrated and in need of fluids. Drinking a glass of warm water with lemon first thing in the morning can help kickstart your digestion and hydrate your body. This simple habit can aid in reducing bloating and promoting regular bowel movements.

Eat a Balanced Breakfast

Skipping breakfast or opting for sugary pastries can wreak havoc on your digestion. Instead, opt for a balanced breakfast that includes fiber, protein, and healthy fats. Foods like oatmeal with nuts and fruit, Greek yogurt with granola, or a smoothie with spinach and avocado can provide the nutrients your body needs to support healthy digestion.

Incorporate Movement

Physical activity can help stimulate digestion and reduce bloating. Whether it's a quick yoga flow, a brisk walk, or some stretching exercises, incorporating movement into your morning routine can help get things moving in your digestive system.

Practice Mindful Eating

Rushing through your meals or eating on the go can lead to poor digestion and bloating. Take the time to sit down and savor your breakfast, chewing your food slowly and mindfully. This can help prevent overeating and improve the efficiency of your digestion.

Sip on Herbal Tea

Herbal teas like peppermint, ginger, or chamomile can have soothing effects on the digestive system. Sipping on a cup of herbal tea after your breakfast can help calm any digestive discomfort and promote healthy digestion throughout the day.

Bloat Be Gone

Your daily or on-the-spot fix for a lighter, more comfortable belly. Its gentle blend of digestive enzymes, ginger, peppermint, and dandelion root tackles puffiness from stress, travel, or indulgences—no matter what’s on the menu. 

By incorporating these simple habits into your morning routine, you can support better digestion and start your day feeling energized and bloat-free. Remember, consistency is key, so make these habits a part of your daily routine so you can feel your BEST, all of the time!

#3017. Why do dogs have cold noses?

Have you ever wondered why dogs have cold, wet noses? It might seem strange for a warm-blooded animal to have a cold, wet nose, but it’s actually a fantastic adaptation that supercharges a dog’s sense of smell and helps to regulate their body temperature.

A dog’s nose is covered in a thin layer of mucus, which keeps it moist. Why is this helpful? Smell molecules travel through the air, but are easier to capture when they can attach to something, in this case, the moisture of a dog’s nose traps tiny smell particles.

Moisture evaporates, and it is the constant evaporation of moisture from the surface of a dog’s nose that makes it cooler than the rest of its body.

Dogs can also smell independently from each nostril, which allows them to work out the direction of the smell.

Humans sweat to cool down, but dogs don’t have sweat glands, so they have to cool down a different way. They do this by panting and using their nose.

Dog noses have lots of blood vessels close to the surface. As moisture on the nose evaporates, it cools the blood passing through the nose, which then travels back through the body, helping to cool the body.

Dogs’ noses also act as heat detectors. They can detect a small animal from its heat from about 1.5 metres away. This only works because a dog’s nose is cooler than the object it’s trying to detect!

A dog’s cold, wet nose is a great evolutionary adaptation with multiple uses, supercharging their sense of smell, helping to regulate their body temperature and allowing them to detect animals even when they can’t see or hear them.

#3018. Gorgeous Rainbow Mountain in Peru With Bonus Red Valley Views…and Alpacas!

If youâve ever wondered why the hype around Rainbow Mountain Peru refuses to fade, hereâs why. Like many epic places or adventures, it’s always better in person than online. For me, this one ranks just under the day I hiked Pisac Ruins in the misty rain, and right up there with exploring the Ollantaytambo Ruins.

This site participates in the Amazon Services LLC Associates Program and other affiliate programs and may earn from qualifying purchases.

After a couple weeks in Cusco, Peru, I finally booked an inexpensive but amazing guided day tour for hiking Rainbow Mountain, and the day delivered big-time: thin air, 360Â° views, friendly locals, and amazing Rainbow Mountain photos I’ll share with you here.

But again, these photos of Rainbow Mountain don’t do the actual views justice. And the fact that the additional short hike to the views of The Red Valley wasn’t even on my radar before the tour to Rainbow Mountain made the day tour even better.

Make sure you check out this article next on all the other things to do in and around Cusco and the Sacred Valley!

Whether youâre winging it, backpacking on a budget, rolling luxury, or working remotely, this is one of those day tours from Cusco, Peru thatâs totally worth setting an alarm…wait…multiple alarms, for.

I was picked up at 3:40 a.m. at Plaza de Armas, which meant a 15m walk in the beautiful, empty morning streets through San Blas. I love empty streets! I was half-asleep and layered in clothing, ready for the different possibilities in weather and temperatures that go hand-in-hand with hiking Rainbow Mountain.

The drive from Cusco takes around three or four hours total, with a quick breakfast stopâ breakfast and lunch after the hike were included in the tourâ before the trailhead assuming you book the inexpensive day tour that I did.

Once on foot, youâll be walking at serious altitude. Starting around 4,600 m (15,100 ft) and climbing to 5,036 m (16,500 ft), the altitude of Rainbow Mountain is no joke.

Every step is earned, and the short distance from the base camp to the peak took a little over an hour because you are moving at a snails pace.

Even though the hike only takes 1â1.5 hours up, the altitude makes it feel double that. I took it slow, stopped often, and reminded myself that this was bucket-list stuff, not a race. And since I have a heart condition and other fun stuff, it was kind of extra important for me to pay attention to my body.

Rainbow Mountain hiking tip number one: donât be a heroâpace yourself! So many of the people younger than me charged out of the gates at top speed, but my slower overall pace had us reaching the peak at the same time.

You can technically DIY this with a driver, or probably with a rental car, but most people join a Rainbow Mountain tour from Cusco for the ease, meals, and safety.

I went small-group, in a van that sat about 16, catered breakfast and lunch, and emergency oxygen for those that needed it. Took almost all of the guesswork out of the day tour for me.

Hereâs the deal: the altitude of Rainbow Mountain is no joke. If youâve just flown into Cusco, Peru, give yourself at least two days to acclimate. For me it took 3-4 to start to feel whole again, but again, I have more issues than most, lol.

Hydrate like itâs your job, skip alcohol the night before, and keep snacks handy. Even seasoned hikers find themselves gasping for air up here. I also had my doctor give me some pills for high altitudes which I took for the 48h prior, and other than the hike being really tough, I had no issues.

And yes, I saw multiple people on oxygen and clearly suffering from altitude sickness at the peak!

If dizziness or nausea hits, rest or descend, and let your tour guide know immediately. Donât try to âpush through.â Many Rainbow Mountain tours from Cusco carry oxygen, but prevention is always betterârespect your limits. You can also rent a horse to get you up to the peak if that’s easier!

Side note…don’t forget to always, always, always consider getting inexpensive travel medical insurance âsometimes as low as $2/dayâfor your trip, and a separate yearly evacuation insurance policy if you travel internationally often! And check out my list of tips for staying safe while traveling abroad.

Planning your trip around weather makes or breaks those epic Rainbow Mountain photos you’re hoping to get. Bottom line though is to suck it up and do the earliest tour of the day you possibly can, because the weather is better and the crowds are at least double by noon!

Clear skies and crisp mornings make this prime time for hiking Rainbow Mountain. Expect cold starts, warm midday sun, and postcard-perfect colors.

Youâll trade smaller crowds for muddy trails and cloudy views. Still, the diffused light can make for surprisingly great Rainbow Mountain Peru photosâthe colors pop softly without glare.

I was in Cusco and did my Rainbow Mountain and Red Valley tour the last week of October. I got lucky, but at that time, I had heard many people complain that the peaks were covered in snow! But if you go at this time it can definitely be a sweet spot: fewer people, mild weather, and a good chance for clear skies.

I almost always travel to these epic places in the shoulder seasons to save money and avoid crowds.

Pack light but smart. Youâll be climbing and shedding layers all day.

Pro Tip for Cusco or Peru in generalâPack Sunscreen from home! Peruvians don’t really use it, so the prices are extremely high. Like I saw upwards of $20+USD per small bottle prices!

Even if meals are included, bring extra snacksâyouâll burn more calories than you think. And always keep camera gear accessible for those surprise alpaca and llama run-ins (of which you will have plenty) which make Rainbow Mountain Peru photos epic.

A typical Rainbow Mountain tour from Cusco lasts about 12-13 hours. Youâll leave in the dark, hike mid-morning, and be back in Cusco by evening. Again, take the earliest tour you can! Thank me later!

Group tours are cheaper ($25â40 USD) and not going to be much different than an expensive private tour. (You can compare different tour company options here and here.) Private tours can run $80â120 but give you flexibility, but I’m not sure it’s worth the money since nearly every condition on the actual hike will be the same as a cheaper (but just as rewarding) tour.

If you want a little more of a hike once you reach the peak viewpoint for Rainbow Mountain, you can ascend a little higher to the ridgeline next to it to overlook The Red Valley.

The Red Valley wasn’t even on my radar, but dare I say that the views were as goodâor maybe even more rewardingâthan the crowded views of Rainbow Mountain.

I followed a faint trail along a ridge where the colors shifted from rainbow bands to deep crimson dunes. Combined with the passing cloudsâwhich actually covered Rainbow Mountain shortly after I left that spotâand the views of the valley were jaw-dropping.

I understand from the tour guides that the soil in the Red Valley is rich in iron oxide, giving it a Mars-on-Earth kind of look. Most people skip it, but this was possibly my favorite part of the day. No crowds, just wind and silence.

It only adds another 30m or so the total route, and you’ve already made most of the ascent, so don’t skip it if you have time!

When booking your Rainbow Mountain tour from Cusco, ask if The Red Valley option is included. If not, some guides will let you decide at the top and pay a small extra fee for entry, around 30 SOL when I did it.

Those colorful stripes are fragile mineral layersâdonât wander off path.

Buy snacks or tea from local stalls. Itâs small money for you but goes a long way for the Quechua families who manage the trail.

Watch the sky. Clouds can roll in fast, and hail isnât rareâit actually started snowing just after I left the viewpoint. Always have your outer shell ready, even if the sun feels warm. And again, sunscreen, sunscreen, sunscreen!

Want to travel more but donât really know where to start? Have a friend or family member that keeps talking about travelâbut clearly needs a little help actually getting off go and making it happen? This is the no-fluff, hands-on guide to finally getting unstuck and on a travel pathâwith confidence, intention, and zero shame.

Before you tackle the hike, hereâs a quick-hit list thatâll make your day smoother:

And make sure to use the base camp bathrooms because you don’t want to be forced to use the pit toilets at the top near the Rainbow Mountain viewpoint!

A few extra Rainbow Mountain hiking tips to lock in the experience:

before leaving your accommodation. Even if your tour includes breakfast, it won’t be for about 2-3 hours after you wake

every 30 or 50 feet on the hike. You’ll be surprised how just stopping for 10 seconds can really help you feel refreshed and help you catch your breath quickly.

before, during, and after the hike. High altitude is dry all-around.

for photos when you want, not only when your lungs force you to.

Rainbow Mountain in Peru really does live up to the hype. The colors shift with the light and the cloud cover, the views stretch forever, and the final ridge feels like standing on the edge of another planet.

Add to that the views of the Red Valley and the round trip tour cost of around $40USD (all-in with tip & extras) seems like a ridiculous steal.

For more Cusco details and adventures, check out this full travel guide for Cuscoâbecause this regionâs full of peaks worth chasing, like hiking the Pisac Ruins in the rain or scaling the side of a mountain wall doing a via ferrata!

Enjoy! Hope this article inspired you to do the thing!

Jason is the author of “The Beginner Traveler’s Guide” as well as the voice behind the words and the eye behind the lens for The Nomad Experiment. “Planning to travel at some point” wasn’t actually getting the job done, so nearing 40 he decided to make it a priority, nomatter how scary that was. A few years laterâthrough the pandemic and a type 1 diabetes diagnosis at age 42ânow living a life of nomadic travel, he’s speaking out to encourage others of any age, or with any serious medical diagnosis, to live an unconventional life.

Letâs just say itâs not a walk in the parkâbut itâs not Everest either. The main challenge of hiking Rainbow Mountain Peru is the altitude, not the distance.

The hike itself is only a couple miles roundtrip, but since youâre hiking between roughly 15,000 and 17,000 feet (4,600â5,200 meters), youâll definitely feel it in your lungs.

Most people can finish in 2-3 hours roundtrip, depending on how often you stop to catch your breath or if you stop to take a million photos of Rainbow Mountain, the glaciers, alpacas, and llamas along the way.

Yesâabsolutely. Spend at least two or three days in Cusco before attempting Rainbow Mountain so your body can adjust to the thin air. Cusco itself sits at around 11,500 feet, which helps ease you into the altitude game.

The dry season (roughly May through September) is your best bet for clear skies and those vivid colors everyone drools over on Instagram. During the rainy season, clouds can hide the mountainâor worse, turn it into a muddy or snowy mess.

That said, shoulder months like April and October can still be lovely and slightly less crowded if you get lucky with the weather. I hiked Rainbow Mountain in late October and it was perfect!

Totally! Most hikers hike to the Red Valley overlook immediately after reaching the main summit, like I did. It only takes an extra 30-60 minutes, but itâs absolutely worth it. The Red Valley looks like something straight out of Marsârolling red hills, streaked with green and grayâand way fewer people. Save some water and energy for this extra leg of hike.

Colder than youâd expect, even when the sunâs out. Mornings can hover near freezing, and the wind at the top can be rough. Layers are your best friend: a base layer, a warm fleece, a windproof jacket, gloves, and a beanie will keep you toasty enough, but you’ll likely find yourself swapping on and off quite regularly.

Technically yesâbut itâs not recommended unless youâre confident with high-altitude navigation and more importantly the transportation logistics. Tours from Cusco are super affordable (usually around $30â40 USD all-in), and they handle everything: transportation, breakfast, lunch, and usually oxygen if you need it.

Going solo means driving (do not recommend!) finding your own driver and entrance ticket, which can be a hassle at 3 a.m. when youâre trying to leave town.

Youâll want layers, sun protection, snacks, water, and maybe a trekking pole or two. The sun can fry you even when itâs chilly, so a hat, sunglasses, and sunscreen are non-negotiable.

Yes. Youâll find a fairly new, large, but basic toilet house near the trailhead and pit toilets midway upâwhich you won’t want to plan on unless there’s an emergency! Bring some coins since TP cost 2 SOL when I was thereâfor about 12 squares, lol.

Yes! Locals along the trail offer horses for rent if the altitude or climb gets too intense. It costs upwards of 100 SOL ($30 USD), and itâs cash only. Just keep in mind that the final steep section must be done on footâhorses canât go all the way to the top.

Yes. Muchos. They’re all along the trail up. And if you’re like me, you’ll probably see some bones from the ones that didn’t make the hike, lol.

It isâbut many photos you see on tour posters are heavily photoshopped and color-enhanced. In person, the stripes of red, gold, green, and blue are still jaw-dropping, just more natural and earthy.

Seeing the colors with your own eyes, under that thin Andean air, makes it way more magical than any photo filter could. And even my photos don’t do it justice to what my brain remembers!

#3019. Madrid 5-Day Itinerary: A Guide to Culture, Gastronomy, and Local Life

Home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city. Though it’s somewhat sprawling, the city boasts stunning architecture, incredible food, and an energetic nightlife that stretches until dawn. Over 10 million people visit the city each year, and the minute you step out to explore, you’ll understand why Madrid is one of Europe’s top destinations.

Like Barcelona, Madrid is a city that starts late and goes slow. It’s a city for night owls, where dinner starts late and the parties even later. But if you can embrace the laid-back pace of life, the slow meals, and the late-night vibes, you’ll have a more authentic visit and uncover the true beating heart of the city’s culture.

I love all my visits to Madrid. I’ve been a few times over the years and the city never ceases to amaze me. The food, the energy, the art (so much art!). Madrid is just cool.

Being such a big city, I know it can be easy to feel lost. Where do you start with what you want to do? Where do you go? It took me a few visits to figure it out.

In this post, I’ll help you plan an epic five-day visit to Madrid that will ensure you not only see the main sights but that you also get off the beaten path and see just what makes Madrid so popular — and all without breaking the bank either!

This first day focuses on a prestigious area designated as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2021. There are over 40 monuments and over 40 buildings on the site. It’s easily one of the most picturesque and historic areas of the city.

The route begins at the Prado Museum, one of the best museums on the planet. Here you’ll find works from El Greco, Velázquez, and Goya, as well as many other masters (such as Rubens, Botticelli, and Caravaggio to name a few). If you only visit one museum in Madrid, this is the one. It’s incredible and worth taking the time to explore. It’s one of the biggest museums in the world, too. Make sure you spend a few hours here at a minimum.

Just a 10-minute walk along the Paseo del Prado, the journey continues at the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum, a private collection spanning from the Renaissance to Pop Art, and culminates at the Reina Sofía Museum. The Reina Sofía National Art Center offers a fantastic collection of modern art. Works by masters like Picasso, Miró, Kandinsky, Dalí, and Bacon can all be found here. The centerpiece is Picasso’s famous Guernica, a 1937 oil painting considered the most moving anti-war painting in the world. While I don’t love modern art, even I enjoyed this museum.

After museum hopping, it’s time to dive into Madrid’s culinary scene. Try Taberna La Fragua de Vulcano for a rustic atmosphere perfect for sampling cocido madrileño. If you are near the Reina Sofía Museum, don’t miss the vibrant garden terrace at Arzábal, renowned for having some of the best croquetas in the city. Finally, for a unique setting, Bodega de los Secretos lets you dine in restored 17th-century wine caves, making it the most atmospheric choice near the Prado Museum.

After a late lunch, spend some time exploring Madrid’s unique ‘House Museums. These are former private palaces that preserve the intimate atmosphere of their original owners. The crown jewel of this collection is the Sorolla Museum, the sun-drenched former residence of ‘the painter of light.’ Following a major architectural renovation, this underrated museum is set to reopen its doors in 2026, offering a refreshed look at its stunning gardens and Mediterranean canvases.

Or if you want something else, there is also the nearby Museum of Romanticism, where you can enjoy a coffee in its secret garden, or visit the Lázaro Galdiano Museum to marvel at a private collection of Goya, Murillo, Velázquez, El Greco, or Bosch housed in a magnificent neo-Renaissance mansion.

In the evening, enjoy some food and relaxation.

The second day delves into the medieval and Renaissance layout of the city, famously known as Habsburg Madrid (Madrid de los Austrias). The central hub is Puerta del Sol, where a photo at Kilometer Zero and the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue are mandatory for a traveler’s geographic check-in. Kilometer Zero is the official starting point of all the highways and railways in the country, making this effectively the center of the entire country. There’s a small plaque you can snap a photo of.

Nearby is the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue (El Oso y el Madroño). The statue shows a bear reaching up to eat fruit from a madroño tree, symbols which come from Madrid’s coat of arms (the bear represents the city and the tree represents the land and nature surrounding it that has helped make it prosper).

From here, walk toward the iconic Plaza Mayor, highlighting its porticoed architecture and the Casa de la Panadería. Plaza Mayor once hosted bullfights, markets, symphonies, tournaments, and even executions. Now it’s ringed with tourist shops, cafés, and restaurants. It’s a good place from which to indulge in some people-watching, offers some good (though overpriced) bars, and occasionally has concerts and events.

For a true “Local Life” experience, stop for a calamari sandwich in the nearby alleys. Your taste buds will thank you.

After a relaxing lunch and some people watching, head to the Royal Palace of Madrid. The largest palace in Western Europe, the Baroque-style palace was built in the 18th century and is home to over 3,400 lavishly decorated rooms. It was originally built on a former 9th-century Muslim fort and today functions much like an art museum with numerous works, including pieces by Caravaggio, Juan de Flandes, and Francisco Goya. Though it’s the official residence of the royal family, they don’t actually live here anymore, and the palace is only used for official state functions. You can walk through the palace (both self-guided and guided tours are available), starting at the grand stairway, and wander through lavishly decorated staterooms. There’s also the Royal Armory, which houses a collection of medieval weapons and armor.

To end the day, head to the Almudena Cathedral. Unlike many of the famous medieval churches in Europe, this one was constructed in the late 19th century. It was finally completed in 1993 and was consecrated by Pope John Paul II. While the exterior has a Neo-Classical design (to match the nearby palace), the cathedral also has a Neo-Romanesque crypt with over 400 columns that you can explore. Be sure to head up to the dome for stunning views out over the city.

Madrid is a paradise for foodies. It’s one of the reasons I keep coming back. While there are plenty of food tours to take in Madrid, I suggest heading off on your own to explore. Begin at the city’s iconic gastronomic markets. The glass-walled Mercado de San Miguel is a must for gourmet tapas near Plaza Mayor. It’s popular with the after-work crowd and is a place I usually visit a few times on my trips. Additionally, local favorites like Mercado de San Antón in Chueca and Mercado de Vallehermoso offer a deeper dive into regional flavors. Just make sure to bring an appetite.

If you do want to take a food tour, consider doing a food tour. This post has more of my suggestions.

For dinner, head to Sobrino de Botín, officially recognized by the Guinness World Records as the world’s oldest restaurant. It was actually a favorite of Ernest Hemingway during his time in Madrid. For a more casual vibe, go ‘tapas crawling’ through the historic streets of La Latina or Barrio de las Letras.

As the sun sets, head to the Gran Vía to experience Madrid’s world-class rooftop culture. Venues like The Roof at Picalagartos or RIU, 360º sky bar offer signature cocktails and dinner with breathtaking 360-degree views of the skyline.

For those who don’t eat meat, Madrid has actually evolved into one of Europe’s best veg hubs, boasting a vibrant vegetarian and vegan scene in neighborhoods like Malasaña, where plant-based versions of traditional Spanish dishes are now a staple of the city’s diverse culinary identity.

Madrid is the only European capital where nature, science, and royal history converge in a UNESCO World Heritage oasis known as the ‘Paisaje de la Luz‘ (Landscape of Light). But this prestigious area, encompassing the iconic El Retiro Park and the Paseo del Prado, is just the beginning of Spain’s monumental legacy. For more UNESCO wonders, take a day trip out of the city.

One popular destination worth visiting is the Monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial, a sprawling imperial masterpiece recognized by UNESCO for its historical significance. El Escorial is located just one hour from the city by car and was commissioned by Philip II in the 16th century. It’s a massive palatial complex that includes a monastery, library, palace, basilica, and tomb for Spanish monarchs. Yet as massive as it is, it feels more austere than other palatial complexes, likely owing to its granite walls and symmetrical layout.

Another option for a day trip is the Royal Palace and Gardens of Aranjuez, a World Heritage Cultural Landscape that rivals the beauty of Versailles. Located just one hour south of the city, this was originally a hunting lodge, also commissioned in the 16th century by Philip II. It’s a blend of Renaissance and Baroque styles, with lavish rooms filled with tapestries, porcelain, and ornate decorations. There is lots of greenery and gardens here, which is partly why the royal family used this as their spring residence.

Lastly, there’s the historic university city of Alcalá de Henares, the birthplace of Spanish novelist, poet, and playwright Cervantes (he wrote Don Quixote). Just 45 minutes away by car, it also holds its own UNESCO World Heritage status, offering a perfectly preserved look into the Spanish Golden Age (1492–1659).

On your last day, it’s time to get further off the beaten path. Step back into the Golden Age at the Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales and the nearby Royal Monastery of La Encarnación, two hidden palaces that house breathtaking royal art collections behind their cloistered walls.

The Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales is a convent founded in 1559 by Joanna of Austria (sister of Philip II). The name “Descalzas Reales” (which means “Royal Barefoot Ladies”) refers to the Order of Saint Clare nuns who lived here in relative austerity. What makes this monastery unique is that many aristocratic women took refuge here, often bringing their artworks and other valuables. Over the years, this turned the convent into a veritable treasure trove of art.

The Royal Monastery of La Encarnación was founded in 1611 by the wife of Philip III, Margaret of Austria. It was a royal convent, meaning it had the direct support of the monarchy. While the exterior has an austere Baroque style, the interior is quite lavish, with ornate chapels, colorful frescoes, and lots of religious sculptures and paintings. It’s also home to several notable relics, including a vial said to contain the blood of Saint Januarius. While tours are available, it’s still an active convent so parts are not open to the public (which, honestly, makes it all the more interesting to see).

To end your day with a local touch, head to the vast Casa de Campo park. This is the largest public park in the city, created in 1931. It covers a whopping 17 square kilometers (6.5 square miles) and includes an artificial lake, lots of paths, a zoo, and even an amusement park. Here, you can enjoy a scenic lunch or dinner at one of the lakeside terraces, offering an unrivaled view of the Royal Palace and Almudena Cathedral across the skyline. It’s the perfect place to end your trip.

While Barcelona tends to get more attention, I think Madrid is one of the best cities in Europe. It boasts a mouthwatering culinary scene, a raucous nightlife, and tons of things to see and do — no matter your interest or budget. I’ve been visiting the city for almost two decades and never get tired of the tapas, architecture, and history. The city just packs so much in and there really is something for everyone here. By following the itinerary above, you’ll see all the main sights while also getting off the beaten path in Spain’s historic capital.

#3022. Bomb Fishing Is Wreaking Havoc on Indonesia's Coral Reefs

This article was originally published by Inside Climate News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

A bomb-fished coral reef in Sulawesi, Indonesia. The Ocean Agency

Fishers operating off the coast of Sulawesi, Indonesia, are detonating more than 8,000 underwater explosives each year, researchers estimate. The practice is turning picturesque coral reefs to “rubble.”

Nicknamed the “Amazon of the Seas,” the Coral Triangle is the world’s most biologically diverse marine ecosystem. Sink below the surface and you’ll encounter the sound of a vibrant symphony of snapping shrimp, crunching crustaceans, and feeding fish.

But then the rhythmic music of life will dissolve into eerie silence, punctured only by the plosive boom of detonating bombs.

Off the coast of Indonesia’s Spermonde Archipelago, underwater microphones captured over 3,500 explosions in just 3,600 hours of recording, according to researchers from the Zoological Society of London.

The source? Blast fishing — a globally banned technique that uses plastic bottles packed with explosives to stun and kill everything in a 90-foot radius. The highly destructive practice has been documented in at least 34 countries, from Lebanon and Libya to Brazil and Ecuador.

While fishers predominantly use the method to catch fish for sale at local markets — identifiable by their ruptured internal organs and burst swim bladders — it’s also a grave threat to colorful coral reef habitats.

“Bomb fishing is quite likely the leading cause of reef loss in this area,” said Ben Williams, the paper’s lead author, noting that a single bomb can wreak 200 square feet of destruction. “These picturesque reefs get converted into a landscape that looks like the moon. It’s just rubble and dead coral with very little sign of life.”

In 2023, researchers from Britain and Indonesia snorkeled down and anchored $150 audio recorders to short stakes in the seafloor. Using A.I. software — which the team has now made open-source — they scoured 16 months of audio in just a few hours to identify possible detonations.

While the A.I. filtered suspected cases, each suggested sound wave was then manually verified to assess if it stemmed from a bomb or a misfiring boat engine.

With sound traveling over four times faster through water than air, the team of marine scientists were able to detect detonations from over 10 miles away.

“When [the bombs] are close, it’s so loud that it can shake you out of your skin,” said Williams. “But if you put your head up on the surface, you probably can’t even see the boat that did it.”

Accounting for stormy-season setbacks and spearfishermen who tampered with the recorders, the team calculated that there were likely more than 8,500 blasts each year — all within an area of just 350 square miles.

With a bomb dropped once every 62 minutes, the equivalent of three football fields of reef are destroyed each year, according to Williams.

Indeed, an estimated 75 percent of coral has been lost in the Spermonde Archipelago since 1990 as a result of human activities, bleaching, and warming waters.

“Repeated blasts create shifting fields of rubble that prevent hard coral recruits from settling and growing, making natural regeneration and recovery of the reefs a difficult or impossible task,” said Melissa Hampton-Smith, a postdoctoral researcher at James Cook University in Australia, in an email to Inside Climate News.

The data revealed for the first time that bomb fishing takes place year-round, peaks during the mornings and significantly reduces on Fridays, the local day of prayer.

While understudied, the incentives for the use of dangerous dynamite fishing are often falsely attributed solely to poverty and desperation. The cost barrier to buying boats, bombs, and detonators means it’s more likely a practice for middle-income fishers, according to experts.

“A combination of factors drives blast fishing, including ineffective enforcement and management,” said Hampton-Smith, highlighting how indiscriminate the explosions are, killing all manner of species, regardless of age, size, or intent.

“Managing all illegal fishing, including blast fishing, is complex and varies from place to place, but in general equitable, consistent, and legitimate enforcement is key,” said Hampton-Smith, who first studied the phenomenon while living and working in East Africa’s bomb fishing hot spot, Tanzania.

Despite the widespread harm, intercepting blast fishers in the act remains an elusive goal in a nation encompassing over 70 million acres of marine protected areas — a region larger than the entire United Kingdom.

Though authorities in neighboring Malaysia successfully confiscated 1,250 pounds of ammonia fertilizer suspected of being used to construct homemade fish bombs this May, patrols currently fail to effectively pinpoint the detonations in real time.

“Restoration efforts struggle to keep up with such rapid rates of destruction caused by bombing,” said Jamaluddin Jompa, coauthor of the paper and a research professor at Hasanuddin University in Indonesia, in a press release. “Immediate work to tackle bomb fishing is needed.”

Williams is hopeful the new research could be used to construct a network of audio sensors with GPS syncs to provide real-time detection and localization for marine authorities.

And not just in Indonesia. From the Philippines to Turkey to Zanzibar, Williams hopes the now publicly available code will be rolled out across the globe to keep biodiverse habitats from being reduced to “rubble.”

Crucially, unlike bleaching events or warming waters, bomb fishing represents a rare form of coral crisis where a local fix exists.

“Because bomb fishing is an acute stressor, you can restore your way out of it,” said Williams. “If bomb fishing stopped, and you went and restored the reefs, they should be healthy and thrive for quite some time to come.”

#3023. Disneyland Discount Tickets: October 2026 Guide

You just can’t argue with that Disney magic. Whether you’re a Disney adult or a begrudging occasional visitor, at some point throughout the day, a little bit of Disney dust will hit you. Maybe it’s the fireworks, or the rides, or the many, many Disney-shaped food items. If not that, it might be seeing the excitement on kids’ faces when they run into a princess, Avenger, or cartoon character IRL. I’m no Disney evangelist, but I would say that if you can’t have fun at a theme park, consider looking inward. (And okay, as a former resident of both California and Florida, I have spent more than my fair share of time at the parks on both coasts.) All that aside, trips to the parks are expensive, so if you’re here to find ways to save, I get it—below, find all the current discounts and promotions to be aware of before planning your next trip to Disneyland.

For the uninitiated, annual passholders are called Magic Key holders, and they can pop in and out of Disneyland as they please (with some terms and conditions in there). Through December 15, these theme park enthusiasts can save up to 15% on select Standard and Premium room types at premium Disneyland Resort hotels. The offer is tailored to Sunday through Thursday night stays at Disney’s Grand Californian Hotel & Spa, Disneyland Hotel, The Villas at Disneyland Hotel, and Pixar Place Hotel. Of note, you must present a valid active Magic Key pass at check-in to secure the discounted rate.

If you're headed to Hawaii, passholders can save even more, with up to 35% off select stays at Aulani Resort in Hawaiʻi that take place between October 19 and December 23, 2026 (with checkout no later than December 24). Those staying five or more consecutive nights can take 35% off; for those staying four consecutive nights, 30%.

Savings are available on an ongoing basis for active-duty and retired US military personnel, including the National Guard, Reservists, the US Coast Guard, the US Space Force, the Commissioned Corps of the Public Health Service (PHS), and the Commissioned Corps of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Tickets start at $98 for kids of these travelers and $104 for adults purchasing a one-day, one-park ticket. These tickets may not be combined with other ticket discounts or promotions, and cannot be sold or transferred.

While going to the parks for just one day is the most cost-effective option, your per-day cost does go down when you opt for multi-day tickets instead. For example, a one-day ticket will run you between $104 and $224 based on the date you select. If you go for two days, your price per day starts at $168; for three days, it drops to $142 and up per day; for four days, from $120 per day; and for five days, from $104 per day.

A few things to note: Disneyland is much smaller than Disney World, with just two parks, so it is possible to cover a good amount of ground in a single day. However, especially if you’re coming from out of town, you may want a few days there so there’s less pressure to squeeze every ride and meal into a single day.

There’s also the question of purchasing one-park-per-day tickets or upgrading to a Park Hopper ticket (an extra $100 per day). If you’re visiting for just one day, I’d suggest the Park Hopper ticket so you get to experience both parks. For multi-day trips, it really comes down to preference; you’ll want to decide between chunking out your park visits or having the freedom to roam back and forth between parks throughout the day (which, size-wise, is definitely doable).

Tickets are one thing, but once you’re inside the park, it’s easy to rack up charges on dining, souvenirs, and add-on experiences. If you’re concerned about sticking to a budget, there are a few surefire ways to cut costs. For one, take a look at the gift card section next time you're at Target, Costco, or Sam’s Club, as they sometimes sell discounted Disney Gift Cards.

If you’re interested in an additional credit card, new Disney Inspire Visa Card holders can earn up to $500 in the form of a $300 eGift to spend at the park and a $200 statement credit after you spend $1,000 on purchases in the first three months of account opening. You’ll also earn Disney Rewards Dollars on all card purchases, including:

When it comes to food, placing mobile orders via the Disneyland App can help you track food spending more easily and find quick options in place of more expensive sit-down meals. Lastly, consider dining off-property or at Downtown Disney to curb costs. On my last visit to Disneyland, I stayed right across the street from the entrance at Park Vue Inn—the proximity was amazing, and it had a pool and hot tub. Rates start at $229 a night, and rooms with kitchenettes are available, which make coming back midday to prep meals a breeze.

#3024. 5 Sneaky Reasons Your Stomach Feels Bloated

Do you often find yourself feeling bloated and uncomfortable and sometimes you don't even know why? It's a common issue that many people face, but the good news is, I know how to beat the bloat!

Let's dive into why you might be experiencing bloating + how you can get rid of it so you can feel snatched all the time! 

5 Reasons WHY Your Bloated

1. Eating Too Quickly

One of the main reasons why you might be feeling bloated is because you're eating too quickly. When you eat too fast, you're more likely to swallow air, which can lead to bloating and gas. Try to slow down during meals and chew your food thoroughly to prevent bloating.

2. Consuming Carbonated Drinks

Carbonated drinks like soda and sparkling water can also contribute to bloating. The bubbles in these drinks can get trapped in your digestive system, causing discomfort and bloating. Opt for still water or herbal tea instead to help reduce bloating.

3. High Sodium Intake

Consuming too much sodium can lead to water retention, which can make you feel bloated. Be mindful of your salt intake and try to limit processed foods, which are often high in sodium. Adding more potassium-rich foods like bananas and sweet potatoes to your diet can help balance out sodium levels and reduce bloating.

4. Lack of Fiber

If you're not getting enough fiber in your diet, you may experience bloating and constipation. Fiber helps to regulate digestion and keep things moving smoothly in your digestive tract. Make sure to include plenty of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and legumes in your meals to increase your fiber intake and reduce bloating.

5. Stress and Anxiety

Stress and anxiety can have a major impact on your digestive system, leading to bloating and discomfort. Practice stress-reducing techniques like deep breathing, meditation, or yoga to help calm your mind and improve your digestion. 

Belly Fat vs. Belly Bloat

It's important to differentiate between belly fat and belly bloat. Belly fat is excess fat stored around your midsection, while belly bloat is temporary and often caused by factors like diet and digestion.

#3025. The datacentre next door: on the frontline of tech’s latest David v Goliath battle

The AI boom is pitting local residents against corporate giants seeking to power their energy-hungry networks – but one Welsh city is fighting back

Dale Johnston opens the gate to his neat suburban garden on the western fringes of Newport in South Wales. There’s a trampoline and a slide on the lawn for his grandchildren, and chairs for him and his wife. He should be enjoying the light draining from the perfect autumnal sky – but almost his entire view is blotted out by a vast expanse of prefabricated panels.

The 23 metre-high grey hulk looming over him and his neighbours is a hyperscale datacentre. It is heralded by the area’s Labour politicians as a job creator, yet all Johnston can think about is what he has lost: “Before, the sun used to come around here and it was lovely.” The way residents have been treated is “disgusting”.

Johnston, who used to work for a chemical company in the city, worries what their lives will be like when the centre is switched on: the 36 sets of air blast coolers, needed to stop the chips inside overheating, most likely generate a constant drone, while regular testing of 60 back-up diesel generators, to prevent costly interruption to the flow of data, could produce harmful fumes. He already has to keep his bathroom window closed to stop the low hum from another facility on the rapidly expanding 46-acre datacentre campus that borders the small enclave of 27 houses. His wife, a nurse who works night shifts, can barely sleep already. He shakes his head in despair: “We just don’t know what’s going to happen.”

Johnston can talk about little else, but he feels no one in authority is listening. He’s invited councillors and MPs backing the development to visit his garden. But “they won’t come around here to see what they’ve done”.

This is the frontline of Britain’s datacentre boom, which is pitting residents against giant US tech firms seeking to build a network of facilities capable of providing the immense computing muscle for powerful AI models. There are 315 hyperscale datacentres waiting to connect to the national grid, which carries electricity from power plants to homes and businesses (hyperscale typically means facilities with at least 5,000 servers and 10,000 sq ft in size). Combined, these new centres will require 73GW of power, 28GW higher than the typical peak energy demand of 45GW on a cold winter’s day.

Wales is one of the main development hotspots outside London. It already has the largest datacentre capacity beyond the capital, with new hyperscale facilities planned for former industrial and urban sites. The Keir Starmer-led Labour government viewed this as an inevitable revolution, which the country must embrace or be left behind. It established five AI growth zones to push more datacentres through the planning system and speed up connections to the national grid. The new prime minister, Andy Burnham, has signalled little will change, turning down calls for a moratorium and insisting datacentres bring economic benefits. But anti-datacentre groups springing up in villages, towns and cities across the country see it rather differently: as the imposition of a resource-hungry, polluting industry that increases profits for often US big tech, with little tangible benefit to local people or the country as a whole.

Digital storage is nothing new. The first home PC users saved files on floppy discs and hard drives; businesses used their own server rooms in the 80s and 90s, then moved to off-site facilities as their needs grew. But the development of cloud computing services in the 2010s, such as Google Drive, and AI chatbots in the 2020s, like ChatGPT, led to even greater information and processing demands, which the tech industry insists can only be met by larger and larger datacentres. This has driven huge speculative bets on hyperscale hubs, which investors and tech firms hope will one day reap the rewards of an AI-led transformation of the economy. Globally, it is estimated spending on new facilities could reach $7tn by 2030 – more than double the cost of the New Deal, the Marshall Plan to rebuild Europe after the second world war and the Apollo space programme combined, even allowing for inflation.

The US is at the forefront of the boom, already hosting roughly half of the world’s hyperscale capacity. But the industry is facing a furious backlash, with three-quarters of Americans now opposed to datacentre development and blaming it for increasing energy bills, threatening water supplies in drought-hit areas and spewing out toxic fumes. More than 500 counties and municipalities have passed permanent or temporary datacentre bans.

Loudoun County in northern Virginia sits in what is known as Data Center Alley because it is home to more facilities than anywhere else in the world. Greg Pirio’s life was turned upside down when a gas-powered datacentre opened 150 metres from his home last year. “This neighbourhood was calm and peaceful, and it’s turned into this nightmare,” he says on a video call. “Our quality of life has been degraded so much.”

The noise from the centre’s eight gas turbines is “like being at an airport with all these engines roaring,” Pirio says. “It has given many of my neighbours headaches. It has kept children up at night.” Pirio, who used to work for the Voice of America radio station, has also developed health problems since it opened, including dry eyes and chest tightness. Once he had to leave his house because he was struggling to breathe: “I know whenever the diesel generators are on, because I feel it in my lungs.”

The UK has not yet seen the same level of opposition as the US. But anti-datacentre groups are gathering momentum. Residents in east London are waging a high-profile campaign against a new datacentre on Brick Lane, including protesting outside the offices of Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, who overturned a council decision blocking the scheme.

Seasoned campaigner Owen Espley, who works for environmental charity Global Action Plan, is helping scores of residents’ groups organise against planned datacentres. “This summer has been wild. Every other week a new group has popped up. Petitions are getting thousands of signatures in days,” he says. “Communities are in uproar, and most politicians are playing catch-up.”

Espley has been taken aback by the gulf between the government’s conviction that there is no alternative and ordinary people’s deepening understanding of the complex issues at stake. “There has been a real grassroots questioning of datacentres that connects British Bangladeshis in Brick Lane with Hertfordshire villagers and communities in Northumberland, who want good jobs to come back,” he says. “It is astounding.”

In fact, there are many alternative pathways to market-­led expansion – from tougher regulation to prioritising publicly-owned data infrastructure – which serve communal goals, such as the heart disease and dementia research powered by Bristol University’s new Isambard-AI facility. “First, we need strong standards for private datacentres,” Espley says. “Second, we need industrial strategy to deliver our own public computer, rather than an assumption that US big tech building and owning everything is the only way forward.”

On the deprived eastern edges of Cardiff, the early morning sunshine is warming a car park dotted with scraggly weeds. The perimeter fence is overgrown with brambles, with patches of singed, blackened grass from a recent wildfire visible just beyond. It looks abandoned but soon cars carrying doctors, nurses and other NHS staff start arriving. They are here to catch free buses to Cardiff’s Heath hospital, the largest in Wales.

Hundreds are said to use the park and ride every day, but it is under threat because Labour-controlled Cardiff council wants to sell the land to a property developer, Curtis Hall, to build a hyperscale data facility. The centre will use up to 150 megawatts (MW) of electricity a year, more than triple the demand of a city the size of Cardiff.

The development is one of the most controversial in Wales. Council meetings have been disrupted and more than 1,200 planning objections lodged. Last month, the new Plaid Cymru-led government ordered the council to put the application on hold while it considered whether to take the decision out of councillors’ hands.

Campaigners are determined to keep up the pressure on the Welsh government. Sue Elias, a retired librarian with seemingly endless reserves of energy, dashes back and forth reattaching her “Ditch the datacentre” banner to the car park fence and taping leaflets to the bus stop glass. “What is going to happen to all the people who use the park and ride? It’s bonkers,” she says.

Elias has leafleted the park and ride every Wednesday morning for six weeks. Today she is collecting signatures for an open letter to prove it is well used – so far she has added the names of 1,300 staff and patients. “I’ve not done anything like this before but I’m told I’m a natural,” she says with a mischievous smile, before breaking off to speak to staff arriving for the next bus.

She belongs to community-based union Acorn, which has campaigned against the scheme, and has taken part in protests, including bursting into a council planning meeting in July. “We’d sent emails, done petitions, but we’d had nothing back – tumbleweed. They’re our elected representatives … They should be talking with us.”

It is hard to find anyone in support of the plan in the queue for the bus, which runs three times an hour. “I use it every day. Without it, I probably wouldn’t continue working at the hospital,” says Ami George, a midwife. “Parking there causes that much stress.”

Across Cardiff’s Rhymney River, which curves around the proposed datacentre development, the area’s newest residents have only recently moved into 100 homes built under the city council’s flagship house-building programme. Nick Richards, a freelance filmmaker and skateboarder, and his wife arrived in November. “It felt like the stars had aligned because there is a brand new skate park up the road … the best in Cardiff. It’s amazing,” he says. “I never pictured myself living in suburbia but when we came we saw kids playing outside and thought, this is a really nice area.”

Like many other residents on the estate, Richards had no idea the council was planning to sell the park and ride to a datacentre developer. They moved in two months before the planning application was submitted. Instead of enjoying their new life, they now fear they will never be able to sell. Their home is 300 metres from what the plans describe as the temporary energy centre, which includes seven giant gas turbines. They are expected to power the facility around the clock for five years, according to documents filed by the developer. “I feel trapped,” Richards says, pacing his kitchen. “I couldn’t look prospective buyers in the eye and not say there’s going to be seven gas turbines right next to them.”

Richards has pored over the planning documents and leafleted every house on the new estate, including a care home, which will be just 150 metres from the turbines. “This datacentre will be powered by gas turbines,” he says. “They will pump nitrogen dioxide into our atmosphere. There will also be fine particulate matter and formaldehyde. All these toxins cause health conditions, such as asthma, COPD and heart disease.”

Air quality assessments commissioned by the developer estimate the emissions will be within safe levels. Curtis Hall says the scheme cannot proceed without 100% compliance with all environmental and public health regulatory requirements.

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

There are more than 100 other planned UK datacentres aiming to use gas turbines due to the long wait to be connected to the grid. Richards doesn’t want his estate to be a test case. “Within a mile of this datacentre are 30,000 people. But the people building this centre don’t live here ... They don’t give two shits about Welsh people.”

A stone’s throw away is Llanrumney Hall, once the home of privateer and slave trader Sir Henry Morgan, who gave his name to Captain Morgan rum. It is now a thriving community centre, with a cafe, recording studio and creche. Labour councillor Lee Bridgeman is vaping on an outdoor table, dressed in a hoodie and baseball cap. He ran the local youth centre until it was lost to austerity-era cuts, and though he’s a high-ranking councillor, jointly responsible for housing and communities, he does regular youth work shifts in the area, one of the poorest in Cardiff.

“Llanrumney runs through my veins,” he says. “I’m not your usual politician. I don’t go to conferences. I got into politics to help the community.”

Bridgeman is charming and friendly – but he is not afraid of a fight. He is one of the few public figures in the area who has spoken out in support of the development, sometimes clashing with anti-datacentre campaigners on local Facebook groups. “Some of the information being spread is scaremongering,” he says. “They are telling residents their electricity bills will go up … the river and reservoir will be drained … It’s false information.”

Many of these fears stem from the US, where the rapid expansion of hyperscale facilities has been linked to rising electricity bills, water shortages and toxic air pollution. Bridgeman argues that “planning processes are totally different in the UK. So whereas [US authorities] turn a blind eye to some of the environmental impacts of those monstrosities, that would never happen in the UK.” He “wouldn’t be comfortable” if the gas turbines were running for five years but thinks they might not be needed if the datacentre can connect to the grid sooner.

The backlash has caught him by surprise, but he blames outside activists. “I didn’t see it coming. I didn’t think there would be this much interference,” he says.

Emotions are running high in the city. Some residents say they have been blocked by councillors when trying to question them on Facebook. Planning committee members have received threatening emails, Bridgeman says. “Threats like ‘I will come after you ... we will make your life hell.’ That shouldn’t happen.”

Although the datacentre will employ only up to 125 people when it is built, Bridgeman believes it could encourage other big companies to east Cardiff: “I’m told the knock-on effect could lead to thousands of jobs.”

Later that day, residents squeeze into the local boxing club for a public meeting about the datacentre plan. It is standing room only, with people lining the walls. Bridgeman repeats his claim that few locals have complained: “I have hundreds of emails from residents ... So far I’ve had two emails with regards to the datacentre.”

Some in the audience react angrily. There are shouts of, “We don’t know you, that’s why” and, “Have you heard of social media?” One woman stands up and says, “Don’t tell me you haven’t been privy to the meetings … or things online.” In a show of hands, roughly three-quarters of the 80 to 100 people in the room indicate they are from Llanrumney, almost all opposed. There are cries of, “There you are … you don’t need emails!” and, “That’s every person!” Almost three weeks later, Bridgeman performs a sudden about-turn, submitting a formal letter of objection to the scheme, noting that he has heard from a large number of residents.

The UK hyperscale buildout has been focused on London, but datacentre developers are increasingly targeting areas outside the south-east, to escape severe electrical grid capacity limits. Wales already has the largest datacentre capacity of anywhere outside the capital. Many more could be coming: five of Wales’s largest new and proposed datacentres will consume more electricity than all Welsh homes put together. While the previous Welsh Labour administration welcomed the building spree, claiming giant tech firms’ investment would generate thousands of jobs, the Plaid Cymru-led government has been more circumspect, with ministers emphasising it must benefit Wales.

In the light and airy Welsh parliament building, which overlooks Cardiff Bay, opposition is growing. Plaid Cymru’s Nick Carter, who is the Senedd member for Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf, which includes Cardiff East, worries that the surging market will benefit developers and US tech firms rather than the public. “As a party, we’re not going to want to see a proliferation of datacentres, haphazardly being built across the country, on what may be an opportunistic basis,” he says.

Carter, who has a background in commercial property, has examined the Cardiff plans in detail. He says the developer, Curtis Hall, has no track record in datacentres; “They could be a front for someone else: Google, Microsoft, whoever. I can understand why these operators need datacentres, but I’m not sure members of the public share the need.” In response, Curtis Hall says it never claimed it would operate the facility itself, adding it had been working on datacentre projects for five years.

Carter is glad the Welsh government has intervened in Cardiff. But he doesn’t believe Wales needs to follow Scotland by imposing a moratorium on new datacentres: “The Welsh government is developing a strategy for datacentres nationally. We’ll see what comes out of that.”

However, it is not clear how the Welsh government can meet its goal to reach net zero by 2040 without limiting datacentre expansion. Carter admits, “It’s massively problematic.” In Westminster, similar questions have been asked. The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology tells me the government will enable the development of datacentres by generating unprecedented amounts of clean power.

A soft autumnal dusk descends on the residents living beside the new datacentre in Newport. Its sleek industrial-grey walls cast shadows across the closest gardens and homes. Much of the anger and frustration that met the original proposals has given way to weariness and resignation. Some residents talk of moving away, while others are mollified by meetings with the US-based data campus operator, Vantage.

Yet their troubles may only just be beginning – right now, only one of the three Vantage datacentres is operational. Microsoft will be opening its own nearby soon. When all are running, there could be upwards of 500 air handling units working at the same time, with back-up diesel generators needing regular testing, so they can immediately fire up if there is a power cut.

Newport council’s chief scientific officer warned during the planning process that the fumes from all the generators had the “potential to cause unacceptable air pollution levels under use, and testing needs to be understood and mitigation proposed, if needed”.

The council tells me it doesn’t have a duty to monitor emissions from generators, but says its officers check air quality management plans, and ask managers to minimise the impact of generator tests. Vantage says all its facilities operate in accordance with noise and air quality controls. It says it will monitor impacts and investigate concerns when the new centre opens.

Some residents have already given up on democratic process. Johnston fought the proposals through the planning process but felt he was ignored. “We’ve been let down by all of them. I’ve had electoral roll cards come through my door. But I’m voting for none of them … I can’t trust them. They don’t care about any of us.”

Over the road are older homes, where staff working on a nearby wealthy estate once lived. Sonia Thomas, a retired teacher, has lived in the same housekeeper’s cottage since 1969. She can remember when orchards and fields fanned out in front of their gardens but now she doesn’t even know if the sun is shining. “From inside you see grey, not blue,” she says, glancing at the datacentre filling the sky. “It’s horrible.”
