#3028. Hiking The Pisac Ruins In The Sacred Valley of Peru: An Unexpected Hike I Fell in Love With

Iâd already been exploring some of the other famous ruins and sites around the Sacred Valley of Peru and beyondâlike the Ollantaytambo Ruins, reaching 16,500ft hiking Rainbow Mountain, the Maras Salt Mines (and Moray), even scaling the side of a valley cliff doing my first via ferrata with ziplines…

I had barely read a single thing about Pisac, Peru before heading there, and was mostly going on the encouragement of the friend I was traveling with. Actually didn’t know much about the ruins, nor had I planned on checking them out. (Read Next: Full Cusco, Peru Travel Guide full of the best things to do in Cusco and the Sacred Valley!)

This site participates in the Amazon Services LLC Associates Program and other affiliate programs and may earn from qualifying purchases.

But as my friend and I stood in the valley looking up at the archaelogical site, he said I really should check them out.

He said it only takes a couple hours, so I grabbed a taxi and headed up by myself, with little more than time and curiosity at hand. It was supposed to be a quick morning visit to Pisac, visiting the Pisac Market, grabbing coffee and food. Instead, it turned into one of the most peaceful and beautifully rewarding solo hikes Iâve done in this part of the world.

The soft drizzle of rain, clouds descending on the valley, silence and surprises around every corner. I was like a kid on Christmas.

The town of Pisac, in the Sacred Valley of Peru, sits about 33 kilometers (20 miles) northeast of Cusco, making it one of the easiest day trips from the city. My plan was simple: grab a colectivo from Cusco to Pisac (for under 10 SOL each wayâcolectivos leave regularly from the Pavitos or Puputi streets in Cusco and drop you off near the Pisac market), explore Pisac for a bit, maybe stop by the Picac market, then head back after lunch. Then I decided to do the ruins.

Once you’re in Pisac, you can either enter the ruins from the bottom of the valleyâwhich means hiking up the entire wayâor taxi to the top of the ruins and hike down. I opted for that route.

You can grab a taxi from the valley of Pisac and pay about $30-40 SOL for the ride up, and the taxi can stop for a moment for you to buy a ticket to the ruins if you don’t have one yet.

Side note…don’t forget to always, always, always consider getting inexpensive travel medical insurance âsometimes as low as $2/dayâfor your trip, and a separate yearly evacuation insurance policy if you travel internationally often! And check out my list of tips for staying safe while traveling abroad.

My suggestion, if you’re planning to visit at least 2-3 of the main sites Cusco or the Sacred Valley of Peru, is to buy the Boleto TurÃ­stico del Cusco, the multi-site ticket that covers most of the major archaeological sitesâincluding the Pisac Ruins, Ollantaytambo, and Moray.

If youâre exploring several places in the Sacred Valley, itâs totally worth it, since most of the main sites are 70 SOL each, so it almost pays for itself after 2 sites. And it’s good for 10 days!

When I arrived, two huge tour buses unloaded just ahead of me. This wasnât what I had in mind for a quiet hike through ancient Incan terraces, but it made me even more determined to explore on my own, going anywhere but where the large crowds were going. Within minutes, the sound of chatter faded as I took every unbeaten side path I could find.

I noticed some paths and routes headed up and up and up, then out towards a peak in the distance, so I headed that way. Then came the drizzle.

That soft, misty kind of rain that doesnât soak you, makes everything shimmer. The mountain seemed to sparkle under the gray sky, and suddenly, I was completely alone.

For nearly an hour and a half, I had the trailâand the entire mountainsideâto myself. I occasionally passed a hiker or two, but for the most part I was all alone.

The Pisac Peru ruins are massive. What starts as a series of terraced hillsides quickly reveals temples, ceremonial baths, residential areas, and walls carved into the mountainside. The Incas knew what they were doing.

I kept following the narrow trail as it snaked along the mountain ridge. Every turn opened up new surprisesâand another sweeping view of Pisac and the Sacred Valley of Peru below. It felt like I had the entire site to myself.

Eventually, once I got as far out on the mountain ridge as possible, the trail started downward, winding and switchbacking until finally reaching the bottom, spitting me back out into the town of Pisac for some much-needed food and another tour through the Pisac markets.

When people talk about things to do in Sacred Valley of Peru, Pisac RuinsÂ can get overshadowed by the more popular sites like Machu Picchu or even the Ollantaytambo Ruins.

But honestly, Pisac Ruins offers something uniqueâa chance to feel truly immersed in Incan history without the massive crowds, especially if you’re willing and able to take the scenic route instead of rushing through.

Exploring on the trail, surrounded by clouds drifting through the valley, I realized how grateful I was that I didnât overplan this day. If I had, I probably would have followed the crowds and missed out on this quieter, more unique experience. (I mean, I probably should have packed more snacks, but hey, that’s what glucose tabs are for?)

After finishing the long trail down through the Pisac Cusco ruins, I eventually found myself back in the town center and the Pisac Market. Even if youâre not much of a shopper, itâs worth a stroll.

Youâll find colorful textiles, local produce, and all kinds of handmade souvenirs. Plus, grabbing a juice or snack from one of the stalls is the perfect way to refuel after the hike.

Just be prepared for a bit of sensory overloadâespecially if you arrive when tour groups are in town. Still, itâs a lively contrast to the quiet solitude of the mountain.

Want to travel more but donât really know where to start? Have a friend or family member that keeps talking about travelâbut clearly needs a little help actually getting off go and making it happen? This is the no-fluff, hands-on guide to finally getting unstuck and on a travel pathâwith confidence, intention, and zero shame.

From Cusco, take a taxi or a shared colectivo (around 8-10 soles, $3-4USD) to Pisac. The drive takes about 45 minutes. It sometimes feels death-defying, but keep in mind people drive these roads…this way…all day long.

If you do want to stay overnight in Pisac, you can check here for current hotel deals.

Youâll likely want the Boleto TurÃ­stico del Cusco. It covers entry to Pisac and other major sites like Moray and Ollantaytambo and costs about 150 Soles. Or you can do the small ticket that’s only for Pisac Ruins for 70 Soles (as of this writing at least).

If you start from the top entrance as early as possible, youâll likely beat the big crowds and have even more solitude.

That said, I started my hike around 11am, and taking the scenic route hike shown here still weeded out the tourists almost immediately. The slight rain also helped.

The weather can change fast. I lucked out with a drizzle, but heavy rain is always a possibility. Be prepared.

Plan for at least 2â3 hours minimum if you want to explore the full circuit and allow yourself to soak it in and get distracted by every hidden corner.

I’m so glad I was encouraged to visit the Pisac Ruins, but even more happy that I didn’t listen to the little voice in the back of my head that sometimes tells me I should rush or that I “should” finish up and move on to the next thing.

I always need a reminder not to “should” all over myself!

I didnât expect hiking the Pisac Ruins to be one of my top favorite memories of my visit to Cusco, Peru and the Sacred Valley, but it is now notched there.

Hopefully all of these beautiful Pisac Ruins photos and words are enough to convince you it deserves your time and patience as well.

Give yourself the time to wander the terraces, get a little lost, and maybe enjoy some drizzle or rain instead of running from it. Because usually, the best memories are hiding just past the point where you think you should stop.

Jason is the author of “The Beginner Traveler’s Guide” as well as the voice behind the words and the eye behind the lens for The Nomad Experiment. “Planning to travel at some point” wasn’t actually getting the job done, so nearing 40 he decided to make it a priority, nomatter how scary that was. A few years laterâthrough the pandemic and a type 1 diabetes diagnosis at age 42ânow living a life of nomadic travel, he’s speaking out to encourage others of any age, or with any serious medical diagnosis, to live an unconventional life.

Entry to the Pisac Ruins is included with the Boleto TurÃ­stico del Cusco. The full ticket costs around S/150 (~$45-50 USD) and grants access to multiple sites across Cusco and the Sacred Valley, including the salt mines, SacsayhuamÃ¡n, and more.

The CuscoâPisac route is about 45m or so by taxi, car or cheap colectivo. Colectivos leave regularly from the Pavitos or Puputi streets in Cusco and drop you off near the Pisac market. For a return trip, just go back to where they dropped you off and wait for the next colectivo back to Cusco. Note colectivos tend not to be as regular after dark, so plan to head back to Cusco before then.

Plan for 2 hours or more if you hike from the top down into town, or a bit longer if you do the bottom up route and you stop often for photos or wander through every terrace like I did!

Yes, but itâs steep! The hike up from the valley of Pisac takes at least 1.5â2 hours and climbs over 400 meters (1,300 feet). Again, most visitors take a taxi or tour bus up to the top entrance to the Pisac Ruins and hike down.

The Ruins sit around 3,300 meters (10,800 feet) above sea levelâwhile Cusco, Peru is about 11,500ft for comparisonâso take it easy if youâre still acclimating.

The dry season (MayâSeptember) offers the best weather, but mornings can be chilly. Shoulder seasons on each side can be more wet or questionable for weather, but hotels and other things will often be cheaper in general. Arrive early to beat the crowds.

Yes. The Pisac market is one of the best-known in the Sacred Valley, packed with local crafts, textiles, and snacksâperfect for a post-hike wander.

Parts of the trail can be challenging, with steep steps, uneven stone paths, or even “caves” that are extremely tight to get through. Wear good shoes, and bring plenty to snack on and hydrate on.

Yes! Cusco to Pisac is an easy day trip, especially if you also want to explore other things to do in the Sacred Valley along the way.

A definite Yes. I mean, if you’ve read this far, you should know that based on my tone and photos! The Pisac Peru ruins are big, less crowded than Machu Picchu, and offer some of the best views of the Sacred Valley, Peruâtotally worth the climb! Send it!

#3029. One of the World's ‘Most Wanted’ Lost Fish Is Rediscovered

The recently rediscovered spinach pipefish. SHOAL

On a vast network of rivers flowing through the jungles of Papua New Guinea, researchers have rediscovered the spinach pipefish, a relative of the seahorse, which had not been recorded in more than 40 years. The fish has long been sought after by conservationists, who feared it had gone extinct.

On an expedition that unfolded like a search for a missing person, researchers spent two weeks traversing the Sepik River and its tributaries, scouring villages and markets for evidence of the missing pipefish. They showed its photo to fishers, vendors, and village elders and asked where it might be found.

The task was daunting. The Sepik River extends across 700 miles of forests, floodplains, and wetlands along the northern coast of Papua New Guinea. “Travel is almost entirely by motorized boat or canoe, often taking many hours between villages,” said Jerrica Agebigo of the New Guinea Binatang Research Centre. The vast scale of the river system meant that scientists were heavily reliant on local knowledge.

Helen Asu, a prawn fisher in Imbando Village, who aided in the rediscovery of the long-lost spinach pipefish. New Guinea Binatang Research Centre

In interviews, villagers consistently reported spotting a long, slender fish in the shallows of the Sepik River. Though they called the fish many names — Karuweng, Inap, Karuwena, Sako — their descriptions matched the profile of the missing species.

In the final days of the expedition, a fisher named Helen Asu managed to nab two pipefish using the handheld net she relied on to catch prawns. Researchers shared photos of her catch with Australian ichthyologist Gerald Allen, one of the last researchers to document the spinach pipefish in the 1980s. He confirmed the rediscovery.

“It makes my heart sing to hear that the spinach pipefish has been recorded anew,” said marine biologist Amanda Vincent, who chairs an expert group on seahorses, pipefishes, and seadragons for the International Union for Conservation of Nature. “To learn that the spinach pipefish still exists gives us hope that other ‘lost’ species are out there, too.”

The spinach pipefish had been named one of the 10 “most wanted” lost freshwater fish species by SHOAL, a U.K. conservation group. Its rediscovery highlights the urgency of protecting freshwater fish, the group said.

In interviews throughout the expedition, villagers reported declines of native fish, which are imperiled by mining, logging, and other threats. Globally, freshwater fish are under growing pressure. A recent U.N. report found that over the last half-century, populations of migratory freshwater fish have declined by 81 percent.

#3030. Capital One Venture Business Card Review

If you’re a traveler like me, chances are you’re always on the lookout for ways to make your trips more affordable. That’s why I collect points and miles: they help me lower my travel costs so I can spend my money on what’s actually important…which is usually booking more trips!

One card that can help you earn more points and miles — which translates to more free flights and free hotel stays — is the Capital One Venture Business card. It’s an easy-to-use card perfect for travels who want to simplify their points and miles collecting. Here’s everything you need to know about the card to help decide if it’s for you. It’s a solid business card for those who don’t want a high annaul fee card but want some added perks besides just getting miles when you spend money.

Table of ContentsWhat Is It?Rental Car PerksTravel PartnersWho Is This Card For?

The Capital One Venture Business card is the new rebranded version of Capital One’s Spark Miles. But it has some noteworthy improvements that I think make it worth adding to your wallet. Here’s a look at the card’s main perks:

The annual fee for the card is just $95, which means it’s effectively free once you factor in the two statement credits. With a default 2x miles for every dollar spent, that makes this card a solid choice for everyday spending. And without a ton of differing spending categories, the card is very easy to use, making it perfect for travelers new to the points and miles game.

In addition to giving you Hertz Five Star status, which lets you skip the counter at select locations while also offering a wider selection of cars, the card also offers rental car coverage when renting a car for business reasons. You’ll need to charge the full fee to your card and also decline the company’s collision damage waiver, but once you do that, you’ll be covered for damage due to both collisions and theft.

While I don’t often rent cars for work, I appreciate the free collision coverage and being able to skip the line (especially at busier rental locations).

With this card, you’ll earn Capital One miles. You can use them like you would any other rewards program: to get cash back, book travel directly, or transfer them to travel partners.

The easiest option is to redeem your miles for travel in the Capital One travel portal, which works like booking through Expedia or any other online travel agency. Doing so is very straightforward. You simply search for and book your flight, hotel, or rental car and choose “miles” as your payment method. It’s basically like using your miles as cash, at a value of one cent per mile.

Both options are super easy to implement, which is why this is a great card for newbies. And if this is the only way that you’ll use your miles, go for it! Using them is better than letting them sit around.

However, you can usually get more for your miles when you transfer them to Capital One’s transfer partners.

The ability to transfer to travel partners is what makes Capital One miles valuable. While the actual value varies based on what you book, you can usually find airline and hotel redemptions worth much more than the aforementioned 1 cent per mile.

Transferring to travel partners is a bit more work than using the portal, but there are more tools than ever to help you maximize your miles (such as point.me for finding flights and Awayz for finding award hotel stays).

Here are their current hotel and airline transfer partners:

This card is best for business travelers who are looking for an easy-to-use card to help them earn points and miles. While I personally think the Capital One Venture X Business card is a better card, it comes with a higher annual fee so, if you want a solid travel card for your business and don’t need the upgraded perks of the Capital One Venture X Business card, this is the Capital One card for you. And since the credits cover the annual fee, the card is essentially free!

The new Capital One Venture Business card has an amazing welcome offer, a respectable 2x on every purchase, and some solid perks for regular travelers. And with its low annual fee, this card is a no brainer for travelers looking for a new business card. I just wouldn’t wait too long — this huge welcome offer isn’t gonna last forever!

With some big AI companies soon to go public on the stock market, the ranks of ultra-rich philanthropists in the United States look set to grow. Compared to government funding agencies, ultra-wealthy research investors tend to support projects that are higher risk and more personally relevant, with fewer strings attached. But there’s less oversight of philanthropic programmes, it’s difficult to assess their success and many are geared towards encouraging the use of the same technology the philanthropists profited from developing.

This celestial map of 1822, closely modelled on an earlier stone stele from 1247, reflects the Taoist conception of the cosmos as a ‘Celestial Bureaucracy’ with the heavens divided into hierarchical offices and ranks resembling those on Earth. This huge coloured woodcut by Yunyou Sanren 雲遊散人 (Shang Huang 黃裳) is on display in Night Maps at the Warburg Institute in London, UK, until 17 April. (©The Sunderland Collection)

Global greenhouse-gas emissions might have plateaued last year and there has been a faster-than-expected expansion of renewable energy capacity, finds the United Nations’ latest report on climate change. But without a major acceleration in emissions cuts, by mid-century average temperatures might hurtle past 2 °C — a ceiling that countries committed to in the Paris Agreement. The emissions slow-down is “definitely good news, but not good enough,” says climate scientist Bill Hare. Under current policies, scientists estimate warming to peak at 2.6 °C to 2.8 °C this century; there is also a smaller chance of warming exceeding 3.4 °C on the current trajectory, which would be catastrophic.

Reference: UN Environment Programme Emissions Gap Report 2026

Palaeontologists have trained a machine-learning model on a huge database of fossil records, then used it to reconstruct a timeline of changes in Earth’s biodiversity over hundreds of millions of years in unprecedented detail. The model, called OneStrata, hints at several possible challenges to big ideas about evolutionary history. For example, it suggests that three of the “Big Five” mass-extinction events were gradual declines in biodiversity, rather than the sudden cataclysms described by other reconstructions.

Physicists have suspended a single positron — the antimatter equivalent of an electron — near absolute zero and in a near-perfect vacuum, for months. Researchers hope to spot subtle differences between matter and antimatter that could shed light on one of physics’ greatest mysteries: why is there something rather than nothing.

A study of more than 11,000 people with depression found that a quarter had a new subtype that makes their condition hard to treat. ‘Circadian depression’ seems to be linked to disruptions in the body’s internal clock, which could be targeted with treatments such as melatonin and light therapy. “Circadian depression is not just depression with bad sleep,” says neuroscientist and study co-author Emiliana Tonini. “There is an underlying biology that is quite distinct from other forms of depression.”

Reference: British Journal of Psychiatry paper

The ‘modern-day Jonah’ film Whalefall, based on Daniel Kraus’s 2023 novel, follows a university student who is accidentally swallowed by a sperm whale while scuba diving. Scientific advisor Joy Reidenberg, a comparative anatomist, and Ilias Foskolos, who researches deep-diving toothed whales, talk to Nature about glowing guts, stomach acids and why we probably don’t have to worry about any of this in real life.

During the film, Jay grabs a glowing jellyfish that was also swallowed by the whale to light his way as he looks for an exit.Credit: 20th Century Studios/Everett Collection

Physicist Neal Lane, former director of the US National Science Foundation (NSF), is among those who say that staff changes at the top of the agency are a sign of its de facto takeover by the administration of President Donald Trump. (Science | 7 min read)

#3032. The Power of Community

Why You Need a Support System to Thrive

We’ve all heard the saying, “If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go together.” But when it comes to health, fitness, and personal growth, this couldn’t be more true.

Having a strong community around you—whether it’s in fitness, wellness, or life in general—can make all the difference in staying motivated, pushing through challenges, and achieving your goals.

We’ve seen firsthand how a supportive, uplifting community can transform not only fitness journeys but also lives. 

Why Community Matters

1. Motivation & Accountability

It’s easy to hit snooze on an early workout or skip meal prep when no one’s watching. But when you have a community cheering you on, suddenly, showing up feels different.

In the Team LSF community, women support each other every step of the way—whether it’s through sharing wins, encouraging words, or just knowing you’re not alone in the journey.

💬 " I also realized how much I appreciate the LSF community. I’ve always had this mentality that “I can do things on my own” – but I think I was confusing that with the feeling that if I needed other people, it meant that I didn’t really do it myself. But the fact that I had a team on my side didn’t mean that I wasn’t the one making all that progress, it was still my own hard work.

What I didn’t see at first was that it wasn’t about tough love, it was about having other people cheer you on, congratulating you, making you feel good about yourself and just being there as someone who is also working towards a goal and wanting to do it in ways that support our health and wellbeing as a whole." - Sara

2. Shared Goals & Inspiration

There’s something powerful about surrounding yourself with people who get it—who have the same struggles, dreams, and dedication as you. Seeing others work hard, overcome obstacles, and celebrate victories fuels your own fire.

Want to connect with an amazing community of women who are on this journey just like YOU 👉 How to Connect with Team LSF

3. Make the Journey FUN

Let’s be real—sticking to workouts, healthy habits, and personal growth can feel hard sometimes. But when you have a community that makes it fun, it doesn’t feel like work/another job you have to do—it feels like a lifestyle.

That’s why Team LSF is more than just fitness—it’s about friendships, challenges, and celebrating every moment. From workout challenges to giveaways and real talk about our struggles, we make it fun, not just functional.

No matter where you are in your journey, having a strong, supportive community makes everything better. The power of community is real, and when you find your people, there’s nothing you can’t achieve.

#3035. Seeking Nirvana With Kate Berlant and Jacqueline Novak

Comedians Kate Berlant and Jacqueline Novak are co-hosts of the wellness podcast Poog. Berlant's latest special, “Parmesan,” was released on HBO on October 16, and Novak's next tour begins November 20.

I'd heard about the Golden Door many years ago from a gently famous, beautiful actress who had gone for a week to lean out after the excesses of the winter holiday. Her positive testimonial was echoed by a downer-loving millionaire who attended with her brilliant and terrifyingly thin mother for her 70th birthday. Zen gardens, sunrise hikes, five-star health-oriented meals, daily scrubs, wraps, and massages—and it’s been offering all this since long before it was fashionable, having opened in 1958.

Imagine my surprise and delight when I got the chance to go with my dear friend and Poog podcast co-host Jacqueline on assignment for Condé Nast Traveler. I'd just filmed my stand-up comedy special “Parmesan,” and I was eager for the week off. Previously, I'd thought the Golden Door was a space I would perhaps only visit in the afterlife. Now that I’ve been, it’s no exaggeration to say that the Door exceeded my wildest fantasies—and I’m plagued by the fear of never returning. We're both still talking about it. Below, Jacqueline and I unpack the experience. —Kate Berlant

The Golden Door, with its zen gardens, sunrise hikes, and wellness treatments, has been open since 1958.

Jacqueline Novak: How lovely that instead of death, it was, essentially, podcasting that got you to the Golden Door. We should tell them why Traveler sent us, two comedians, to write about this place.

Kate Berlant: Our podcast Poog is an ongoing conversation about wellness, beauty, and travel. It’s Goop backwards.

JN: But it’s not a satire. As touring acts we are constantly in hotels analyzing their features together.

KB: And a core tenet of the podcast is trying to get luxury items or spa experiences for free.

JN: I would argue this was our biggest “get.”

KB: Yes, even bigger than the Lyma laser.

JN: Remember the first night at dinner when we had to introduce ourselves in front of the group, I referred to the Golden Door as “our white whale,” which made sense to no one.

KB: This was moments before a woman stood up and announced it was her 118th visit. An elder. And she credited the place with…this is a direct quote: saving her life.

JN: The first visit saves your life and then visits two through 118 are more like…

KB: I really want to crunch those numbers.

JN: We did, remember. In my room before bed. It equaled 1.5 million. But profits go to charity.

KB: If you go over 100 times you get a brass plaque.

JN: And they hang it on a brass tree in the bamboo forest. We walked by it on our last day.

JN: So we knew ahead of time the Japanese gardens were immaculate, the luscious grounds were expansive, the dining was world-renowned. But for me the wow factor started weeks out with a leisurely but extremely detailed call with a kindly staffer who took down all of our details. Allergies, preferences…

KB: What classes I might want to try. Intuitive pottery. Taiko drumming. Chakra Yoga?

JN: Spring water or Alkaline in your room daily? I said, “What did Kate get?”

KB: Spring. Would you like a Keurig in addition to your daily French Press?

JN: Whenever I was unsure, the staffer said, why not both?

KB: They say, please don't bring jewelry, makeup, perfume. You could truly show up with only underwear and you'd be fine. They provide your clothing. They ask you details of your diet and how large you want your portions to be—small, medium, tall, or tall plus.

JN: And they offer to pick your ass up and drop you off at the end.

A visit to the Golden Door begins at its namesake gilded entrance.

KB: On arrival, we were escorted across a wooden bridge to the famous ornate jewel-laden golden door.

JN: Halfway across, under the canopy of Camellia trees, they ask you to pause. The bridge changes direction. It goes fifteen degrees to the left. The idea is dark energies can’t follow a direction change.

KB: So they ask you to take a moment to reflect on what you want to leave outside the doors.

KB: Right then a couple from New York blows past us. We hear them explain they’ve been here many times before. This was our first glimpse of another guest.

JN: The place runs on a weekly rhythm. A group arrives Sunday and departs on Sunday.

KB: The Golden Door warns you on the website not to bother notable people nor solicit donations.

JN: When we got to our rooms, I was shocked to see a printed list of the guests’ names and cities of origin.

KB: This way I was able to instantly Google and see we were sharing space with billionaires and authors and Gestalt therapists, oil heiresses, venture capitalists.

JN: You sent me a screenshot of an article about someone and his picture popped up on my phone screen, thankfully in front of nobody. I left my phone in the room after that.

KB: The confidence of giving guests a list, as if to say, we know you bastards want to know who you’re sitting with at dinner. We'll save you the uncomfortable line of questioning: So what do you do?

JN: It gets it out of the way. So you can compose yourself in your room if someone important to you is there. So many details of the Golden Door were like that, clearly the result of the wisdom of the gazillion years they’ve been doing this. They also give everyone a chance to add their email to a list before the end of the week so no one’s trying to secure anyone’s contact.

KB: To be clear, there were no celebrities from film or television or the stage. There were some well-known people from the finance world.

JN: One “handsome financier” mentioned that if he ends up in the piece, he’d like to be referred to as such. You’re welcome, Herbert. That wasn’t his name. I didn't get the feeling anyone was back in their room googling us though. The second morning on the 5:45 a.m. hike, a group of New Yorkers asked what we did.

KB: I ended up screaming “we're both Emmy-nominated!” in order to endear myself to the venture capitalist.

JN: You also said we were accepting scholarships.

Novak and Berlant with their new bff, Chef Greg

KB: Initially I had anxiety about being trapped there for four nights. The communal meals. I’d even said to Jacqueline, you know we can have meals in our room. But the uncanny happened. We made friends.

JN: We ended up taking every meal with the group. There’s a middle school lunch vibe because you do choose where to sit. So to offset that, we tried to sit with different people. I almost wish they assigned seats for each meal.

KB: We were there during co-ed week. Most weeks at Golden Door are women’s weeks, but they also have men’s weeks and co-ed. I initially wanted Women's Week.

JN: It was fun to meet couples, lifers who keep coming back. Going as a couple, by the way, is not a money-saving technique. The $13,000 rate is per person.

KB: One couple was celebrating their anniversary. But you see people go there in times of grief, of desperation, of sadness. You can really imagine it helping to reset a bitch.

JN: I was fantasizing about securing more money and more problems in the future so that returning to Golden Door would be inevitable. I want to one day be burnt out but rolling in it, and be dropped on their doorstep.

JN: I was nervous the portions would be too small, so as you know I smuggled in a box of Ezekiel cereal and several Dr. McDowell’s ramens, but didn’t end up needing them.

KB: A multi-year veteran of the Door told us that in the old days they used to weigh and measure you on check in.

JN: They’ve rightfully moved away from that approach.

KB: They were very accommodating with food.

The Golden Door Table, a new cookbook, includes 100 recipes from the propery.

Chef Greg Frey Jr., the executive chef at the Golden Door, at work in the kitchen.

JN: Like when you saw my black bean tempeh ramen or my mochi dessert, you were jealous, and they swiftly prepared one for you too.

KB: When I returned famished from a hike, and felt my breakfast tray wasn’t going to cut it, I requested more, and in under seven minutes sourdough pancakes arrived.

JN: The thick coconut yogurt and berries.

KB: Almost all ingredients are foraged directly from their sprawling farm. At the helm is Chef Greg, a towering and—I'll say it, gorgeous!—chef, who one day I found myself high-fiving wildly in the pool, while playing water volleyball for the first time.

JN: And scoring the game-winning point, if I recall.

JN: The garden was immense. It was like walking through the aisles of a grocery store built by the earth.

A majority of the ingredients served at Golden Door come from the onsite farm.

The garden is “like a grocery store built by the earth” Novak recalls.

KB: An Edenic paradise. Edenic, a favorite word of mine.

JN: Even the little flowers in the drinks came from their garden.

KB: Best iced tea of my life. Best tempeh I've ever had in my life.

JN: Bento Box day. The potassium broth poolside midday, with pepper and turmeric and flax fixings.

JN: A pot after every meal. Made of a fresh ginger slurry.

KB: Also you're not deciding what to eat four times a day.

JN: In general, the reduction of decision-making to easy choices was, for me, possibly the most relaxing element of all. Falling into the Golden Door daily rhythm, floating through the day according to the printed schedule, from activity to treatment, all optional.

KB: Like it’s 12 p.m. I could go to a Pilates class. I could do water volleyball. I could do a butterfly tour in the garden.

JN: Or walk the grounds. Hang at the pool. Float up to the art studio.

KB: I took everything from Japanese calligraphy to Ikebana to Archery.

JN: I learned taiko drumming. Found out my Aura might be green. You were shocked yours was yellow.

Activities like mah jong entertain between treatments.

Yoga and pilates classes are also on offer at the Golden Door.

KB: My favorite thing was the five-mile hike departing at the impossible hour of 5:45 a.m. I thought I'd go the first day just to experience it and never return, but I ended up doing it every morning.

KB: Rolling out of the deliriously comfortable bed and into my provided hiking gear. Leaving in the dark and hiking as the sun came up. Thinking, this could be my new life!

JN: One morning we were led on a silent hike with another couple and a leader that involved sun salutations to the actual rising sun.

KB: Followed by a contemplative labyrinth walk and silent breakfast.

JN: In the first couple days I kept hearing people go, you know, it's summer camp for adults. You were saying it felt like we were in kindergarten, munching on dessert while they made announcements.

KB: Everyone's in their identical Yakuta robe. Some people have hair wet from the shower or the pool. You're tired, you're satisfied. And then a sweet person who works at the Golden Door comes out and goes over some of the activity updates for the next day.

JN: It was a little vintage, like Kellerman’s from Dirty Dancing, but amidst the Japanese Gardens.

KB: Then there's the communal walk after dinner to the golden door gates.

JN: Knock three times and set intentions.

KB: The ten-minute stroll reduces glucose sensitivity…or does it increase glucose sensitivity? I never know.

Quiet spaces and intention setting are part of every day at the Golden Door.

JN: Though stays are usually seven nights, we were initially booked for just four, but pretty quickly I started to feel somber that we'd be leaving early. On the morning we were supposed to leave I sent an email begging them to let us stay. We had already made a big show of our early departure and goodbyes to the fellow guests, but then showed up at dinner to say, we’re staying.

KB: To think I was worried I’d feel trapped after four nights.

JN: There were many elements that felt surprisingly simple and wholesome. Stopping by the pool to take in the lunar eclipse on the way back to their rooms.

KB: Laughing and whispering in the pool during our night swim.

JN: You bringing your breakfast tray over to my patio to dine and discuss the day.

KB: Hunched over bowls of berry-speckled oatmeal, overlooking the Koi pond on the property’s impeccable Japanese gardens.

JN: The nightly evening programming, if you weren’t too sleepy. There was a self-love coach who led us through a ritual of flowers and affirmations.

KB: A magician. We crowded into a small, overly lit room with not enough seats to watch him.

JN: I was looking around during the magic show thinking, okay, the uber-rich are paying to have a sort of goofy evening, to not be overly accommodated by the staff. Having to figure out the chair situation themselves. And you won an Almond Joy. And one guest attempted to sabotage the magician’s trick.

KB: By shuffling the cards when he wasn't supposed to.

JN: You and I were staring at each other, identifying more with the hired act, of course.

KB: We lay in bed after analyzing the various characters and actions.

JN: Why would someone want to sabotage the magician’s trick? I loved chatting in your ice-cold room before you fell asleep. Then I’d sit on my patio, surely the last one up.

KB: Other programming included a self-love coach…

JN: An electric cello concert and light show.

The Golden Door is inspired, design-wise, by traditional Japanese ryokans.

KB: A breath work guide who played the singing bowls, where you had your big release.

JN: Yes, the second night’s program. We were lying on our backs in the dark for a sound bath while engaging in a 20-minute breathing practice.

KB: Two inhales through the mouth, one exhale through the mouth. I thought, this could get me high.

JN: Halfway through my hands and feet went numb, then felt like fire, and then contorted into strange positions like lobster claws. I was physically unable to open my hands. Like in an exorcist film. The teacher whispered in my ear that I could stop the breath if it was too uncomfortable.

JN: But I took it as encouragement to power through in case I was on the brink of nirvana. The teacher afterward said I’d had a big heart chakra opening.

KB: I was envious. Because I had felt my hands tingle and got scared and slowed my breathing.

JN: But you were right to. In bed I was googling what I’d experienced and the internet said it was Tetany, brought on by a CO2 imbalance where the body lets the extremities “go” first. I choose to believe both are true.

KB: Definitely. The founder of the Golden Door by the way is still alive and apparently “sharp as a tack” at 104. So she knows something. It was said she enjoys tuna melts and a daily mushroom tea elixir. Needless to say, I'm listening. By my fourth day, I was crunching the numbers, convincing myself this was actually a deal.

JN: I think by your fourth hour. The real question though: Would we pay out of pocket to return?

KB: Seven nights will run you about $13,000 with tip.

JN: Should someone save for years to go? Would the Door want someone to come on those terms?

KB: I’ve heard some people leave early because it's not, quote, nice enough. It really is so fucking luxurious, but it's not geisha level.

JN: A woman did perform tea service on her knees for me during check-in.

KB: Oh right. But there's a certain kind of person who wants a person's back broken, bent over, in servitude. Or amenities. Like our bathrooms. They could be considered too dated for someone.

JN: Right, and yet I never noticed the bathroom. It all felt right. The Golden Door has this vibe, like they’ve been around long enough to not chase trends. They know better than you. They know that you don’t actually need a free-standing soaking tub.

Amenities like a bathhouse and watsu pool blend wellness and lounging by the water.

KB: You don't need the self-warming floors. Or a TV in the mirror.

JN: Or anywhere. The resort knows exactly what it is. They are exactly who they are.

KB: They're fucking exactly who they are.

JN: The history of the place gives it credibility and confidence. It’s not insecure. Which can sink a place that has otherwise good features.

KB: And service is unmatched in terms of what matters.

JN: You ask to move a facial and then they appear at dinner to drop off your new schedule. It’s excellent service, like a militaristic operation under the surface,

KB: I left something under my dinner chair. The next morning, it’s resting atop my breakfast tray.

JN: I lose my shades and they appear on my nightstand.

KB: One of the things that I love is that while it’s a prohibitively expensive, luxurious experience, it still retains this feeling of old California health food culture. It feels free from the overwhelming polluted space of optimization and wellness culture that is so soulless. People who are going to the Golden Door can go anywhere, they can afford to go anywhere on earth. And they are choosing to come here.

JN: If you’ve worked every day in your life, and you say fuck it, I’m gonna cash out and finally leave this two-horse town, your first trip probably shouldn't be Golden Door. Your first stop should be Europe. Or a beach vacation. Not because those are better. But because the Golden Door is a sophisticated and nuanced experience. It’s the billionaire's last stop, where he finally finds a place worth returning to. Or if you can swing it, an opportunity to cosplay as one. To imagine you’re tired of all the empty luxury and peak experiences, that you just want to have a meaningful place to commune with family and friends.

KB: I will say I left Golden Door as I was entering an extremely emotionally stressful week and I swear to God, on some level, I felt like I was more able to cope with it. I felt like Amy Jellicoe, Laura Dern's character in the Mike White series Enlightened.

JN: After she connects with that tortoise underwater.

KB: When she leaves her Hawaiian retreat, she feels like a new person. Of course, I found myself desperate to hold on to the Golden Door. So I bought the Golden Door broth. A gorgeous loaf of sourdough, which I froze, and I've been eating in pieces.

JN: I bought nothing, but since coming home I have instituted the Golden Door post-meal gate walk, where my fellow and I walk to the gates of our own apartment complex and knock three times.

KB: They also send you off with a packed lunch. That helps.

JN: The daughter of a brass tree guest told me that on the last day, her mother pulled her aside and offered a somber warning.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#3036. AI firms say UK has a year to head off datacentre protests before construction is threatened

Exclusive: Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco taskforce urges ministers to offer areas greater benefits from tech infrastructure amid fears of US-style opposition

AI companies have told ministers they have 12 months to head off public opposition to datacentres in the UK or risk US-style protests that could threaten their construction.

Successive dry summers and rising energy bills are increasing public scrutiny of plans for the huge computer warehouses that are used to train and run AI models, says a submission to the Labour government from a group including the AI infrastructure companies Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco.

Amid increasing anti-datacentre activism in the US and Europe, they are calling on ministers to create a “compact” that would show how communities can benefit from hosting datacentres, including allowing councils that host them to retain more tax revenues.

The move by the Sovereign AI Leadership (SAIL) taskforce reflects rising concern among tech companies that arguments that have blocked datacentre developments in parts of the US are taking hold in Britain. Microsoft has promised to invest $30bn (£22bn) in UK AI infrastructure.

Microsoft has built a datacentre in Acton, London and another is under construction in Newport, but wants to build several more facilities and is engaging with local and national leaders, including the prime minister, Andy Burnham, over the balance between the potential benefit of AI to the economy and public opposition to datacentres.

The SAIL group said: “In the United States, organised local opposition has stopped fully permitted datacentre projects, and moratoriums have been announced even in states that are otherwise pro-growth.

“Reporting from those places shows that AI itself is only a surface-level concern; distrust of corporate and government promises, fear of stranded assets and electricity costs run deeper. The same arguments have begun to appear here.”

It added: “Britain has a window – we think of roughly 12 months – to build a compact that earns public consent before that pattern takes hold.”

The taskforce is calling for the government to create a clear framework for councils and mayors to follow that will set out recommended terms for local benefit, including an indicative contribution – likely to be financial or in terms of facilities – scaled to a site’s size.

Opposition to datacentre construction is being fuelled by widening public concern about the safety of AI systems, after a summer in which some of the largest companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google appeared to lose control of some of their most cutting-edge AIs. Some protesters have begun resorting to direct action and the membership of anti-AI campaign groups has been growing rapidly.

The datacentre companies are determined to head off that opposition. The chair of the SAIL taskforce, Steve Rigby, said: “By establishing a clear prosperity compact between government, industry and local communities, we can build the infrastructure we need, equip our workforce with future-ready skills, and ensure Britain’s digital destiny. This taskforce’s goal isn’t another strategy document, but high-impact actions that materially accelerate the UK’s transition to an AI-enabled economy.”

It has not calculated the cost to central government finances if councils that grant permission to datacentres are allowed to keep all of their business rates.

Responding to the proposals, Joseph Miller, the director of PauseAI UK, which campaigns for a global pause to datacentre buildout, said: “People are going to feel it is undignified to be bought off by huge tech companies who do not share their interests.”

He said tech companies were “absolutely right to be worried” about US-style public opposition to datacentres growing in the UK. Kat Jones, the director of Action to Protect Rural Scotland, which campaigns against datacentres, said tech companies had already “missed the boat on containing community opposition to hyperscale AI datacentres”.

“In Scotland, we have 15 community campaigns already working incredibly hard opposing these environmentally destructive developments locally, and a growing national campaign,” she said. “Even the titanic lobbying efforts of US big tech are going to find it a real challenge to change the winds of public opinion, which have already shifted solidly against hyperscale AI datacentres.”

Donald Campbell, the director of advocacy at the tech equity campaign Foxglove, said: “Big tech firms have spent years trying to force vast, highly polluting datacentres through the planning system under a blanket of secrecy and misleading information. Now, with the public waking up to the fact that these facilities plunder resources and wreck the climate, the US tech giants have decided that there’s a problem.”

He warned that incentivising councils to back datacentres by allowing them to keep more of their business rate revenue would mean “these wealthy tech giants would not pay a penny more” while boosts to council funding would “come from the pocket of central government services like the NHS”.

A government spokesperson said datacentres “should create British jobs and supply chains, and provide investment to the communities in which they are built, as well as prioritising clean power, using water responsibly”.

“For most proposed datacentre developments, community benefits are considered through the relevant local planning processes,” they said. “We have already announced measures which will enable local authorities hosting datacentres in AI growth zones in England to keep all the additional business rates they generate.”

#3037. Balancing Ice Skater STEM Challenge

This simple balancing ice skater STEM challenge is the first of a series of Winter Olympic themed science activities. The idea is to make a cardstock skater attached to a small piece of dowel, balance on your finger! It seems impossible, but with a bit of clever science, it works really well and looks amazing.

It’s a great way to learn about the centre of mass and balance, while patiently making small adjustments and observing how they change the position of the skater. Play-dough works well as you can easily adjust how much you use and its position.

Cut the skater image out from the template page or draw your own.

Attach a small piece of dowel to the skater as shown in the photo.

Try to balance the dowel on your finger, the skater should fall off.

Attach two straws to the back of the skater using tape, so they point downwards diagonally on each side.

Try to balance the skater again. If it falls off, add a little Play-Doh to the bottom of each and adjust until the skater balances.

The ice skater stays balanced when its centre of mass is directly above the wooden dowel. Gravity pulls downwards, and if the centre of mass isn’t lined up over the dowel at the bottom, it creates a turning force that tips the ice skater over.

Adding straws and Play-Doh changes the centre of mass of the ice skater and the dowel. Adjusting the straws and Play-Doh bit by bit moves the centre of mass over the dowel, balancing the skater.

Last Updated on January 25, 2026 by Emma Vanstone

#3038. Rising CO2 Speeds the Growth of Grasses on the African Savanna

Kruger National Park in South Africa. Åse Elin Langeland

On the arid African savanna, grasses are growing faster than they were a generation ago, boosted by rising levels of carbon dioxide from the burning of fossil fuels. That is the finding of a new study that warns that faster growth could fuel larger wildfires and alter the distribution of wildlife.

Since the dawn of the industrial age, the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere has grown by half, which is helping to speed photosynthesis and cause many plants to grow faster. The phenomenon, known as “carbon fertilization,” has been well documented in forests, and some experts believe it may be responsible for the greening of drylands around the globe.

It was long assumed, however, that grasses on the African savanna gain little from the extra carbon dioxide, as they already employ a highly efficient form of photosynthesis. But researchers are now finding otherwise. An analysis of three decades of data gathered from experiments and observations across Kruger National Park in South Africa shows that rising carbon dioxide levels are prompting faster growth.

Between 1989 and 2021, grass production rose by 28 percent, a shift that could not be explained by changes in rainfall, temperature, grazing, fire, or other drivers, according to the study, which was published in Nature. Researchers say that extra carbon dioxide is allowing grasses to use water more efficiently, which is helping them to grow more quickly, even through dry spells. Modeling suggests that savanna grasses will continue to benefit from the surplus carbon dioxide even as warming intensifies heat and drought.

The faster growth brings new risks, however. Researchers say more grass means more fuel for wildfires. It also means more forage, which could boost the number of grazing animals. And there is no guarantee that the additional carbon drawn down by grasses will stay locked away.

“The wider impact depends on where the extra grass ends up,” said lead author Kimberley Simpson, an ecologist at the University of Sheffield. “If it is eaten by animals or burned in fires, much of the carbon is quickly released back into the atmosphere.”

Later on I’ll get into the good, bad, and ugly, the weather, getting around, and all those things. But I know you want to know the fun things to do in Cusco or the Sacred Valley area of Peru. Thereâs no shortage of things to see in Cusco, but here are the highlights Iâd recommend to anyone visiting.

But first, make sure you consider travel medical insurance. I’ve never regretted always having it! It can be as cheap as $2/day!

Side note…don’t forget to always, always, always consider getting inexpensive travel medical insurance âsometimes as low as $2/dayâfor your trip, and a separate yearly evacuation insurance policy if you travel internationally often! And check out my list of tips for staying safe while traveling abroad.

If you love people-watching and sampling local snacks and fruit drinks on the cheap, these are the places to do it. Eat cheap, haggle a little for souvenirs, and just soak up the Cusco energy.

Once plated entirely in gold, it was the spiritual center of the Inca world. Still has some near-perfect Inca stonework that still anchors the colonial church built on top.

An underrated gem and a way to get away from the noise and pollution in Cusco when you need a break. Uber or taxi up, and if it’s daylight, hike back down. You can do it on your own or by horseback on a guided tour!

A massive stone fortress with panoramic views of Cusco. A fairly cheap taxi ride if you want to do it yourself, or you can book a half-day tour for pretty cheap and hit multiple important stops and ruins in Cusco in one fell swoop.

Take a cusco guided tour or collectivo to this ancient Inca town. The terraces and the Ollantaytambo Ruins are awe-inspiring, and the vibe is slower than in Cusco. I spent a day there exploring and hanging with the alpacas, and having one of the best sandwiches of my life. More about this one below.

Colorful market, sweeping mountain views, and a massive and overwhelming Inca ruin complex. Itâs one of the best things to do in Sacred Valley, and hiking the Pisac Ruins in the rain was hands down one of my most unexpected favorites of my trip. It’s also one of the easiest and best day trips from Cusco. More on this one further down in this travel blog.

Pisac Ruins is easily one of the best day trips from Cusco and a must-do if you’re there. You can also get a Hotel in Pisac if you want to experience sundown and sunup in the Sacred Valley.

Yes, itâs Insta-famous, but itâs famous for a reason. Go early or book a Rainbow Mountain tour with smaller groups to beat the crowds. Don’t skip the Red Valley views. It’s 16,500 feet, so make sure you’re acclimated!

Harness up, clip in, and scale the cliff face. Climbing the side of a cliff is wild, but itâs safe, and itâs one of those epic adventures you brag about later. It was my first via feratta, but it definitely won’t be my last!

Small but fascinating Inca sites close to town. Perfect half-day hikes while acclimating to the altitude of Cusco Peru.

Honestly, one of the best things to do in Cusco, Peru is just wander aimlessly. If you want to get beautiful photos of Cusco with no people, explore the alleyways and stairwells in the old town near San Blas in the rain or near dawn.

Of course the thing most people come to Cusco, Peru for a trip to Machu Picchu. Plan early and book an all-inclusive tour now (you can always cancel for free in advance), or you could miss your chance, like I did. Womp Womp. Check guided tours for Machu Picchu here.

Cusco is the launchpad for dozens of day trips. And a list of things to do in Sacred Valley would take up this whole travel blog post, but hereâs a shortlist…

The ruins in Ollantaytambo were pretty darn epic. The way the Incas put together structures with rocks by making them fit together perfectly may sound like an odd thing to be stoked about, but honestly, it’s pretty impressive. GoÂ all the way to the top of the trail where very few venture for some of the best views of the Ollantaytambo and the Sacred Valley.

Ollantaytambo Ruins is easily one of the best day trips from Cusco and a must-do if you’re there.

Pisac is super easy to get to by 45m collectivo from many spots near San Blas and it will run you less than 10 SOL each way. Hiking the Pisac Ruins in the rain was easily one of the best things I did while I was in Cusco, since I took the hard route where nobody goes and had amazing views and ruins exploring time to myself.

I highly recommend that you plan for a full day in Pisac to get the most out of it and take it slow.

The salt pans of Maras shimmer like a science-fiction landscape, while Morayâs circular terraces look like crop art from space. You can get a guided tour like I did for around $20+ USD if you want to take the guesswork out of it, which I highly recommend.

I did my first via ferrata in the Sacred Valley in Cusco, Peru, but it won’t be my last. Talk about an adrenaline rush.

A little pricey at first glance, but while I was hanging off the side of a mountain, I was all “TAKE MY MONEY PLEASE!”

I can’t wait til I can do my next via ferrata. Read all about my first via ferrata experience in the Sacred Valley here.

Whether you book guided tours in Cusco (easiest is through sources like GetYourGuide or Viator IMO) , or go DIY, the Sacred Valley is pretty easy to navigate and has endless epic memories to be made and photo opps to be had.

Just a few of the things I loved about Cusco to whet your appetite. I’ve spent over a 16 months in Latin American countries over the last few years, and Cusco has many of the reasons why!

Interactions with the people living in Cusco is almost always a pleasure.

While Gringo pricing can be real, most of the time it’s honest interactions with kind people simply trying to make a living.

Personally, I’m not much of a haggler or negotiator, since I’m happy to give a tiny bit more of my money since I know it’s important to the hard working folks. But that’s just me.

I’m a hopeless romantic, and I just love me a good old cobblestone street. Getting lost in the alleyways after dark will forever be one of my favorite ways to pass time. Add a little rain and it completely changes the vibe, in the best way possible. Go out at sunrise and you get the added luxury of little to no tourists or honking taxis.

There are tons of places to eat in Cusco, and you can get amazing meals for one person for anywhere up from $4 USD. One Cusco travel tip would be to eat at San Blas Market at least once a day to get some delicious food for hella-cheap.

Even at the mid-range restaurants you can easily spend around $20-30 per person (less drinks) and have an absolutely stunning meal. But for me, I stick to the $4-15 meals because I find them equally imaginative and delicious, and more bang for my buck than some super fancy place. But you do you boo.

There are always some “bad” things you’ll want to keep in mind about most locations you travel to. Traveling in Cusco, Peru is no different. Here are just a few of the more…real things… to keep in mind when you travel to Cusco.

Taxis are constantly honking to get the attention of tourists and locals. And I mean constantly. And it seems like anything with an engine is out to get you, since traffic flows like water, but not in the tranquil way you might want.

Stopping at stop signs and respecting divided road paint are optional, and passing at full speed with limited sight lines on curvy mountain roads seems mandatory. Pack a puke bag for any tours, or when you go long distances in a taxi, Uber, or collectivo. You’ve been warned!

No filter isn’t a good thing when it comes to exhaust and fumes.

The data says, on average, air quality in Cusco hovers between 60â90 AQI (moderate to unhealthy), largely due to old diesel vehicles and limited emission controls.

But while you’re getting crop dusted by black fumes every 20 seconds you’ll likely think it’s much worse. (Luckily there are so many ways to get into nature in the Sacred Valley you can get some reprieves!)

Yeah. I said it. Cusco seems to have even more street dogs than many places I’ve been in Latin American , and that means more dog poop landmines to evade. Personally, I’ve had or seen too many scary encounters with street dogs, so I prefer not to pet them or get too close.

But I almost always give a “hola perro” as I walk by because…doggos are still the best. ð

You can visit Cusco year-round, but your experience will likely be effected pretty drastically with the seasons. The wet months can get a ton of rain, and the dry months are really, really dry, especially at Cusco’s high elevation.

The shoulder seasons can save you some cash and be cheaper for travel in Cusco.

Guided tours around Cusco, in the Sacred Valley or the mountains can be cheaper, but you might deal with different types of weather than in the high travel season. Pick your poison!

Whichever season you choose, give yourself a couple of days to acclimate to the altitude of Cusco Peru. Walk slowly, drink coca tea, skip the Pisco Sours for a day or two until you’re grounded.

Here are just a few foods to try when in Cusco.

Meals in local joints and mercados run USD $3â10. Fancy dinner with a view? USD $20+. Lots of places take credit cards, but you should always carry some local cash!

Cuscoâs old town and tourist center is best explored on footâthough youâll definitely feel the altitude of the Andes on uphill climbs. Don’t worry, that subsides the moment you stop climbing.

You can join small-group Cusco guided tours for most destinations if you donât feel like driving or dealing with any logistics.

Exchange rate at the time of writing: 1 USD â +/-3 Peruvian soles. For me the easiest way to keep that straight was to think: 30 SOL = About 10USD. Or 10 SOL = About 3 USD. That rough math always keeps me under budget!

Street food is cheap and filling, so stop at San Blas Market or into a local restaurant for your early meals then splurge on dinner. Youâll find coffee for $2-3, craft beer for $5â6USD, and Uber or taxis around town will usually only run you about 5-15 SOL (around $2-6USD).

Cusco feels safe, but basic street smarts still apply. (Check out this post with 18+ tips for staying safe while traveling.) Keep your phone close in busy markets and donât flash big bills. When visiting sacred Inca sitesâwhich can be found littered around Cusco and the rural areasâstay on paths and be respectful. Locals treat these as living spiritual places, not just photo ops.

Altitude sickness can sneak up fast. If you start feeling woozy and get a strong headache, drink coca tea, hydrate, and rest. Thereâs no trophy for pushing through the altitude of Cusco.

Taxis and collectivos in or around Cusco, or to the Sacred Valley area, are considered pretty safe. But when in doubt, Ubers are readily available.

When in doubt, read this article about tips to reduce your fear of traveling anywhere!

My biggest advice? Donât rush Cusco. Again, I spent 5 weeks there (working, taking 20 hours of Spanish classes a week, and exploring…), and barely scratched the surface. You* won’t* be able to do it all, so don’t even try! Slow down and enjoy!

There are endless things to do in Cusco, Peru, but the magic often hides between the planned stops. Chat with a shop owner. Wander down a street because a dog looked at you funny. The mountains are ancient here, and they reward curiosity over checklists.

Unexpectedly getting lost by myself while hiking the Pisac Ruins was the best misadventure of my whole trip to Peru!

Take it easy with the altitude, sip your coca tea, and let the Andes show you their pace. When you finally tackle that via ferrata climb or watch sunrise from Rainbow Mountain, youâll realize how worth it every slow breath was.

Jason is the author of “The Beginner Traveler’s Guide” as well as the voice behind the words and the eye behind the lens for The Nomad Experiment. “Planning to travel at some point” wasn’t actually getting the job done, so nearing 40 he decided to make it a priority, nomatter how scary that was. A few years laterâthrough the pandemic and a type 1 diabetes diagnosis at age 42ânow living a life of nomadic travel, he’s speaking out to encourage others of any age, or with any serious medical diagnosis, to live an unconventional life.

Cusco sits around 3,400 m (11,200 ft). It can take a day or two (or more if you have a major medical condition or heart issues like me) to adjust, so hydrate and take it slow.

You can book online, at your hostel, or through dozens of local agencies offering early-morning departures. But if you don’t speak great Spanish, that could be tough, so I would suggest checking out this all-inclusive. Yeah, the early morning wake-up can be rough, but getting to Rainbow Mountain before the crowds is totally worth it.

The basecamp of Rainbow Mountain in Peru sits at roughly 4,326 meters (14,189 feet), but the viewpoint of the actual Rainbow Mountain Peaks is at 5,036 meters (about 16,522 feet). The relatively short hike (under a mile) took over an hour because you have to hike it really, really slow and take lots of breaks. Luckily there are plenty of Alpaca to chat with!

Yesâgear is provided, guides are professional, and the views are insane. Itâs a must to do the via ferrata with 5 different ziplinesâone over 700 meters longâif you’re an adventure seeker like me. Check out how my via ferrata went hereâwell worth the price tag. Book it early!

The Pisac Ruins were my absolute favorite, only 45 minutes from Cusco. Take a tour to Ollantaytambo to check out my next favorite ruinsâor tale a collectivo for cheap and take your time. Temple of the Sun, Temple of the Moon, and SacsayhuamÃ¡n are either in or super close to Cusco and definitely a few of the bestÂ things to see in Cusco.

About 1â2 hours to get from Cusco to the Sacred Valley by car, collectivo, or bus, depending on where youâre headed. Perfect for an Ollantaytambo day trip,Â Pisac day tripÂ to check out the best bang for your buck ruins around Cusco (in my humble opinion), or more like 3-4 four hours for an epic tour of Rainbow Mountain.Â

Expect $30â80 depending on comfort level and whether itâs a group or private guide. There are tons of adventures and tours around Cusco, so plan ahead!

Very much so. Just use normal caution and trust your instincts. If you’re drunk and out after midnight by yourself, then you’re tempting fate in any city in the world, and that goes for Cusco too.

After speaking with many locals, the consensus says you’re generally safe in the historic districts of San Blas and Plaza De Armas areas, but in high tourist season especially, you can do a lot of things to make yourself a little safer. Check this article for many of those things!

AprilâMay or SeptemberâOctober for great weather and fewer crowds. These windows are considered the shoulder season, so just be careful to look at the seasons since snow at higher elevations could be an issue and could dampen your day tours to places like Rainbow Mountain or other high-altitude tours.

Taking it slow! Too many people try to see everything without acclimating to the altitude of Cusco, Peru first. It takes a minimum 24-48 hours or more to acclimate.

With my heart condition and type 1 diabetes, I didn’t feel “good” until about 3-4 days in.

I met people who literally landed at midnight (from 30 hours of flights from Australia) and were climbing the side of mountain doing this via ferrata and zipline adventure with me less than 10 hours later, and planning to start the Inka Trail 24 hours later. One star, do not recommend that approach!

#3040. Outsite Review: The Best Place to Stay for Digital Nomads

Balancing travel and remote work will always be one of the biggest challenges on the road. When you’re a digital nomad, it’s always a struggle to balance sightseeing and also get your work done in a nice, quiet environment. No one wants to spend hours searching for a coffee shop or be in one that is uncomfortable. It is something I’ve struggled with a lot in the past.

Working from the road used to mean hunching over a tiny hostel common room table or arguing with an Airbnb host who swore their internet was “super fast” (only to find out it couldn’t even load a basic email).

But, as remote work has expanded post-pandemic, a ton of coliving spaces have popped up that combine the benefits of a coworking space with the social atmosphere of a hostel (but without the dorm-style basic amenities). They are meant for those digital nomads who want a nice place to stay where they can not only get work done but also meet other travelers (as remote work can be isolating since you’re doing it alone)!

The biggest and most popular platform for remote workers doing this is Outsite, which has a lot of beautiful locations around the world.

And, in this post, I’ll go over everything you need to know about them and my experience staying with them on a recent trip to Bordeaux.

Founded in 2015, Outsite is a global network of coliving and coworking spaces designed specifically for remote workers, location-independent entrepreneurs, and digital nomads.

They started with a single house in Santa Cruz, California, aimed at people who wanted to surf and work. Today, they have over 5,000 members and 50 locations you can choose from.

Currently, anyone can book a stay at Outsite but if you’re a member, you get access to more perks and better rates. You can pay a yearly membership of $199 or pay once for a lifetime membership at $499. Perks include access to members-only locations, 1 week free in new destinations, 50% off in flash sales, 40% off extended stays, new member mixers, a job & sublets board, and some lifestyle perks.

It’s easy to use, too. You just browse their website, filter by destination or the type of vibe you want (beach, city, mountains), and book your private room.

Outsite operates like a boutique hotel meets a coworking space. When you book an Outsite, you are booking a private bedroom. Most rooms have their own private en-suite bathrooms, though some budget-friendly rooms share a bathroom with one other person.

Every location features massive, beautifully furnished communal areas. You get to enjoy fully-equipped chef’s kitchens that you could never afford in a solo Airbnb. Plus, you get spacious living rooms, outdoor patios, and often roof decks or pools (location depending).

Every single location has a dedicated coworking space built right into the house. I’m talking ergonomic chairs, plenty of outlets, monitors you can plug into, and blazing-fast, enterprise-grade Wi-Fi. You can wake up, make your coffee, and be at a proper desk in a state of deep focus within five minutes.

Plus, there’s a social aspect to all Outside locations. Every location has a dedicated Community Manager. Before you even arrive, you are added to a local WhatsApp group and locations organize weekly events like family-style dinners, group weekend trips, Friday night tapas crawls, and morning yoga sessions. You really get a lot of chances to meet people.

And the community manager is a great resource. During my stay at their Bordeaux location, they were available to share tips, suggest places to eat, and just be there to answer any questions I had. It was really helpful.

First, the properties are really nice. Their place in Bordeaux had modern furniture, comfy chairs to work from, laundry facilities, and even a small gym. The rooms were really nice too. I had a private desk, a comfy bed, and a really lovely bathroom (the water had GREAT shower pressure!).

The shared kitchen was super clean (cleaners come daily) and the counter space was huge. It was the kind of kitchen I wish my house had. You could cook some really good meals here. (Coffee and tea are always provided for free!)

Plus, I love the design. The spaces are designed with natural light, plants, and local art. It feels incredibly far removed from the sterile environment of a corporate hotel. It feels like you are staying at your very wealthy, very cool friend’s house.

However, for me, the main draw for using Outsite is the community aspect. Being a remote worker means you’re often working alone. Whether in a hotel or a coffee shop, it’s just you and your community. It’s hard to meet people.

At Outsite, you are surrounded by your fellow digital nomads who can relate to your life experience. They aren’t backpackers on a trip wondering why you are sitting on your computer all day when you should be exploring. Because everyone is there to work and live, there’s a shared bond. You’re there to work and have fun. Most people at the Bordeaux location were there for at least two weeks. Our community manager organized a bunch of weekend events to help people get to know each other, too.

First, Outsite is not a budget backpacker option. If you are used to spending $15 a night in a dorm room in Southeast Asia, Outsite is not for you. You are paying a premium for the private room, the guaranteed workspace, and the community curation. That said, when you factor in the cost of renting an Airbnb plus buying a monthly pass to a local coworking space, Outsite likely comes out cheaper.

Second, the popular locations book up fast. If you want to spend July in their Lisbon house or January in their Costa Rica location, you need to book months in advance. You can’t always be spontaneous with their most sought-after properties.

Do I have to be a member to book a stay? No! Anyone can book a stay at Outsite. However, if you plan on staying for more than a few days, the $199 annual Membership pays for itself almost immediately through the discounted nightly rates.

Is there an age limit? There is no official age limit, but you must be at least 18 (and in some locations, 21) to book. The vast majority of guests are working professionals in their late 20s, 30s, and 40s. It definitely skews a bit older and more professional than your average backpacker hostel.

Is there a minimum number of nights required? For most locations, the minimum stay is just 2 nights, making it easy to pop in for a weekend. However, some specific locations (especially in major cities with strict local housing laws like New York) may require a 30-day minimum stay.

Can I bring my pet? Generally, no. Because it is a shared living environment with communal kitchens and living spaces, most Outsite locations do not allow pets to ensure the comfort of all guests (and to prevent allergy issues).

Living the digital nomad life shouldn’t mean sacrificing your career progression, your comfort, or your social life. You shouldn’t have to choose between traveling the world and having a comfortable desk chair, or seeing new cities and having a consistent group of friends. I met some cool people while I stayed with them in Bordeaux.

Outsite is a great platform for people who want the perks and comforts of a private home, the productivity of an office, and the social life of a hostel. I think sharing a home creates a sense of intimacy, and you will absolutely make some friends out of it.

Be sure to check them out on your next trip and go find your tribe!

My New York Times best-selling book to travel will teach you how to master the art of travel so that you’ll get off save money, always find deals, and have a deeper travel experience. It’s your A to Z planning guide that the BBC called the “bible for budget travelers.”

Click here to learn more and start reading it today!

Book Your Flight Find a cheap flight by using Skyscanner. It’s my favorite search engine because it searches websites and airlines around the globe so you always know no stone is being left unturned.

Book Your Accommodation You can book your hostel with Hostelworld. If you want to stay somewhere other than a hostel, use Booking.com as it consistently returns the cheapest rates for guesthouses and hotels.

Don’t Forget Travel Insurance Travel insurance will protect you against illness, injury, theft, and cancellations. It’s comprehensive protection in case anything goes wrong. I never go on a trip without it as I’ve had to use it many times in the past. My favorite companies that offer the best service and value are:

Want to Travel for Free? Travel credit cards allow you to earn points that can be redeemed for free flights and accommodation — all without any extra spending. Check out my guide to picking the right card and my current favorites to get started and see the latest best deals.

Need a Rental Car? Discover Cars is a budget-friendly international car rental website. No matter where you’re headed, they’ll be able to find the best — and cheapest — rental for your trip!

Need Help Finding Activities for Your Trip? Get Your Guide is a huge online marketplace where you can find cool walking tours, fun excursions, skip-the-line tickets, private guides, and more.

Ready to Book Your Trip? Check out my resource page for the best companies to use when you travel. I list all the ones I use when I travel. They are the best in class and you can’t go wrong using them on your trip.
