#3041. How to Build Habits that Stick

We all start with the best intentions—whether it’s exercising regularly, eating healthier, or prioritizing self-care. But let’s be real… sticking to new habits can be hard. Life gets busy, motivation fades, and before you know it, you’re back to old patterns.

So how do you create habits that actually last? The key isn’t willpower—it’s strategy. By setting yourself up for success, you can build healthy routines that feel effortless and become part of your lifestyle.

Here’s how to make your habits stick for good!

1. Start Small & Be Specific

One of the biggest mistakes people make is going too big, too fast. If your goal is to work out every day, don’t start with an hour-long workout. Instead, commit to at least 10 minutes a day—something so easy you can’t say no. Once that’s locked in, build from there.

Example: Instead of saying, “I want to eat healthier,” say, “I will add a serving of veggies to my lunch every day.” Making your goals specific make it easier to follow through!

2. Habit Stacking

One of the easiest ways to build a new habit is to pair it with something you already do. This is called “habit stacking” and helps your new habit feel more natural.

Example:

  • Want to start journaling? Do it right after brushing your teeth in the morning.
  • Want to drink more water? Have a glass before your morning coffee.

The more effortless it feels, the more likely you are to stick with it!

3. Make It Easy

If a habit feels complicated or overwhelming, you won’t stick with it. Remove obstacles so it becomes the easiest choice.

Example:

  • Want to work out in the morning? Lay out your workout clothes the night before.
  • Want to eat healthier? Meal prep snacks so you always have good options on hand.

Set yourself up for success by making the habit as easy as possible.

4. Track Your Progress

There’s something powerful about seeing your progress—it keeps you motivated! Track in my MOVE APP or in the #GOALS PLANNER.

Even if you miss a day, don’t let it derail you. The goal isn’t perfection—it’s consistency!

5. Focus on Identity, Not Just Behavior

Instead of just thinking about what you want to do, shift your mindset to who you want to become. When you identify with your habit, it becomes a part of you.

Example: Instead of saying, “I’m trying to work out,” say, “I am someone who moves my body every day.” When you believe in your new identity, your actions will follow.

6. Reward Yourself (But Not with What You’re Avoiding)

Positive reinforcement is key! Celebrate your wins—big or small—to keep yourself motivated.

But here’s the trick: Don’t reward yourself in a way that contradicts your habit.

✅ Good reward: Bought a new yoga mat after sticking to a month of workouts.
❌ Not-so-great reward: Cheat days filled with unhealthy food and no workouts as an “reward."

Keep your rewards aligned with your goals!

7. Give Yourself Grace & Keep Going

Nobody is perfect. You will miss days, and that’s okay. What matters is that you get back on track quickly instead of quitting altogether.

Make It a Lifestyle!

Building habits that stick isn’t about temporary motivation—it’s about creating a lifestyle that supports your goals. By starting small, making habits easy, and tracking progress, you can create lasting change and feel amazing while doing it!

#3043. ‘Black October’: cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over new era of AI-enabled hacking

After discovery of severe bug in the PHP programming language, executives warn of ‘vulnerability tsunami’

Leaders in cybersecurity are sounding the alarm after the discovery of a major vulnerability this week. They are predicting that artificial intelligence tools will expose more fundamental weaknesses in global internet infrastructure in the months to come.

“I no longer think we’re going to be able to patch all bugs,” said Sam Altman on Thursday evening, joining the chorus of executives. In the midst of what’s being called “Black October”, for which researchers used AI to help identify critical flaws in a coding language that is used across millions of websites and may have been unpatched for years, tech executives are warning about the ways AI will be used both to identify and exploit security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented scale and pace.

The next few months will see a “vulnerability tsunami”, according to Jason Clinton, Anthropic’s deputy chief information security officer. “There won’t be enough time to patch critical infrastructure,” Clinton said in a post on X on Thursday evening. Marc Benioff, the Salesforce CEO, agreed and called it a “code red”.

AI is uniquely able to find and identify security flaws in a way and at a pace that will feel catastrophic because the security community will not be able to move quickly enough to address them, said Matthew Prince, the Cloudflare CEO. “It’s going to feel like the sky is falling. It’s going to feel like there’s nothing we can do.

“The next two years are going to be incredibly, incredibly, incredibly fraught with new tools that have infinite patience to go look for vulnerabilities across the Internet,” he wrote in a post on X.

While cybersecurity experts have been warning about a “vulnpocalypse”, or the ability for AI to more easily identify security bugs for months, it wasn’t until “Black October” that researchers were able to use AI to find a flaw as fundamental and critical as the one announced on 21 October.

Massive bugs were found in a programming language called PHP, which may have left the millions of websites that run on it vulnerable to hackers for years. Some experts estimated 70% of all the sites on the internet were at risk of hacking.

However, in the same way AI will be used to aid in identifying security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented pace, tech leaders worry it’ll also be used by malicious actors to exploit those bugs at an unprecedented pace.

Attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerability have already begun.

After the vulnerabilities were announced, government and private websites across the US and UK temporarily took down their sites to patch the bugs. The US National Security Agency (NSA) issued an alert recommending any site that runs on PHP implement the patches immediately. Malicious cyberactors may seek to further exploit these bugs to access servers without authorization, the NSA said.

“Such an access vector could help attackers steal sensitive data, disrupt services or move deeper into a network,” the warning read.

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

In a post on X, Prince said CloudFlare, a security provider, had seen evidence of thousands of people trying to exploit the PHP flaws in the 10 hours before it was announced.

“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now,” he wrote.

In a blogpost, researchers at AI security platform Wiz said that this was “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history”.

“The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” they wrote.

#3045. Filipino Cacao Growers Learn to Live With a Hotter Climate

In “Chocolates Melting Away” — the First-Place Winner of the 2026 Yale Environment 360 Film Contest — Breech Asher Harani explores how cacao growers in the Philippines are developing new techniques to protect their crops from increasingly turbulent weather.

In the Philippines, ideal growing conditions for cacao have fueled an industry with a market value of more than $400 million. In the Davao region, on the island of Mindanao, growers tend trees, harvest fruits, and produce premium chocolates for the domestic market. But climate change, which has brought drought, floods, more humidity, and extreme heat to the region, has presented growers with serious challenges.

Based in Davao, filmmaker Breech Asher Harani set out to document the concerns of cacao farmers at two artisanal operations and speak with agricultural researchers about the industry’s efforts to adapt to changing conditions. Farmers demonstrated how they use intercropping, produce fertilizers from agricultural waste to increase yields and quality, and employ innovative irrigation systems to minimize water loss.

“These farmers are very well versed when it comes to climate mitigation strategies and sustainable farming techniques,” Harani says, noting that he never sensed a feeling of hopelessness among growers. Not only do the cacao farmers seem “ready to face the battle,” Harani says, “they are also ready to show others what they are doing so their methods can be replicated.”

Harani hopes his film elevates the importance of farmers, “whose hard work sustains our everyday needs,” and that viewers will feel motivated to take action against climate change, “which is already reshaping what we eat.”

About the Filmmaker: Breech Asher Harani is a filmmaker and artist whose work spans narrative, documentary, experimental, and animated forms. In 2019, he was named a JCS International Young Creatives awardee at the International Emmy Awards, and was subsequently listed on Forbes Asia’s 30 Under 30 for the Arts. Harani is the first recipient of a Climate and Labor Film Grant, awarded jointly by the Pulitzer Center, the Financial Times, and One World Media.

About the Contest: Now in its 13th season, the Yale Environment 360 Film Contest honors the year’s best environmental documentary shorts from around the world. This year we received 596 submissions from more than 80 countries across six continents, with the winners selected by the editors of Yale Environment 360.

#3047. How the Antigravity 360 Drone Will Change Your Travels

Drones are huge. And, while there’s lots of restrictions around them, a lot of travelers take them on road because they produce some amazing sweeping aerial shots.

There’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1. Released in late 2025, attempts to render the traditional gimbal obsolete for a vast segment of creators. By leveraging a dual-lens 360-degree capture system, the A1 records everything in every direction simultaneously. The result is a “fly now, frame later” experience that feels less like piloting a drone and more like directing a virtual camera in a pre-recorded digital environment.

I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.

What make’s Antigravity 360’s so special is the two lenses. Most drones feature a single lens that points forward. However, the A1 features two ultra-wide-angle lenses positioned on the top and bottom of the central fuselage that each captures a 200-degree field of view. When those images are combines, they overlap to create a seamless 360-degree sphere.

And, in the final exported footage, the drone itself is digitally removed, creating the illusion of a camera floating in mid-air with no visible means of support.

The sensors themselves are 1/1.28-inch CMOS units. While smaller than the 1-inch sensors found on some “Pro” level photography drones, they are massive compared to typical 360 action cameras. This allows for significantly better low-light performance and a higher dynamic range, capturing details in the highlights and shadows that would typically be lost in the harsh contrast of a midday sun.

Most countries require drones weighing 250 grams or more to be registered and subject to stricter flight rules. Antigravity clearly understood the importance of this threshold because they made the A1 to weigh exactly 249 grams with its standard battery meaning it’s not considered a commercial drone so you don’t have to register it.

And the drone feels remarkably sturdy. It utilizes a high-grade carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer that offers a better strength-to-weight ratio than the standard ABS plastic found in cheaper models. The folding mechanism is satisfyingly tactile, clicking into place with a precision that suggests long-term durability. When folded, the drone is roughly the size of a large smartphone, though about three times as thick.

The Vision Goggles: These are sleek, lightweight, and feature dual 4K micro-OLED displays with a 120Hz refresh rate. The latency is nearly non-existent and they have integrated head tracking. Because the drone is recording in 360 degrees, you aren’t limited to seeing what is in front of the drone. When you turn your head to the left, the goggle feed pans to the left. If you look down, you see the ground passing beneath you. This provides a sense of presence and spatial awareness that is simply impossible with a traditional fixed-camera drone.

The drone uses a single-handed motion controller. You point the controller where you want to go and pull the trigger to accelerate. Tilt your wrist left to bank, or raise the nose of the controller to climb. It is an incredibly intuitive system that allows even a novice to fly through complex environments within minutes. For professional FPV pilots who prefer the precision of manual acrobatic flight, the A1 does support a traditional “Mode 2” stick controller, but the motion controls are so fluid that most users will likely never switch back.

The marketing for the Antigravity 360 proudly displays “8K Resolution.” In a traditional camera, 8K means every pixel is packed into a 16:9 rectangle. In 360 video, those pixels are spread across a full sphere. When you “reframe” that 8K sphere into a standard flat video, you are looking at a “crop” of the total image.

The color science is noticeably improved over previous 360 cameras. The A1 features a “Vivid” profile for those who want punchy, social-media-ready colors, and a 10-bit “Log” profile for professional editors who need to match the footage to other cameras in a color-grading suite. The stabilization, powered by Antigravity’s “FlowState” algorithms, is nothing short of miraculous. You can fly in 20mph winds, and the footage remains as steady as if the camera were on a tripod.

The “Antigravity Studio” app allows you to download footage wirelessly (at speeds up to 80MB/s) and reframe your video using your phone’s gyroscope. You simply watch the video and move your phone around to “film” the scene in real-time. The app also features “Auto-Frame,” an AI tool that identifies subjects and automatically generates a cut that keeps them in focus. For a solo creator, this effectively provides a virtual camera crew that never misses a shot.

Battery technology remains the bottleneck for all small drones. The A1’s standard Intelligent Flight Battery provides a theoretical 24 minutes of flight. In real-world conditions with moderate wind and constant recording, expect closer to 19 or 20 minutes.

While 20 minutes sounds short, the “work per minute” is much higher than a traditional drone. Because you don’t need to re-fly a path to get different angles, a single 20-minute flight can yield the same amount of usable footage as three flights with a Mavic. For those who need more time, the “Pro Battery” (which pushes the weight over 250g) offers a staggering 39 minutes of flight time, though it does compromise the drone’s agility slightly.

In terms of flight dynamics, the A1 is a “cinewhoop” style flyer. It is stable and predictable rather than aggressive and twitchy. It has a top speed of roughly 36 mph, which is plenty for following bikes or cars, but it won’t keep up with a professional racing drone. The “Turtle Mode” is a life-saver; if you crash and end up upside down, the drone can flip itself over using its propellers, allowing you to take off again without a “walk of shame” to recover the aircraft.

The Antigravity 360 is a niche product that is rapidly becoming mainstream.

The Antigravity 360 (A1) is the most exciting drone I have tested. By removing the need for a gimbal and the stress of manual framing, it allows the pilot to focus on the one thing that truly matters: the story they are trying to tell.

While the image quality isn’t quite at the level of a high-end cinema drone, and the lenses are admittedly delicate, these are small prices to pay for the creative liberation the A1 provides. It bridges the gap between traditional cinematography and the immersive world of VR.

If you are a creator who is tired of the same old “drone shots” and want to push the boundaries of what is possible in the air, the Antigravity 360 is an essential addition to your toolkit.

#3048. Science Activity Ideas for Chinese New Year

Chinese New Year marks the start of the New Year based on the lunisolar calendar, which falls on the first new moon between 21st January and 20th February. It’s a chance to celebrate the move from Winter to Spring and involves family reunions, decorations often with a red theme, gifts, dragon dances and fireworks. The celebrations begin with the new moon and end 15 days later with the full moon.

Each year is associated with one of 12 Zodiac animals, which are a fantastic source of inspiration for science activities.

I’ve created a science activity themed to each animal. You can print a single activity, or the whole pack is available at the bottom of the page.

If you’d rather kids’ crafts for Chinese New Year, Red Ted Art has some fantastic ideas!

Horses are four legged mammals, with a long mane and tail. They are fast and strong with large hearts and powerful muscles.

This walking horse is a brilliant low-cost science activity that requires only paper, scissors and something to make a ramp from. The horses can be a bit fiddly at first, but they are worth the effort.

Cut the small triangles from the bottom of each leg, then cut up the legs, stopping at the middle section.

Bend the four legs down and fold the tail upwards.

Fold up the neck and again at the top to make a head.

Set up a ramp from a stack of books and thick cardboard, and place the horse at the top.

If it doesn’t move, gently push the legs until it starts walking.

When the horse is at the top of the ramp, it has potential energy due to its height. As it moves, this is converted into kinetic energy.

The small triangles you cut at the bottom of the horse’s legs make it slightly unstable, so it rocks from side to side when gently pushed. As the horse rocks onto one leg, the other legs are lifted up, as it is on an incline, gravity pulls the lifted legs forward.

Goats are well known for their climbing and balancing skills. Several features help them achieve their gravity defying skills.

Cut a small piece of carrot and insert a wooden skewer approximately 2 inches long into the bottom. Most of the skewer should be outside the carrot.

Place the skewer on the top of the bottle, it will fall over.

Push the pointed end of two skewers into opposite sides of the carrot, and push a marshmallow onto the end of both.

Place the carrot onto the bottle lid. It should now balance!

Add two more marshmallow skewers to the carrot and see if it still balances.

Experiment by moving the marshmallows up and down the skewers.

The carrot ( goat ) stays balanced when its centre of mass is directly above the skewer. Gravity pulls downwards, and if the centre of mass isn’t lined up over the skewer at the bottom, it creates a turning force that tips the carrot over.

Adding skewers and play dough changes the centre of mass of the carrot. By adjusting the skewers and play dough bit by bit, you bring the centre of mass back over the bottle and the skewer at the bottom, keeping the carrot balanced.

Have you ever wondered how monkeys swing through trees so effortlessly? Monkeys are natural acrobats with exceptional dexterity, making them a great animal to learn about through a fun science activity.

This balancing monkey challenge is great for learning about Centre of Mass. For a monkey to balance on a tree branch, its Centre of Mass needs to be under the branch. Monkeys use their tails to help them balance in the trees. Adjusting the position of their tails helps monkeys shift their centre of mass, making it easier to balance as they swing through the trees.

Cut out the monkey shape from the template below (or draw your own) and try to balance it on your finger. The monkey will fall over.

Place 2 paperclips or a coin on the bottom of the arms and try again. The monkey should balance.

Add an extra paperclip and watch what happens.

Extension challenge: try other small objects instead of paperclips. A small coin or Play-Doh also works well.

Roosters are famous for the crowing noise they make in the morning! They have an excellent internal biological clock, which means they Cock-a-doodle-do at the same time every morning.

A rooster’s crow can reach 130 decibels, which is about as loud as a jet taking off! To prevent hearing damage, roosters have a clever built-in earplug. When they open their beak to crow a flap of soft tissue partially covers their eardrum to protect it!

This simple sound activity using a paper cup demonstrates how sound can be amplified.

Thread the ribbon through the hole and tie a small knot at the end. The ribbon should be about 30 cm longer than the end of the cup.

Attach the paperclip to the ribbon so it rests on the bottom of the cup.

Fold the paper towel around the ribbon and pull it down!

The cup acts like a soundboard. Try rubbing the paper towel down the ribbon without the cup attached. There’s no noise. The cup amplifies the vibrations created by the movement of the paper towel down the ribbon, making a louder noise than you’d get without the cup.

A dog’s sense of smell is around 10,000 times better than a human’s! This simple activity tests your sense of smell as you hunt for scents around a room.

4 foods with a strong smell or flavoured essences, eg, vanilla extract, peppermint extract, garlic, ginger

Place either a cotton wool ball with flavoured essence or a strong smelling food into each cup.

Hide the cups one at a time around a room and ask a friend to try to find them.

If it’s too easy, cover the cups with foil and try again.

Things that smell give off tiny smell particles that float around the air. You smell these when they reach your nose! Dogs have superpowered smelling power partly because they have cold, wet noses that the smell particles can attach to more easily than a warm, dry nose!

Pigs are smart, have great long-term memories, can eat almost anything, and are surprisingly athletic thanks to lots of clever adaptations! In this activity, you’re going to learn about the incredible features of pigs that make them special.

Pigs roll in mud to cool themselves. Mud dries and holds onto the water, which then evaporates slowly, providing a long lasting cooling effect for the pig.

Pigs have an excellent sense of smell that allows them to detect food buried in the ground!

Pig snouts are prehensile (they can move and feel), allowing them to move objects out of the way with their noses!

Pigs have a layer of subcutaneous fat that helps keep them warm because they don’t have much fur.

Pigs have a good long-term memory. They can remember where food is hidden months later!

Pigs have very large lungs for their body size, allowing them to move quickly for short periods of time.

Pigs can eat roots, fruit, grains, vegetables, dairy, and eggs. They are omnivorous foragers with a tough digestive system.

Pigs have cloven hooves, meaning they have two toes split down the middle instead of a single solid hoof. When walking in soft mud, pigs can split their toes, which increases the surface area of their hooves, spreading the pig’s weight over a larger area and helping it avoid sinking in wet mud.

Put your new pig knowledge to the test with this fun challenge to design a superpowered pig!

Rats are agile, social and smart animals with a great memory and amazing vibration sensing abilities.

In this activity, we’re going to pretend to be rats and identify objects without using our eyes.

Rats rely more on their whiskers than their eyes and use them to identify the shape, texture and location of objects in the dark.

A whisker is more than just a hair. It grows from a follicle that is sealed by a capsule of blood, called a blood sinus. When a whisker touches something, it bends and pushes against the sinus, which triggers nerves that send a message to the brain. The rat uses information from its whiskers to identify and locate objects.

The idea behind this activity is to use a pipe cleaner (a pretend whisker) to identify objects you can’t see in a box.

Whiskers are so sensitive that they can detect very small changes in air currents and surface textures.

Try to identify the different objects in the box using only a pipe cleaner or a toothbrush.

An Ox is a cow that has been trained to work, usually pulling heavy loads. Oxen are most often male and over 4 years old.

Like all cattle, Oxen have four separate compartments in their stomach that allow them to break down tough, fibrous grass for energy.

Rumen – like a huge storage tank where bacteria start to break down tough fibres.

Reticulum – filters out anything the animal shouldn’t have eaten.

Omasum – a series of folds that squeezes water out of the food.

Abomasum – acids and enzymes continue to break down the food, ready for the intestines.

Ruminant animals also regurgitate food. After its first trip into the rumen and reticulum, it’s regurgitated back up to the mouth to be chewed and swallowed again and again until it’s small enough to digest!

The rumen is like a huge tank where microbes break down tough plant fibres by a process called fermentation. Methane and carbon dioxide are produced during this process. We’ve used yeast to represent the microbes in the Ox’s stomach.

Pour the yeast and sugar into the empty plastic bottle.

Fill the bottle about halfway with warm water, then quickly place the balloon on top.

You should see the balloon start to blow up.

The yeast in the bottle breaks down the sugar, releasing carbon dioxide, just as microbes in the rumen break down plant fibres.

As an extension task, you can try bicarbonate of soda instead of yeast!

Tigers are the largest of the wild cats, they have 100 cm long tails, 7 cm teeth, and can be 4m long from nose to tail!. Tigers are strong, powerful predators who hunt alone. They have thick necks and strong jaws, making them exceptional hunters capable of killing animals much bigger than themselves.

Sadly, tigers have been overhunted for a long time, and their population has declined as humans have encroached on their habitat.

Each tiger has a unique stripe pattern, with orange fur and dark stripes.

Tigers are Apex Predators, which means they are at the top of the food chain. There are 6 subspecies of tiger, based on where they live and slightly different characteristics. The most common type of tiger is the Bengal Tiger, which makes up about half of all wild tigers.

Imagine what would happen if you removed the tigers from the chain. The population of primary consumers would increase, leading them to eat more plants and potentially destabilising the ecosystem.

Print the sheet below and cut out the images. Use them to create a food chain for tigers living in the glasslands and another for tigers living in the wetlands.

Rabbits are small, social mammals with long ears, soft fur, and fluffy tails. Domesticated rabbits are kept as pets, but rabbits are also found in the wild. Rabbits mostly eat grasses, but are also known for eating their own poo! This allows them to digest nutrients they didn’t digest the first time around! One rabbit can have 50 offspring in a single year!

Rabbits are also known for their distinctive hop. They can quickly jump through the air, thanks to their powerful hind legs and strong leg muscles.

Rabbits have very strong, long hind legs, which are the main reason they can jump so high and so far. They also have light, hollow bones, which allow them to jump with almost explosive power.

This activity shows how a rabbit’s hind leg is like a lever, allowing it to jump high without too much effort.

Place the ruler on a table with about 5 cm hanging over the edge. Place a pom-pom on the edge farthest from the table, then push it down. The pom pom will fly into the air.

This time, move the ruler so that  10cm hangs off the edge. Measure how far the pom pom flies. The longer the lever (rabbit’s leg ), the further the pom pom ( rabbit ) will jump!

The longer the lever arm, the further the pom pom flies. Levers make work easier. In this case, the longer the rabbit’s foot, the easier it is to lift the rabbit off the ground.

Snakes are incredible hunters, amazing eaters, and great at disguising themselves! They are cold-blooded, scaly creatures found in most parts of the world. Snakes can unhinge their jaws, which allows them to swallow animals bigger than themselves whole!

The longest snake in the world is the reticulated python, which can exceed 6.25 metres! Reticulated pythons are found in Southeast Asia. They are non-venomous and can climb trees!  In contrast, the smallest snake in the world is the Barbados threadsnake, which is a tiny 10cm long!

This activity uses household objects (and hands and feet) to demonstrate the length of a reticulated python. It can also be adjusted for other snakes.

Measure the length of your building block or other small object in cm or inches if you prefer. Divide the length of a python, 625cm, by the length of the building block to work out how many blocks are the same size as a python.

Measure 625 cm on the ground and mark with chalk. Walk from the start to the end point and count how many of your feet long a reticulated python is.

Measure your height in cm and work out how many of you are the same length as a python.

Dragons are fictional animals usually depicted as large, powerful dinosaurs or lizards with four legs, a long tail, and wings. They are famous for breathing fire and often live in the mountains.

If dragons were real animals, they would most likely be cold-blooded reptiles who hatch from eggs and sit at the top of the food chain!

For a dragon to have any hope of flying, it would need strong, but lightweight bones. Birds have hollow bones filled with air sacs connected to their respiratory system, which provides a constant supply of oxygen needed for energy, allowing them to fly!

This easy science activity demonstrates how strong a hollow tube can be!

Add books to the top of the paper plate until the columns collapse.

Try this again, but with paper columns folded into triangles and squares.

You should find that the circle shaped columns can hold the most books without collapsing.

Iâll be honestâwhen I first heard about via ferratas on my buddy Jason’s Zero to Travel podcast, I had to do one. Little did I know that there was a via ferrata in the Sacred Valley of Peru, south of Cusco, where I was about to spend a few weeks. Done and done!

This was my first ever via ferrata, and the idea of hanging on steel cables over Peruâs epic cliffs sounded equal parts thrilling and slightly deranged, but I never had a doubt it might be a life-changing new adventure.

This site participates in the Amazon Services LLC Associates Program and other affiliate programs and may earn from qualifying purchases.

This via ferrata immediately quickly became one of my favorite things to do Sacred Valleyâa half-day adventure packed with adrenaline, mountain air, and jaw-dropping views.

And there was plenty else I did during my time in Peruâlike exploring the Ollantaytambo Ruins, hiking the Pisac Ruins in the rain, hitting 16,500ft at Rainbow Mountain, and the Maras Salt Mines and Moray.

If youâre an adventure traveler, a DIY explorer, or just someone looking to push your comfort zone, this via feratta is a must-do activity thatâll have you grinning all the way back on the break-neck roads back to Cusco.

If you’re a seasoned via ferrata climber, this “first-time” guide probably isn’t for you. But if the above gets you stoked, read on and let me know how your first via ferrata goes!

Without further ado, here’s your complete guide to what to expect if you do sign up for this epic half-day tour from Cusco, Peru!

For this half-day adventure you’ll get picked up in Cusco, where transportation to the Sacred Valley is included, much like most day tours from Cusco Peru.

After about an hour and a half of driving through the sometimes-nauseating roads of the Andes, youâll reach the base of the cliff. Your heart rate will probably spike a little when you spot the tiny ladders stretching up the first ascent.

Side note…don’t forget to always, always, always consider getting inexpensive travel medical insurance âsometimes as low as $2/dayâfor your trip, and a separate yearly evacuation insurance policy if you travel internationally often! And check out my list of tips for staying safe while traveling abroad.

Before you even touch the rock, your guides walk you through every piece of via ferrata equipment: the full-body harness, helmet, gloves, and the all-important lanyard system with two locking carabiners and an energy dissipator.

Itâs the safety system that keeps you safely attached to the steel cables at all times…assuming you do what you’re told during the instruction!

If youâre wondering, âIs via ferrata safe?â the answer is *generally *yesâwhen done with professional instruction and proper gear. Youâre always connected to the cable by at least one carabiner, so even if you miss a step, you wonât go anywhere but into your harness after a short fall. Are injuries during this via ferrata possible? Of course, but if you listen to and follow instructions, any missteps should cause minimal damage, lol.

After a quick safety talk and practice run, itâs time to hike about 100ft up to the wall, clip in and start the climb.

The first step is literally a 10-15ft metal ladder straight up the rock wall. Quite the introduction!

From there, steel rungs are set into the rock face itself, and within minutes youâre a few stories off the ground, realizing how different âstepsâ feel when theyâre bolted into a cliff. Oh, and wait til you step on one that’s just a* little loose.* Good times!

This first vertical section of the via ferrata Cusco climb gets your adrenaline pumping right away.

All-in-all during the via ferrata you’ll ascend over 300 vertical meters!

The ladders and steel rebar steps are surprisingly sturdy, but the exposureâthose vast drop-offs belowâwill make you very aware of your every move.

Each step upward rewards you with better and better views of the Sacred Valley: terraced farmlands below, jagged peaks in the distance, and the river snaking through it all. Your via ferrata guide will be along for the entire journey. We had 5 people on ours.

Thanks to my new friends from France and Australia for taking pics of me along the way!

Once youâve conquered the first climb, youâll start a horizontal traverse that lets you breathe a little easier. Youâre still clipped in, of course, but now youâre moving sideways across the cliff, sometimes with your feet on small rock ledges and other times on steel steps drilled into the wall.

Then comes the rope bridgeâtwo parallel cables strung across an airy gap between rock faces. Your feet walk the lower cable while your hands balance on the upper one. Itâs a mental game of focus and trust, but crossing it is pure fun.

Pause in the center for a few seconds like I did and take in the view of the gorgeous Sacred Valley below. You’ve earned it!

After the rope bridge, youâll face another vertical pushâthis time even higher than the first. Itâs around this point where the wind picks up and youâre grateful for the early start, since the wind picks up as the day rolls on. Just look at the trees along the river leaning sideways for proof!

Pro tip: do this via ferrata as early in the morning as possible. The cliff face sits in shade until late morning, which means cooler temperatures and far less sweat while youâre working those quads.

The climb is steady and well-paced, with plenty of spots to rest, drink water, and take in the landscape and plenty of pictures. Remember to bring plenty of water or hydration and a small backpack with layers, since the higher you go, the chillier it gets especially in the shade.

And this via ferrata is rain or shine, so be ready for any elements Pachamama might throw at you.

Once you top out on the cliff, youâll traverse again along the rock to reach the zipline platforms. This section is more relaxedâyour arms get a break, and your adrenaline starts to shift from climbing mode to âholy crap, Iâm about to flyâ mode.

You’ll also stop for a minimal but welcome bagged lunch, with plenty of time to chat it up with new friends and take in the Sacred Valley views.

The zipline portion is just as epic as the climb. There are six in total, ranging from shorter warm-ups to one run over 700 meters long, with another clocking at around 500 meters long. The speed, the view, the sensation of floating for over 35 seconds on the longest run is truly epic. Plenty of time to look around and take it all in!

Between each line, your via ferrata guides handle all the setup and safety checks, making sure youâre clipped and ready to go. Itâs the perfect payoff after all that vertical effort. By the time you land on the final platform, if you’re like me, youâll be wondering whether you can bribe the guides for another run at the entire route again!

The Sacred Valley has a distinct dry and wet season. The best time for this via ferrata tour is during the dry months, roughly April through October. Youâll get clear skies and minimal rain, though temperatures can swing dramatically between morning and afternoon.

I did this via ferrata in early October. While we dodged a couple raindrops, it was nearly perfect weather in the valley.

Mornings are bestâhands down. The cliff stays shaded early, so youâll climb in cooler conditions and avoid the intense midday sun. Even during the dry season, the wind can pick up at higher altitudes, so layers are your friend.

If you visit during the rainy season (November to March), plan accordingly since the Sacred Valley and Cusco get* a lot* of rain in their rainy season!

Safety is the backbone of any via ferrata, and this oneâs no different. Via ferrata equipmentâfrom the harness to the helmet to the dual carabiner lanyardâis designed to keep climbers (…you) secure even on steep verticals.

#3050. How to Reset & Get Ready for SSD

Spring is around the corner, which means it’s time to refresh, reset, and get ready to feel strong, sculpted, and confident just in time for summer! Let’s not spend another year wishing we had put in the work to feel amazing on vacation. Instead, let’s start now and make those goals a reality!

The Spring Slim Down Challenge is your ultimate reset—designed to help you banish bloat, tone up, and feel your absolute best in just 8 weeks.

Whether you’re looking to tighten up before bikini season or simply want to build stronger habits, SSD is your chance to sculpt, sweat, and SLIM DOWN!

How to Reset & Get Ready for SSD

If you want to maximize your results, a little preparation goes a long way. Follow these simple steps to get your body, mind, and kitchen ready before SSD officially kicks off on March 10th!

1. Detox & Debloat

Start fresh by hydrating and cutting back on foods that cause bloating. Drink at least 80 oz of water per day, add lemon to your water for digestion support, and focus on whole, unprocessed foods. 

2. Set Your Goals

What do you want to achieve during SSD? More energy? A toned waist? Better consistency with workouts? Write your goals down and be specific—having a clear vision makes all the difference in staying motivated!

3. Clean Out Your Kitchen

Your environment plays a huge role in your success. Ditch the processed snacks and stock up on nutrient-dense, whole foods like lean protein, fresh produce, and healthy fats. When you have the right foods on hand, making smart choices becomes effortless!

Grab the Slim Down Nutrition Plan so you can meal prep and get ready for healthy, high protein, and delicious meals!

4. Move Every Day

Even before SSD starts, get in the habit of daily movement—whether it’s a 10-minute stretch, a walk outside, or a Sweat Sesh. The goal is to build momentum so you’re ready to crush the challenge from day one! Join our MOVE app & get 7 Days FREE if you are NEW!

5. Get Your Mind Right

Your mindset is everything. Visualize how you want to look and feel by the end of SSD. Imagine yourself feeling strong, confident, and radiant in your favorite bikini on the beach! When you see it, you believe it—and that belief will fuel your motivation and success.

You Deserve to Feel Your Best!

Don’t let another summer pass by wishing you had started sooner. This is your time to SLIM DOWN! The Spring Slim Down Challenge will give you the tools, motivation, and community support to help you sculpt your body, boost your confidence, and feel incredible from the inside out.

Join us for our Spring Slim Down Challenge and make this your strongest, most confident Summer yet!

#3052. Burnham to reveal plans for AI unit to tackle wildfires after scorching summer

PM will also announce funding for specialised protective gear and the deployment of military aircraft

The UK government is to create an AI Cobra unit to spot wildfires after this year’s record-breaking summer saw devastating blazes across the country.

The country experienced its hottest-ever summer this year, with prolonged dry periods and extreme heat fuelling wildfires that triggered an emergency alert to mobile phones in England and Wales. Figures released on 8 October showed a clear upward trend in the number of fires recorded each year.

The Met Office found that the climate crisis made this extreme heat about 130 times more likely.

At the government’s first wildfire resilience summit on Friday, Andy Burnham will announce plans for a new wildfire AI unit in the National Situation Centre, which is part of the Cobra briefing rooms.

Businesses including Google, Airbus and VodafoneThree are expected to attend the summit to set out how satellite monitoring and early warning systems can help fight fires. The government said its new AI unit would enable it to “spot and fight fires faster”.

The prime minister will also announce £45m for fire crews to buy wildfire-specific personal protective equipment (PPE).

This comes after the Guardian revealed that more than half of the 29 fire services that responded to requests for information had no wildfire PPE.

They included the Suffolk fire and rescue service, which had to deal with an “apocalyptic” wildfire earlier this summer that burned close to the Sizewell B nuclear power station and destroyed vast areas of a protected nature reserve.

Standard particle-filtering respirators do not protect against dangerous gases such as carbon monoxide, which are heavily present in wildfire smoke.

Standard PPE can also be too hot and heavy for wildfire conditions. This can cause crews to overheat, or remove their PPE altogether, exposing them to greater danger from heat, smoke and radiation.

The prime minister will also announce that military planes and helicopters will be made available to fight wildfires on remote moorland, steep hillsides and other hard-to-reach terrain.

The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said: “As the threat of wildfires in the UK grows, defence will step up to provide greater support to our emergency services and protect military training areas across the country.”

The government will also look at tougher local restrictions or product bans to stop people starting fires when the risk is high. In August, Burnham announced a temporary ban on sales of disposable barbecues. He has also been criticised for failing to address the climate emergency in his wildfire response.

Farmers will also be given funding to make landscapes more resilient to fires. This announcement comes after the government quietly scrapped plans announced under the Conservative government to prepare the countryside in England for wildfires.

This revelation led Alistair Carmichael, a Scottish Liberal Democrat MP and chair of the Commons environment, food and rural affairs committee, to raise “serious questions about whether this summer’s wildfires could have looked different with more resources on the ground”.

The government also said it would allocate £25m to restore dried-out peatlands in England so they hold more water and act as natural firebreaks, as well as provide financial support for farmers to fireproof their land.

This new grant scheme is expected to run from April 2027 to April 2029.

Environmental campaigner and author Guy Shrubsole said: “For decades, wealthy grouse moor owners have drained our peat bogs, turning them into a tinderbox. This grant will help reverse that destruction, but must be followed by a new round of landscape recovery funding, and duties on landowners to repair the damage done. It’s time to make England wet again.”

The prime minister said: “I stood in Stourbridge and watched families lose everything. I will never forget it. Our firefighters were heroes that day, but heroes shouldn’t have to fight with one hand tied behind their backs.

“Crews will now have the kit they need to stay safe and military aircraft will stand ready to help tackle wildfires from the sky. We cannot put people through another summer like this one.”

#3053. The Golden Rules of Airplane Etiquette—Because We Have Simply Seen Enough

It is my firm belief that everyone—no matter their age, gender, race, or Delta SkyMiles Medallion Status—needs to learn proper airplane etiquette, and the earlier the better. As a freelance travel writer, I get on lots of flights to and from different parts of the world, and I’ve seen the same silly mistakes, rude behavior, and even downright harmful stunts enacted by all types of travelers. But by that same token, I’ve also witnessed acts of generosity and helpfulness that all people universally appreciate.

So what, exactly, are the rules at 35,000 feet? To draft such a constitution, I tapped three of Condé Nast Traveler’s Top Travel Specialists who are experts in air travel, in addition to my own first-hand experience: Sophie Caulcutt, co-founder of The Voyager Club; Vikram Seshadri, co-founder of In Residence; and Paul Tumpowsky, chief revenue officer of Fora. And to get the real insider take on how we should behave in the air, I spoke with two working flight attendants: Rich Henderson, a flight attendant for a US-based airline and co-host of the podcast Two Guys on A Plane; and a US-based flight attendant and content creator (@lifeinlayovers on TikTok) named Liam.

In general, we agreed that there’s no environment where etiquette (or the lack thereof) matters more than when you’re sitting shoulder-to-shoulder with dozens of other seatbelt-strapped passengers inside a metal tube hurling through the skies. And while commercial air travel may not always be kind to us, we can choose to be part of the solution. As Tumpowsky of Fora pleads,: “Perhaps we can look inside ourselves to make the overall traveling experience better for us and our fellow travelers.”

In the spirit of doing unto others as we would have them do unto us, below are the golden rules of airplane etiquette. Keep these principles and good habits in mind, and you’ll find that, even when everyone else around you is behaving badly, you’ll feel all the better for being a kind and considerate traveler. A true professional, some may even go so far to say.

Among travelers, especially those seated in economy, no one is dying to spend more time on the plane than they have to. So instead of crowding the gate—a rookie move that will earn you the unattractive nickname of “gate lice”—be patient and wait to board last. Your assigned seat will still be there at the end of boarding. (After all, a queen is never late. Everyone else is simply early.)

Jostling to get on board early to secure overhead bin space? The crew will almost always find a spot, even if it’s not directly above your seat; or they’ll check your bag into the hold at no extra cost. To mitigate the inconvenience, pack light and put together your “seat bag” so you have all your essentials (more on these points below).

Are you flying in business or first class? Fabulous. “Linger in the lounge, enjoy the restaurant, and board last,” says Seshadri of In Residence. “Your overhead bin space is dedicated and waiting for you.”

For parents traveling with kids, you might actually want to be among the last passengers to board. “Why spend an extra 30 or 40 minutes sitting on a plane with young children if you don’t have to?” Tumpowsky says. “But I completely understand why new parents, in particular, may want to board early to make sure they have enough storage within reach for everything they’ll need during a long flight.”

Make your personal item count: Before getting on the plane, prepare a “seat bag” that contains all your in-flight must-haves and keep it close to you in your seat. For me, that’s usually my fanny pack with my passport, boarding pass, phone, AirPods, eye mask, lip balm, hand cream, phone charger, and battery pack. Maybe my Kindle or a copy of The New Yorker; a toothbrush and toothpaste for overnight flights. This will eliminate or reduce the need to rummage through the bag under the seat in front of you, or step out into the aisle to reach for your luggage in the overhead bins.

Turns out, doing this is also helpful for the people around you, according to Henderson of Two Guys on a Plane: “Boarding is basically a giant traffic jam, and one person standing in the aisle reorganizing their entire suitcase can hold up a hundred people behind them. Have what you need for the flight ready before you board, find your seat, put your bag away, and step out of the aisle as quickly as possible.”

First off, acknowledge the flight attendants when you board with eye contact, a smile, a quick hello. These are the people here to make sure you stay safe on the plane and everything goes smoothly, first and foremost. Be a good human and treat them with the dignity they deserve, and you’ll get the same treatment in kind. At the end of the flight, do the same thing and thank the crew—you all made it!

Next, carry-on bags. People tend to overpack heavy carry-on bags because most US airlines do not weigh them, explains Liam of @lifeinlayovers, so boarding becomes even more hectic and slow when you can’t lift your own stuff into the overhead bins. Try to pack only what you can literally carry. Consider too your own physical abilities, height, and strength, and pack accordingly. And if you see someone struggling with putting away their carry-ons and you can help, do so. It helps everyone out, and makes the boarding process go more smoothly. The flight attendants will thank you. Speaking of: Note that many airlines discourage flight attendants from helping with your overhead luggage because of the risk of injury, says Henderson, so don’t expect that every FA can or will lend you a hand.

While we’re on the topic of overhead bins, Henderson says, “Please don’t put your small purse or jacket in the overhead bin when people are still looking for space for their actual suitcases.” Save putting them away in the overhead space until boarding is mostly complete; there will always be space on the plane for your stuff, Liam says.

As for deboarding the plane, a few more best practices: Do not get into the aisle while the plane is still taxiing to the gate. Once the plane comes to a complete stop, that’s when deboarding can begin. Wait for the rows in front of you to get up and head to the exit, rather than scrambling to snatch your items from the overhead bins and just crowding the aisle. As space opens up in the aisle, that’s when you stand up, get your bags, and exit.

It’s possible someone behind you will react exasperated, believing you should have gotten your stuff earlier—when there was no room to do so. If that happens, give them a smile (or a sly wink, if you’re feeling cheeky), and retrieve your luggage calmly, knowing that you’re in the right.

When you’re transiting and have limited time to get from Flight A to Flight B, kindly inform a flight attendant prior to landing. “I believe the appropriate protocol is to speak with a flight attendant rather than attempt to negotiate your way to the front of the aircraft,” Tumpowsky says. “The crew can assess just how tight your connection really is, determine whether special consideration is warranted, and, if appropriate, make an announcement asking other passengers to remain seated. That request carries considerably more authority coming from the flight crew than from a passenger who has decided that their connection is more important than everyone else’s.”

Caulcutt of The Voyager Club agrees, saying that the crew may even consider it essential to move your seat closer to the exit—or at least closer to the aisle—if your connection is extremely tight or if they anticipate a delayed arrival. When approaching the crew, Caulcutt says, “I often find that a trip to the galley, during boarding or shortly after, to politely explain the situation one-on-one works best.”

My seat, my choice! When we select our seats on a plane, especially when we pay to get assigned places or use status benefits to do so, we are well within our rights to keep it. Able-bodied spouses, families, and friends can reunite after the flight. You can politely and firmly refuse to swap. (Exercise caution if using the correct but risky phrase: “Your lack of planning is not my problem.”)

“But just apply common sense,” says Caulcutt. “You don't want to separate an elderly couple,” who may physically need each other for assistance, or “a mother from a weeping child.” Because did you really want to sit next to that wailing five year old anyway? Swap with the parent who can calm them down.

Some of us love making friends wherever we go, but when you’re going to be stuck on a plane with hundreds of other people in a steel projectile hurtling through the air, the rules of social engagement get a touch more delicate. So what’s acceptable, and where do you draw the line?

“A brief conversation and a little cordiality are perfectly appropriate,” says Tumpowsky. It’s not a bad idea, though by no means required, to establish some rapport with those around you—but don’t force anything. “If your seatmate engages and the feeling is mutual, by all means, enjoy the conversation,” Tumpowsky continues. “But no one should feel obligated to continue a conversation longer than they're comfortable with. A polite exchange of pleasantries is not a binding commitment to discuss your respective life stories until the landing gear is employed.”

If you’re traveling with a friend or friends and you’re all prone to yapping, keep a few things in mind: “Keep the tone of the conversation low,” says Caulcutt. “People in planes tend to talk louder than they realize because of engine noise. Try to keep your voice at a level that your seatmate can hear comfortably but the rows around you can’t easily follow.” Try to keep topics light and disagreements to a minimum, she adds. If you get into a fight, you won’t have much room to put some distance between you on a plane.

And on night or red-eye flights, the lights in the cabin are usually dimmed and people are trying to sleep, Caulcutt says, so keep conversations to a whisper whenever possible. Otherwise, save them for later on the ground.

Be patient, and take deep breaths. “No one hates it more than the parents,” says Caulcutt. Period!

OK, well, it really is for our own safety in the air. As Henderson says, “I promise we flight attendants are not doing the safety demonstration for our own entertainment!” Do as advised and check where your nearest exits are; and see where the closest bathroom is, while you’re at it. Brush up on the brace position appropriate for the cabin you’re in. Enjoy the safety video, if there is one (the Philippine Airlines “Safetynovela,” depicted as a soap opera, is my current favorite). If the FAs are doing a live demo, give them your attention and a smile.

This is all the more important when you’re seated in an exit row. When the FAs check in with you about the responsibilities you have in the case of an emergency, answer truthfully regarding whether or not you're physically, mentally, or even spiritually able to carry out what needs to be done. This is the cost of the exit-row legroom. (Also, the exit-row legroom comes with the price of not being able to stow luggage in front of you, as there’s no seat to keep them under, so bear that in mind when picking your place on the plane.)

The fasten-your-seatbelt sign is not a suggestion. “Turbulence can happen without warning, even when the sky looks perfectly clear,” Henderson says. Liam explains that the flight deck turns on the sign when there's a forecast of bad weather up ahead, either from radar or aircraft ahead of the plane you’re on. So keep your belt fastened whenever you’re seated, Seshadri says, “even if loosely! You’ll never regret it.”

All our experts and FAs agree that reclining your seat is fair game. That’s what it’s there for. As Tumpowsky says, “Whether it’s the overhead light, window shade, or reclining, I generally believe you have the right to use the product as it was designed.” And everyone is also on the same page when it comes to meal time: Don’t do it while the person behind you is eating. It’s just good manners.

“A little courtesy goes a long way,” Seshadri says. “Recline slowly, be mindful if the person behind you is using it—like working on a laptop—and put your seat upright when the crew asks, especially for takeoff and landing.” On a plane, as in life: Be considerate of others.

This is another point on which all our experts were in agreement. The flight attendant call button is absolutely there to be used, especially if you need assistance, have a medical concern, or there’s something that requires a crew member’s attention—like if your phone fell into the cracks of the seat. (A very real concern! If the machinery ends up cracking your phone and the battery leaks, it could be a fire hazard.)

“But if the FAs are visibly in the middle of beverage service and you just want another soda, it’s usually easier to ask us when we reach your row,” Henderson says. And don’t use the button to summon them every five minutes for things that can wait. There are sometimes hundreds of other passengers and only a few of them. Liam says, “Staffing has decreased and cabins have expanded. Please be patient with us, especially when we’re busy with service or there’s turbulence.”

Again, among our experts, this is a universally acknowledged truth: “The middle seat passenger deserves both middle armrests,” Henderson says. After all, the window passenger gets the window, and the aisle passenger gets a little extra breathing room. “The poor person in the middle deserves something!” he says. (Liam agrees: “As someone who often gets the middle seat when flying standby on benefits, please, for the love of all things good, give me both middle armrests.”)

“No bare feet on display ever!” Caulcutt says. And rightly so. You can remove your shoes, especially on long-haul flights; our feet do swell in flight. Keep your socks on (try compression socks); swiftly and discreetly swap into a fresh pair if you’ve lost the ability to smell yourself. Do not ever prop your feet up on the armrests, seatbacks, or tray tables. (Quick trick: Use your backpack or duffel bag, under the seat in front of you, as a foot rest.)

Henderson’s advice: “Never walk into an airplane bathroom barefoot or even just in socks. That mysterious liquid on the floor is probably not water.” And Seshadri’s: “Please never clip your toenails or file them on a flight!”

For better or worse, Wi-Fi connectivity is getting better on planes, meaning that what often used to be a relatively quiet airborne sanctuary is now another space in which the cacophony of modern life can invade. So, again, don’t be a jerk about it.

Our experts agree that headphones and earbuds are a must, whether you’re listening to music, watching a movie on your own device, or scrolling through Instagram Reels. Do not take your high-level meeting from 35,000 feet in the air. “Voice and video calls are usually prohibited by airline policy or regulations,” Henderson says. “An airplane is a shared space, not your personal living room or office.”

Expect these principles to be sticking points in the coming years. “High-bandwidth internet—and potentially the ability to make calls more easily in the air—is going to create the next battleground in flight etiquette,” Tumpowsky says. “Just because technology allows you to do something doesn’t necessarily mean 200 other passengers want you to do it.”

Alas, from personal experience, it has to be said! And think about your surroundings when you’re watching a movie and there’s a graphic scene in the story, whether sexual or otherwise. Consider speeding through if there are, say, children around. That said, it’s really up to you—especially if the movie or show in question is offered through the in-flight entertainment system. I was once on a flight watching an episode of And Just Like That… and they got to the infamous Snapple scene in Carrie’s apartment and, well, I didn’t skip it since I was pretty much alone in the business class cabin.

As long as you’re not doing a full-on downward dog in the aisle, Caulcutt says, stretching in the aisle is fine. Keep it quick and respectful. Do some standing spine twists, lymphatic taps, and gentle walking, then return to your seat. Don’t do it during meal service or when the FAs are working. If an FA tells you to return to your seat, don’t make a fuss and sit back down.

“We encourage passengers to get up and move around when it’s safe, especially on long flights, but the aisle is a workspace for flight attendants and an important pathway for everyone on board, especially in the event of an emergency where we must move quickly,” Henderson says. So don’t block the aisle, congregate around the bathrooms, or interfere with the crew doing their jobs. “A little stretching is one thing, but turning the plane into a yoga studio is another,” he says.

There’s nothing wrong with politely waking someone if you need to get out of your row to reach the toilet. Just be considerate (there it is again, basic kindness). Liam says, “I’d hate to be woken up after I’ve just gotten comfortable; for me, that’s having an eye mask and headphones on. Watch out for those signs. But if you have to go, you have to go.” Wake someone up the way you’d want to be woken: Respectfully.

The flip side is that if someone in your row gets up to use the bathroom and disturbs you, it might be a good opportunity for you to go as well. “Think of it as airplane efficiency,” Tumpowsky says. “You may save everyone another round of climbing over one another later in the flight.”

Whether they physically need to or not, many people allow their intrusive thoughts to win and grab the top of the seat in front of them to pull themselves up. This is awful and rude. If you really need support, Tumpowsky says, “the proper etiquette is to use your own row of seats for support whenever possible. Pulling on the seat in front of you can jolt the person sitting there—and if they’re sleeping, you’ve just unnecessarily woken them up.”

I was gonna say, “leave the bathroom the way you leave yours,” but the mileage may vary on that one. Keep the place tidy, wipe anything you made wet as a courtesy to the person who comes in after you, and dispose of any waste properly, as the laws of common decency intend. “Just because you don’t want to push down the flap to discard your trash doesn’t mean you can just start a pile of it on the ground or counter,” Liam says. “And for the love of aviation, wear shoes in there!” Henderson adds.

Maybe there was once a time, in a faraway land, when dressing nicely for a flight might have improved your chances of an upgrade. No longer. “Today, upgrades are much more likely to be determined by status, algorithms, bidding, or other systems, so I don’t think your wardrobe is moving you up the list,” Tumpowsky says. “Dress comfortably. Being comfortable will have a much bigger impact on your flight experience than looking like you belong in first class.”

You can do so comfortably! May I interest you in a cashmere jogger set or a wrinkle-free traveling suit? Figure out a travel uniform that works for you—something comfortable that also makes you feel put-together. It’s a proven fact (by me, anecdotally) that looking good helps you feel good, like you can handle any travel hiccup like flight delays or lost baggage with dignity and grace. But hey if it’s not your literal style, no one says you have to.

“Always be polite to the plane crew,” Caulcutt says. Flight attendants aren’t responsible for the weather, delays, baggage fees, or most airline policies, so don’t take your frustrations out on the people who are there to keep you safe and comfortable to the best of their abilities.

Patience and kindness can go a long way, Henderson says, and Seshadri reminds everyone to extend that respect to the airport staff and your fellow passengers. Moving with respect and courtesy, he says, “will earn you not just a better flight but a good dose of karma and happiness too.”

Yes, cabins are getting stuffed with more seats, and those seats are getting smaller, while crew staffing keeps getting cut. And yet, even in the face of all this, on top of everything going on in our world, we get to travel. So it’s more important than ever to cultivate a sense of solidarity as travelers. As Liam puts it, “We’re truly all in this metal tube together.”

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#3056. A London Scheme to Cut Car Pollution Restored Lung Growth in Children

A controversial scheme aimed at slashing car pollution in Central London was a boon to children in the area, whose lungs grew faster after the program was launched, researchers found.

Established in 2019, the Ultra Low Emission Zone initially covered around 8 square miles in Central London. To drive in the zone, owners of older, more polluting cars, buses, and trucks would have to pay a daily fee, equal to around $17 for most drivers, with fines for those who skirted the fee. The scheme led to a steep drop of nitrogen dioxide pollution, which is known to impede lung growth.

To study the impact on children, researchers followed more than 3,400 students, between the ages of 6 and 9, at schools in Central London and in the town of Luton, roughly 30 miles away. Between 2018 and 2022, they regularly measured the lung volume of each child.

Before the emissions scheme was introduced, researchers found, children in London had stunted lung growth. But within five years of the program’s launch, they saw a turnaround. While exposure to pollution fell in both Central London and Luton over that period, in Central London it fell by more than twice as much. And as pollution dropped, the lungs of the children in London grew faster, until they had caught up with children in Luton.

The findings have significant health implications, as children without fully developed lungs are at greater risk of asthma and other health disorders. As pollution fell in Central London, researchers found, the proportion of children with impaired lung function also dropped, from 14 percent to 9 percent. The research was published in The Lancet Public Health.

U.K. Health Minister Karin Smyth said the study “is a powerful reminder of the impact that air quality has on children’s lung health, and will help to improve our understanding of how reductions in air pollution can restore normal lung growth among children, reduce the risk of respiratory illnesses in adulthood, and support our goal to give every child the best start in life.”

The Ultra Low Emission Zone was expanded in 2021 and again in 2023, and now covers all of Greater London. Under the scheme, officials estimate, levels of roadside nitrogen dioxide have fallen by 27 percent across London, while deaths linked to toxic air have dropped by 40 percent.

Despite its effect on pollution, the zone has proved highly controversial, sparking widespread protests over the fees and vandalism. Londoners have damaged or stolen hundreds of the more than 3,700 cameras installed citywide to monitor traffic.

#3057. Why This Company is One of the Best for Finding Work

Most travel is extractive and passive. You show up somewhere, take photos of the same landmarks everyone else takes photos of, eat at a restaurant the guidebook recommended, and hit up some bars. You take some tours to learn about the place and, if you’re lucky, get to meet some locals on your trip. You don’t really go deep.

Even long-term travelers who talk about how they “aren’t tourists” do the same – just at a slower pace and while trying to spend less money.

And there’s nothing wrong with that. That’s just the nature of travel. While we all imagine dropping into a place, befriending locals, and having this crazy time like we’re in some movies. But that doesn’t happen. Because we’re just passing through and, for the most part, locals don’t want to become friends with tourists. In fact, most locals don’t interact with tourists. (I mean it does happen but it’s not the norm.)

If you really want a deep travel experience, you need to stay. If you want to understand a place, you need to stay. The most transformative travel experiences I’ve ever had involved contributing something and staying somewhere long enough to build real relationships. It was being embedded in a place rather than just passing through.

I think that more travelers should give back when they travel. In the old days, it was hard to find out what organizations and opportunities were legit, vetted, and actually made the lives of locals better.

Now, there’s a ton of companies that can help you not only find meaningful volunteer jobs when you travel but also paid jobs when you travel and one of the best ones is Global Work & Travel. Use code NOMADICMATT to unlock a discount on your next trip.

Global Work & Travel is the world’s largest gap year company and has been placing people on working holidays, volunteer programs, teaching positions, internships, and more for nearly 2 decades. They’ve helped over 116,000 people and they cover destinations across, the UK and Europe, the Americas, Asia, Africa, and the Pacific.

Even for experienced travelers, moving abroad can be difficult. Finding employment as a traveler, securing permanent accommodation or getting stuck in shared rooms for months on end, transport costs in a new city, interview after interview competing against locals… This is just the beginning of what long term travelers need to consider.

Fortunately, companies like Global Work & Travel provide the scaffolding or safety net that makes working abroad possible for people who don’t want to figure everything out themselves. They handle job matching, pre-departure support, visa guidance, placement, and ongoing assistance through their gWorld portal, a personal trip management app that keeps everything organized in one place. For first-timers especially, having that support structure can be the difference between actually going and endlessly deliberating. The programs they offer span a wide range:

For the past decade, “digital nomad” has been the aspirational version of long term travel. Work remotely, earn in a strong currency, live somewhere cheaper, repeat.

But that model only really works for a small subset of people. You need a remote job, a certain income level, and often a level of career stability that most younger travelers simply don’t have yet.

Instead of bringing a job with you, you get one when you arrive. You integrate into the local economy instead of floating above it. You meet people through work, not just coworking spaces or short-term hostels. And you build a life somewhere, not just a temporary routine.

In a lot of ways, working holiday makers are having a more grounded and accessible version of what people think digital nomad life is. You’re not just passing through, you’re actually living there. You have coworkers, a schedule, a reason to stay longer than a week, and a chance to build real lifetime connections.

It’s also far more realistic for most people. You don’t need a remote business or years of experience. You just need the willingness to go and the right setup to make it happen.

That’s why I think we’re seeing a shift. Less “how do I work remotely?” and more “how do I actually live and work abroad for a year?”

And that’s exactly where structured programs like Global Work & Travel come in. They remove the biggest barriers, finding a job, navigating visas, getting set up, so people can actually make that shift from idea to reality.

For a lot of travelers, this isn’t just an alternative to digital nomad life. It’s a more sustainable, accessible, and realistic way to actually live and work abroad.

Volunteering abroad has a complicated reputation, and it’s worth being honest about that. There are lots of bad volunteer programs out there in the world. Programs that don’t really give back and are designed to make travelers “feel” like they did something but really are just profit driven campaigns. Global Work & Travel’s vets programs in the areas such as wildlife conservation, community development, education, and healthcare in the locations and countries it operates so you know the program you sign up for is legit.

The case for ethical, well-structured volunteering is genuinely strong. When you work alongside local Zanzibar communities on problems they’ve defined as priorities, or with wildlife and conservation in South Africa or Elephant rehabilitation in Thailand — something shifts in how you understand the world. Not only are you helping to give back to a place but you also understand the true needs of a the people and ecosystems living there, but also helping overcome the struggles they go through. It opens your mind and shifts your perspective.

Their Global Animal Welfare Fund also channels resources directly into conservation projects at their partner sites, so the impact extends beyond individual placements.

Working holidays let you truly experience a country instead of just visiting it. You immerse yourself in the culture by living like a local every day. You meet more people both locals and fellow travellers while building real friendships. Best of all, you get paid to travel, so you can stay much longer instead of rushing through in a few weeks. This lets you experience local life deeply, discover hidden spots, and understand how people really live in different places. You also build valuable skills, boost your resume with international experience, and make long-term travel more affordable since your income covers the costs. Plus, you gain a real cultural understanding that no short holiday can match. All that while stil getting paid? Not bad right?!

Working holidays turn travel into a true lifestyle, not just another 2 week vacation.

Global Work & Travel are the world leaders in long term travel and offer a ton of options for travelers looking to volunteer, work, or spend extended time in a destination. Some things I like about them.

Do I need prior experience to work abroad with Global Work & Travel? For most trips, generally nothing more than basic work experience is required. Teaching programs include TEFL training, and volunteering can be started from no experience.

What’s the minimum age? Most programs are open from age 18. Working holiday visas typically cap at 35 depending on the destination country but volunteer and teach programs are open to ages 18–80.

How long does the whole process take? It varies by programs and destination. Most people book their trips 6-12 months in advance for proper planning, job matching and visa quotas. You can get started for as little as $1 here.

Is my money safe if things change? Global Work & Travel and their lifetime deposit policy means your initial payment doesn’t expire. They are also members of many consumer protection services to further support travelers.

Can I go as a solo traveler? Yes, and this is actually one of the most common scenarios. The gWorld Community and programs group connections mean you’ll be meeting others in the same position quickly.

Travel has always been best when it’s been more than tourism. The moments that stay with you — that you actually tell people about five years later — are never the ones where you queued to see a famous landmark. They’re the ones where you connect with people. They are the moments where you did something.

#3058. Invisible Beaker STEM Challenge

The invisible beaker is a classic science activity and a fantastic example of “science magic” that’s sure to provide a wow moment to children (and adults) of all ages! It’s inexpensive and very easy. You need a large and a small glass beaker and enough clear cooking oil to cover the small beaker when it’s placed inside the larger one.

The beakers must be made of borosilicate glass, such as Pyrex, or the demonstration won’t work. The secret to the small beaker disappearing is because of something called the Refractive index.

Optional challenge – draw a picture on the smaller beaker and watch as it seems to float inside the big beaker.

Usually, when light travels from one material to another, it changes speed and bends. It is the bending of light which allows us to see the edges of a transparent object.

Oil and glass have the same refractive index (approximately 1.47), which means that light passes through them as if they were a single solid substance. Light doesn’t bend as it passes from one to the other, so our eyes cannot detect the small beaker!

You can see the edges of the larger beaker as the refractive index of air is 1.0. Light bends as it passes from the glass to the air, and so the edge of the beaker is visible.

Make a jumping bean with kitchen foil and a marble. A jumping bean takes less than five minutes to make and leaps around like it has a life of its own.

Push pencils through a plastic bag filled with water and be amazed when it doesn’t leak!

Use another clever refraction trick to make a coin disappear!
