Like I said, this build took into consideration a lot of things about how I used my first Jeep storage & bed platform build and how I planned to use this new one. Here are some details and reasons I did what I did. I highly suggest thinking deeply about these and expanding on these ideas so you can adjust for your own use case!

Since this bed platform has a fairly unobstructed flat sleeping surface, there’s not much in the way moving around the main space. You can even access the under bed storage by lifting one “wing” at a time when inside.

To sleep in a Jeep, with two people nonetheless, it tight and cramped. Imagine a proper 2-person tent; not a ton of room, but it does the job. If you’ve never done it, I suggest looking close at the measures here and testing with your partner in a tent before assuming this bed platform or sleeping in a Jeep is right for you!

Contouring the part of bed top I call the “wings” around the center console and cupholders essentially dictated the size of panels. You can adjust or make sexier curved cuts if you want, but I went with simple, straight cuts to save time.

Note that the depth of the drawer in the Jeep storage space is based on my computer backpack which is about 5″ or so inches deep when loaded. For me that works, but you could adjust the measures more or less based on your needs.

This design puts the cooler on the back shelf, then up into the roof space when not being used, so it’s pretty much out of the way. And when driving the shelf is dropped and should be secured with a bungie or two to make sure things aren’t moving in transit anyways.

Getting back and forth from the front seat without getting out of the Jeep is not only a convenience but a safety issue. No worries with this build, since access to the front seats is easy: Just flip back the part of the “wings” at the head, slide seats back, and hop up front!

With the Jeep tailgate closed and locked, the 32″ drawer is really hard to get to, even with the back of the drawer cabinet not having an actual back. Not impossible, but at least it makes it one of the most secure places for valuables.

But my Tuffy lock boxes under my front seat (below) serve for true locked storage for money and other stuff, and I highly recommend them!

Especially when I was running a soft top, but now still with a hardtop, I’ve sworn by Tuffy’s products. This lockbox is robust and bolts into the frame under the seat. You can get one for the passenger side too. (Used to run their trunk storage box back in the day.)

READ NEXT: Jeep Wrangler Upgrades & Accessories to Make Your Jeep Life Fun as Hell!Is Life An Adventure Anymore? Reflections from Camping in Cathedral Valley in Capitol Reef National Park

Iâm giving you general Jeep bed measurements I used for my custom build here, so this how-to is for reference only! Measure your Jeep Wrangler multiple times and build to your own variables between year and make and any aftermarket Jeep accessories and parts you might have. Mine is a 2015 Wrangler JKU Sport.

Main sleeping platform dimensions: 52â³ wide & +/-71â³ long,  wider at the doors and narrower at the Jeep tailgate Hinged RV cooler shelf: 39â³ wide & 14″ deep, with about 13.5″ underneath when extended up on its legsDrawer storage: Actual drawer is +/-5″ deep but had room above inside the enclosure to give around 6″+

Some things to keep in mind before and during the actual build. Oh, and I suggest reading this article a few times with your own pen and paper and tape measure to adjust before even buying materials or starting your build!

Find some big cardboard pieces. You can likely ask an appliance store if you don’t have any. It’s a huge time and money saver assuming it saves you from wasting expensive wood.

Plus, being able to âseeâ the bed platform before cutting and being able to use your template for general tracing on the wood is really helpful. (Just make sure you use a straight edge for true lines.)

Start with the spine, then the storage drawer and drawer enclosure, then tops and wings, and finally the cooler shelf. Raise up the upper piece to fit it. Build all that then confirm the upper storage box before cutting, etc.

Pay attention to the tailgate latch enclosure, driver seat position, window crank accessibility, cupholders, and any other nuances your Jeep might have.

You can likely get all of your bed top pieces and the shelf out of one single sheet of 4’x8′ heavy-duty plywood if you plan well. And I suggest using the factory straight edge to your advantage whenever possible knowing those edges are already true and straight.

You can do this with a circular saw (I suggest using a guide to get straighter cuts) but I highly suggest a proper table saw and a new blade for the easiest, best and straightest cuts.

Find some big cardboard piecesâyou can likely ask an appliance store if you don’t have any. It’s a huge time and money saver assuming it saves you from wasting expensive wood. Plus, being able to âseeâ the bed platform before cutting and being able to use your template for general tracing on the wood is really helpful. (Just make sure you use a straight edge for true lines.)

I love these tie down anchors and I use them everywhere in Jeep my bed builds. For less than $2 a piece, they’re good in the Jeep, workshop, or wherever else you need strong tie downs for bungies or ropes.

Step 1. Remove the back seats and cover for the original equipment jack stand and storage compartment. Removing seats for the first time can be a major pain, but once you break the Loctite itâs a breeze. Get yourself a long lever or proper breaker bar to put over your wrench/socket handle to give you some leverage.

Step 2. Using the general measures from all of these DIY instructions and images, grab a tape measure and detail on a sheet of paper and detail what your specific bed measures need to be. Keep in mind window cranks, center consoles, extra speakers, seat positions, etc.

Step 3. Using the 48â³ T-square, transfer your measures to large pieces of cardboard to use for templates. Even if your Jeep Wrangler JKU make and model match my 2015, I suggest doing cardboard cutouts so you can “see” how things will fit before building!

Once you cut templates out you can add too or take away material to get your fits just right. My final pieces looked like a cardboard Frankenstein’s monster because I had cut and added to them.

Step 4. Measure and confirm the size and placement of the spine support of your Jeep bed platform. Don’t worry, you’ll confirm things next without cutting much.

Step 5. Soft-assemble to confirm size, height, etc., that will give you other measures. Cut your 2″x4″ spine legs and simply place in the jeep and set on of the 1″x4″ boards extending out the doors if you want, until you confirm measures. You can then place the other 1″x4″ on top going out the back of the jeep and simply prop that up to height.

Step 6. Confirm measures for the 2″x8″ main spine support pieces that go over the body floor articulations. Note in the image below that the main 2″x8″ sits on the frame in the back, and it only needs the small supplemental foot piece to raise it up to be level. I suggest you wait to cut and assemble this until you get through step 9 below.

Step 7. Before cutting and constructing the whole spine, cut and sort the 2″x8″ uprights that make the drawer enclosure. This is simple, since the only thing necessary is cutting to length (go longer than shorter if necessary), measuring notches and cutouts, then setting them in.

NOTE: The backmost edge of these uprights are based on the tailgate door latch enclosure. Look close at the plan drawings to see how those things line up!

Step 8. Cut a template for the bed top that goes on the enclosure based on the measure images. Don’t forget that there will be pieces of 1″x4″ on top of the enclosure legs that help to add some surface area for the top and wings to sit on.

At this point, the back of the spine near the tailgate is simply propped up by something (a spare 2″x4″ piece?) so you can see things lining up, test the side locations, etc.

Step 9: Dry set up the central spine, drawer uprights and bed top. This step is really just so that you can really confirm that things are level and your measures are correct before cutting and putting together your spine and the remaining pieces. Make sure the enclosure legs fit night and from front-to-back your drawer has equal room top to bottom.

Now you can likely complete your central spine build and add the 1″x4″ and 1″x6″ top boards to the enclosure verticals. Don’t worry, these get the bed top applied overtop, so if you have to affix then take apart and adjust, it’s not going to be visible.

At this point you’ve constructed the spine and have the storage box sides cut, notched, etc., applied the top boards to those uprights, and you have a template for the bed top. I suggest at this point finding a spare 2×4 or other spare boards to allow you to attach a front and back to the drawer enclosure sides just for the use of making it square while you finish installing the top.

Step 10. Now place the enclosure exactly where it will live once all bed is built, make sure the side have equal and parallel side-to-side measures where your drawer will go later, and set your template on top. Near the passenger seat area you should have about 2.5″ or so of the 1″x5″ top boards showing, which your wings will sit on later. Make sure all of your measures are plumb and things are straightâ¦

NOTE: You’ll want to close the tailgate with all of these parts sitting where you want them to make sure you have clearances!

Step 11: Cut your heavy duty plywood for the drawer enclosure top. All of these checks and balances for measures have led to thisâcutting the most expensive piece of material you’ve bought. If you’re confident in your template, place it with the middle of the bed edge against the perfectly cut edge of the sheet. Put your template on top, mark lightly, then come back with a straight edge to true your lines, then cut!

Step 12: Set your plywood on top, close the tailgate, true everything up, then connect with screws. If you’re unsure at this point, just add enough screws to hold things together and you can come back towards the end of the build (mainly after your drawer is in and done) and add more screws.

At this point you essentially have a finished back part of your bed, ready to build and install the drawer.

Step 13. Construct the drawer box. Make sure you take into consideration the material depth of the heavy-duty drawer slides and leave room for the tailgate latch enclosure. Your drawer slide width and any play in your slides will determine your drawer materials measures. I’ll leave those details up to you.

NOTE that you’ll want to leave about 1/2″ under the drawer so that it’s actually raised up off of your Jeep floor and you can put things in your OE “trunk” underneath.

For the drawer bottom, a 1/2″ thick standard plywood is likely enough, which is what I used. Construct the edges all together, cut your plywood to size, set on top and screw together.

Step 14. Paint your drawer before adding the heavy-duty drawer slides. Up until now I’ve avoided painting, but I’m a details guy. At this point I would suggest painting the whole box (and enclosure if you’re solid) before adding the slides so that you can have a super clean and tight paint job when you’re done, even behind the mechanical parts. Make sure you do any sanding of hard corners first if you want some fine details!

Step 15. Once your paint is dried, install the drawer slides and drawer. Honestly, installing drawer slides on drawers and the enclosure is hella tricky IMO. I suggest that if you’ve never done it, you just measure a lot, mark truly, and go at it, maybe securing minimal screws until you’re sure it’s set up right.

You can always undo and adjust to a degree or use shims if things aren’t aligning perfectly. Good luck!

At this point you should have a finished back portion and the spine in place to where it’s some easy confirmation of the “wing” piece measures before cutting. Just remember that near the front seats the hinged part of the wings the fold forward will sit midline on the 1″x4″ spine tops for support. (Look closely at the black and white plan imagesâ¦)

Step 16. Confirm your measures for the wood and lay out on your remaining heavy-duty plywood. Again, lay it out so that the edges that are already perfectly straight on the original 4’x8′ are used for edges that you need perfectly straight, like where they meet when bed is put together. Measure thrice, cut once!

Step 17. Cut chamfered angled edges on the opposite side of the pieces where your hinges will go. You only need to make it about 1/2 width, but this will make sure things move smoothly when lifting and moving hinged pieces.

I suggest you actually hold off and cut the remaining pieces (for the shelf) and paint everything before actually assembling, but that’s up to you!

Step 18. Assemble the hinged pieces. Cut your hinged pieces to length then assemble. This is easy enough just laying all of the hinged pieces together on a flat surface, predrilling your holes first.

Step 19: Cut the vertical support legs for the “head” pieces of the wings. These are simple 2″x4″ pieces that will have a small dowel/hole on one end and they’ll just use gravity to stay in place. Easy peasy. I suggest thinking about what storage used the space around these might need and place them accordingly.

For instance, if you know you have a battery system like this one, place it in, then figure out where the best place for your legs will be. We’ll get to the dowels later.

Admittedly, the shelf is where you can likely improve on this design, but hey, my first try works pretty well. The hinged pieces simply use door hinges, since they fit pretty perfectly on the 1.5″ edge of a 2″x4″ or 2″x8″, which as you know are actually 1/2″ less than those measures. And the heavy duty nature of hinges like this had me feeling better than any piano hinges I found.

Where you can likely improve is either finding hinges that lie perfectly flat (so that the round part isn’t thicker than the hinges), or adding a 1/8″ shim on the side of each hinge that would allow them to sit perfectly flat when the shelf is up.

Step 19. Measure your space to make sure your cooler fits up in the ceiling of your Jeep when extended, then dry fit everything! The tops of your shelves are made of the heavy-duty plywood, so cut them after confirming measures, then just play builder and set everything up without connecting so that you’re sure you have it set up right. Paint and assemble when you’re confident!

The hinge mechanisms are a little tricky to visualize, so much better to play with them before connecting everything.

A few finishing touches are up to you, but I think this is where the extra touches can really elevate things. And this is your bedroom, so make it nice!

Add small dowels to the corners of the wings where they sit against the drawer bed top. This is simple if you just put it all together and use a tiny drill bit straight through the top into the structure underneath. Then take them out and measure dowel depth, drill, use wood glue on the dowel side, finito.

Don’t forget you’ll also need these in your leg supports. A single dowel piece go in end of each 2″x4″ and the receiver hole goes on the bottom of those wing pieces.

Add tie-downs here, there, and everywhere! These tie-down’s are cheap and useful for so many things, so I buy a multi-pack and go nuts on every new build. You’ll definitely want some around the cooler shelf for when a cooler is in tow or just to hold the shelf down when not in use. Other spots I have them are on the spine legs.

For the cooler shelf support (when up) I used a 2″x4″ and created a horizontal “bar” that I simply wedge under the shelf. This works fine, but you can likely improve on it. I have a hard top, so there are some slim “lips” on the sides that I sit this bar on.

It’s not sexy, but it’s only meant to keep the shelf up when parked and I would never leave the shelf up when driving!

What’s the final step? Grab a beer and enjoy your work!

I’m really happy with this build, even though there are always improvements I see after the build is done. I hope that’s where you’ll take these ideas and run with them!

Where this Jeep bed excels is in the lack of wasted space because of the minimal structure. So much storage which leaves all that space on the bed to sleep two comfortably.

Things I need while in the Jeep are easy for me to get to, especially in the âattic storageâ bungee net system rigged up. (Images below)

The metal tie-downs are inexpensive and really helpful. I was worried about the metal tie-downs jingling or making noise, but thatâs never been an issue.

The secure drawer storage makes me feel safe when around town, but again, I keep the really important stuff locked in a Tuffy lockbox under my front seats. Highly recommend. I’ve had a version of this box in both of my Jeeps, so for about 15 years now.

Let me know in the comments if you build this and whether you make any changes or modifications! Iâm just a hack with some power tools, and I know there are better ways to do things than the way I do âemâ!

Make sure youâre using these just as recommendations and fit your specific vehicle and needs to find whatâs right for you!

Figure out where you are going & how are you getting there…I suggest using at least 2 to 3 different travel search sites. Start with Skyscanner or Orbitz or Booking …or whatever aggregator site you prefer. Then when you see what airlines to use, check their respective sites for better deals or rewards flights.

Figure out where you’re going to stay…If you’re interested in hostels, search Hostelworld or Hostelling International. For longer-term or more private digs, look at Airbnb, VRBO, colivings, or you can look for hotel rooms in the links from the search engines listed above.

Get comprehensive travel insurance, or in the least, travel medical insurance if internationally…Especially with COVID not going anywhere, you need travel medical insurance nomatter what! Start with an insurance aggregator or with SafetyWing,Â World Nomads, or another. Then decide what is important to you; trip cancellation, baggage coverage, medical, or all of the above. And get a yearly evacuation plan, since you’ll have to get home after your emergency!Â

#3062. Experts cast doubt on Anthropic report detailing how AI has altered work at the company

Anthropic claims AI will shift how work gets done and labor demand – but some experts are skeptical of the vision

Last year, the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, warned that artificial intelligence could eliminate half of entry-level white-collar jobs and that in six months it would be writing 90% of code. Neither of those predictions came to pass.

Now, in a report Anthropic published on Thursday, the company said it was hiring fewer junior technical workers and that human attention has become the new “bottleneck” as it increasingly relies on its Claude AI agents.

Anthropic says AI has changed the way work gets done, and as a result, restructured employment at the company. The report suggests its changes foreshadow the future of work more broadly: as more companies adopt AI agents, software engineers could face a tougher job market while entry-level tech workers struggle to build necessary skills and experience.

“As AI diffuses and improves, the organization of work could shift,” Anthropic’s report reads before offering a potential future. “One possibility is single-person startups, each with a human founder steering swarms of agents to rake in billions in revenue.”

In its report, Anthropic touts its “deep adoption of AI”, which it claims resulted in “producing more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts”. By outsourcing some coding and sales-related tasks to AI agents, Anthropic said it raised productivity within a few months.

From May 2026 onwards, AI agents logged more work hours than human employees, the report said. Employees now spend about 22% of their time managing Claude agents, more than double the amount a year ago, based on Anthropic’s analysis of their chat summaries.

It also says since March 2025 – soon after the release of its agentic AI coding tool Claude Code – entry-level technical hires dropped from nearly 30% to 9%, and headcount dropped from about 21% to 14%. It attributes the shifts to AI usage, and described its workers as merely “a thin layer atop a growing contingent of AI agents”.

While the report provides a small glimpse of the inner workings of the AI heavyweight, some AI researchers are skeptical that it will herald big changes across companies or industries. Instead, they say the findings are probably Anthropic’s attempt to drive its valuation ahead of its initial public offering – similar to how SpaceX boasted about proposed space datacenters to boost its market debut in June.

Anthropic’s claims seem to back some tech executives’ view that AI is behind recent waves of corporate layoffs, but research complicates that.

Morgan Frank, a Case Western Reserve University researcher on how AI and technological changes affect workers, recently posted a paper that’s in peer review showing that AI-exposed job markets deteriorated well before the arrival of ChatGPT in November 2022 and Claude a few months later. State unemployment claims reveal that job markets tanked starting at the beginning of 2022, months before ChatGPT’s release, according to the paper.

“It doesn’t appear that the launch of ChatGPT corresponds to any major increase in loss or worsening outcomes,” he said.

Frank said several factors could explain recent job losses, including cutting pandemic-era hires and “AI-washing”, where some bosses credit AI for layoffs they might have made anyway.

Julián Posada, a Yale social scientist, also questions Anthropic’s motives for publishing its report.

“It is written from the perspective of a company that wants to sell shares, a company that really wants people to invest in it,” said Posada, author of the book Platform Extractivism: Data Work and the People Powering Artificial Intelligence.

Unlike an economics study, the report lacked an independent assessment by outside auditors, Posada said. Its figures and graphs only tell part of the story, without revealing how Anthropic’s workers feel about their work or how they are actually engaging with the models, he said.

Dylan Baker, lead research engineer at the non-profit Distributed AI Research Institute, was also curious about how Anthropic’s developers feel about the changes. Shifting some software development to AI, while hiring few entry-level workers and having the remaining engineers wrangle AI agents seems “shortsighted”, they said.

Baker is also surprised by Anthropic’s human “bottleneck” characterization.

“That’s such a strange way to put it,” they said. “It fundamentally misunderstands how software is written, architected and designed. It’s such a social, interpersonal and human process.”

Anthropic’s report quotes an unnamed engineer, who described facing “an army of Claudes, with every one asking for my attention”. That doesn’t sound like a fruitful work environment, Baker said. “I wouldn’t think really thoughtful, well-designed products are coming out of that team.”

As generative AI products proliferate, a majority of Americans are wary of AI, with particular concerns about AI-related job losses, according to Pew Research Center. In its report, Anthropic suggests that tech employers should offer their workers stock ownership, posing this as a potential solution to rising concerns. “It is difficult to imagine a version of pro-worker AI adoption in which workers do not hold a financial stake in successful rollout,” it said.

Anthropic did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.

Anthropic, which could debut on the stock market as soon as November, released its employment report one day after pledging to commit 5% of its shares to the “public good”, though it did not provide details. Critics noted that philanthropy has long doubled as a reputation builder used by tech titans like Bill Gates and Mark Zuckerberg.

But Anthropic, and its claims that it is improving how work gets done could face tougher scrutiny as it nears its IPO. A draft of the company’s S-1 filing revealed that Anthropic had an $80bn net loss over the first half of this year, and that it received a junk credit rating in June. Considering Anthropic’s slowing revenue growth, investors now project a valuation of $1.5tn, down from earlier estimates of $2tn or more. At the same time, Anthropic’s cloud computing partner, CoreWeave, has become swamped in AI debt and its stock is plummeting, fueling concerns that the AI bubble may begin to deflate.

Regardless of when or whether the bubble pops, software engineers and other tech workers will surely be affected, Baker said. The question is how that will play out.

“My hope is that there is a reckoning, a reassessment or re-evaluation of how much this has always been about human work,” they said.

#3064. 13 Dreamy Airbnbs in the Middle of Nowhere

There’s a reason so many people talk about leaving Wi-Fi, cell service, and city lights behind for a remote Airbnb that lets them connect with nature. For some, it’s their greatest nightmare. For others, the height of luxury. The middle of nowhere might be divisive in its allure, but there’s no denying what it can offer a certain type of traveler. Perhaps you want to connect with the great outdoors, or look deeper within yourself; maybe your motivation is as simple as getting some distraction-free reading done. Whatever the case, a remote Airbnb promises peace, quiet, and unparalleled access to nature—whether that looks like the craggy cliffs of an Icelandic fjord, or the lush Green Mountains of Maine. The properties on this list, which span from a vegetable farm in North Carolina to the Andean peaks of Patagonia, will offer you an experience unlike any other.

In the case of these excellent spots, “remote” doesn’t always have to mean inconveniently out of the way; some of these rentals, like a cottage in the Faroe Islands or a cabin in Tennessee, are within 20 minutes of an airport or major city, offering the best of both worlds. Below are 13 remote Airbnbs for when you want to disconnect from the world. Read on for something for every level of adventure, whether you dream of experiencing the stillness of the high desert in California or hanging out at the top of a mountain in Peru.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Hot tub, wood-burning fireplace, vinyl collection

It’s tough to say whether this White Mountain hideaway looks better in the summer when it’s sprinkled with wildflowers, or in the winter when it’s blanketed in snow. Facing westward, the alpine home captures golden afternoon light and mountain sunsets from every room. The living area is a midcentury-modern dream, with its record player and expansive vinyl collection, while the outdoor patio is ideal for stargazing at night, thanks to a catamaran net that allows you to lie flat while staring up at the sky.

Location: Norway, MaineThings to do nearby: Norway Brewing Company, Pennesseewassee Lake, Roberts Farm Preserve Trails

Number of guests: 6Bed & bath: 2 beds, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Infrared sauna, firepit, access to red rock hiking

Set at the base of a private sandstone peak, this luxury container home is pure Utah magic. Crafted from two high cube shipping containers, it features modern finishes, oversized tubs, smart beds, and an expansive 1,000-square-foot deck made for stargazing and sunrise coffee. With a cedar sauna and cozy indoor fireplace, it's as perfect for winter cocooning as it is for summer hikes. It’s a prime base for national park adventures (it’s close to Capitol Reef National Park and within driving distance of Bryce Canyon National Park) and intimate group getaways.

Location: Teasdale, UtahThings to do nearby: Bluebell Knoll, Larb Hollow Overlook, Capitol Reef National Park

Number of guests: 4Bed & bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: EV charger, private patio, long-term stays allowed

If reconnecting with nature is a top priority, this two-bedroom, one-bathroom cabin fits the bill. With its floor-to-ceiling windows and 180-degree vistas, you'll never want to leave. Set on 42 acres, yet just half an hour from Nashville International Airport, the views are of trees, trees, and more trees. Take in the scenery while preparing a meal in the state-of-the-art kitchen (peep those copper pots and pans) or while birdwatching on the terrace. Cozy touches like a wood-burning stove and cushy leather furniture encourage travelers to silence their phones and disappear into a good book.

Location: Goodlettsville, TennesseeThings to do nearby: Cedar Hill Park, Union Hill Trading Post, Nashville

Number of guests: 2Bed & bath: 1 bedroom, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Unobstructed Sierra views, deep soaking tub, desert solitude

On the edge of the vast Owens Valley near Death Valley National Park, this poetic desert cabin is framed by Mount Whitney and a sea of grazing cattle. Inside, find unobstructed views from the floor-to-ceiling windows, a wood-burning fireplace, and a warm bedroom with direct access to the outdoor bathtub. You come here not for polished amenities but for the romance of the Wild West—sunrises over red rocks, coyotes in the distance, and the feeling of stepping back in time. It's ideal for writers, dreamers, and anyone chasing the stillness of the high desert.

Location: Lone Pine, CaliforniaThings to do nearby: Mount Whitney, Shark Fin Trailhead, Turtle Creek Trailhead

Number of guests: 3Bed & bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Scandinavian interiors, wood-fired hot tub, cedar barrel sauna

This 200-square-foot tiny home proves small can be spectacular. Tucked on eight quiet acres outside Hillsborough, it features Scandinavian design paired with lovingly handcrafted details. Whitewashed pine, handmade ceramics, and East Fork pottery fill the space; outside, a porch nearly the size of the house leads to a sauna and hot tub surrounded by trees. There’s no TV, but you won’t miss it once the stars come out. This spot is perfect for adult duos looking to slow down and soak up some backcountry bliss.

Location: Efland, North CarolinaThings to do nearby: Kings Highway Park, downtown Hillsborough, Mebane Historical Museum

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Hot tub, sauna, rain shower

An ideal stop along the Ring Road, this sleek mirrored home beautifully reflects Iceland’s stunning coastline. Inside, enjoy floor-to-ceiling windows, a queen-size bed, and a bathroom with a rain shower. Right outside, guests can soak in a hot tub while taking in the fresh air, or retreat to the separate unit that houses a private glass sauna with views of the fjord (just imagine how magical it’d be to take in the northern lights while breaking a sweat). While you will feel like you’re in the middle of nowhere, the home is only a five-minute drive from the town of Búðardalur, where you can grab a bite to eat.

Location: Búðardalur, IcelandThings to do nearby: Hólar Farm, Eiríksstaðir (Viking Longhouse), Ásgarðsgrund beach

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Ocean and mountain views, wildlife sightings, proximity to the airport

Located just a five-minute walk away from the world-renowned Múlafossur Waterfall, this one-bedroom home in the Faroe Islands feels undeniably remote, but is located just a 20-minute drive away from the airport. One of six cottages on the property, you may run into a small community of like-minded travelers as you bask in the dramatic Faroese scenery. You might even spot sheep, birds, and highland cows—and if you’re really lucky, the northern lights. Do note that the house can accommodate two extra guests for an added charge.

Location: Gásadalur, Faroe IslandsThings to do nearby: Drangarnir Sea Arch, Fjallavatn Lake, Fjósið restaurant

Number of guests: 2Bed & bath: 1 bedroom, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Private deck, mountain views, fast Wi-Fi

This sleek and cozy “bothy” (Scottish cottage) is a minimalist dream in the Scottish Highlands, with vaulted ceilings, soft Skyeskyns rugs, and uninterrupted views of the Quiraing and Trotternish Ridge. Open-plan and sunlit, it has everything you need to escape: a full kitchen, an en suite bath, and a wooden deck perfect for stargazing (or spotting the northern lights). It’s a peaceful retreat for hikers, writers, or couples who want to immerse themselves in Skye’s cinematic beauty without roughing it. Bonus: you’ll wake to total silence—and maybe a few sheep.

Location: Isle of Skye, ScotlandThings to do nearby: Staffin Beach, Kilt Rock Waterfall, Loch Shianta

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: River access, bicycles for rent, mountain view

If you’re planning a trip from Tokyo to Kyoto, consider stopping in the countryside to stay at this 100-year-old traditional home once owned by a green tea farmer. Surrounded by lush mountains, bamboo forests, tea fields, and a river, the house is designed to let the outside in, with wide windows and paper sliding doors. To get the most out of this remote retreat, consider booking a bamboo weaving workshop with the host Daisuke (guest reviewers gush that he is the nicest man to ever exist), or rent a few bikes to explore Fujieda.

Location: Fujieda, JapanThings to do nearby: Utoge Waterfall, Kashiba-ya Museum, Mount Bikuishi

Number of guests: 2Bed & bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Hot tub, firepit, free parking on premises

Set in Argentine Patagonia, this whimsical yet serene pod‑like shell (inspired by the Welsh dragon masks created in the region) is one of a kind. It offers sweeping views of the Andean peaks and forests—you may even catch a glimpse of the snow-dusted summits, depending on the season. Inside, the materials and light are simple—thoughtfully composed wood, glass, and metal. Ideal for solo travelers or couples who want to dive into Patagonia’s wild energy: glaciers, trails, cold rivers, and long skies are all part of the package here. Come to unplug, to let nature take center stage, and to sleep in a sculpture.

Location: Trevelín, ArgentinaThings to do nearby: Laguna Brychan, Trevelin lavender farm, Molino Andes museum

Number of guests: 2Bed & bath: 1 bed, shared bathroomTop amenities: Unobstructed views, gourmet meals included, zip line access

Not for the faint of heart, this skylodge offers the chance to sleep in a fully transparent pod suspended 1,200 feet above Peru’s Sacred Valley. You arrive via zip line or a Via Ferrata climb—and the reward is staggering: 360-degree mountain views, an included gourmet dinner and breakfast, and an unmatched adrenaline rush. Best for fit travelers, thrill-seekers, and couples who want a night they’ll never forget (or stop posting about), this is truly a once-in-a-lifetime stay.

Location: Urubamba, PeruThings to do nearby: Flowers Path, Rancho Valle Dorado, Hacienda Puka Punku restaurant

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Hot tub, patio, mountain view

Situated on a working farm in South Africa’s Overberg region, this off-grid cabin is an unforgettable way to take in the Riviersonderend Mountains. It comes equipped with a king-size bed, a well-stocked kitchen, Wi-Fi, air conditioning—and arguably the best part—an outdoor patio housing a massive wood-fired hot tub. “It felt like my husband and I were the only two people there in the world,” one guest reviewer wrote.

Location: Riviersonderend, South AfricaThings to do nearby: Lord’s Wines, Greyton Nature Reserve, Eseltjiesrus Donkey Sanctuary

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Outdoor bathtub, covered porch, access to trails

As the host puts it, this New Zealand hut is so wonderfully secluded, “you won’t see a neighbor close by.” Tucked away in the valleys of Mount Somers, the one-bedroom home offers 360-degree views of the surrounding mountains, perhaps best enjoyed from the windows encompassing your bed. You’ll find all the modern comforts too, like built-in USB chargers, heated towel racks, and electric blankets, but perhaps most convenient is the list of nearby hiking and biking trails that guests receive upon booking (there’s a pair of Moustache e-bikes available to use as well).

Location: Mount Somers, New ZealandThings to do nearby: Emerald Pool, Lake Clearwater, Awa Awa Reserve

#3065. Collapse of Atlantic Currents Could Drive a Surge in Warming

A vast system of Atlantic currents appears to be weakening, and scientists say its collapse could lead to dramatic cooling in northern Europe. A new study suggests an additional risk: a surge in warming across the rest of the globe.

The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, or AMOC, carries warm water from the tropics toward Europe. As the water flows north, it cools, becoming more dense, and descends to the depths, where it flows back south. But as oceans warm, those waters are not so cool, nor so dense, as they once were, and measurements suggest the system of circulation is slowing down.

Complicating matters further, the melting Greenland ice sheet is unleashing into the North Atlantic large amounts of fresh water, which is less dense than salty water, further slowing circulation. If the AMOC were to collapse, temperatures in northern Europe would drop by 9 to 27 degrees F (5 to 15 degrees C), according to one estimate.

The weakening is not a new phenomenon. The AMOC has undergone hundreds of weak periods over the last 2.7 million years as the climate shifted. And scientists have long assumed that each time the North Atlantic cooled, southern latitudes warmed by an equal amount. The total amount of heat remained roughly constant, they thought. It merely shifted from place to place.

But the new modeling study reveals a more dramatic change, showing that when AMOC previously weakened, the Earth grew hotter overall.

“The AMOC works like a heat valve that controls the energy budget of the planet,” said lead author Christo Buizert, of Oregon State University. With a strong AMOC, warm water flows to the North Atlantic, where the heat is lost to the atmosphere. But with a weak AMOC, the study found, heat instead builds up in the ocean.

Buizert said that past weak periods produced the same amount of warming as 10 years of human emissions would today. The research was published in Nature Geoscience.

Buizert noted that studies of past shifts in the AMOC are not a perfect comparison for changes underway today, but they can help scientists make sense of what may be in store as temperatures rise.

Why Fears Are Growing Over the Fate of a Key Atlantic Current

#3066. Don’t Visit Ko Lipe

After 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006. Back then, it was one of those super off-the-beaten-path destinations that few but the most intrepid travelers visited, where electricity only ran a few hours a day, basic bungalows right on the beach cost something like $2 USD, and there really was a last boat for the season.

There was much to do here but that was the point. You hung out on the beach, read a book, went snorkeling, went back to the beach, drank beers at the one beach bar on the island, rotated meals between the five restaurants there, and went to bed early.

It was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck. Days easily turned into weeks here.

If you asked me what the highlight of all my travels was, I would be the time I spent on Ko Lipe. I made incredible friends, lounged around, got to know the locals, learned a bit of Thai, and, overall, lived that idyllic backpacker life we all dream about.

Over the years, I’ve avoided going back to Ko Lipe because the memory of my time there is so strong that I didn’t want to ruin it. Any re-visit would simply be trying to recreated a magic that couldn’t be recreated because the people that it special wouldn’t be there. I’d be chasing travel ghosts. And, since I know my sleepy paradise has been developed greatly over the years, I was also too afraid seeing that would make me sad.

Tourism in Thailand tends toward the unsustainable. No island really develops in a good way. It’s all build, build, build.

And I didn’t want to see my Ko Lipe like that.

But as I was planning my recent trip through Southeast Asia, returning to Ko Lipe made sense. I was heading down the Indian Ocean side of Thailand on my way into Malaysia and I’d pass by it.

And, since I was looking for a lively place for New Year’s Eve, it seemed liked the best choice. I knew there would be travelers there and there were no other nearby islands that would work, especially since Ko Lipe has a boat to Langkawi, which was my next stop.

And I’m sad to report that Ko Lipe took the Ko Phi Phi model of tourism and is now extremely overdeveloped.

Most of the island is now paved over, the old dirt footpaths having become concrete for the cars and construction trucks. Swaths of palm trees are now the sites of high-end resorts with pools (on an island with no natural water supply). Construction of more resorts continues at a fast pace. The coral around the island is dying, a victim of all the boats, anchors, pollution, and overfishing. Beaches are now lined with boats, their exhaust spilling into the ocean, leaving a shiny film you can see as you swim. And the restaurants cater to tourists looking for bad Western food, not great Thai cuisine.

The island’s boom has displaced many locals, who were forced to sell to mainland developers, and much of the island’s workforce is now from the mainland. They see little of the benefits this tourism boom.

So lies Ko Lipe, another victim of Thailand’s all too common overdevelopment and exploitation of limited resources.

I met lots of people there who loved the island. If it’s your first time, I can see why you would love it. After all, the area is postcard perfect, the water is perfectly an azure blue, the sand is a beautiful white, and since you’re surrounded by a national park, a lot of tours take you to some secluded islands.

And, in comparison to Ko Phi Phi, Krabi, or Phuket, it is less developed so I can’t fault someone stepping here for the first time going “wow!”

But, as I reflect on the island and its overdevelopment, I have come to the same conclusion I have about Ko Phi Phi: people shouldn’t visit.

I’m not against growth, but I’m against this kind of growth. It’s not sustainably managed and going there will only tax the island’s limited resources even further. You can’t put the genie back in the bottle and no local is going to say “sure, I’ll stay broke so you can an idealized vision of the world.”

And, with so many other islands to visit that are well managed (Ko Lanta, Ko Jum, and Ko Mook, to name three nearby), I think you should skip Ko Lipe.

A visit there will only make things worse.

It pains me to say that, because it was such a beautiful place, and my original visit had a huge impact on my life. But if we’re going to be good stewards and travelers, sometimes you just have to say enough is enough.

And Ko Lipe is a place where enough is enough.

Go somewhere else that is better managed.

Riding elephants in Thailand went away when consumers became more conscious of it. Eco lodges got big because of consumers. Overtourism is talked about by consumers as much as it is by locals.

Maybe if enough people start to do something, Ko Lipe will change.

But, at the very least, by not going you are at least no contributing to the problem.

#3067. How are storms named?

Have you ever wondered why and how storms are named? It may feel like a random process, but storm names follow a strict international system. Naming storms has been found to increase awareness and encourage people to prepare if needed. It’s also easier for news reporters to use a single name rather than a longer, less memorable name composed of scientific terms.

The naming process depends on the type of storm and its location.

Tropical storm and hurricane names are maintained by the World Meteorological Organisation, which uses six alphabetical lists that rotate every six years.

The first storm of the year starts with an A, the second wth a B and so on through the year. Names alternate between male and female and have done so since 1979.

Q, U, X, Y, and Z are usually missed out because there aren’t enough names starting with those letters.

Names of particularly severe storms are retired to avoid confusion in subsequent years and as a sign of respect.

The Atlantic list of storm names for 2025 has been released and includes Dexter, Jerry and Melissa.

Storms in the UK are named only when they are expected to have a medium to high impact, typically associated with an Amber or Red Weather Warning.

Names are usually chosen from a shortlist suggested by the public. The storm names for 2025 include Amy, Bram and Hannah!

If there are more than 21 named storms, the names go back to A and start over.

#3069. Human Being Or Human Doing? Burnout, Acceptance, & Recovery: Reprogramming A Toxic Productivity Mindset

It was the oddest of things. Always attempting to look like I “have my sh*t together” while also being fairly mindful, the moment really caught me off guard. It probably stemmed from a few months of delving deeper inside and uncovering some somewhat uncomfortable realities that I had been casually ignoring about the past few years and personal projects, my lifestyle goals, and other things I had chosen to backburner concentrating on the true mechanics of.

Regardless of the reasons for the breach, there was no more ignoring it; I was overwhelmed and burned out.

This site participates in the Amazon Services LLC Associates Program and other affiliate programs and may earn from qualifying purchases.

I can’t remember it specifically. But it was something like a simple sepia-toned image of a small pond, a tree off to the left side, a little faded… quietly framing a version of a quote I had read dozens of times over the years. But this time, it read slightly differently, and it cut me to the bone.

“If you keep doing what you’ve always done, why would you expect anything different?”

Yep, I’m sure you’ve heard some version of it, just like I had. But again, somehow this timeâthe way it was phrased or maybe the quiet moment I was inâit hit me differently. “Why would you expect anything different” looked me right in my eyes as it spoke to me, and demanded an answer.

It demanded me to stop ignoring a status quo that kept me just comfortable enough to ignore what might be beyond if I intentionally searched for whatever “it” could be.

Cue the waterworks… the moment the dam broke and I lost it. In the middle of a normal afternoon, standing by myself in my $500/month 2-bedroom apartment in beautiful Bansko, Bulgaria, I started bawling my eyes out. Something gave.

Somewhere in between happy enough and truly enjoying happiness, my soul was wondering why “somewhere in between” was good enough for me to have settled into.

Fast forward a couple of hours, as I was on a video call with my super-smart and patient partner… who also happens to be a personal coach with a penchant for helping people dig a little deeper to find what’s holding them backâor what’s holding them hostage emotionally… and some of the reasons for my overwhelm started surfacing.

The short of it was that I was considering building another side project, hoping for that ever-elusive dream of “passive income” to finally become a reality. But the idea of doing something because I knew I could execute it, because it made sense, or because I knew it was viable, was no longer enough.

I had spent well over 6-7 years inside the side hustle culture of building and executing nonstop. Between my graphic design work (that actually pays the bills), TheNomadExperiment.com, writing, designing, and publishing a book, journals, youtube, and more, the idea of another so-so execution involving hundreds of extra hours over the following six months had caused the dam to break.

BTW. Passive income through blogging, item creation, etc., in my opinion is a complete lie, at least the way weâve been sold it over the past 10-20 years. Itâs another full-time job, with the same potential for burnout, so just donât fool yourself. But Iâll leave that discussion for another timeâ¦

The real problem wasn’t even putting in the work, or even whether it would be successful or not; the real problem was the question of why I would choose to do it. It ended up coming down to this ingrained “need” for me to do, to execute, to look like I’m always busy, to somehow prove to myselfâand othersâthat I’m valid and not lazy. For lack of a better labelâToxic Productivity.

Toxic productivity is defined as a mindset that involves working excessively to the detriment of other aspects of life, such as physical and mental health. It can manifest as a need to be constantly “doing” or “producing.” Signs of toxic productivity are burnout, depression, anxiety, and other physical and emotional health consequences.

After spending some time digging deeper, it was clear that I was extremely uncomfortable with the idea of being irrelevant, or seeming lazy, or looking like I wasnât working my ass off to earn whatever I had in my life.

Looking like I deserved and earned instead of actually taking time to enjoy the life I was attempting to build for myself.

If you’re still here, good on ya! But I think it’s time for the disclaimer. I’m so grateful for my life, scars and all, and I know I’m lucky to have the things and opportunities I do.

I also try to discourage myself and others from playing the comparison game. It’s important to work to be a good world citizen and attempt to do better for the world, but not to let those things overshadow the need for each of us to find what we need personally. Whether that’s with material things, or with “effort-based” ideas, or modeling someone else’s toxic productivity output.

My partner, having heard me say a couple of different ways that “I just don’t want to spend another 6 months doing nothing but work only to have another mediocre project out in the world that doesn’t feel greatâ¦or even produce,” finally asked me a question that I could never thank her enough for:

“If you’re scared of spending all that time and effort over the next 6 months with a result you won’t be happy about, what’s stopping you from just taking the time you would spend on that project and instead concentrating on enjoying the life you’ve built?”

This time though because the idea she was presenting made so much sense. Fortunatelyâ¦or unfortunately depending on how you look at itâ¦the answer to her question of “what is stopping you” was literally… me. I was the thing that was stopping me from choosing that.Â

It was the uncomfortable ideas inside my mind of letting off the gas and the fears of “them” not thinking I was working hard enough. My self-worth was somewhat wrapped up in these unrealistic expectations of what I “should” be doing with my time.

That I might be viewed as not appreciating the opportunities I had in life by working myself nonstop. Or confronting the fact that I had kind of forgotten what it felt like to not work all the time…and that scared me.

My association with enjoyment and play had been programmed over the years to be akin to laziness or being spoiled or wasteful. I’ll blame my Midwestern, middle-class, “if you don’t take the overtime and overwork, you’re wasting opportunities” upbringing.

I had… no have… a really hard time balancing the ideas of working hard and taking time to enjoy the life I’m working so hard for.

Remote work and being nomadic give the freedom to work whenever I want, but that can be a slippery slope when your work hours and personal time become so intertwined that it’s hard to truly “turn off” and combat toxic productivity gremlins.

I used to literally put in my calendar blocks titled âbe spontaneous,â which Iâm pretty sure is exactly the opposite of what spontaneity is, lol! I canât ignore that this is just part of who I am or was, even if Iâm aware that mindset needs some updating.

After our 2-3 hour conversation I went inside myself. I spent a day or so wandering aimlessly, journaling, making lists, asking questions, staring into the ether, and everything in between.

I questioned what my days could look like if I only concentrated on making the money I needed to pay the billsâand keeping the insulin comingâwhile taking a break from all of my current or prospective side projects.

Ideating on what I could fill all of that extra time with if I chose to reclaim “play” or a more intentional use of my time over constantly chasing productivity or overworking.

I literally made a 3-page list of all the things I could do if I had more time devoted to play or enjoyment instead of work. I highly recommend this exercise!

About 48 hours after my burnout breaking point, I decided to consciously choose to spend the next 3-6 months doing just that.

That was about five months ago (as of this writing), and let me tell you, the time in between then and now has been both beautiful and grueling.

Wandering aimlessly around new streets in new cities with no destination in mind or time constraints.

Buying armfulls of flowers and then spending multiple hoursâ¦on multiple occasionsâ¦creating flower arrangements. For my room and for decorating the common areas at my last coliving spot, just because I enjoyed it and it made me happy.

Or just choosing to hang out, linger, and “waste timeâ because it just felt right to be with people living life instead of behind my computer working away.

The exact opposite of toxic productivity or hustle culture normsâpaying attention to my mental and physical health first, and truly trying to achieve a good work-life balance.

Iâm much happier now, but itâs a work in progress reprogramming all of that old mess inside about what I âshouldâ be doing with my time.

Prioritizing mindfulness and intentional living isnât a set-it-and-forget-it way of lifeâ¦it requires more mindfulness and intention to stay focused. And even with that dedication, there are so many moments of retraction and stepping backwards or falling into complacency.

Balancing real priorities and necessitiesâlike taking care of financial responsibilities and medical responsibilitiesâand hoping the future is taken care of isnât exactly easy.

But letâs be honest, âfinancial securityâ is kind of unattainable, since for many of us, one (more) diagnosis, or emergency in our lives will have us back in figure-it-out mode regardless of how financially secure we trick ourselves into thinking we are in the short term.

So why not find a way to do the best you can for yourself now and in the future while really giving yourself the opportunity to slow down more often, play, include self-care and wellness, and literally stop to smell the roses everyâ¦singleâ¦time you see some roses that need smellinâ? Break the cycle of toxic productivity that might be holding on to you and give yourself time to rest and recharge.

Cheers friend. Appreciate the time you spent here. Talk again soon. (Please share this article if you know someone it might help!)

Oh. And I donât know whatâs next. But Iâm writing when it feels right, and sharing when it feels right. Not because I should. Iâm hoping that the Universe will show me the right path now that my eyes are a little more intent on paying attention, and my heart is a little more open to saying yes.

#3070. Interest rates unlikely to reach 4.75% by next summer, say City economists

Experts say Bank of England unlikely to increase rates by full percentage point – and could lower them by end of 2027

Financial markets are wrong to predict the Bank of England will raise UK interest rates by a full percentage point or more by next summer, City economists believe.

According to market-implied interest rate expectations, the Bank is likely to raise interest rates at least four times over the next year, lifting the bank rate from 3.75% today to 4.75% by the end of July, and possibly to 5% – meaning five rises – by December 2027.

But a number of City experts believe such a sharp tightening cycle is unlikely, given there is little sign that the rise in energy costs is pushing up other prices sharply.

“If you look at the swaps market, and you look at what’s priced in for the Bank of England, you’ve got four rate hikes and then no cuts ever. And I think you’d be hard-pressed to find anybody that really agrees with that,” said James Smith, a developed markets economist at the Dutch bank ING.

“By next spring, I think they [the Bank] could be sounding the all clear, and by the end of next year they could be cutting rates again,” Smith told a briefing in the City last week.

Market-implied interest rates are calculated from the prices of a range of financial instruments, including derivatives such as “swaps”, to establish where traders think interest rates will be in future.

Economists cite several reasons why market-implied interest rates expectations are high. One is that these expectations have been closely correlated with oil prices since the Iran war began.

The higher oil prices have risen, the more rate increases have been priced in. An investor could be right that interest rates won’t rise as far as markets think, but if oil prices keep increasing in the meantime, they would face mark-to-market losses and potentially margin calls.

“It can get pretty painful, so a lot of traders are quite reluctant to take this risk until there’s greater certainty about energy supply and the extent of inflation this winter,” said Smith.

Many traders got burnt at the start of the current Middle East crisis, when most were positioned for further rate cuts this year, he said.

Sanjay Raja, the chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, also doubts that the Bank will raise rates as fast as the market pricing suggests.

“I do not believe that any mainstream forecaster thinks the Bank of England will hike to 5% by the end of next year with the information set we have today,” Raja said. “It’s not to say it won’t happen. But based on current projections, it seems less likely.”

He has calculated that a lot of the forecast interest rate rises is actually “baked-in risk premia” – where investors require an extra return to protect them from uncertainty or instability.

“Once we strip that out, we have estimated that there is only really ~50bps [half a percentage point] of hikes pencilled in,” he said.

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

Deutsche Bank’s base case is for the Bank of England to take the bank rate to 4.25% by next February and then hold rates there until the end of 2027.

The Bank of England is widely expected to raise interest rates to 4% at its next meeting, on 5 November, after UK inflation rose further above its target in September to 3.5%.

Last month Goldman Sachs said its probability-weighted forecast path for the bank rate remained “notably below market pricing”, although it does expect the Bank to raise rates to 4% next month.

Morgan Stanley’s base case is for rises in November and February, with rates on hold thereafter. But in a new research note, it suggests there could be additional pressure to raise interest rates if the Low Pay Commission recommends a larger increase in the national living wage than expected.

Oxford Economics, a consultancy, also thinks the UK rate-raising cycle will be much less pronounced than what is currently priced into financial markets.

“We forecast the [Bank’s] monetary policy committee will raise interest rates by 25bps [a quarter of a percentage point] at its November and February meetings, taking the bank rate to 4.25%. This is significantly below the peak in money market expectations, which currently point to the bank rate peaking between 4.75% and 5%,” they told clients last week.

Even Huw Pill, the Bank’s hawkish chief economist, has suggested market expectations are running too hot. He told an International Monetary Fund meeting in Bangkok this month he was sceptical that the Bank would need to raise interest rates four times over the next year.

#3072. Apple Watch Ultra 4 review: longer battery life but still awaiting new features

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Biggest Apple smartwatch gets better health tracking and new readiness tools with a battery and chip boost in preparation for controversial audio AI

As the Ultra enters its fourth year as Apple’s biggest and beefiest smartwatch it gets the best kind of spec upgrade – longer battery life – while waiting for something potentially more transformative.

That’s because several of the key features announced as part of Apple’s new smartwatch lineup for 2026 have yet to be enabled, awaiting updates towards the end of this year. That leaves the £749 (€899/$799/A$1,349) Apple Watch Ultra 4 the top dog, but basically the same as last year’s model.

The Ultra 4’s body, screen, colours and design are identical to the previous versions. It weighs about 1g more, but the bigger changes are on the back and inside.

Upgraded sensors on the back of the watch take heart rate (HR) readings every five seconds during the day, up from every five minutes on previous generation Apple Watches. They also enable the measurement of your heart rate variability (HRV) during the day, not only at night, which feeds into some new recovery metrics.

The Ultra 4 is the first Apple Watch in several generations to get a meaningfully faster chip with the new S11. The battery life for general use in my testing now stretches to 79 hours, too, meaning the watch lasted well into its third day between charges. Most will be able to charge it every third morning, or less if you use the low power modes, although that is far behind the week-plus stamina of top adventure watch rivals.

The new watch charges at 10W with its little magnetic puck, up from 5W of previous generations, and reached 82% in under an hour and 100% in less than 90 minutes.

Connectivity: Bluetooth 5.3, wifi 4, 5G RedCap/4G, UWB

Sensors: HR, ECG, spO2, temp, depth, dual-band GPS, compass, altimeter

The Apple Watch features some of the most comprehensive health tracking available on your wrist, which on the Ultra includes extremely accurate dual-band GPS tracking for exercise. The more frequent HR and HRV measurements enable a few new features for the Ultra 4. The Vitals app, which monitors your stats overnight, now works during the day giving you an assessment of your general health. It can let you know when your HR and HRV are outside your usual baseline, indicating strain or sickness that might be on the way.

The new readiness app adds a popular feature from sports watches, which looks at your activity, vitals and sleep and works out whether you have properly recovered from strenuous exercise or stressful days. It gives you a score out of 10 and some advice on how ready you are for exercise, which can be a useful tool for training for a race or goal.

The Ultra 4 runs watchOS 27, just like Apple Watches back to the Series 9 and Ultra 2, which includes Apple’s new Siri and improved AI tools, some of which are available now, while other exclusive features are awaiting updates planned for later this year.

The upgraded Siri is available to talk to and behaves very similarly to that on a modern iPhone, including the Siri app for reviewing previous interactions. The new Siri Modular watch face features the top timely widget, which has been surprisingly useful. It shows simple things such as the timer when you have one running, or the weather when it starts raining. It also puts your vitals front and centre in the morning, or your calendar if you have an upcoming event, replacing the need for multiple complications.

Shazam music recognition is now significantly faster, while the sound recognition accessibility feature, which listens out for certain sounds, such as a fire alarm, doorbell, car horn or baby crying, and sends an alert to your wrist could be very useful.

But the marquee “audio intelligence” features that could be transformative and controversial are not yet enabled, being expected in “late 2026”. Siri Recap promises to transcribe conversations all day before delivering them as an AI summary. It doesn’t record audio or keep full transcripts, just the text summaries, but the Live Rewind feature can show you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation so you can see what you missed.

Apple says the battery should last more than 1,000 full charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity and can be replaced for £95. Damage repairs cost £539.

The watch contains more than 45% recycled material, which is broken down in its environmental impact report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling for devices.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 comes in a choice of two colours and multiple bands costing from £749 (€899/$799/A$1,349).

For comparison, the Apple Watch Series 12 costs from £369, the Watch SE 3 costs £219 and the Garmin Fenix 9 costs from £860.

The Ultra 4 is the best smartwatch Apple makes. It has a great screen, rugged looks and all the trappings of other Apple Watches, including Apple Pay, comprehensive health tracking and full integration with an iPhone.

The faster charging and longer battery life are welcome, lasting about six hours more for general use than previous versions in testing. The more frequent heart rate readings and daytime heart rate variability monitoring are additive rather than revolutionary. The readiness and recovery monitoring add to the existing suite of training tools to close the gap to top-tier sports watches from Garmin and others.

Upgraded Siri is more useful on your wrist, and the new Siri Modular watch face was a surprisingly good addition. But the new audio intelligence features are not here yet.

That makes the Ultra 4 a great Apple Watch, just not a significant upgrade on those that came before.

Pros: great screen, rugged yet sophisticated design, hands-free gestures, three-plus-day battery life, 4G/5G and satellite SOS/messaging, comprehensive health tracking, great activity tracking with dual-band GPS, recovery/readiness tracking, better Siri, extra action button, 100-metre water resistance and 40-metre dive-ready, long software support.

Cons: no big upgrade on previous model, very expensive, only works with an iPhone, no third-party watch faces, shorter battery life than adventure watch rivals, marquee AI features not yet available.

#3073. The United States Just Got a New National Park For the First Time in Six Years

The US national park list is growing for the first time in nearly six years. Chiricahua National Monument, located in southeastern Arizona, was officially designated as the 64th national park in the US on October 20, 2026 following President Trump's signature on the Chiricahua National Park Act.

The new park lies just over an hour from the Arizona–New Mexico border and is nicknamed the “Wonderland of Rocks” for its towering rock spires and unusual formations, the result of a volcanic eruption about 27 million years ago.

Chiricahua was originally established as a national monument in 1924, and today boasts more than 17 miles of hiking trails for exploring on foot, as well as the Bonita Canyon Scenic Drive, a picturesque road that winds through rock formations.

For outdoors lovers, the designation is big news. The last US landmark to receive a new national park designation was West Virginia’s New River Gorge National Park & Preserve in 2020, home to one of the oldest rivers in the world and the deepest and longest river gorge in the Appalachians.

Chiricahua joins three existing national parks in Arizona: The Grand Canyon National Park in the north, Petrified Forest National Park in the northeast, and Saguaro National Park just under two hours west of Chiricahua near Tucson. If you're planning a trip to the newest US national park (or perhaps all four Arizona parks), here's what to know.

Chiricahua National Park is famous for its hoodoos and balancing rocks.

Chiricahua National Park is incredibly biodiverse thanks to its unique location in the Chiricahua Mountains between the Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts, an environment known as a “sky island.”

The park spans roughly 12,000 acres of grasslands, desert scrub, riparian, and pine woodlands, which means there is a huge variety of wildlife and habitat types to see and explore. Aside from the almost 200 species of birds, there are also over 70 species of mammals, 46 species of reptiles, and 8 species of amphibians. Keep an eye out for everything from banded rock rattlesnakes to cactus wrens, whitetail deer, and white-nosed coatis.

While immersing themselves in nature, visitors can also experience the areas's rich cultural history; the park is the ancestral home of the Chiricahua Apache and has ties to prehistoric Indigenous communities, Buffalo Soldiers, ranchers, and the Civilian Conservation Corps.

Visitors can experience the best of the park's offerings by taking the scenic drive to Massai Point, Echo Canyon, and Sugarloaf; hiking the 17 miles of wilderness trails through the rocky landscape; exploring the Faraway Ranch historic district, home to Swedish immigrants in the late 1800s; or stargazing in the area (did we mention it's an international dark sky park too?).

Because Chiricahua was already protected as a national monument, not much will change on the ground besides the new name (and updated signage). Guests can still camp in the park overnight, enjoy scenic drives through the volcanic landscape, go on hikes, and spot plenty of wildlife. For now, parking and the entrance fee to Chiricahua remain free, as they did before the new designation.

The largest impact will come from the increased attention that national park status will bring to the area. Based on a report done in 2018 by independent nonprofit research group Headwaters Economics, in reference to White Sands National Park's change in designation from a national monument in 2019, national parks often see higher visitation rates than national monuments, resulting in increased spending per visitor, and more overnight stays. That means visitors can anticipate higher tourism rates in and surrounding Chiricahua National Park in the near future—which could also lead to more crowds, traffic, and increased development in nearby towns.

Like many national parks, Chiricahua is remote, and doesn't have an overwhelming amount of accommodation options nearby. The nearest city to Chiricahua National Park is Willcox, Arizona, which is roughly 30–45 minutes away by car. Tucson (where guests from farther afoot will likely fly into) is about two hours away. There are a few smaller cities and towns—like Bisbee, Douglas, Portal, and Bowie—scattered within 100 miles of the park, but expect the drive from your accommodations to the park to be on the longer side. For those who want to sleep under the stars, you can camp directly in the park at the Bonita Canyon Campground.

#3074. So Far This Year, China Has Wasted Enough Clean Energy to Power Mexico

Power lines in Tianjin, China. Yucun Tang via Flickr

China is leading the world on renewable energy, last year installing more wind and solar capacity than every other country put together. But its buildout has unfolded at such a ferocious pace that China is now generating much more electricity than its power grid can handle, meaning that huge amounts of clean power are going unused.

When the grid is at capacity, operators must reject electricity from wind and solar plants to prevent overloads and blackouts. In the first six months of this year, China rejected 360 terawatt-hours of clean energy, enough to power Mexico for a year, according to a report from Global Energy Monitor and the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. “Had this electricity been absorbed, the additional power supply could have met all demand growth and allowed coal power generation to fall,” analysts said.

The problem, analysts say, is that China lacks the transmission infrastructure necessary to ferry its abundant clean energy from where it is generated to where it is needed. Also stymying the consumption of clean energy is a policy that guarantees the purchase of electricity from newly built coal power plants.

Despite a pledge to shift away from coal, China continues to permit and construct new generators. “Coal capacity is still growing because of legacy approvals and policy protections, even as plants run fewer hours and large volumes of clean electricity go unused,” said Qi Qin, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. The new report finds that China rejected 26.1 percent of its wind and solar output in the first half of this year, far more than official figures would suggest.

Other countries with large amounts of renewable energy are also dealing with wasted power. In India, clean power capacity just surpassed fossil fuel capacity for the first time, but transmission infrastructure has yet to catch up. On a single day in March, India wasted 34 gigawatt-hours of clean electricity, enough to power about 5 million homes, according to an analysis from the think tank Ember. The core of the problem, analysts said, “is a growing mismatch between the pace of renewable energy development and the readiness of the transmission infrastructure.”

As It Boosts Renewables, China Still Can’t Break Its Coal Addiction
