#3075. How I Got My Visa to France

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand showed me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”

I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

Well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.)

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:

The student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

But this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

Additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you plan to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

The paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

But does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

The gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

For this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this company, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.)

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:

I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment said the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

At the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

The worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most important things to have perfect on your application.

Once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.)

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

So, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other issues or questions, it’s important that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!

#3076. Large-scale single crystals printed layer by layer

Gregory S. Rohrer is in the Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania 15213, USA.

The dazzling gemstones used in jewellery are single crystals of minerals, prized for their beauty and uniformity. Single crystals of materials also have crucial functions in silicon microprocessors and jet-engine turbines. However, technological applications have been limited because such crystals are rare in nature and are difficult or expensive to make for most synthetic materials. The breakthrough reported in Nature by Liu et al.1 is therefore newsworthy: the authors have discovered a way to produce single crystals of metals in a wide range of shapes and sizes, including complex geometries that cannot be achieved by established crystal-growth methods. The method they used is a type of additive manufacturing — which means that it works like a 3D printer2 — and has the advantage of being implemented using readily available equipment.

#3078. Crayon Resist Snowflake Pictures

It’s freezing cold outside today, so we’ve been trying some indoor winter science activities. These crayon resist snowflake pictures have been a big hit, and they are very easy to create.

Younger children love to watch the images appear as they paint over them, but this activity is also a fun way for older children to learn about wax. Wax is a very useful material as it repels water and has a low melting point.

Draw a snowflake on the paper using the white crayon. You might need to press down hard. It can be a bit difficult to see what you’re drawing, but all will be revealed when you paint over the crayon.

Using the watercolour paint, gently paint over the crayon snowflakes. They should become visible as they are painted over.

The same technique works for leaving secret messages for friends or drawing other pictures.

Crayons are made from wax, which repels water. They are hydrophobic. As you paint over the crayon, the paint slides off.

Washable crayons are not quite as good for this activity as wax crayons, but they work well enough to make a good picture.

Wax has many properties that make it a very useful material.

Repels Water – as well as being used to waterproof clothing, wax is useful for coating machinery to protect it from oxygen and water, to prevent rust from forming.

Doesn’t conduct electricity – this means wax can be used to seal electrical parts.

Low melting point – wax melts easily, making it great for candles and for making moulds and crayons.

Malleable – wax is easy to shape, making it ideal for shaped candles and craft projects.

Wax is used in a lot of health and beauty products as it is slippery and so gives lipsticks and lip balms a texture that allows them to glide over the skin, as well as providing a protective barrier and glossy look.

Beeswax, carnauba and lanolin are examples of wax used in cosmetics.

Wax is often used to protect tablets from moisture and to make them easier to swallow.

Some fruits and vegetables are covered in a thin layer of edible wax to preserve them by reducing moisture loss.

Some cheeses are dipped in wax to preserve their freshness.

Gummy sweets often contain wax to stop them from sticking to each other and to give a shiny appearance.

#3079. Emirati-linked firms’ ownership of Manchester land ‘up 39%’ in ten years

Economic ties face scrutiny after scandal over Manchester City’s financial rules

‘That’s the way the city works’: how the UAE changed the face of Andy Burnham’s Manchester

Emirati-linked companies own almost 40% more land in Greater Manchester than a decade ago, Guardian analysis reveals, as the city’s economic ties face scrutiny after Manchester City’s financial rules scandal.

The number of land titles in Greater Manchester owned by United Arab Emirates-linked companies increased from 51 in 2016 to 168 in 2026, equivalent to a 39% rise in the total area owned in a decade, from 73 to 101 hectares (180 to 250 acres).

Among them, there are at least 34 land titles currently owned by Manchester City FC’s owner Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan through one of his companies. That includes the Etihad Stadium, as well as properties in Ancoats and New Islington, among others. In total, two-thirds of the Emirati-owned land in Greater Manchester as of 2026 was owned by one of Mansour’s companies.

Andy Burnham has faced weeks of scrutiny over the Manchester City FC cheating scandal after he appeared to initially sympathise with City’s owners, who he described as a “huge partner in the building of modern Manchester”, and said that he would be “really concerned” if they sold the club.

The prime minister has been urged to reveal all of his meetings with Manchester City’s owners after he initially said he had one “significant” meeting with the Abu Dhabi executives only for five other meetings to come to light.

The scale of UAE investments in Manchester has been revealed by the Guardian after Manchester City were found guilty of an “unprecedented” nine-year breach of financial rules under the current ownership. The analysis shows that while there has been strong growth in land ownership, Emirati money is only one part of the foreign investment that has helped drive Manchester’s recent economic success.

Prof Jonathan Silver, a University of Sheffield researcher who has analysed Manchester’s deals with Abu Dhabi, said the growing buy-up of land and property by Emiratis raised “major concerns about the fragility of the ‘Manchester model’ and its reliance on attracting flows of international finance, whatever the cost”.

He added: “This is not ‘just a football story’ but rather a story of a city-region in northern England aligning its economy into the orbit of an authoritarian state in the Gulf, accused of human rights abuses at home and terrible war crimes in Sudan.

“It’s put city leaders in a position in which they celebrate the radical democratic history of Manchester but act against such traditions in the present, all justified by the demands of economic growth.”

The total stock of all foreign investment in Greater Manchester increased by 25% between 2015 and 2024. Looking at the most recent investments only, the latest ONS data shows that the north-west received the highest net foreign investment in 2024 of any region outside London. Greater Manchester received almost £2bn net from overseas entities that year, the highest city region after London, Edinburgh and the south-east of Scotland, and Cardiff.

Although published ONS data does not specify investments in Greater Manchester by the UAE, other figures suggest that it is a relatively small contributor overall. Asian countries outside Japan made up less than 5% of the total stock of foreign investment in the city region at the end of 2024. A further 10% was from UK offshore islands – through which some Emirati money may have flowed.

At the end of 2024, the total stock of foreign direct investment from the United Arab Emirates accounted for just 0.3% of all foreign investments in the UK.

Although UAE investment in the country is small, it is growing. Property experts say the UK has seen a surge in demand from international investors in recent years, with buyers in the UAE, the wider Middle East and Europe said to be the fastest-growing markets.

The rise in the amount of land owned by Emirati-linked corporations in Greater Manchester has been mostly driven by UAE-based companies other than those owned by Mansour. That includes 15 titles owned by the Abu Dhabi government – most of which were acquired as part of their purchase of Circle Health Group, including Alexandra hospital in Cheadle, Highfield hospital in Rochdale and Beaumont hospital in Bolton.

Other wealthy Emirati investors include Dr Ali Saeed Al Ameri, a Gulf oil executive, who owns £1.3m worth of apartments through a company registered in the British Virgin Islands, which is famed for its corporate secrecy.

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

Another is the multimillionaire property mogul Mohammed Ahmad Aldallal, who develops luxury homes in Dubai while owning at least £10m worth of comparatively unglamorous buildings in Bolton, Oldham and Manchester.

These include Oldham’s historic Grand Theatre, where the Beatles are said to have performed, which he demolished last year to make way for an 11-storey apartment block. Aldallal, who comes from a line of super-rich property developers, said last year it was a “great honour” to invest in Oldham, where he spent seven years at college and “almost every day” at Riley’s snooker club, which was based in the now-demolished Grand Theatre.

Separate Guardian analysis of public contracts from all Greater Manchester-based public bodies – including NHS trusts – shows that £84.4m was spent on firms ultimately owned in the UAE between 2016 and 2026. Of that 85% was NHS spending on Circle Health Group, which was ultimately taken over by the UAE government in 2024.

The figures – from the public sector market intelligence firm Tussell – show Manchester city council spent £6.3m on UAE-backed companies, more than half of which went to Manchester City Football Club.

Leader of the Manchester city council Garry Bridges said: “I came to Manchester in 2005 and it is inarguable that the city is in better shape now than it was then, and unrecognisable from the city of the 80s and 90s.

“Ancoats in particular was a derelict, largely abandoned neighbourhood and one which the council was committed to regenerating for some time. To suggest that the story has been anything but positive from a regeneration point of view is ludicrous.”

The Guardian analysis combines data from the Land Registry and Companies House to track ownership of land between 2016 and 2026. There is no information on beneficial owners of companies before April 2016.

It includes land titles that are owned by companies based in the UAE and titles whose beneficial owners are the Abu Dhabi government or Emirati nationals based in the UAE. The analysis does not include land owned directly by individuals as this information is not publicly available.

Additional reporting by George Francis Lee

#3081. Delicious Oaxaca City, MEX: My Favorite Centro Restaurants, Food & Tacos…for $1-20USD per person

I have no idea how I lost weight while in Oaxaca, Mexico for two months, because I made strong work of trying so much of the amazing food in Oaxaca! And it’s often so cheap to eat amazing food if you stay out of the tourist traps. (Many of the tacos on this list are under $1USD each!) But before we dig in to my favorite places to eat in Oaxaca, you need to understand why Oaxaca is such a big deal.

Oaxaca City is renowned for its rich culinary traditions and diverse flavors. It’s often considered the gastronomic capital of Mexico, partly because of the indigenous Zapotec and Mixtec flavors, combined with Spanish and other international influences.

This site participates in the Amazon Services LLC Associates Program and other affiliate programs and may earn from qualifying purchases.

The markets in Oaxaca City are full of vibrant produce, spices, and traditional, local ingredients. Mercado Benito JuÃ¡rez and Mercado 20 de Noviembre are popular spots where you can immerse yourself in the food culture. But don’t forget that any Mercado in Oaxaca is worth visiting and sampling.

Just a heads-up on a couple of terms you need to know when talking Mexico. “Centro” means literally central, or center. And typically it’s where everything happens.

A “Zocalo” is literally “the public square or plaza of a Mexican city or town,” and if it’s significant, it’s also often right in the middle of the touristy area.

Zocalos can be massive (Mexico City) or pretty tiny (Queretaro), but the Zocalo in Oaxaca is about the size of a good city block and full of festivities nomatter the time of year!

READ NEXT: Queretaro, Mexico: Centro Restaurants & Foodâ¦for $2-20USD/meal!The Prettiest F*cking Sintra, Portugal Travel Guide Youâve Ever SeenâAKA: Isnât It Romantiâ¦cism?

Oaxaca is famous for its rich and complex mole sauces, which come in different types like mole negro (dark mole), mole coloradito (red mole, and my favorite so far), and mole verde (green mole). These sauces are typically made from a blend of chilies, nuts, seeds, herbs, and spices, resulting in a symphony of flavors, and you can find them pretty much everywhere.

Another Oaxacan specialty is tlayudas, which are like large, crispy tortillas topped with a variety of ingredients such as beans, meat, cheese, and salsa. They are often enjoyed as a snack or a main dish and offer a delicious combination of textures and flavors.

Or after a night out to soak up some alcohol. I’m not a huge fan, since they tend to be more bread than I care for (#type1diabetes), but they’re a staple.

Oaxaca city is also known for street food, but then again, that goes for most Mexican cities. You can find tamales, empanadas, memelas, and quesadillas being freshly prepared and sold by street vendors at any hour of the day. If you’re up for it, try chapulinesâtoasted grasshoppers seasoned with lime and spicesânot my jam, but when in Rome?

Word to the wise, make sure you see a lot of washing of dishes with (semi-) fresh, filtered water around the food stands. And going earlier is always better than later from a tum-tum danger zone standpoint.

Oaxaca is also famous for its mezcal. The traditional Mexican spirit is made from agave plants and offers a smoky and complex flavor profile. Mezcal tasting tours and visits to mezcal distilleries are popular, but there is also an opportunity on nearly every block in centro to step into a Mezcaleria and sample from around the state.

The Mexican Peso has been averaging around $17-20MXN per $1USD in recent years. For my calculations, I like to use a rounded-up figure of $20MXN/1USD. It’s just easier, and we’re only talking $.05-.10 difference here.

Now, here comes the math part (nerd alert!) that I do in my head. I take the cost in MXN pesos, drop the zero, and divide by two to estimate the USD equivalent.

Let’s say something costs $200MXN. I drop the zero, divide by two, and it comes to around $10USD. For instance, a hearty egg/veggie torta (with cheese, of course) priced at $50MXN, which is the size of my head, will only set me back about $2.50USD. Now that’s what I call eating well without breaking the bank in the Mexican neighborhood my friend!

Check out the newest Lonely Planet Mexico (Travel Guide) check price

My travel style is definitely more budget-minded, but without feeling like Iâm crushing my and eating goals.

My daily spend (all-inclusive) was less than $63/day for almost two months as a digital nomad in Oaxaca.

I only spent about $13/day on average for eating out and fresh groceries from mercados and local stores for eating in! I usually have coffee and work 2-4 hours in the AM before eating a big brunch/lunch, then have a late dinner. The portions are typically huge, so really two-three meals a day is beyond plenty!

Now, take this with a grain of salt, since there was no way for me to visit every food stand or restaurant in Centro Oaxaca! But did try a lot of different places in the two months while I was there! When it comes down to it, my list of best food and restaurants in Oaxaca comes with a healthy balance of reasons:

READ NEXT: Queretaro, Mexico: Centro Restaurants & Foodâ¦for $2-20USD/meal!Jaw-Dropping Images Of Pena Palace & Gardens in Sintra, Portugal

Again, tacos are a dime a dozen (ok, not literally…), but I tried a lot of different places that were top rated. There are quite a few Oaxaca taco spots here, all worth trying. And since you can eat at each of them for easily less than $5-10 totalâless than $1 a taco usuallyâwhy wouldn’t you try them all?

Oh, I do prefer vegetarian, but all bets were off and I took full advantage of trying all the meats as it came to tacos in Oaxaca!

This joint does one thing: Tacos De Lechonâslow-roasted pork tacos, tostadas or tortas with salsa verde and pickled jalapeÃ±os (on the side). 4-5 tacos or 2 tostadas or 1 tortas will do you, and eating them with a cerveza on their gorgeous, plant covered patio is fantastic. They have a huge tree right in the middle! Make sure you try their desserts too.

What to eat at Taqueria Ta’ BihuiTheir slow roasted pork also comes in  “chicharron” variety, which adds kind of a crispy texture to the meal. So definitely try the tacos in both styles!

Tacos Roy is the closest to a “chain” on this list, but they are definitely good tacos. Many swear by the El Pastor tacos, but I was actually a bigger fan of the Carnitas. Almost every taco on their menu is around a $1, but oddly the vegetarian tacos were $1.50? Regardless, in and out and with a full stomach of tacos for under $5 ain’t bad.

What to eat at Tacos Roy Restaurant in OaxacaEl Pastor tacos are all the rage, but try the carnitas, and the Gringo if you’re nasty.

This food stand in only serves one type of taco: tacos de tasajo. Hey, when your one thing is this good, don’t screw with it. For less than $1 a taco, it’s the best taco deal I found in Oaxaca. Make sure you add all the toppings too, like pickled onions, cilantro, and salsa, since that’s where the “authentic” way of eating mexican tacos is at!

What to eat at Tacos Del Llanno Food TruckStraight up just a bunch of tacos de tasajo. Start with 3 (you don’t pay till you’re completely done) and go back for a couple more…and a couple more…

Maybe one of my favorite taco spots overall, ever. This tiny vegan taco restaurant is only maybe 10’x15ft, with room for 6-7 to sit while the two owners take care of cooking everything from scratch right in front of you.

This place serves their delicately crafted vegan tacos with love and care, but the tastes are out of this world.

What to eat at Herbivora VeganTry them all, because you can do it for about $1.50 a taco…but make sure you have the fried potato tacos. Wow.

Easily the fanciest and more expensive on my list, Humar Seafood is more of a middle-high dining taco or seafood spot. But the beer-battered tacos are delicious and the presentation is off the hook. All while sitting next to an open door out to the street while comfortably inside their trendy spot on the outskirts of Centro.

What to eat at Humar Seafood in OaxacaRaved as one of the best restaurants in Oaxaca for beer-battered cod tacos. Get those and whatever else your budget will afford you on a splurge kind of night!

Never got to try this taco stand personally, but my friends swore by it. It’s hit or miss as to when it shows up on the corner it’s supposed to, so good luck!

With tacos out of the way, we’ll back up to the most important meal of the day. These are some of the best breakfast restaurants I found in Oaxaca.

This place is legit, and definitely one of the best restaurants in Oaxaca. Chain across the door because it fills up and sometimes has a line, but super quaint and chill on the inside. The breakfast sandwiches are the size of your head and plenty to share. Granola bowls that are Instagram ready. Baked goods that will make you close your eyes and moan…in a public space. (Raises hands slowly…)

What to eat at Onnno Loncheria Restaurant in OaxacaThe breakfast sandwich. If there are multiple options, the one I’m recommending had their fresh baked bread, an egg crepe filled and folded with cheddar cheese, avocado, etc. Amazeballs. Bolus early if that’s your jam.

Another tiny breakfast joint that is hard to spot from the outside. This place felt trendy and was a little more pricey, but we’re really only talking about an extra dollar or two at the end of the day.

What to eat at Yegole CafeAgain, the breakfast sandwich on a buttery, melt-in-your-mouth brioche bun. The only sandwich I had served on brioche in my 2 months in Oaxaca, and it stood out.

Gluck is a super vibey and trendy vegetarian/vegan restaurant in Oaxaca, but it’s so approachable and the two staff that are usually on put a lot of care into everything. And the little notes that accompany the coffees or plates delivery a tiny, thoughtful message to help improve your day. Bravo.

What to eat at GlÃ¼ck Vegetarian in OaxacaThe avocado toast is off the hook. It has red beet spread and chia seeds and is simply amazing. Yeah, those things sound weird, but trust me; worth it. Lots of good vegetarian options to pick from.

READ NEXT: Mexico: Murals & Street Art of Oaxaca â A Bakerâs Dozen of Badass #04Queretaro, Mexico: Centro Restaurants & Foodâ¦for $2-20USD/meal!

What a cool space Centro GastronÃ³mico De Oaxaca is. When you enter, you’re greeted with this contemporary structure with small food stand eateries scattered throughout the bottom. Up top there are even more small stands with a stage and central eating area. Tons of food options on the cheap, especially on the weekends when it’s a little busier.

Centro GastronÃ³mico De Oaxaca also hosts cooking classes, food workshops, and culinary events. These things help visitors learn about traditional cooking techniques and heritage of the Oaxaca region. Definitely make a stop here!

I had the tamales from the stand right inside the main door for about $1 per tamale!

This Italian restaurant was an unexpected surprise. I was walking about with a friend and we realize we were hangry and looked around to see what was near. Sicilia Pizza Y Pasta had great reviews, so we went. It’s a super quaint spot on a fairly loud and busy street with only about 4-5 tables inside.

What to get at Sicilia Pizza Y Pasta Restaurant in OaxacaThe bruschetta, hands down. One of the tastiest I’ve tried, and I try a lot of bruschetta! We also had a pizza, which was giant and delicious. I’m guessing it’s hard to go wrong with anything here!

I ate here three times, the third being a complete throw-down for two where we filled an entire four-seat table with food and drinks! Herba Dolche is easily one of the best restaurants in Oaxaca, and the reviews prove it. The experience is amazing, and the foundation and ethics behind the restaurant and the food speak loads. From the Herba Dolce website:

We offer plant-based food, we cook with ingredients from local trade and clean cultivation. A completely deindustrialized restaurant, we prepare everything from the base, without accelerating cooking or fermentation processes. No added sugars and oils.

Beautiful setting, amazing visual plating of every dish or drink, and top notch food and flavors. It presents like a lot of fine dining restaurants, but without the pretentiousness. Do it.

What to eat at Herba Dolce Restaurant in OaxacaTo drink, try the tepache, a fermented pineapple-based drink. Then try the Inked Huitlacoche mushrooms on tostadas, the Pibil mushroom tacos, Ceviche, and any of the soups.

Huitlacoche, also known as corn smut, is like the “Mexican truffle” of the corn world. It has a deep, earthy taste. It’s often used in quesadillas, tacos, soups, and tamales. It’s considered a delicacy in Mexico.

Casa Taviche is a little more of a spend, but still, not too bad. It’s a nice little sit-down restaurant with plants everywhere and a quaint little bar area. The presentation of the food and drinks is beautiful, and the food was delicious.

What to eat at Casa Taviche Restaurant in OaxacaTry any of the salads. They’re also known for their mole, so never a bad thing to try wherever you go in Oaxaca!

If you love plants, you’ll love Muss Cafe. But here’s the trick; there’s a tiny coffee shop off the street, but you have to go past that, through the courtyard, and up three flights of stairs to the real magic. That’s where you’ll find the rooftop terrace at Muss Cafe, completely enveloped in floor to ceiling plants.

One of the best coffee shops in Oaxaca I found for just sitting and writing and reflecting.

Check out the newest Lonely Planet Mexico (Travel Guide) check price

Not one of the best cups of coffee ever, but the atmosphere at Boogie Cafe in Oaxaca is my jam. Two little indoor library/lounge areas complete with cats sprawled out wherever they please. And there’s a nice rooftop as well, so make sure you grab a drink and head up there in the evening when it’s cooling off.

Yep, GlÃ¼ck is back on the list. Possibly some of the best brewed lattes I had in Oaxaca, and the presentation alone is worth the trip. Delicious coffee with a bit of inspiration? Yes please.

This small coffee and pastry shop near the city center in Oaxaca gets you out of the tourist madness on a busy day. Delicious pastries and plenty of drink options in a cute little space.

Easily up top for the best bakery in Oaxaca City, Mexico. The have a cafe/restaurant that you can sit down at, but you can also just swing through their pastry counter if you’re out exploring the city. Breads, pastries, quiches, and tons of delicious desserts. Go nuts.

I fell in love with Son De Aqui on my first night in Oaxaca. A bunch of new friends met up there and we spent an hour or so sipping drinks while watching the sun set over the city. It’s a cool artsy space with really expensive art, but this cool rooftop bar area. In the later evenings a DJ sets up spinning chill beats and a local food artisan sets up to cook Oaxacan dishes.

Son De Aqui is easily one of the best places to watch a sunset in Oaxaca. Beautiful views of the city day or night…but especially night!

What to have at Son De Aqui Rooftop Terrace in OaxacaTry the local Kombuchas. Some of the best I’ve had, and they’re made locally. I even reached out to the maker and purchased some quarts at a much better cost than what you pay at a restaurant or bar! Or Mezcal is always a good option since it originates in Oaxaca!

This little spot will hold memories for me for years, since I visited with a group of about 15-20 friends and we packed the tiny 15’x15′ room where the live music is. (And 15×15 is generous!) Great memories. And being so close to the local musicians is such a nice vibe.

Oaxaca, Mexico, is a feast for the sensesâfull of color, culture, and ridiculously good food. If you’re thinking about traveling there, here are some details to help you plan your trip like a pro.

Oaxaca City is tucked down in southern Mexico, about a six-hour drive (or a quick flight) southeast of Mexico City. Itâs the capital of the state of Oaxaca, which is a hotspot for culture, landscapes, and mole.

Oaxacaâs got altitudeâabout 5,000 feet above sea level to be exact. That means cooler nights and mild days, even though itâs technically in the tropics. Youâll get warm days (80Â°F/27Â°C in summer), crispy cool nights in winter, and a rainy season (MayâOctober) where it usually just dumps rain for a bit in the afternoon before clearing up. Pack layers and maybe a lightweight rain jacket, especially if you’re going in the rainy season.

Of course that depends on your travel style, but here is the lowdown:

If youâre flying in, XoxocotlÃ¡n International Airport (OAX) is your spot. Itâs a small airport, about 30 minutes from the city center. (You book get a cheap shuttle from the airport…) There are direct flights from Mexico City, Monterrey, and even some U.S. cities. For a more adventurous vibe, long-distance buses from places like Puebla or Mexico City are affordable and surprisingly comfy.

Once youâre in the city, youâre golden. Oaxacaâs super walkable, especially in the historic center where most of the action is. If youâre heading out to nearby spots like Monte AlbÃ¡n or Hierve el Agua, you can book a rountrip tour.

There you go. Results from my exhaustive âresearchâ from living as a digital nomad in Oaxaca, Mexico for over two months! I loved my time there, experiencing the kind people, culture…and food! Iâll be back!

Jason is the author of “The Beginner Traveler’s Guide” as well as the voice behind the words and the eye behind the lens for The Nomad Experiment. “Planning to travel at some point” wasn’t actually getting the job done, so nearing 40 he decided to make it a priority, nomatter how scary that was. A few years laterâthrough the pandemic and a type 1 diabetes diagnosis at age 42ânow living a life of nomadic travel, he’s speaking out to encourage others of any age, or with any serious medical diagnosis, to live an unconventional life.

Figure out where you are going & how are you getting there…I suggest using at least 2 to 3 different travel search sites. Start with Skyscanner or Orbitz or Booking …or whatever aggregator site you prefer. Then when you see what airlines to use, check their respective sites for better deals or rewards flights.

Figure out where you’re going to stay…If you’re interested in hostels, search Hostelworld or Hostelling International. For longer-term or more private digs, look at Airbnb, VRBO, colivings, or you can look for hotel rooms in the links from the search engines listed above.

Get comprehensive travel insurance, or in the least, travel medical insurance if internationally…Especially with COVID not going anywhere, you need travel medical insurance nomatter what! Start with an insurance aggregator or with SafetyWing,Â World Nomads, or another. Then decide what is important to you; trip cancellation, baggage coverage, medical, or all of the above. And get a yearly evacuation plan, since you’ll have to get home after your emergency!Â

#3082. Websites across world hit by millions of attempts to exploit PHP code flaw

Problem in language that underpins 70% of sites has led governments and companies to pull sites offline to patch fault

Tell us: have you been affected by the PHP code flaw?

What is PHP, and how bad is the computer language flaw causing website shutdowns globally?

Websites around the world have been hit by millions of attempts to exploit a recently discovered vulnerability in their code, cybersecurity companies have said, as the US warned the flaw could allow attackers to take control of web servers, steal data and disrupt services.

The problem in the PHP programming language, which underpins about 70% of the world’s websites, emerged on Wednesday causing governments and companies to pull their websites off the internet before they could be attacked and so they could patch the fault.

In the UK, 32 government services had been taken offline, the cybersecurity minister, Liz Lloyd, told parliament. She said this “largely resulted from precautionary measures” while updates were applied. Downing Street said no public-facing critical services had been affected and “some limited services may be temporarily offline” but this did not mean they had been hacked.

The website for the BBC’s Traitors was one of those that was down on Thursday, while the government declined to name the affected sites, saying services were being reviewed, updated and coming back online. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) sent out 50,000 alerts to affected organisations, but said it had no reports of successful hacks as a result of the flaw. Other sites reportedly temporarily affected included the Internet Archive, Wikipedia and 4Chan.

The vulnerability sparked particular concern about the ongoing vulnerability of systems used by schools, local governments and charities, which may not have dedicated cybersecurity support to execute the fix. The NCSC said the scale of the vulnerability was “unprecedented” and the patch would not work for some organisations running older systems, and these would have to be replaced. The British Chambers of Commerce, which represents thousands of employers, said it was not yet causing firms any significant difficulties.

Ciaran Martin, the former chief executive of the NCSC, described the flaw as “very bad”, saying that while most internet software vulnerabilities did not matter, this was “the most serious vulnerability discovered for five years”. The former GCHQ chief David Omand warned that Russia and China could look to exploit the bug.

However, Ryan Austin, a researcher at the cybersecurity company Calif, who was key to discovering the flaw, said: “At the moment it doesn’t look like exploitation has taken off or been widespread.”

The flaw prompted governments into action, with the US National Security Agency saying it could allow attackers to seize control of web servers, steal sensitive data, disrupt services and move deeper into a network. Government websites were quickly taken down so the patch could be installed with many coming back on line soon afterwards.

In an update overnight on Wednesday, and into Thursday, Matthew Prince, the chief executive of the cybersecurity business CloudFlare, said the company encountered tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the weakness in the 45 minutes after the problem was announced, rising to “hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now”.

Amazon Threat Intelligence, another cybersecurity company, said PHP2Shell, as the vulnerability is known, was “now being broadly exploited in the wild” and it had identified several attempts from multiple actors to test ways to capitalise on the vulnerability before the fix was released by the PHP developers on Wednesday.

CloudFlare also said that in the 10 hours before the vulnerability was publicly announced, it saw thousands of attempts to exploit it, amid concern over the handling of the alert. One cybersecurity expert, Prof Alan Woodward, said the flaw was revealed a day before the patch was released, and that “somebody let the cat out of the bag”.

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

The PHP vulnerability could allow hostile actors to “grab the resources” of exposed sites, said Michał Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert. A website, such as Slack or Wikipedia, has access to computing power, servers, and IP addresses which locate it on the internet. In many cases, this infrastructure is managed and mediated by PHP.

Criminal groups, state-sponsored hackers, or crypto miners might “nest” themselves into exposed sites using this PHP vulnerability, and then exploit those resources for their own aims. A hacking group could use an exposed site’s IP address to launch attacks that could not then be traced back to it. Crypto miners could use a server’s computing power to run their energy-intensive calculations for free.

It was unclear at what scale this has been done, said Woźniak, and many sites would not even be aware of it.

Wiz, one of the research organisations that uncovered the vulnerabilities, said it was arguably among the most severe software vulnerabilities ever discovered. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” it said in a blogpost. “Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”

“Cyber-actors are likely to weaponise PHP2Shell,” the NSA said. “These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across US government departments and agencies.”

The government of South Korea said on Thursday it was activating emergency response measures, raising its private sector cybersecurity alert level and issuing guidance to tens of thousands of companies on how to fix the problem.

China’s industry ministry urged organisations to immediately inspect their systems and upgrade to the latest secure version of PHP, and recommended strengthening cybersecurity monitoring, changing passwords and keys. The prime minister of Japan encouraged businesses and organisations to patch the vulnerability – or shut down their sites.

#3083. Japan is Making it Harder for Non-Citizens to Become Permanent Residents

Tourists from around the world continue to flock to Japan’s bustling megacities and quiet onsen towns, generating a record-setting (and sometimes unmanageable) influx of travelers: an increase from 25.1 million in 2023 to 42.7 million in 2025, according to the country’s tourism board. In the face of this boom, Japan is setting more boundaries with visitors, including levying an increased tourist tax and, as of October 1, making it harder for non-citizens to obtain residence status.

The number of foreign residents in Japan reached a record 3.96 million people in June 2025, prompting Japan’s immigration agency to tighten its eligibility guidelines for the country's permanent residency permit, which is available to foreign workers who have continuously lived in Japan for at least 10 years. The new rules are just one part of a larger framework of policies adopted by the Japanese government on January 23, 2026 called the “Comprehensive Measures for the Acceptance and Orderly Coexistence of Foreign Nationals.”

The government says the policies are designed to address “anxieties and feelings of unfairness felt by some citizens as the number of foreign residents increases,” Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi wrote in a September 26 post on X. That means applicants to Japan's foreign residence permit will soon face stricter language proficiency requirements, more expensive fees, and a higher income threshold.

If you're pursuing permanent residency or a long-term stay in Japan, here's what you need to know.

The new requirements dictate that applicants must earn more than the average Japanese household income (which was about $36,350 per year in 2024, according to a survey by the country’s health, labor, and welfare ministry). In addition, applicants must now show pension benefits that match what they would have received after 30 years in the country’s employee pension program. (If the applicant falls short on the pension requirement, the guidelines say they can supplement with additional “financial assets," but does not provide specifics beyond that.)

The government also announced a dramatic 20-fold hike in the application fee, which is now 20,000 yen, or about $1,260. That said, the cost is still relatively affordable compared to permanent residency-related applications in countries like the UK, which cost 3,226 British pounds (about $4,261), and the US, which can cost upwards of $10,000, according to Arton.

Qualifying for Japan's permanent residency visa isn't just about financial eligibility. Applicants will also need a proficient understanding of the Japanese language, which the guidelines define as at or above a B1 level on the Japanese-Language Proficiency Test; however, it’s not yet clear how applicants will be asked to demonstrate their language ability.

The income changes will retroactively affect applications filed from April 2026. Other changes, such as the pension requirement, will be implemented starting April 1, 2027.

“For Americans thinking of making Japan their long-term home, the message is clear: financial security alone is no longer enough,” Armand Arton, CEO of citizenship firm Arton Capital, tells Condé Nast Traveler. “Applicants must also demonstrate a genuine commitment to living and working in the country, as well as integrating into Japanese society.”

To apply, you need to have lived in Japan for 10 continuous years, with at least five of those years under a work or residence visa. If you’ve been out of the country for more than six consecutive months without a “reasonable” justification, or for a total of two-and-a-half years over the decade, your application could receive “negative” marks.

That said, there are exceptions to the 10-year rule: For example, if you’ve been deemed a “highly skilled foreign professional” or if you’ve been married to a Japanese resident for at least five years (and your spouse has lived in the country for at least three continuous years).

Japan doesn’t want new residents who will bounce in and out of the country, but rather those who will commit to building a life locally: “It’s offering quality of life and cultural immersion, rather than passport power and access,” says Arton.

If you meet these payment, income, language, and residency requirements, you can submit your application to a local immigration office in Japan. Applicants should prepare documents such as a copy of your health insurance card and proof that you’ve paid your resident taxes on time (through means such as providing a copy of your bank passbook)

After everything has been submitted, expect a four-to-six-month processing timeline (all form and application details are available at Japan’s immigration agency website).

If you don’t meet the requirements for a permanent residency permit, Japan offers several temporary relocation pathways.

If you’re deemed a “highly skilled professional” who will drive the local economy and academic research, you could get a five-year highly skilled professional residence visa. If you work as an entertainer, a chef specializing in an international cuisine, or in one of the other qualifying industries, you could apply for a working visa, which lasts between three months and five years. (You can check whether you qualify for the highly skilled professional or work visa by checking the evaluation guidelines on Japan’s immigration services website.)

If you have Japanese ancestry, consider applying for a long-term resident visa, which grants you between six months and five years in the country. Or, if you work remotely and want to stay in Japan for six months, the digital nomad visa may be the best fit.

A comprehensive list of all of Japan’s visas is available on its foreign affairs ministry website.

#3085. In Australia, a Home Battery Boom Has Helped Cut Wholesale Power Prices in Half

A little more than one year ago, Australia rolled out a program to heavily subsidize home batteries, part of a larger effort to make use of the huge volumes of solar energy that were going to waste. On Friday, officials announced that more than 500,000 batteries had been installed under the plan, helping to slash wholesale power prices roughly in half.

Energy Minister Chris Bowen said that Australia now has more home batteries than the United States, which has a population 12 times larger. “This is a story of global significance that Australian households have achieved,” Bowen said in a press conference.

Australia is the world leader in rooftop solar, with panels installed on more than one in three households, the highest rate of adoption globally. But abundant solar power has created a new dilemma as the grid faces a surge of electricity from connected rooftop arrays. Power prices plunge. Centralized power plants are forced offline, threatening grid stability. And much of that solar power goes to waste.

The government has moved to make use of this surplus solar energy, including by offering free power in the early afternoon to homeowners in Queensland, New South Wales, and South Australia, regardless of whether they have solar panels on their roof or not. The goal is to spur more consumers to run appliances or charge electric vehicles during this window.

With its home battery subsidy program, launched in July 2025, the government is aiming to help households use more solar energy by providing a 30 percent discount on residential battery systems connected to solar arrays.

The subsidy program has spurred a boom in installations. Australia is on track to more than double its home battery capacity this year, Bloomberg reports. The program has also been a boon to the grid. By relying on batteries in the early evening, when demand peaks, homeowners are reducing the need for utilities to fire up additional power plants during those hours, which is helping to lower costs for other ratepayers, officials say.

The subsidy program has been “the major factor in the wholesale price of energy falling in Australia by 47 percent in the last 12 months,” Bowen said. “Australia is one of the very, very few countries in the world which is reducing wholesale prices in the midst of a global energy crisis.”

#3086. How Do Snowflakes Form?

Did you know that no two snowflakes are the same? Snowflakes all take slightly different paths to the ground as they form, which is why each one is unique.

Snowflakes start with a tiny speck of pollen or dust floating in a cloud that acts as a seed. When a very cold water droplet hits the seed, it freezes to form a tiny ice crystal.

This happens over and over again to form a six-sided shape. As the hexagon snowflake moves around in the cloud, it bumps into more water vapour, which freezes onto the corners of the hexagon to form the arms of the snowflake. The shape of a snowflake depends on the condition of the air.

The largest snowflake ever recorded was in Montana in 1887. The huge snowflakes were reported to be 38 inches wide!!!

Snowflakes fall at a speed of 1-4 miles per hour.

Each snowflake is made from approximately 1,000,000,000,000,000,000 (one quintillion) water molecules.

A snowflake is about 90% air and 10% ice!!

#3088. Nationwide to slash 275 jobs in latest round of cuts since takeover of Virgin Money

Exclusive: Bosses tell staff cuts part of effort to ‘simplify’ operations and ‘remove duplication’ across wider workforce

Nationwide building society is slashing another 275 jobs in the latest round of cuts since bank bosses pushed through a £2.9bn takeover of Virgin Money.

Bosses made the announcement to staff on Wednesday, saying it was part of efforts to simplify the bank’s operations and “remove duplication” after absorbing thousands of staff in to the group’s wider workforce.

The cuts are to fall across its retail division, including those working on mortgages, as well as in HR, the chief operating officer’s office, customer operations, communications and finance.

Nationwide said no customer-facing staff would be affected, which appears to be in line with its pledge to keep its 700 branches open until at least 2030.

It follows closely behind the last round of job losses, which were announced in June and affected 600 staff.

Commenting on the latest cuts, a spokesperson for the lender said: “As we integrate Virgin Money into Nationwide, we’re making a limited number of changes. No customer-facing colleagues are at risk and we’re supporting those affected, including through retraining and redeployment.”

The Virgin Money takeover was a boon for the building society sector when it was first announced two years ago, having marked a rare moment when a member-owned lender – traditionally focused on mortgages and savings – was snapping up a commercial high street bank. However, the move also proved controversial, with Nationwide having refused to give members a vote on the deal.

Virgin Money had more than 7,000 staff around the time Nationwide formalised its takeover in late 2024, when the building society had about 18,000 of its own employees, according to its 2025 annual report. Its total workforce now sits at roughly 27,000 today.

Executives had confirmed back in 2024 that there would be “limited workforce changes” to deal with overlapping roles but that they would undergo a formal review of its employee base in the years that followed.

A Nationwide spokesperson stressed that the cuts were not linked to any growing use of AI.

#3089. Anthropic sued for allegedly using 274 Elvis Presley songs to train AI models

Authentic Brands Group says AI company infringed on rights of songs by the King such as Can’t Help Falling in Love

The owners of Elvis Presley’s music catalogue are suing artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic for allegedly using Presley’s songs to train their models without permission.

Authentic Brands Group, the licensing organization that has ownership of both Presley’s music and likeness, is accusing Anthropic of infringing on the rights of 274 songs by Presley. The lawsuit, first reported by Billboard, was filed on Friday.

While AI firms have already faced copyright infringement claims from the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) and music labels such as Sony, Universal and Warner Records, this case represents one of the first major legal challenges brought directly by an artist’s estate against an AI developer. The result could set a broader precedent for how AI companies are allowed to use existing music catalogues.

“The Elvis plaintiffs bring this action to enforce these exclusive rights against the defendant that has built its entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before,” lead attorney Richard Busch wrote in the lawsuit.

The lawsuit claims that “from its inception, Anthropic’s AI model, ‘Claude,’ has created infringing output of copyrighted material of virtually every song from every catalog available on the internet”.

It further accuses Anthropic of utilizing 274 of Presley’s songs to train its AI model. These works include Can’t Help Falling in Love, All Shook Up and A Little Less Conversation. The plaintiffs are seeking $150,000 per infringed track, or about $41m (about £31m).

Get the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning

“Even Anthropic’s institution of guardrails (albeit ineffectively) to purportedly limit outputs which infringe upon music copyrights, after being caught, along with its knowledge that its guardrails were ineffective to stop creating outputs which infringed music copyrights, demonstrates that Anthropic knowingly engaged and continues to willfully engage in copyright infringement of others’ musical works,” the lawsuit states.

AI music platforms work by analyzing large amounts of recorded music in order to learn the sounds, structures and expressions of songs, and then allows users to create their own AI-generated music via text or speech prompts.

Musicians have repeatedly expressed concerns that their music and voices are being used without their permission by AI models, as well as fears that AI-generated “slop” music could replace human-made songs.

Some AI bots have even begun impersonating real living artists on music streaming platforms. Last week, music streaming giant Spotify announced it had removed about 50m songs considered AI slop from its recommendations to users over the past year.

#3090. Tips On How To Use An Emergency Hiking Whistle…And Why You Should Have One

I have to admit, when I got certified as a Wilderness First Responder I had no intention of putting much of what I learned into use. I thought it would be a “nice to have…just in case” and a good line on the resume for seasonal jobs and such.

Also, growing up withÂ “The More You Know”Â commercials on the TV every hour programmed me to always search for more knowledge and to be better prepared. Fast forward to theÂ secondÂ time I had to put my skills into useâwhich included heavy use of my emergency hiking whistleâand I wasÂ reallyÂ thankful for my preparedness.Â

Even if you just came for the tips on how to use (or buy) an emergency whistle, please read this little throwback to understand why it’s such an important thing for you to have when recreating in the backcountry…and how quickly things can hit the fan even when you’re in places you know and frequent.

And to respect my friend’s privacy, I’ll be somewhat vague and not use names and details about the ordeal or recovery.

This site participates in the Amazon Services LLC Associates Program and other affiliate programs and may earn from qualifying purchases.

It was about 30 minutes after dark; well past when my friend should have been home had he left the mountain bike trails while it was still light. I knew he didn’t have his heavy-duty night-riding lights and gear, so I shot a text to his wife who was out of town. He’s been warned that he’d be in trouble if he doesn’t share a Strava beacon with her every time he heads out.

“Can you check his beacon? He went riding and I don’t think he took his lights. He should be home by now and he’s not replying to my texts.”“He’s on Torn Shirt Trail and has only moved a few feet in the past half hour…”

When she asked if I could go find him I had already grabbed my backpackâwhich always has a headlamp, backup batteries, and other emergency gear packed and ready to goâand was getting in my Jeep. Luckily the trailhead was only about a 5-minute drive away and I knew it somewhat well. She sent me GPS markers and I worked my way to him as fast as I could.

SHOP FOR: Metal Emergency Whistle2-Pack Plastic Emergency Whistles

First I found his bike a few feet off the trail, then I saw him about 20 feet further down the hill…in a patch of poison ivy no less. Loss of most of the movement below his neck meant he couldn’t reach or take off his backpack to get his phone. He was alert and oriented, but beyond that, he was pretty screwed.

I was staying in contact with his wife, who had already called 911 to get emergency services en route. But until they got there, it was a matter of keeping calm and checking vitals and for other injuries so that I could report when they arrived.

Unfortunately the emergency response teams, from multiple stations in the immediate area, had zero understanding of the trails or how to get to injured riders.

I had to bounce back and forth from talking to 911 on the phone and giving directions as best I could to using my emergency whistle so they could get to us…for about 20 minutes after they were on the trails trying to find us…until they finally got to us.

READ NEXT: Yesterday I had to Use My NOLS Wilderness First Responder Trainingâ¦âEverybody Poopsâ¦Sometimes In The Woodsâ & 10 Other Things You Might Hear At Wilderness First Responder Training

All in all, they weren’t able to get him out for about 2 hours from the time I arrived, and the execution was beyond dicey. I had four emergency responders standing near me afterward telling me how important it was that I was able to find him and that I had my whistle to signal for help to be able to find us.

Did I mention that none of the emergency responders had an emergency whistle or any other way of “being loud” other than yelling?

Afterward, my friend had to spend a week in the hospital to get back basic movements of his extremities to the point where he could head home to start recovering. Over a year later and he’s still in regular physical and motor therapy to try to improve a percentage of his old abilities that are still absent, but he’s at least able to send it on the trails again.

A well-formatted and explanatory letter was sent (thanks to a family member of my friend) documenting many of the things that went wrong with the rescue and how they could potentially improve preparedness and responses in the future…for the benefit of the many people that ride those trails.

And I’ve gotten much more respect for that tiny little whistle that’s always dangling from the front of my lime-green osprey backpack.

READ NEXT: More Articles About Type 1 Diabetes & My ExperiencesI just got diagnosed with Diabetes and Iâm FREAKING OUT!Diabetes Symptoms For Noobs â My Type 1 Diabetes Symptoms & Diagnosis StoryTravel Medical Insurance, Pre-Existing Conditions, & Type 1 Diabetes

While a hiking whistle might seem like a fairly simple tool to shop for, there are a few features to be aware of. At the end of the day, you need a loud whistle that will be durable given the way you hike. Here are a few features to weigh the importance of when buying an emergency signal:

Plastic hiking whistles are compact and easy to carry, and they emit a loud, high-pitched sound that can be heard over long distances. A lot of times a plastic rescue whistle will come free on an expensive backpack, but I suggest upgrading to a metal whistle or carrying a metal whistle as your primary and a plastic whistle as a backup or for a friend.

Metal whistles are more durable than plastic whistles and may have a slightly different sound. They are often used by professional hikers and outdoor enthusiasts who require a more heavy-duty option. Yes, they’re more expensive, but they also do the job better and won’t get crushed like a cheap kids toy when throwing your backpack around.

SHOP FOR: Metal Emergency Whistle2-Pack Plastic Emergency Whistles

The decibel level of an emergency whistle can vary depending on the specific design and construction of the whistle, for instance, whether it’s metal or plastic, pealess, or with a pea (see below).

For the most part, the highest decibel level for an emergency whistle is typically around 120 decibels (dB), which can be heard from a distance of up to two miles away in open terrain.

The distance at which an emergency whistle can be heard can depend on many different factors, including the design and construction of the whistle (for instance whether it’s metal or plastic, pealess or with a peaâsee below), the ambient noise level, and the environment in which it is being used. As a general rule, a quality emergency whistle with a loudness level of around 120 decibels (dB) should be audible up to 2 miles away in open terrain, assuming no significant background noise.

Here are some general distance ranges for emergency whistles at different decibel levels, based on a typical open terrain scenario with little background noise. As you can see, there’s a big difference in how far you’ll be heard for different levels!

Some hiking whistles also have built-in compasses, which can help you navigate your way out of trouble spots. These types of whistles are typically more expensive than basic plastic whistles. I think these are two different tools for two different reasons, but you can check out one of these combos here.

Similar to whistles with built-in compasses, some hiking whistles also have built-in thermometers, which can help hikers monitor the temperature and weather conditions. Again…C’mon man.

Most hiking whistles come with lanyards or cords that can be attached to backpacks, jackets, or belts, making them easily accessible in case of an emergency. Honestly, a quality emergency whistle should come with a lanyard.

SHOP FOR: Metal Emergency Whistle2-Pack Plastic Emergency Whistles

When it comes to emergency whistles, there are two main types: pealess whistles and whistles with a pea. Honestly…you should only have a pealess whistle, and here’s why:

These whistles do not have a pea inside and instead rely on a specially designed chamber and shape to produce sound. Pealess whistles also work in a wider range of temperatures and conditions.

They are generally more reliable than whistles with a pea because they do not require air to pass through a small opening, which can become clogged with dirt or debris.

These whistles have a small ball, or “pea,” inside that vibrates when air passes through it, producing sound. They are typically louder than pealess whistles and may have a distinct sound that is easier to recognize. However, they can be less reliable than pealess whistles in harsh conditions, as the pea can become stuck or frozen.

No matter what you call itâan emergency whistle, a hiking whistle, a safety whistle, a survival whistleâthere’s not much to using it. Hell, you could throw these tips out the window and just start belting notes as loud as you can on a whistle and you’re pretty much guaranteed to signal someone to your locationâwhether to help you or to kick your ass for being annoying!

Three short, consistent blasts is the universal distress signal for a backcountry emergency. That’s it. It’s really that simple. If you are lost or injured, blow three 2-3 second blasts with a short pause in between. Then wait for a few secondsâto listen for a responseâand repeat the signal.

But there are a few more tips I can give you that will up your game in any situation you encounter where an emergency whistle is needed.

Here are some tips to help you know how to use an emergency hiking whistle effectively, starting with probably the most important one!

Make sure to keep your whistle with you at all times, either on your keychain, in your pocket or attached to your backpack. But optimally it should be on a lanyard, attached to something on your pack, and readily accessible. This way, you can quickly access it in case of an emergency, but it’s also not “loose” so that it can fall out of a pocket or get lost.

When blowing your whistle, make sure you are in an open area, where the sound can carry farther. Avoid using it in a valley or a dense forest, where the sound may not travel as far. And if possible, avoid being up against a “wall” that will only allow the sound of your three blast signal to be heard in one direction.

If you are lost or stranded, blow your whistle at regular intervals, such as every 5-10 minutes, to increase your chances of being heard. You should adjust this tip as needed to your situation, and if the emergency is dire, use your whistle as much as your lungs will allow.

If you only have a limited amount of air, use it wisely. Take deep breaths and blow hard and long blasts on your whistle, instead of short, weak ones. You need to be blowing loud enough to have the sound extend as far as possible!

In addition to blowing your whistle, make sure to stay visible by wearing bright clothing, waving your arms, or using reflective materials. Consider putting signal “flags” of bright items on high locations if you think search crews will spot them.

Only use your whistle in case of an emergency. Blowing it unnecessarily can confuse and may desensitize others to the sound. Think “the boy who cried wolf.”

By following these tips, you can use your emergency hiking whistle effectively and increase your chances of getting help in case of an emergency. It’s this simple: If you don’t have a survival whistle, buy a reliable, pealess whistle now.

Then remember that three short blasts, consistent at about 2-3 seconds eachâon your survival whistle and repeated at regular intervals, are your best bet to signaling a rescuer in a backcountry emergency. This little bit of knowledge and preparedness could save your life or the life of a friend.Â

Don’t forget to hit me up on Instagram and join the conversation! And sharing this article with someone would really help me out!

Jason is the author of “The Beginner Traveler’s Guide” as well as the voice behind the words and the eye behind the lens for The Nomad Experiment. “Planning to travel at some point” wasn’t actually getting the job done, so nearing 40 he decided to make it a priority, nomatter how scary that was. A few years laterâthrough the pandemic and a type 1 diabetes diagnosis at age 42ânow living a life of nomadic travel, he’s speaking out to encourage others of any age, or with any serious medical diagnosis, to live an unconventional life.

After blowing the whistle, pause and listen for any response. Repeat the signal if necessary, and continue to listen for a response.

Both metal and plastic emergency whistles can be effective in signaling for help in an emergency situation. But metal whistles are often considered more durable and can withstand extreme temperatures and weather conditions. Metal emergency whistles also tend to be louder than plastic whistles, which can be an advantage in a noisy or windy environment.

Compared to metal whistles, plastic whistles are generally less expensive, often lighter, and less likely to corrode or rust, making them a good option for use in wet environments. Plastic whistles may not be as loud as metal whistles, but they can still produce a loud and clear sound.

In summary, both metal and plastic emergency whistles can be effective. Choosing between them should depend on personal preference, intended use, and environmental conditions.

If weight isn’t an issue with your pack, I suggest carrying both a plastic and a metal emergency whistle. That gives you options depending on your circumstances, or just a spare whistle to let your irresponsible friend borrow during the trek! (J/K…kind of.)
