#3116. ‘Synthetic twin’: Why Socceroo Cristian Volpato is the latest footballer to license his AI clone

Athletes’ scramble to control – and monetise – their digital identities at the cutting edge of AI rights deals

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

The Socceroos star stares at the camera as he strides through an enormous atrium, the sound of his football boots on polished concrete echoing around him. Suddenly, he spawns four digital clones that peel off out of view to re-emerge in different settings around the world.

This scene from a social media video is fake and generated by artificial intelligence. But it has been authorised by the very real 22-year-old footballer, Cristian Volpato, the latest professional athlete to licence and monetise his AI likeness.

Draped in a white linen suit with his feet on the sand, Volpato’s “synthetic twin” turns towards a photographer as the limestone stacks of the Twelve Apostles tower behind him. Another dominates a large digital billboard wearing a football jersey. One smiles into a mirror while adjusting a sharp grey suit.

This video was produced by a new company that acts as an AI licensing agent for professional athletes. Experts believe it is one small part of a nascent online industry that could transform the future of image rights and sports content.

As bookmakers, broadcasters and brands increasingly use athletes’ images in AI generated content without their permission, some players are fighting back.

In mid-September, Volpato, who plays for Italian Serie A club, Sassuolo, struck a deal with the California-based company Callandor to license his AI image.

As part of the deal, Callandor was given exclusive rights to Volpato’s digital likeness, voice, biometric profiles and performance data. The company will monetise his AI image by landing brand deals, taking a cut, and help restrict content that does not have his approval.

From Los Angeles, Callandor’s co-founder, Michael Fisk, tells Guardian Australia he’s in the business of making “synthetic twins”.

“Cristian is constantly training,” Fisk says. “He’s constantly out there playing. If he has any free time whatsoever, he’ll probably want to spend it with family and friends, so he loses on a lot of opportunities on brand placements.

“A synthetic twin could be used 24-7, year-round by brands. Assuming it’s approved, right?”

Founded in February, Callandor has a small stable of athletes, including Brazilian footballer Jorginho and American sailor Chris Poole. Its campaigns are only in the pilot phase, but Callandor is pursuing an array of opportunities beyond traditional advertising.

Fisk, a former executive at Sony Pictures and MGM, talks of creating AI-generated book voiceovers with foreign language editions. His team is also plotting apps that offer fans a personal relationship with a synthetic twin.

“Ultimately, the holy grail of an athlete is to have that one-on-one interaction with fans,” Fisk says.

He raises the prospect of creating an app that monitors how people play football. A digital clone of Volpato would give real-time instructions.

“He’s realising I’m not handling the ball well [so] his synthetic twin can tell me, ‘Hey, you should be doing this and this and this’,” says Fisk.

“Volpato would never be able to do that one-on-one with [them].”

Volpato’s deal with Callandor is at the cutting edge of AI rights deals, but he isn’t the first to embrace the technology. In June, Brazilian superstar Neymar licensed his AI likeness to a Chinese-owned entertainment platform that created short videos published during the FIFA World Cup.

These projects are being launched as governments across the world consider basic regulation of AI. At the moment, player contracts with major Australian sporting leagues make no mention of AI.

But technology isn’t waiting for regulation to catch up and Fisk says his synthetic twin clients are blurring the lines between real and fake.

“It’s becoming almost impossible to detect, that look and feel, the difference, particularly when you see it on a mobile device,” he says.

William Saunders leads a small Sydney based start-up, Hyperknown, that’s trying to cut similar deals. He says athletes are beginning to realise that if they don’t monetise their AI image, others will.

Earlier this month, the AFL told its gambling partner Sportsbet to stop using AI images of players without their consent. This was prompted by a complaint from the players’ union, which is considering whether stricter rules should be negotiated.

“Sportsbet shows us what happens when companies and technology get ahead of consent,” Saunders says.

“Volpato represents the counter-move: people establishing their rights before others start making decisions about their identities.

“We’re watching a race between what technology can do and what people have actually authorised.”

Many in the Australian sports industry, including content creators, bookmakers, broadcasters and athletes themselves, have started embracing the technology.

Earlier this month, Australian cricketer Travis Head personally appeared in an ad for the broadcaster Kayo. He joked that his AI clone had already finished filming the ad, before throwing to vision of him riding a flying kookaburra.

Brand deals and endorsements have become major money makers for athletes, with some securing multimillion dollar contracts. It remains unclear whether brands will be willing to pay as much for an AI clone, as opposed to the real deal.

But Saunders, whose company has only just launched, says the opportunities are enormous. He talks of AI clones selling products in foreign languages in nations athletes have never visited.

“The next trust signal won’t just say ‘made with AI’,” he says, referencing a tag often used by social media companies. “It will say ‘made with this person’s permission’.

“AI can make content abundant. It can’t manufacture someone’s permission. That’s becoming a new commercial requirement.”

Jonathan Harlen, an expert in intellectual property law at Southern Cross University, says the rise of AI brokers is “the obvious next step” in a “supercharged global market”.

From a legal perspective, he says this new industry presents “a tangle of different interests and rights” that need to be carefully negotiated.

“While copyright already subsists in voice recordings, artistic works and cinematographic images, it is only recognised where there has been human authorship, as well as a degree of independent or creative human effort involved in the making of the work,” Harlen says.

Celebrities and athletes do have some protection against AI-generated content using their image and voice without consent. But these “passing off” laws only apply when public figures can prove they have suffered an economic loss.

This has not slowed an explosion of deepfakes generated by increasingly sophisticated off-the-shelf software.

In the UK last month, a campaign was launched by some the world’s top footballers, including Cole Palmer and Lucy Bronze, which highlighted their concerns about deepfakes and the inability for regulation to slow their explosion. This campaign was backed by the global player union, Fifpro.

One offshore casino used a deepfake video of Manchester United player Bruno Fernandes in advertising earlier this year.

Not all unauthorised deepfakes will be unwanted, however. Fisk says a heavy-handed crackdown on “fan art” using AI tools might be counterproductive.

“You don’t want fans to use your image and put you in [content] using brands that you don’t use, or saying something that you would never say,” he says.

“Obviously, anything with religion and drugs, or whatever it might be, you have to be very, very careful. So it does complicate things a bit, but the opportunities are phenomenal.”

But in this emerging realm, the consequences may be hard to predict.

#3117. Cutting ‘red tape’ is nothing but a red herring – and arguably counterproductive | Heather Stewart

Blaming a moribund economy on too many rules is a hackneyed neoliberal trope – UK plc needs smarter regulation, not less regulation

Before becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham pledged to “end 40 years of neoliberalism”. But as he prepares for his first budget on Wednesday, his government is yet to let go of one of its most tedious cliches: red tape.

In the run-up to the chancellor John Healey’s high-stakes Commons address, the government issued a press release last week promising his plans would include measures to “slash the red tape choking firms”.

Named after the tape once used to tie up government bills, and popularised by the historian Thomas Carlyle, the phrase is straight from the neoliberal playbook and has long outlived its usefulness.

Getting the interfering state out of the way of the wealth creators was a trope of Thatcher and Reaganite economics, and on this side of the pond it has been repeated ad nauseam by every government since.

Thatcher unleashed the City with her “big bang” deregulation drive, and her successor John Major was enthusiastic about “hacking back the jungle of red tape”. It was the man he appointed for the job – Michael Heseltine – who coined what has become the most hackneyed description of this particular approach: the “bonfire of red tape”.

With Labour back in power, Gordon Brown celebrated a light-tough regulatory regime for the UK’s hard-driving financial sector – until the Treasury had to bail out the banks after the 2008 financial crisis.

Boris Johnson wanted to unfetter Britain’s businesses from “Brussels bureaucracy” and waffled on during the Brexit campaign about bendy bananas. Yet, after Brexit, business groups said their members would rather comply with longstanding EU standards in many areas than adopt an entirely new UK regime. And bananas are no more or less bendy than before.

Rachel Reeves had a more unpleasantly graphic way of making a similar point, referring to regulation as a “boot on the neck” of British business.

There is nothing wrong with ensuring the interaction between business and the state is smooth. But even during the early years of neoliberalism, the free market good, regulation bad dichotomy was always unhelpful, for several reasons.

First, good regulation – a robust competition regime, for example – is essential to make markets work well. And even most enthusiasts for a laissez-faire approach would acknowledge the need for some basic quality standards – for food and medicines, for example.

When it comes to the labour market, Labour has unashamedly adopted a pro-regulation stance. Its Employment Rights Act is the most significant increase in workers’ rights in a generation – but it inevitably, and deliberately, increases the rules firms must follow.

That is to the benefit, ministers rightly argue, of low-paid employees trapped in insecure work. But a bonfire of red tape it is not. Labour posing as a champion of deregulation will seem unconvincing, given that context.

Second, and ironically, the march of neoliberalism itself is a reason regulation has mushroomed in recent decades. As the Labour MP Yuan Yang argued in a recent lecture for the journal Renewal, as the state retreated from providing important services, watchdog institutions to oversee the private sector became necessary.

As she put it: “The neoliberal illusion, that privatisation liberated markets from state interference, obscures the reality that the state already significantly controls our privatised utilities, but through a maze of arm’s length regulatory agencies which operate outside democratic influence.”

For the water sector, privatised in 1989, these include Ofwat, which sets bills (with the Competition and Markets Authority acting as an appeals body in the event of a dispute); the Drinking Water Inspectorate; the Environment Agency; and the Consumer Council for Water.

Yet, as Yang points out, none are responsible for drawing up a coherent plan for the sector as a whole. “Everyone knows how this story ends: with our rivers polluted and our water infrastructure dangerously lacking.”

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

Hacking away at the regulatory thicket fails to deal with the structural features of the economy that make the rules necessary in the first place.

Mat Lawrence, the director of the thinktank Common Wealth and author of The Productive State, a policy paper influential among those close to Burnham, calls this “the regulatory state”. He cites affordable housing targets for private developers as another example of regulation taking the place of stuff the state once did itself.

The third reason the endless red tape discourse is unhelpful is one raised by Mike Clancy, the general secretary of the Prospect union, which represents workers at many of the regulators.

He has urged the government to lay off these often not lavishly paid staff, who are trying to do their jobs with stretched resources. “Regulators continue to be labelled as ‘blockers’ despite the vital work they do keeping us safe and protecting our natural environment,” he said.

Prospect has been urging the government to ditch a promise to “cut the administrative burden” of regulation by 25% by the end of the parliament, arguing it is arbitrary and potentially counterproductive.

Finally, we would all benefit from some over-mighty businesses being reined in by regulation, not least the tech firms, which insouciantly concede that their AI agents have been busting through safety controls and may be about to start spawning spontaneously.

Embracing the tired idea that red tape is “choking” business is hardly likely to help the government make the case for the more stringent approach that is clearly necessary.

As it happens, Bonfire Night is almost upon us. If Burnham really wants to embrace a different approach to the economy, he could start by consigning the phrase “red tape” to the flames.

#3118. How to Make Light-Up DIY Christmas Cards with Paper Circuits

These light up paper circuit cards were much easier to make than I expected and only need a few inexpensive materials.

They’re a great way to learn about circuits and electricity. You can make a simple, basic circuit or a more complicated series or parallel circuit. I’ve created a free template to make the activity as easy as possible.

Electric current is the flow of charge around a circuit, it can only flow if the circuit is complete. This means that if there’s a gap in the circuit the LED won’t light up.

A battery acts like a pump, pushing the electric charge around the circuit.

Use my free card templates or draw your own!

Adult supervision is needed with this activity.

Either print out one of my templates or draw a picture on the outside of a folded piece of A4 card that you can insert a coloured LED into.

Look at the LED, the long leg is postitive + and the short leg is negative -.

The top of the battery is positive and the bottom is negative.

A simple circuit has one battery, one LED and a complete square made with copper tape.

We left a gap in the circuit that is only closed wheh the card is closed. This means the LEDs light up only when the card is closed and the circuit is complete.

When making the cicruit the copper tape attached to the long leg of the LED should lead into the positive side of the battery.

Check the circuit, try flipping the battery or the LED.

Press down on the copper tape to make sure there are no looose connnections.

Make sure the copper tape isn’t touching itself by the LED legs or the battery as this can cause a short circuit.

Once you’ve mastered a basic circuit, try a parallel circuit with 2 LEDs.

If you enjoyed the activity, don’t forget to check out my other easy electricity projects.

#3120. Audi kündigt Milliarden-Investition in den USA an

Die Volkswagen-Tochter Audi baut ein eigenes Werk in den USA. Angekündigt wurde das auf einer Wahlkampfveranstaltung der Republikaner von US-Präsident Donald Trump. Noch sind allerdings Fragen offen.

Der amerikanische Präsident Donald Trump sagte in der Stadt Perry im US-Bundesstaat Georgia, Audi investiere vier Milliarden Dollar in das Werk. Jährlich sollten dort rund 200.000 Fahrzeuge vom Band laufen.

Audi-Chef Gernot Döllner bestätigte die Ausführungen Trumps und erklärte: "Wir planen, unsere größten und hochwertigsten SUVs hier in Macon, Georgia, zu produzieren". Er ergänzte: "Dies ⁠ist ⁠eine langfristige Investition, weil wir an den amerikanischen Markt glauben."

Die Ankündigung des deutschen Autobauers spielt dem amerikanischen Präsidenten in die Hände. Am 3. November stehen in den USA Zwischenwahlen an, und seine Republikaner drohen, die Mehrheit im Kongress zu verlieren. In Georgia wird zusätzlich auch der Gouverneur neu gewählt. Trump will deutlich machen, dass seine Zollpolitik der US-Wirtschaft hilft. ​Der republikanische US-Senator Bernie Moreno sagte, das Audi-Werk wäre "ohne eine wirtschaftsfreundliche Regulierung niemals zustande gekommen".

Kritiker führen dagegen an, dass die ​von der Trump-Regierung auferlegten Zölle Autos verteuert und Investitionen verzögert haben. Audi importiert derzeit die Fahrzeuge für den US-Markt aus ​Europa und Mexiko. Ein ‌eigenes US-Werk steht seit mehr als einem Jahrzehnt auf der Wunschliste der Ingolstädter.

Audi zufolge sollen durch die Investition rund 4500 Arbeitsplätze entstehen. Der Baubeginn für das Werk in Macon sei für das kommende Jahr geplant, die Produktion solle Anfang der 2030er-Jahre anlaufen. Jährlich sollen rund 200.000 Fahrzeuge gebaut ‌werden. In dem Werk der Volkswagen-Tochter sollen die Modelle Audi Q7, Q8 und Q9 montiert werden, sagte ein US-Regierungsvertreter der Nachrichtenagentur Reuters. Zudem plane ‌Audi, ​jährlich 25.000 Fahrzeuge im benachbarten South Carolina zu bauen, auch für den Export.

Volkswagen-Chef Oliver Blume sagte, Nordamerika sei ein fester Bestandteil des Zukunftsplans. Die Region sei ein wichtiger Markt, um profitabel zu wachsen. "Ein mögliches Werk für Audi in den USA würde dafür weitere Voraussetzungen schaffen: Lokalisierte Produkte aus den USA für die USA." Derzeit spielt Audi auf dem US-Markt kaum eine Rolle. Die von Trump eingeführten Zölle hatten den Autobauer im vergangenen Jahr mit 1,2 Milliarden Euro belastet. Der Absatz von Audi ging in den USA in diesem Jahr bislang um 16 Prozent zurück.

Ungeachtet der von Präsident Trump und Audi-Chef Döllner gemachten Erklärungen zum Bau eines eigenen Audi-Werkes in den USA steht die Zustimmung des Volkswagen-Aufsichtsrats noch aus, und dort dürfte die Ankündigung für ⁠Gesprächsstoff sorgen. ​Niedersachsens Ministerpräsident Olaf Lies sagte, es sei strategisch richtig, den US-Markt noch besser zu erschließen. Allerdings dürfe das ​nicht zulasten der deutschen Werke gehen. "Wachstum in Amerika muss Arbeit und Wertschöpfung hier sichern und darf sie nicht verdrängen." Das Stammwerk des Volkswagen-Konzerns, zu dem Audi gehört, befindet sich im niedersächsischen Wolfsburg.

IG-Metall-Chefin Christiane Benner, die auch stellvertretende Aufsichtsratsvorsitzende bei Volkswagen ist, forderte verbindliche Perspektiven für die Beschäftigten ​an allen Standorten. Ein Sprecher der IG Metall sagte, es sei mehr als befremdlich, wenn ​sich ein deutscher Auto-Boss zum Wahlkampfhelfer eines US-Präsidenten mache, ⁠der aus deutschen Autobauern amerikanische machen wolle.

"Trump hat nie verhehlt, worum es ihm geht: Er will unsere heimische Wirtschaft schwächen, allen voran die Automobilbranche, Wertschöpfung und Arbeitsplätze sollen über den ⁠Atlantik wandern, seine Zollpolitik ist dafür das Werkzeug", sagte ​der IG-Metallvertreter. "Dass Gernot Döllner ausgerechnet in dieser Lage Trump die Hand reicht, ist schwer zu begreifen. Zumal sein eigenes Unternehmen hierzulande Werke und ganze Regionen infrage stellt."

Das Volkswagen-Management und der Betriebsrat streiten derzeit über den weiteren Kurs bei dem Autokonzern. VW-Chef Blume will bis 2030 weltweit weitere 50.000 Arbeitsplätze streichen. Ab 2030 steht die Produktion in vier deutschen Werken zur Debatte. Es geht auch um die Audi-Fabrik in Neckarsulm.

Redaktionsschluss 17.30 Uhr (MEZ). Dieser Artikel wird nicht weiter aktualisiert!

#3122. Namibia' Black Rhino Is One of Africa’s Most Exciting Conservation Stories

We’d been looking for nearly five hours—scanning the dry grass for upturned pebbles and the horizon for a dark, lumbering shape—when we spotted the rhino bull. Next to me, tracker Mensley Karutjaiva shook his head with a resigned chuckle. We’d been up since daybreak, alongside three other members of the Save the Rhino Trust, looking for critically endangered black rhinos in Damaraland, a land of flat-topped mountains, rocky hills, and stark plains in the Kunene region of northwestern Namibia. While we scrambled about in the heat, the bull had been dozing in the shade of a milk bush. We watched as he stood up, as if posing for us, before lying back down to resume his nap.

I was traveling in a loop around northwest Namibia that took me to three new (or recently renewed) camps. Since photographic safari tourism began here over a century ago, Namibia has largely been known amongst international travelers as a self-drive vacation—a destination with plenty of do-it-yourself road trips through otherworldly desert landscapes. Unknown to many visitors, though, human-wildlife conflict—population activities that negatively affect animals through habitat loss or resource competition— has been an ongoing challenge, and past decades of poaching threw rhinoceros populations into a tailspin. But, in the past few years, Namibia has seen a lot of positive conservation momentum, with these northwest reaches acting as a bellwether. From innovative government measures to an Indigenous-stewarded private reserve, this region is now a story of forward-looking change.

In May 2026, the country’s government launched a new conservation finance deal called Namibia for Life in partnership with the World Wildlife Fund. Worth approximately $63 million, it sets aside funds for Namibia’s 86 community-supported conservancies, which span more than 49 million acres.

Gazing at the black rhino, I felt a thrill as my eyes followed the magnificent swoop of the animal’s two intact horns, the larger of the two over three feet long. In an attempt to deter poachers, wildlife management will often cut down a rhinos’ horns—a humane, if humbling, procedure—so that the sight of a rhino, especially one of this critically endangered sub-species, often entails seeing just nubs.

Wild black rhino populations in Namibia came close to extinction in the mid 90s, but thanks to conservation efforts, have recovered.

Rhino horn can fetch up to $5,400 a pound in the illegal wildlife trade—so just seeing this intact horn was a triumph in itself. Decimated by poaching throughout the 1970s and 80s due to demand in Asia and the Arabian Peninsula, wild black rhino populations had dropped by 96 percent in the mid 90s. They came so close to extinction that only 2,410 were left on the entire planet.

That sighting was a harbinger of better days to come. Thanks to conservation efforts, today some 6,000 black rhinos now roam free, with an estimated half of those living in Namibia. In July 2026, the World Wildlife Fund announced that Namibia had experienced a 53 percent drop in rhino poaching since 2024, reaching its lowest numbers of rhino poaching instances in over a decade.

“Over the past 39 years of visiting Namibia regularly, I’ve been heartened to see a growing understanding of the importance of conservation and community-based tourism–and more recently, how to sustain it,” said travel advisor Nicola Shepherd, who arranged my itinerary. “Namibian organizations such as the nonprofit Integrated Rural Development and Nature Conservation are investing in practical ways to reduce conflict and protect both people and wildlife.”

The founder of the conservation-focused Explorations Company, Shepherd and her team have been arranging customized trips to this country for decades. In the past few years, she’s noted a shift in the advent of luxury accommodations, including Zannier Hotels, Habitas, and others, that have broadened the country's appeal to travelers seeking high-end experiences. It’s all welcome news for the country, which is experiencing an uptick in traveler interest—just two months after my trip, local publications reported that the country’s hotel room occupancy was having one of its strongest years.

More than twice the size of California, Namibia’s expanse includes coastline, semi-arid desert, dry and wet woodlands, and golden savanna. The northwest corner is a rich mix of these terrains–including the otherworldly, white-tipped grasslands I walked through as we returned to Wilderness Desert Rhino Camp after our morning rhino sighting.

“In this area of the Palmwag Concession, the rotation of tourism helps protect rhinos,” Karutjaiva told me. I heard this sentiment echoed wherever I went, although specific numbers are carefully guarded. “It’s a state secret. The only thing I can say is that the population is growing,” he said. The guardedness is understandable, as the threat of poaching is still everywhere. And growth isn’t restricted to the rhino populations.

The lounge area at the intimate Wilderness Desert Rhino Camp, which was formerly a field station for wildlife research.

At Desert Rhino Camp, a full rebuild in 2024 resulted in six stand-alone tented suites, where materials like timber, leather, and stone evoke a modern, desert-chic style. With the Etendeka Mountains rising in the distance, red basalt boulders form the walls of the open-air dining lounge where I enjoyed a delicious slow-cooked lamb potjie stew for dinner.

“We really realized how important tourism was during the pandemic, when most businesses closed and a lot of people lost their jobs,” lodge manager Fanus Katondoka told me that evening, as we sipped on rooibos iced teas. “Now we know it. Operators are building a lot of facilities, lodges, hotels–it's booming.” That growth means more resources for community-supported conservation, so Karutjaiva and his team can continue their work protecting rhinos and other species.

Rhinos have adorned conservation headlines recently, but they’re far from the only draw in northwest Namibia. A new camp from outfitter Natural Selection recently opened about an hour’s flight north, in the desert Kaokoveld region, highlighting another species of desert-adapted wildlife. A few days later, I was headed to see it.

Sitting in the cockpit seat of a tiny four-seater Cessna, I waved goodbye to the rhino trackers and flew over the Namib Desert, one of the oldest arid regions in the world. The landscape flowed in ridges and mountains of faded yellow and whisper pink, where welwitschia–large, low-lying plants that live to be hundreds of years old–sprawled like relics from a Dune film set.

The Namib Desert stretches along the Atlantic coast of Namibia and features some of the highest sand dunes in the world.

It was a fitting introduction to my next stop: the Hoanib Valley, home to a new camp with a mission that’s a bit bigger than rhinoceros. I quickly learned what that something was when guide Howard Groenewaldt picked me up from the airstrip, nosed our vehicle toward camp, and then abruptly cut the engine.

We had stopped at the Hoanib River, a seasonal waterway that runs west from the desert until it reaches the Skeleton Coast on the Atlantic Ocean. Now in the dry season, it turned into a sandy avenue lined with camelthorn and giant ana trees that age more than 100 years old. It was a nature-born runway—and something was stirring around a bend.

A giant, desert-adapted elephant slowly walked toward us. His long tusks were pale white; the bottoms of his feet splayed out wide under his skinny legs, the better to stabilize on sand. There was no sound except the breeze that was stirring the wizened, banana-shaped seed pods in the branches above my head, and the soft fwump of the elephant’s footsteps. I watched, transfixed, as he paused and delicately trailed the tip of his trunk on the ground

The author looks on at a desert-adapted elephant.

This is exactly the kind of encounter the new Natural Selection Hoanib Elephant Camp was built around. Located off the northern bank of the river, its 10 solar-powered suites bring a new level of comfort to the valley. Between game drives, guests here lounge on the veranda overlooking the desert hoping to spy more elephants, or relax in their suites with a massage or nap. Each of the natural-hued suites include a private plunge pool, a deep king-size bed, and a writing desk. Dinner is a multi-course affair in the shared lounge; afterward, a bonfire crackles under the stars. During my stay some visitors curled up on the couches against the evening desert chill, sipping hot drinks spiked with Amarula, a South African liqueur, surrounded by flickering candles.

While the resort is stylish and deeply comfortable, Natural Selection’s approach to community partnership also reflects the shift in this region toward local collaboration. The evening I arrived at camp, I met Petty Daniels, who hails from the nearby Torra Conservancy and brings an acutely local perspective. Years ago, she began working in hospitality as a waitress—today, she’s the manager of both this new camp and its giraffe-focused sister property, the Hoanib Valley Camp. Roughly 97 percent of staff are from surrounding community conservancies, creating a working model of local investment in supporting companies that protect their homeland.

Sundowner drinks are accompanied by a knowledgable guide on a Hoanib Elephant Camp safari.

Within Daniels’ generation, change has been flourishing in the hearts and minds of locals. “Before tourism, people drove wherever they wanted, shooting animals to provide food for their families,” she said. “Not anymore. People are getting into conservation tourism and understanding why they shouldn’t do that.”

Even so, human-wildlife conflict is still a problem. Elephants ramble into gardens and cheetahs kill the occasional goat, but the overall opinion of locals is shifting, especially as the Namibian government signals support for conservation that’s more in step with local interests.

Namibia’s Hoanib Valley was made famous by its desert-adapted elephants.

“Namibia’s communities already help look after lions, elephants, rhinos, water, plants and open land,” Rob Moffett explained a few days later, soon after I arrived at my third and final destination in northwest Namibia. “Instead of saying, ‘Good luck finding money every year,’ the Namibia for Life fund says, ‘Here is a proper money box, a rule book, and a team to help you keep protecting nature.’”

Moffett is the general manager of sales and marketing at Ongava Game Reserve, a private stretch of savanna and mopane woodlands that stretches more than 74,000 acres next to Etosha National Park, one of the country’s biggest visitor attractions. It’s also the site of another positive–and long overdue–story of change.

Wilderness operates single-engine flights from camp to camp that come in handy.

To reach it, I rented a gas-electric hybrid car from ATI Holidays and drove east from the Hoanib Valley. This type of travel is still popular in Namibia, with strong infrastructure supporting visitors. After a detailed briefing with an ATI staff member, I was kitted out with a folder packed with maps, a Namibian cell phone pre-programmed with key contacts, and a first-aid kit. I drove for several hours, listening to music and watching the desert scenery flash by. But driving solo can be tiring, and I was glad for the air travel between previous camps, seamlessly arranged by the Explorations Company. For US travelers unaccustomed to driving on the left side of the road, and often juggling a few shorter vacations, brief single-engine flights from camp to camp are increasingly preferred by high-end resorts opening in the northwest.

The new Horizon by Ongava, where I had arrived, is one of those. Consisting of just three hilltop villas, the property debuted from renovations and a name reset in April 2026, and prioritizes seclusion and comfort. My accommodations unfolded in a graceful series of rooms with couches, a four-poster bed, and a dual-vanity bathroom. Outside, overlooking a plain of the greenest scenery I’d seen so far, a wide deck hugged the hillside, and included two dining spaces, an outdoor shower, and a private plunge pool. My favorite touch was the large bench in the walk-in dressing room, carved in the shape of a serval—a wild cat native to sub-Saharan Africa.

The dining, led by chef Festus Ilyambo, is a feat in its own right. That evening, in the open-air lounge, I asked Ilyambo for the recipes behind his potato pavé—thinly sliced, buttery potatoes infused with organic thyme and fresh cream, then sautéed with garlic—and filet mignon, served with a jus and cognac sauce.

Raised walkways lead to villas at the new Horizon by Ongava.

Alfresco dinners at Horizon by Ongava are a highlight of the day.

The next morning, longtime guide Pascalis Kazimbu led me on a private walking safari in Ongava Game Reserve, pointing out everything from lilac-breasted rollers to white rhino mothers with calves tottering close behind and wildebeest that bleated—“gnuu, gnuu”. Later that afternoon we set out on a game drive, pausing at a watering hole for sundowner drinks as dusk began to settle. I was sipping a local Tafel lager in the safari vehicle when a deep, reverberating roar sounded behind me, vibrating in my bones. Moments later, a male lion strolled out of the thin trees behind me, settling by the pond for a drink.

With game viewing like this, verdant Ongava and its neighboring Etosha National Park are a welcome coda to the scenes of desert and dunes I’d left behind. The circular route of my trip is a popular one: travelers arrive into the capital of Windhoek, travel in a rough circle that begins with awe-inspiring desert and ends near Etosha, and then head back to Windhoek to begin their journey home.

A new community-led concession and lodge in Ongava will protect thousands of acres and help conserve species, including the Southern Yellow-billed Hornbill.

But a coming Ongava project will add a new element for curious travelers. In 2024, the Indigenous San (or Bushmen) Hai//om community and Ongava agreed to a legally binding agreement to partner to manage a new concession, including a new lodge, on the southeast border of Etosha National Park. Slated to open in 2028, the new reserve will secure thousands of acres of land, strengthening wildlife corridors and helping to protect an important waterway called the !Gobaob Spring, where black rhinos and many other species gather to drink in the dry season.

“That place is a miracle,” Ongava manager Moffett said. “In the Hai//om’s oral history, it’s the one spring that has never failed in their entire existence.”

The implications of this new initiative, called the Ongava-Hai//om Joint Venture, extend far beyond wildlife. The concession carries profound historical significance because it includes part of the ancestral homeland of the Hai//om people, who were forcibly removed from Etosha by the government in the 1950s. “Today, most Hai//om people are living scattered on the outside of the park, but this is their home,” Moffett said. “For them to reclaim management and ownership of this concession has the potential to become one of the most special community conservation stories of our time.”

When the 25-year joint venture ends in 2049, the entire business will transfer from its current shared management to the Hai//om community. By protecting endangered wildlife while empowering the Hai//om people to build long-term prosperity, the new concession promises benefits for all involved, including visitors.

The stakes are high for the black rhino, but now, there is also hope.

Learning about this project felt like an encapsulation of everything I’d seen and heard on this journey in northwest Namibia, where community-focused conservation held hands with high-end hospitality. I thought back to the rhino I’d seen in my first days here, and the slow but steady work locals like Karutjaiva are doing to protect the species from the knife’s edge of extinction.

In Namibia, the stakes are high, but so is the promise of a more prosperous, wild future.

I hit the road for the first time after collegeâwith over $20,000 of student debtâto work as a tour manager running a charity event where kids raced tractors around a course we set up in a big box retail parking lot. Not the typical post-college job, I know.

In the suburbs of Philadelphia where I grew up, going to college, getting into debt, and then working a ârespectable jobâ to pay off said debt was the norm.

Why? Who the hell knows? Itâs just what people did, without thinking too much about it! In hindsight, going that âtraditionalâ way seems way crazier to me than becoming a nomad. Back then there were no reassuring podcasts, blogs, social media travel âinfluencersâ or amazingly helpful books like this oneâgiving you the how-to on the digital nomad lifestyle while praising you on bucking the status quo and going after your travel dreams.

If you told someone you were traveling around and sleeping in a van, their first thought wasnât, âWow, you’re living the dream!â It was, âDude…Iâm sorry you’re homeless and maybe mentally ill.â

Accepting the status quo lifestyle is the norm, while going against it can make you an outsider. At times, this caused me some serious anxiety.

These types of questions popped up from time to time but I always came back to one thingâI just wanted to do what made me happy. And travel is what made me happy, so I just kept doing it.

Thatâs why I consider myself an accidental nomad. I wasnât intentionally avoiding settling down. I just loved the nomad lifestyle so damn much that I kept choosing it over anything else.

Most people go on vacation. They take a break from their regular life only to (reluctantly) return to it. For nomads, travel is regular life.It’s not a trip, it is a lifestyle.

If returning home from a vacation and stepping back into your regular life feels like walking into a prison, maybe itâs time for a change. This Seth Godin quote captures the essence of what the nomadic lifestyle is all about for me:

Instead of wondering when your next vacation is, maybe you should set up a life you donât need to escape from.

Iâm guessing that if youâre reading this, you are ready to take Sethâs advice, or at least will be by the time youâre finished.

Think of all the ways you can travel as an a la carte menu. You can order up what works best for you now based on your goals, then order up something new at any time. When you are flexible you have an unlimited amount of ways you can startâand keepâtraveling.

#3124. Last Month Was the Hottest July on Record for the World's Oceans

Oceans globally recorded their hottest July ever last month, according to a new analysis. The severe ocean heat was evident around Europe, which is coping with a scorching summer.

Outside the polar regions, the ocean surface averaged 69.73 degrees F (20.96 degrees C), breaking the previous July record, set in 2023, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service. Ocean heat was particularly severe in the Pacific, thanks to an intensifying El Niño.

Land surface temperatures were only slightly less severe. Across both land and sea, last month was the second hottest July on record globally.

Daily sea surface temperatures between the 60th parallel south and 60th parallel north. Copernicus Climate Change Service / Adapted by Yale Environment 360

In Europe, heat records continue to fall. “July 2026 was the third consecutive month of exceptional heat in Western Europe, bringing the combined temperature for June and July to a new record for the region,” said Samantha Burgess, deputy director of Copernicus.

Recurrent hot spells and meager rainfall have desiccated soils across Western Europe, making heat more severe. “As soils dry out, they lose their ability to provide natural cooling, allowing heat to build more readily,” Burgess said. “This is a clear example of how climate change is intensifying heat extremes, with heat and drought increasingly reinforcing one another.”

Drought has also drained rivers across Europe. Low water levels on the Danube River, on the border between Serbia and Romania, have revealed dozens of World War II shipwrecks. The ships belonged to a Nazi fleet that was sunk near the end of the war to slow the advance of Soviet forces. Elsewhere on the Danube, in Slovakia, authorities recovered an unexploded WWII bomb.

#3125. Cookie theft: how fraudsters get the digital key to your accounts

You’ve had a busy morning of life admin, logging into various accounts to check balances and make payments. At the end of a productive few hours you close your laptop and move on to your next job.

“They don’t need your password, they don’t trigger a login alert, and they can often bypass your multifactor authentication (MFA).”

It looks like a regular session on the web. At some point you will have logged in and given your password, and maybe used MFA to prove it’s you.

If it’s a social media or email account you may discover it’s been used by scammers to trick other people. If it’s your bank they could access your account, or they could use details they find to perpetrate an impersonation scam.

And if you were shopping online, the fraudsters could change and redirect your order and charge it to your saved payment details.

You may be alerted by a security alert from a site, for example, a message asking if you have tried to change any details.

Be really careful about the extensions and software you download, because that’s where infostealer malware will usually be hidden.

Look out for signs that your laptop or phone has been infected with malware. Briedis says red flags include your device suddenly struggling with simple tasks, a battery that drains faster than it should, frequent crashes, or a browser that starts behaving oddly with redirects, pop-ups, or a changed homepage.

He suggests moving passwords out of your browser and into a dedicated password manager.

If you suspect you have been compromised, run an antivirus scan. Also log out of your accounts on every device and change your passwords.

Use MFA on accounts, as it does still offer more protection than a simple password.

Alert your bank if you notice any suspicious payments.

#3126. What is the £100k income ‘cliff-edge’?

The tax-free personal allowance starts to be taken away when you hit six figures, and in England you lose access to childcare subsidies

Believe it or not, there are downsides to earning more than £100,000 a year – particularly if you have small children.

“It’s the ambition of many people to reach an income of £100,000, but it does come with an unexpected sting in the tail,” says Sean McCann, a chartered financial planner at NFU Mutual.

Those who make it into six figures face a 60% tax bill on some income. That is because the tax-free personal allowance starts to be taken away once you earn more than £100,000.

For every £2 of income over that, you lose £1 of the £12,570 annual tax-free personal allowance.

“This means that any earnings between £100,000 and £125,140 are effectively taxed at 60%,” says McCann. “When you add on the 2% national insurance payable, that means you only keep £38 of every £100 earned.”

An estimated 800,000 people are in this position, according to a freedom of information request by NFU Mutual.

In England, high earners also lose access to government childcare subsidies once a parent has an adjusted net income of more than £100,000 for a tax year.

As a result, a family with two young children loses roughly £30,000 of financial support if either parent earns even £1 more than the threshold, according to the investment platform AJ Bell.

There are three components to this: tax-free childcare; free hours’ childcare; and child benefit.

AJ Bell’s maths is for a family with a nine-month-old baby and a two-year-old, and puts a value of £4,000, £23,872, and £2,337 on the respective elements.

Sarah Coles, the platform’s head of personal finance, says parents “lose a big chunk” of support as soon as they hit the earnings limit: “It isn’t tapered away gradually, hence the ‘cliff-edge’ moniker.”

All entitlement to tax-free childcare (worth up to £2,000 a child a year) goes, Coles explains.

You also forgo the 30 hours funded term-time childcare for children aged nine months old to three years old, and half the 30 hours for children aged between three and four.

And at this level, all the family’s child benefit entitlement (currently £27.05 a week for your eldest or only child, and £17.90 for each additional child) is clawed back by the high-income child benefit charge (a tax “penalty” that kicks in when someone’s income exceeds £60,000).

So how many missed out on funded childcare because a parent exceeded the income threshold?

Official government data suggests that between 50,500 and 99,000 children in 2025-26. That is according to a freedom of information figures obtained by the wealth management firm Quilter. That is up sharply on just two years earlier, when it was estimated at between 15,600 and 30,800.

#3128. Walking Reindeer Challenge

These walking reindeer made us laugh so much. They work brilliantly, but can be a little fiddly to get going. This activity is traditionally called the walking horse, but as it’s nearly Christmas, we’ve made reindeer!

The reindeer *walk* down a ramp or slope, because of a combination of forces including gravity and friction.

Print the template below to make this activity even easier! If you don’t have a printer, just draw the shape on paper.

Cut the small triangles from the bottom of each leg, and then cut up the legs, stopping at the middle section.

Bend the four legs down and fold the tail upwards.

Fold up the head and again at the top to make a head.

Set up a ramp from a stack of books and thick cardboard, and place the reindeer at the top.

If it doesn’t move, gently push the legs until it starts walking.

When the horse is at the top of the ramp, it has potential energy due to its height. As it moves, this is converted into kinetic energy.

The small triangles you cut at the bottom of the reindeer’s legs make it slightly unstable, so it rocks from side to side when gently pushed. As the reindeer rocks onto one leg, the other legs are lifted up, as it is on an incline, gravity pulls the lifted legs forward.

The reindeer rocks from side to side, moving forward with each cycle, which creates a walking type motion.

If you like this activity, don’t forget to check out my other Christmas science activity ideas.

Last Updated on December 19, 2025 by Emma Vanstone

#3130. Großbrand am Kehlsteinhaus: Feuer wieder aufgeflammt

Der Brand an Hitlers Kehlsteinhaus im früheren Nazi-Sperrgebiet Obersalzberg war gelöscht. Nun musste die Feuerwehr in der Nacht erneut ausrücken.

Nach dem Großbrand am historischen Kehlsteinhaus auf dem Obersalzberg in Berchtesgaden in Bayern ist das Feuer in der Nacht zum Sonntag erneut aufgeflammt. Es habe "nochmal zimmerhoch gebrannt", sagte ein Polizeibeamter. Die Feuerwehr rückte aus und löschte die Flammen. Dass ein Feuer wegen Glutnestern nach dem eigentlichen Brand wieder aufflackert, sei nicht unüblich, sagte er.

Am mehr als 1800 Meter hoch gelegenen Kehlsteinhaus war in der Nacht zum Samstag ein Großbrand ausgebrochen. Nach Angaben des Polizeipräsidiums Oberbayern Süd in Rosenheim löste ein Rauchmelder des Gebäudes am Freitagabend gegen 21.15 Uhr Brandalarm aus. Die alarmierten Feuerwehren sahen bei der Anfahrt hoch aufschlagende Flammen, vor Ort wurde dann "der Vollbrand des Gebäudes feststellt". Die Flammen hätten es "weitestgehend zerstört".

Etwa 200 Rettungs- und Einsatzkräfte von Feuerwehr, Rotem Kreuz, Polizei und Bergwacht waren ausgerückt. Der Schaden geht nach ersten Schätzungen des Zweckverbands Bergerlebnis Berchtesgaden in die Millionen.

Einsatzkräfte nahmen einen 33-jährigen Verdächtigen fest, der aufgrund mutmaßlicher psychischer Erkrankung vorläufig in ein psychiatrisches Krankenhaus eingewiesen wurde. Es würden mögliche politische Motive geprüft, hieß es am Samstag von der Staatsanwaltschaft. Der Mann war laut Ermittlern am Freitagabend unmittelbar nach Brandausbruch von eingesetzten Kräften auf einem Motorrad gestoppt und festgenommen worden.

Das 1937/38 erbaute Kehlsteinhaus bei Berchtesgaden war Teil des sogenannten Führersperrgebietes Obersalzberg und sollte NS-Diktator Adolf Hitler als Repräsentationsgebäude dienen. Seit 1952 wird es als Gaststätte genutzt, eine Ausstellung erinnert an die Geschichte des Hauses. Bayerns Innenminister Joachim Herrmann kündigte bereits den Wiederaufbau an. Das Haus sei wichtig für die "Erinnerungsarbeit".

If you have something specific in mind, know that you can select the “Notify Me” button on any item page to receive an email notification when the size and color you're looking for becomes available.

Away’s appeal goes beyond its minimalist design—it’s the thoughtful details that make the brand a trusted travel companion. Orders over $100 ship free, and if something isn’t quite right, you can return or exchange unused items within 100 days, either online or at one of Away’s 17 stores. Every suitcase is backed by a lifetime warranty, covering functional repairs so your luggage lasts trip after trip.

There’s purpose behind the polish, too: With sustainability in mind, Away incorporates more recycled materials into its luggage and ships everything in 100% recyclable packaging. And with Shop Pay, you can choose interest-free installments to make investing in quality gear a little easier.

If your Away promo code isn't working at checkout, don't panic—there are a few simple things you can do. First, double check that the code is spelled correctly with no extra spaces or typos. If that doesn't work, take a look at the exact details of the promo code to make sure it's still active and hasn't expired already. Keep in mind that some discount codes have a minimum spend requirement, so you'll want to be sure you've hit any necessary criteria for the deal. If everything looks right and your Away promo code still isn't working, clear your browser's cache and give the page a refresh. Shoppers can also contact Away's customer service for help.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#3132. Mountain Lions Are Keeping Deer Off the Road, Study Finds

A puma crossing a road on the Olympic Peninsula in Washington state. Nicolás Lagos / Panthera

Mountain lions in Washington state may be cutting down on traffic accidents by scaring deer away from roads, new research finds.

Deer often avoid open spaces, including roads, when predators are nearby. But while it has long been suggested that predators might tamp down on traffic collisions with prey, that has never been demonstrated in areas where big predators are well established, researchers say.

The new study tracked wildlife across the Olympic Peninsula in Washington state, comparing collision data with photos from camera traps that revealed the whereabouts of mountain lions. The big cats, sometimes referred to as cougars or pumas, prey primarily on deer.

Researchers found that where mountain lions were active, deer avoided roads. Overall, deer in those areas were 15 percent less likely to be found near roads, which led to a 67 percent drop in the odds of a traffic accident involving deer. The findings were published in the journal Current Biology.

“When we talk about pumas, we often focus on the risks they pose,” said coauthor Mark Elbroch of Panthera, a conservation group working to preserve wild cats. “But we rarely stop to consider the many ways they benefit us as well.”

#3133. The Best Blogging Tools For Beginners: Software I Use For This Site, Photography, & Designing Books

Iâve had many fellow travelers ask me how I do all the things needed for this travel blog and everything that goes into it. The answer usually comes down to having some seriously strong digital and blogging tools in my toolbox. This is my massive breakdown of blogging tools for beginners along with lots of practical advice if you’re thinking of starting a blog. Some of these tools, software, and apps are free, yet some aren’t freeâbut well worth the investment.

And yes, as of this writing Iâm still creating everything on this website solo. A labor of love my friend.

This site participates in the Amazon Services LLC Associates Program and other affiliate programs and may earn from qualifying purchases.

As a graphic designer by trade (hereâs the hard proof), Iâve been using many of these apps and software in one form or another my entire professional career. Whether blogging-specific or simply design and photography related, they work together.

Back in the day, these were typically only available on desktops. But nowadays most of the programs have extremely capable apps that allow me to work seamlessly while mobile, which is pretty handy.

Iâm literally writing this sentence while on my tablet…on a train from Barcelona to Valencia, Spain.

Of course, the first thing you need if youâre starting a blog or site is to have a home for it. Thatâs where a host (or server) comes in. If youâre starting a new blog, you can definitely go with a big gun like Bluehost, Hostgator, or similar. Iâve used both in the past.

Many host providers like Bluehost or Hostgator have “free hosting” or extremely cheap “shared” hosting options that are great tools for beginner bloggers.

Just keep in mind that shared hosting means your site is on a server with potentially hundreds of other sites. This can cause speed issues as well as vulnerability issues.

Eventually I needed a more personal touch and the speed and security that comes with dedicated server hosting. Now I use a smaller, independent host, but they’re attentive and availableâbut not taking new clients at the moment.

Not having a lot of money means that going with free or cheap hosting with Bluehost, Hostgator, or similar is necessary when youâre just starting a blog or website.

READ NEXT: The Ultimate Wanderluster, Nomad Adjacent, Chronic-preneur Gift Guide

As with half the world, I use WordPress for the bones of this website. If you looked at my site pre-2022, it looked different. Before the current design, I used an Elegant Themes page builder. They have many good options and a pretty fantastic âpay for lifeâ plan for all of their WordPress themes.

But be careful with page builders, as they can leave a lot in the background which makes changing themes really difficult. They’re a little more geared toward bonafide websites than blogs.

Now I use the Kadence theme and keep it simple, allowing the words and the photography to shine…hopefully.

For keyword research and SEO optimization researchâwhich are really, really, really important, I use Keysearch almost primarily. It allows me to do all of my own research, make lists of keyword topics, and also spy on some other sites and what theyâre doing. I use this before writing any content because keywords are literally what people may type into a search engine.

Knowing what people are searching for helps you write, so this is easily one of the most important and best blogging tools for beginners.

There are plenty of others, but they tend to cost more than Keysearch does.

I use the Yoast SEO plugin in the backend of WordPress to optimize posts when theyâre actually going into the blog. Yoast has free tools, but I pay a little more for robust WordPress tools that can help me when creating and pre-publishing posts inside WordPress.

Essentially, it’s like having a checklist built into your WordPress builder so that you don’t miss any important things before hitting publish.

Yoast SEO is a great free blogging tool, but well worth the yearly cost if you’re committed.

Google Analytics is pretty much the industry standard for understanding how traffic is getting to, spending time on, or leaving your blog or website. And since Google pretty much runs the world of SEO, why not use this free blogging tool?

You have the option to dive extremely deep into your traffic, down to demographics, time on page, bounce rates, and anything you would like to know. One of the best things is that you can leave notes on your timelines in tools like Google Analytics to mark important events.

For instance, I marked a note when I launched the redesign of this site. Then I noticed that over the next few months my “time on page” per reader almost doubled!

That means the hundreds of hours and financial investment were well worth it! Validation for the win!

Skillshare has been pivotal to me in learning new software and improving my skills in video, social media, and all the other things you need if youâre a creative. I’ve been using Skillshare for years and continue to go back to the well when I need schooled on both old and new software. Seriously…

There are some wicked smart and extremely polished educators on this platform. Highly recommend.

For photography, which Iâm passionate about but still have a lot to learn about, I almost always spend a couple of minutes editing or processing before you see anything. Whether it’s published in blog posts on this site, on Instagram, or any other social media platform.

One day I hope thatâs one of the things that makes this site stand out from the restâattention to quality photography.

The software I use for photo and video is from the Adobe Creative Suite, specifically Lightroomâboth on laptop and mobile. Lightroom allows me to take shots on mobile, import, edit and use, then syncs with my account so I can continue on the laptop. I also use if for RAW photos from my DSLR because those take some horsepower.

Organization is key when you have a lot of photos and destinations, and Lightroom is also built for organization. Beyond that, I also use Premiere Pro for serious video edits for YouTube.

Itâs one of the industry standards for video editing. On mobile, Iâll use Adobe Rush for quick edits for Instagram or YouTube shorts.

When posting to YouTube, I highly recommend TubeBuddy, since it makes âchecking all the boxesâ of best practices easy. TubeBuddy helps with SEO, keywords, card insertion, end screens, etc., and can also make batch changes to descriptions, which means you save time. (You can see The Nomad Experiment YouTube channel by clicking the icon below.)

I saw a significant improvement in people seeing my videos in search resultsâthus more viewersâonce I started using their interface. I suggest you start with a small, inexpensive plan then go up once you know whether YouTube is your jam.

TubeBuddy kind of ended up being a blogging tool too, since I learned a lot about SEO and keywords by using the Tubebuddy YouTube plugin.

Similar to photography, I use Adobe Creative Suite for page layout, and I have been for a long time. As much as I didnât like Adobeâs subscription model in the beginning, Iâve been won over by it because I literally have all the software and apps I need for so many needs, both on laptop and mobile.

I use Adobe InDesign 90% of the time for page layout and print design. It allows me to add hyperlinks throughout designs and create fillable fields that all export out to PDFs that end up being freebies on this site.

Oh, and I designed my entire 300+ page âBeginner Travelerâs Guide To Going Nomadâ 100% with Adobe InDesign.

I also use Canva occasionally, as it’s free and easy to use. But I use Canva mostly for image thumbnails or Instagram slideshows. Adobe also has “Adobe Express” which is similar to Canva, and it’s included in a Creative Suite subscription, or as a standalone.

I use Quip a lot for drafting contentâI’m literally drafting this article in Quip. Probably because itâs just an old go-to for me and I donât like how much control Google has over my data, so I don’t use Google docs much. I’ll then copy and paste into other tools like Grammarly. I use Grammarly for…well…grammar, punctuation, and tone issues.

I really like how Grammarly allows me to choose the tone of the article I’m writing and keeps me on track with that.

For much more broad, long-form content like writing The Beginner Travelerâs Guide to Going Nomad, I use Scrivener. They have large manuscript organization and tools on lock. Itâs kind of like Word on steroids. Not too many bells and whistles or sexy UI design, but it really helps with clearing away and allowing you to organize and write long-form content.

Regardless of whether you travel all of the time or are a nomad, you should have a VPN running at all times when using public wifi networks. Itâs literally a blogging tool beginners often overlook. But using a VPN is super helpful, since a âlack of stressâ is what it gives you. If you’re logging into your precious blog and a hacker gets your password, good luck!

And I know youâre using public wifi networks all the timeâbecause I do! (I’m literally writing this sentence from Metalo Cafe in Cape Verde, Africa on a public network.) Itâs so ridiculously easy for a hacker to get your passwords and content, yet itâs also ridiculously inexpensive to simply use a VPN nonstop.

I’m currently using Surfshark VPN and I’ve been very happy with it, but Iâve used ExpressVPN in the past and also recommend. Pretty much all VPNs will also give you the ability to use your VPN plan on at least 3 devices simultaneously, on the same plan.

Surfshark VPN has a feature where I can turn on âKill Switchâ which wonât even allow me to use the web unless the VPN is connected, which is a brilliant safeguard!

Obviously, I just implored you to get…and use…a VPN. But literally on the same level of concern should be using a password manager. If youâre still using some whack combination of your birthday or your last dogâs nameâin only 2-3 different variationsâthen if a hacker gets one of your passwords itâs not long before they have access to everything.

The best password managers will help you make every password unique and robust, then autofill fields for you so you never have to remember those super-tricky passwords.

This is a great blogging tool for beginner bloggers because starting a blog means a lot of new passwords and logins! Only $20-30 a year to save you the possibility of some major headachesâand potential financial loss or credit report havocâseems like a small price to pay.

Iâve used 1Password for years, but there are many reputable password managers out there. Find the one that fits you!

One thing I was extremely bad about back when I was new to blogging was growing an email list. This is the second most important thing to do next to owning your blog or website, which allows you to control all of your intellectual property. If Instagram, Facebook, or YouTube goes away, you still have your blog and your content. But…

without an email list of past readers, you’ll have very limited ways of contacting them and monetizing!

I’ve been using Mailerlite for a couple of years now and really like it. Mailerlite is a simple, drag-and-drop email marketing and list management app that has some really good tutorials.

More importantly, they have a free plan that allows you to build a fairly large email list before you need to pay. (Oh…the email optin form below will pop your email directly in my Mailerlite list. Hint, Hint.)

Skip aggressive but useful tools like ConvertKit until you have a substantial list built, since they tend to cost a chunk of change each month.

READ NEXT: Virtual Mailbox 101: What is a Virtual Mailbox & How I Get Mail While Traveling Full-Time

If youâre going to start a blog, or build any small business, I highly suggest you track your time on major time-sucks. Yes, even if youâre unlikely to make money for a long time. First, itâs good to know where your time is going…or not going.

Second, youâre less likely to lose your mind with the âI feel like Iâve been busy but I feel like I have nothing to showâ head game that happens when you get lost in time-consuming work.

I use Toggl Trackâs free plan for this and itâs more than enough. Itâs definitely one of my favorite blogging tools for beginners, but also just for any small business. I create a project regularly for longer-form posts so I can see how much time from start to publish it takes me. Then when I start hiring out, I at least have a good baseline for the time involved.

For project management I sometimes use Trello, but honestly Iâm sh*t at project management for this travel blog. Often times it just feels like Iâm battling a dumpster fire, haha!

I switched from the cult of MAC when I went nomadic because I didnât like the idea of always being force to pay 100% of an a phone bill if I was going to be on wifi a majority of the time. Apple iPhones aren’t Google fi native, so I jumped ship. Google fi and a Google Pixel was where I went, and no I use a Samsung Galaxy S20 because it allowed for an expansion SD card.

Since Google Fi allows calls on wifi and allows me to use my US number in hundreds of other countries, I rarely have to worry about landing somewhere and getting a SIM card (which means a new number, ugh). No, this isnât technically a blogging tool, but it makes life easier and itâs tech, so it made it on the list!

Google fi still has some kinks to work out. But saving upwards of $300-400 a year because I am smart about my data use makes it well worth the investment.

Especially when our phones can cost as much as a decent computer these days.

Obviously with any blog comes the dream of making âpassiveâ revenue in the background. What facilitates those are affiliate networks. Essentially, companies pay bloggers and others for âmarketingâ their products through referral links. Obviously, I only support products Iâve used or that come highly recommended, so itâs a win-win.

Affiliate networks like Awin, Partnerize, etc., help facilitate those relationships between advertisers and websites. So as you advance your blogging career, youâll want to create relationships with them. Some companies like Safetywing travel insurance run their own affiliate program.

Keep an eye out for great products and pay attention to whether they have an affiliate network they use or if they run their own program. Add these blogging tools to your toolbox only if your blog can actually get readership and clicks.

When you get enough content on your site, reach out to see if youâre a fit for to work with them. I actually donât suggest dipping your toes in this pool yet if youâre just starting a blog. Wait a little while.

The best advice I can give you is to have realistic expectations of how long building something as a second income can take, especially if starting a blog is that second income stream! It takes a lot of time and effort to grow your blog.

Iâve been writing and blogging for over 5 years now and I still only pull enough to pay for the expensesâand barely. Can you do it faster? Absolutely. But…

I suggest setting your expectations for a longer timeline and then putting in the work and maybe being happily surprised when you hit your goals earlier. If youâre starting with a strong social medial following, that will definitely help.

But if you know nothing about keywords, SEO optimization, email funnels, and management, or even how to edit good photos and videos, you likely have much more learning in front of you than you expect.

Ben een paar maanden geleden bij Lalabet begonnen en om heel eerlijk te zijn had ik er weinig van verwacht. De lobby is gewoon dik in orde: zo’n 2500 tot 3000 games voor zover ik kan zien. NetEnt, Play’n GO en Pragmatic zie je overal terug, en de bekende namen als Gates of Olympus, Sweet Bonanza en Book of Dead zitten er gewoon tussen.

Waar ik zelf het meeste hang is het live gedeelte. Die tafels draaien op Evolution en dat is gewoon kwaliteit: live dealers waarvan er een paar Nederlands praten, met Crazy Time en Monopoly Live erbij. Beeldkwaliteit is prima, zelfs op mobiel data.

Over de bonus: het is 100% tot 500 euro en 200 gratis spins, en 50 gratis spins zonder dat je iets stort. Doorspeelvoorwaarde is 35x, gemiddeld voor de markt, zeg maar. Ik had de voorwaarden vooraf doorgespit, de achtergrond van de club vind je op [url=https://unidosporcristosocial.com/read-blog/35828]Lalabet Review – Online spelen in 2026: een praktische spelersgids[/url] als je twijfelt. Een account maken is zo gebeurd en je kunt al vanaf 10 euro los.

Betalingen gaan via iDEAL, Visa, Mastercard, Skrill en Neteller, ook Bitcoin gaat er doorheen. Uitbetalen bij Lalabet duurde bij mij ongeveer 24 tot 48 uur, met e-wallet nog wat vlotter. En dat is meteen mijn irritatiepuntje: de KYC-check sleepte een paar dagen, daarna ging alles vlot.

Klantenservice zit in een chatvenster, antwoord komt doorgaans snel. Lalabet heeft gewoon Nederlandstalige support, al kreeg ik een keer duidelijk een standaardantwoord. Een echte app is er niet, het schaalt netjes naar je scherm dus dat mis ik eigenlijk niet.

Ze draaien op een Curacao-licentie, dus geen Nederlandse toezichthouder â dat moet je zelf afwegen. Ik heb er tot nu toe geen problemen mee gehad, maar ik speel dan ook met bedragen die ik kan missen.

Been playing at Nonebet for about four months now, mainly late nights, and might as well write something up since a few blokes here asked. Registration took me like two minutes â email and a password, that’s it, although the ID verification hit me later, which is normal enough. Minimum was $10 which is fine for a casual punter.

There’s a stupid amount of games â I’d guess around 4,000 titles last I looked. Play’n GO dominates, so Gates of Olympus, Big Bass, the usual suspects are sitting right on the front page. I tend to grind Yggdrasil and Betsoft titles when I’m not chasing. NetEnt back catalogue is there as well. The live section is Evolution-powered, which means real croupiers, roulette running 24/7 plus Crazy Time which I watch more than I play.

Bonus-wise the offer was 100% to $500 with 150 spins, rollover sits at 40x which is about average. They also had a no-deposit spins offer at one point but don’t count on it. Offers rotate a lot so have a look at [url=https://motoride.sk/?login=PeterNovakc982]Nonebet Casino – Real-Money Gaming in 2026: A Practical Player Guide[/url] before you claim anything. What did get on my nerves is the $5 max bet cap during bonus play â I busted it by accident once and lost the lot. Lesson learned.

Cashouts at Nonebet have been fine, mostly. Crypto came back in under an hour every time I’ve done it, Skrill and Neteller were about a day, but the Visa one dragged out to nearly four days which felt long. Funding is instant via card, Skrill, Neteller or crypto.

Support answered me at 2am, actual humans once you get past the bot. Nonebet doesn’t have a proper app as far as I can tell â it’s just the mobile browser, works well enough on the iPhone. It’s a Curacao licence, which isn’t the ACMA, obviously, make of that what you will for us down here.

I’ve been on Single Bet Calculator for the best part of a year, mainly on mobile, so this is just my two pence. Found it after a mate mentioned it, wasn’t an ad.

The game selection is frankly enormous â somewhere north of 3,000 games according to the filter counts. Pragmatic Play stuff dominates, so Book of Dead and the usual suspects are present and correct. I mostly stick to Betsoft games since the maths feels fairer to me. One gripe â the search function on Single Bet Calculator is a bit rubbish, filters half work.

The live dealer bit is Evolution-run, which is fine by me. Actual dealers, the stream holds up on 4G, and Crazy Time and Lightning Roulette is rammed on a Friday. Fair to note the UK tables are properly staffed from about 6pm onwards. If you want to compare the current terms I’d have a nose at [url=https://franciscopumari.com/acca-calculator-review-overview-for-uk-bettors]single bet calculator free[/url] since the offers shift about.

Welcome offer on Single Bet Calculator is ?100 matched plus 100 spins on Book of Dead. Wagering is 40x which is about par these days. They also ran a ?5 no deposit token when I registered. Min deposit is ?10, registration was quick, ID check was same-day.

Cashouts are decent. Card payments land in a couple of days, Skrill came through in under 12 hours, and Bitcoin is quickest if you use it. Took out about ?250 recently with no drama. Single Bet Calculator’s support was on me within five minutes â human, not a bot script. Properly licensed for UK players, so at least there’s a complaints route. No standalone app, which is mildly annoying but the site works fine.
