Make sure you regularly assess and correct, if needed, any of the following areas where you may be spending your time absorbing positive or negative vibes. While youâre at it, consider changing the channel to something that gives you more travel inspiration!

Whatâs the saying? You can pick your nose, but you canât pick your family? Well, I guess thereâs some truth to that, but you can choose how much and how often certain family members add to or detract from your life.

Have âfriendsâ in your life that you only tend to hang out with when you donât have better plans?

End up feeling like you need a warm shower to scrub off the negativity when youâre done hanging out with these “friends?”

At some point, youâll need to address whether thatâs a good use of your extra time or whether you should cut strings with some of these people and redirect your precious time somewhere else.

Some would say that itâs almost impossible to change who you work with or the fact that you have to be around them. Well, Iâm not having that. Life is long.

Some studies show that the typical adult will hold more than 10 different jobs by age 40 and more than 15 over the course of their lifetime.

If it ainât working, actively work to change it. I could even argue that a small pay cut or a less-than-perfect position is worth it to surround yourself with positive vibes and room or opportunity for growth.

While youâre at it, make sure your next job allows you to work remotely!

Yep, if you spend a lot of time volunteering youâre likely soaking up some good juju on the regular. Props to you my friend. More of this please! Just keep in mind that some places you volunteer can still be very draining or have management that makes the sacrifice on your part borderline toxic.

You can always choose to find other places to volunteer so that things are optimal and beneficial both ways, regardless of your long history with a certain organization.

Maybe yours is all body-positivity and inspiration-laden, but I know plenty where negativity and self-deprecation is the âmotivationâ used to get results. If the latter kind of gym is where youâre spending your time, maybe rethink that membership.

The old standby, so it cannot be overlooked. Good old, analog, snailâs pace reading, whether on paper or a screen reader.

Slowing down is necessary in this fast-paced worldâjust pay attention to what and how much youâre consuming, and whether the perspective is balanced.

Itâs getting harder and harder to consume authored works that arenât heavily slanted towards one political direction or another, or overly positive or negative. Be aware of the root of the messaging and try to balance your intake, thus keeping your ability to absorb and constructively argue contrasting views…like a grown ass-adult should.

Want to travel more but donât really know where to start? This is the no-fluff, hands-on guide to finally getting unstuck and on a travel pathâwith confidence, intention, and zero shame.

The reality of most of these sources is that theyâre âownedâ by someone or some kind of corporate machine with very specific intentions and influences. Yes, even more than the book authors mentioned above. Those influences tend to affect the slant in which the information is delivered. Again, pay attention and attempt to only consume channels that are as balanced or unbiased as possible.

I listen when I drive, walk or hike. Thatâs typically anywhere from 5-15+ hours per week. That author I listen to for 10 hours is probably spending more time influencing me than anyone in my family this week.

I use free sources/apps like Hoopla, Libby, or Cloud Library, which connect your library card and have a virtual library of books you can âcheck outâ on multiple devices. Or you can pay for a streaming audio service like this one for even more options.

Endless possibilities. If you so choose, Brene Brown, Tony Robbins, Seth Godin, and so many more will drop up-to-the-minute knowledge, inspiration, and motivation on the regular for your feasting ears. I also have friends that consume raunchy comedy for hours on end via podcasts.

To each their own, but Iâll take content that lights my brain on fire. Plenty of travel-centric options too!

The Location Indie Podcast, Zero To Travel, and Extra Pack Of Peanuts are literally three of the most influential podcasts I’ve ever listened to and played heavily into my getting over my travel anxiety and finally going nomadic!

There are tons of interesting channels out there from National Geographic to Curiosity Stream to Skillshare and all things in between.

Yep. I just went all meta on your ass. That little voice in your headâ¦or letâs be honest…voicesâ¦are something you literally canât get away from. But by maintaining positive external prompts you canhelp to control some of the negativity of your internal dialogue or the impact of memories.

#3153. How tech became the villain of the US midterms

Datacenters, AI and distaste for the billionaires developing it has soured Americans on big tech

How will Trump’s mass deportation agenda shape the US midterm elections? Our reporters answer your questions

The campaign ad begins with a clear, idyllic stream that suddenly turns sludge-brown as two concrete datacenters slam on to its banks. Another facility thuds down on a peaceful suburban park, and two more crush-green pastures as an ominous soundtrack to a disaster movie blares.

“They’re coming for our rivers. Our neighborhoods. Our farmland,” a deep-voiced narrator says. “Because Brent Taylor wrote the law allowing datacenters to take over Tennessee.”

The attack ad, paid for by the Democrat-aligned Three Star Pac and targeting a Tennessee Republican congressional candidate, is one of more than 150 midterm election campaign commercials across the US focused on datacenters or the artificial intelligence industry. At debates and at rallies, in mailers and online ads, the burgeoning AI industry has taken center stage, as both Republican and Democratic candidates try to convince voters that their opponents will put the unpopular facilities in voters’ backyards.

And it’s not only datacenters – the public anxiety over AI and distaste for the billionaires developing it, as well as backlash over encroaching tech such as surveillance cameras, has turned the tech industry into a ubiquitous villain this election cycle. As with big pharma before it, candidates are straining to distance themselves from big tech.

The stigma of the tech industry has even forced prominent Republicans to break with Donald Trump’s pro-AI party line, with candidates like Ken Paxton, campaigning for US Senate in Texas, calling for a slowdown. In Tennessee, Taylor’s campaign ran its own television spot that claimed he was tough on tech and datacenters.

The campaign ads focused on tech have sprung up alongside an ecosystem of pro- and anti-AI political action committees, which have collectively spent hundreds of millions of dollars to influence elections and back candidates. The breathtaking amount of spending has pushed tech into the forefront of the midterms, even as polls show issues like the economy, democracy and healthcare still rate as more important among voters.

Super Pacs funded by tech billionaires are among the top spenders in this election cycle. Leading the Future, formed by the OpenAI president, Greg Brockman, and venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, has raised more than $75m to back tech-friendly candidates. Elon Musk has sunk $366m into Republican causes, more than he spent on the 2024 presidential election. AI money has also been funneled into pro-regulation Pacs seeking to counteract the influence of deregulation groups.

Including Musk’s contribution to various Republican-aligned Pacs, the tech industry and its leaders have spent more than half a billion dollars to influence elections and ballot proposals in 2026.

The cumulative effect of such vast spending, lobbying and advertising is that tech issues and the tech industry have become far more pervasive in the midterms than previously seen in US elections, marking the first major test of how American voters will react to the AI boom.

Concern over AI’s potential effect on society has grown over the last year, and the backlash has been most intense where there is a physical target for voters’ ire. None of those targets have loomed larger than the sprawling datacenter facilities that are part of the tech industry’s multitrillion-dollar infrastructure build-out. Although campaigns have nodded to AI regulation and fears over the technology’s risks, it is datacenters that candidates have repeatedly and specifically called out as a real, tangible threat to constituents.

“Datacenters are now a campaign question in nearly every race in the nation,” said Brad Carson, the head of a pro-AI-regulation group Public First Action and a former congressman.

The growing animosity toward datacenters has also been reflected in nationwide protests and polling. A Pew Research poll from last month showed that the percentage of US adults who believe that datacenters are bad for the environment, energy costs and quality of life has risen across demographics since January. Only 4% of respondents believe the facilities will be good for the environment or home energy costs.

Datacenters have become toxic enough that some candidates have even begun using the facilities as an epithet to tar their rivals.

“Data Center Derek gave the billionaires and greedy corporations a $2bn tax break. Driving up our electric bills, destroying Ohio farms,” declared a Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee attack ad against the Ohio Republican candidate Derek Merrin.

At least 20 candidates for governor across the US are calling for moratoriums on datacenters, according to the policy tracking firm MultiState, while fewer than 10 candidates across 36 gubernatorial races are backing the projects without any calls for increased regulations.

Along with datacenters, the public backlash against AI-enabled Flock surveillance cameras that automatically scan license plates has also bled into campaigns, including in key battleground races. In Michigan, the Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed ran a Flock-focused ad that accused his Republican opponent Mike Rogers of pushing a surveillance state by backing the cameras. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico has similarly spoken out against the company and its data collection.

“Flock cameras have no place in Texas,” Talarico said last month at a rally. The state’s Republican governor, Greg Abbott, surprisingly agrees with him, blocking state agencies from spending on Flock cameras in August.

Elsewhere, legislation has targeted not just tech infrastructure but the billionaires behind it. In California, voters are considering a ballot measure that would levy a one-time 5% wealth tax on any resident of the state worth more than $1bn. The state’s ultra-rich have feverishly mobilized against it, raising more than $340m and spending more than $1m a day to fight the measure. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone has contributed at least $102m to oppose the tax.

The collective backlash against the tech industry has put its leaders in a bind. Companies are facing internal and external criticism of their products and politics, but accepting more intense government regulation or halting datacenter construction would threaten their growth.

The pushback has caused a shift in at least one company’s calculus – OpenAI has distanced itself from Leading the Future in recent months, and Brockman backed out of a planned $25m donation to the Pac.

Musk, Brin and other tech moguls, however, have doubled down on their efforts to swing votes their way.

“They have never met a problem that they didn’t think they could solve by throwing more money at it,” said Charles Blaettler, political director of the pro-AI-regulation Pac Guardrails Alliance. “They’re realizing there’s an intense backlash to their ideas.”

The political landscape of the tech industry is vastly different from the last time the US held midterm elections. Anthropic, now potentially set to go public at a more than $2tn valuation, was just one year old in 2022. OpenAI had not publicly released ChatGPT. Musk had not yet allied himself with Donald Trump’s campaign.

The tech industry has become increasingly entrenched in government and determined to shape regulation in the period since. Tech leaders have simultaneously built up immense campaign finance and lobbying arms that have come into full force in this year’s midterms.

Meanwhile, Americans feel negatively about how AI will affect a range of issues from personal relationships to the economy to elections, multiple polls show, as well as broadly opposing datacenters in their communities. More Americans oppose a datacenter being built in their area than oppose a nuclear power plant, according to a Gallup poll from earlier this year.

The public distaste for the AI industry also extends to its leaders, with polls showing that the US generally views executives such as Musk, the OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, and the Anthropic, CEO Dario Amodei, as untrustworthy and unlikable.

“There’s this very deep-seated sense of anxiety people have about the direction this technology is taking and who’s in control of it,” Blaettler said. “People just feel like they don’t have any agency in their lives any more.”

The enormous spending from the tech industry has largely flowed to Republicans, but it has also inspired a new category of pro-AI-regulation Pacs that have formed to counter groups like Leading the Future. Some of these pro-regulation Pacs have received money, counterintuitively, from AI companies and workers with different views on how government should oversee the technology. Anthropic contributed more than $40m to Carson’s Public First Action, while the Guardrails Alliance and its associated non-profit have raised more than $11.5m.

One of the early tests for this type of battle was in the Democratic primary for New York’s 12th congressional district in June, where pro- and anti-AI groups, including Carson’s, cumulatively spent $24m on the race – largely targeting candidate Alex Bores, who was running on a pro-regulation platform. The result of all the spending was hard to determine, with Bores coming second in a crowded field and losing to similarly pro-regulation candidate Micah Lasher. After the vote, Lasher sought to distance himself from both Anthropic and OpenAI’s spending.

“I have some news for the two big AI companies who’ve taken such an unusual interest in who won this congressional seat,” Lasher said in June. “I won’t be taking my cues from either of you when it comes to protecting our kids, our jobs, our environment.”

While the spending frenzy on pro- and anti-AI campaigns has helped fund some of the fights over tech in the midterms, leaders of pro-regulation Pacs say these are issues that voters already organically care about and are mobilizing around. The message from the AI industry has for years been that their products will usher in a utopian era of abundance and affluence, but this election cycle has shown there is deep skepticism from everyday voters that they will benefit from the boom.

“It’s now a world where most people on the street have a view about AI,” Carson said. “And it’s mostly negative.”

#3154. Tech firms should pay the creators whose work they use | Letter

It could raise up to £300m a year, providing UK creators with additional income, write Barbara Hayes, Tayyiba Nasser, Christian Zimmermann and Paul Seheult

Anthropic’s proposal (AI firm Anthropic to commit 5% of shares to fund for ‘public good’, 19 October) raises an important question: who should benefit from technological progress? Before pledging money for the public good, AI companies such as Anthropic should first pay the creators whose work they use.

Device manufacturers have a separate responsibility under the same principle: creators should share in the value their work generates. Smartphones, computers and other devices enable creative work to be copied and stored, yet UK creators receive no private-copying payments, unlike their counterparts in more than 40 other countries.

The proposed Smart Fund would require manufacturers and importers to make modest contributions on devices used to copy or store creative work. It could raise up to £300m a year, providing creators with additional income and supporting skills, cultural programmes and affordable workspaces.

For creators on persistently low and falling incomes, these payments would make a tangible difference. Visual artists’ median annual earnings are just £12,500 – 47% lower in real terms than in 2010. Authors earn a median of only £7,000 from writing, down from £11,300, according to surveys published in 2022 and 2018 respectively. Audiovisual performers report median annual earnings from performing of £17,500. Yet it is creators’ work that attracts people to technology, sustains their engagement and drives innovation. Those creators should share in the value their work helps generate, so they can continue creating and powering that cycle. The government should turn this principle into action by introducing the Smart Fund. Barbara Hayes Chief executive, Authors’ Licensing and Collecting Society (ALCS) Tayyiba Nasser Chief executive, British Equity Collecting Society (BECS) Christian Zimmermann Chief executive, Design and Artists Copyright Society (DACS) Paul Seheult Chief executive, PICSEL

#3156. Easy Last Minute Christmas Elf Ideas

We’ve all been there, the last-minute elf panic, wondering what simple but exciting mischief the Elf on the Shelf can get up to.

This year, Science Sparks makes elf antics easy with 24 easy science-based elf ideas and a sprinkle of festive fun to delight elves and children alike.

There’s an elf activity card for each day with full instructions and a list of materials. The ideas include tidying up with static electricity, making an elf zip line and supersized candy!

I’ve tried to make each day as simple as possible, using templates for some activities and mostly only very basic materials that hopefully you already have at home.

You can print off the whole elf ideas pack or just a selection of 4 days.

The days can be mixed up, or choose your favourites.

Leave out a balloon and tissue paper chopped into small bits. You could cut these into candy cane shapes if you want to be extra fancy.

For this one, boil one egg and leave the other uncooked. The boiled egg will spin more smoothly than the raw one.

One of my favourite science activities to do with young children is to ask them to draw around themselves and add in organs, skeletons or even muscles. For this activity, draw around your elf on a piece of paper and leave it next to the elf with some pens. The challenge is for children to draw what they think is inside an elf. Will it be human-type organs or bones made from candy canes?

This activity involves building a snowman from marshmallows, liquid glucose and icing! It’s a fun activity, STEM challenge and snack in one.

All you need for this festive optical illusion is a straw or pencil, tape and the template from the downloadable pack.

Use the template to create North Pole signs and leave them out with a glass of water. This is a fun, festive demonstration of refraction.

This is a super simple science activity that shows how gummy sweets seem to grow magically if left in the water! Simply pop the sweets in water and watch what happens.

Set up a science investigation to discover what happens to marshmallows in hot chocolate.

For this activity, you’ll need some boxes from the recycle bin, bubble wrap and tape. The idea is to create packaging to protect a potato chip/crisp or another delicate object.

Testing this one is the best part. Throw the packaging around with the crisp inside and see if it stays in one piece. Post the package to a friend to take it to the next level.

Cut the arrows and boxes from the template and leave them out with the elf to be put back together!

Imaginary festive food chains are fun, too.

Backwards messages can be written and read using a mirror. For an extra challenge, ask children to write the message with their non-writing hand.

This one is easy! Set up a bowl of water and some festive items to test. Use the table in the pack to record results.

For this activity, the elf needs to make snow angels with different items. It’s a bit messy, but worth it!

This activity aims to test how strong a candy cane is by hanging different items from the end. Keep adding until the candy cane snaps.

Set up an elf zip line by tying a string to two points inside or outside. You might need to construct a pipe cleaner harness to hold the elf in place.

Build a simple marshmallow launcher with a cup and a balloon, and leave it with some marshmallows or pom poms for children to experiment with.

Use materials from the recycle bin to design and build an elf clubhouse. As an additional test, try different materials to find one that makes a roof waterproof.

This colourful skittles display is super easy to set up and looks great too. Experiment with warm and cold water to see which is faster.

Shadow puppets are a great way to learn that light only travels in straight lines. Use the template or draw your own!

Let the elf build the first tower and challenge the children to make a taller one.

A basic parachute can be made from a square of paper with a section of string tied from each corner. This is also a fun way for the elf to arrive if you want to use this idea for day 1.

Create a cone Santa hat using red paper. Place the cone on top of an empty milk jug and squeeze hard. The hat will fly up into the air.

This simple flying Santa hat activity is a great way to learn about forces.

Attach the elf to a wall inside a pair of pants ( completely optional ) and leave some paper underneath for children to make the elf a paper plane so he can get down.

Whether you’re forward planning or looking for last-minute elf ideas, hopefully, you’ve found at least one activity to use!

#3157. How tech billionaires are disrupting biomedical science

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

Illustration: Mr.Nelson design; adapted from Minh Connors/Bloomberg, Michael Kovac/Breakthrough Prize, Sean Gallup, Angela Weiss/AFP (all via Getty)

It’s boom time for billionaires. In the next few months, the world could see a fresh crew of technology entrepreneurs join that club, and the numbers of multi-millionaires would swell even more.

How a new wave of science philanthropists can have the greatest impact

How a new wave of science philanthropists can have the greatest impact

Two giants of artificial intelligence, OpenAI and Anthropic, plan to go public in the next year or so, floating stocks that are expected to rocket some of their employees into the ranks of the ultra-wealthy. Some analysts have projected that Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) might bring in US$2 trillion, the largest in history. OpenAI is reportedly targeting $1.4 trillion for its IPO, although the company delayed going public until 2027 amid renewed concerns about AI safety.

If these IPOs go as planned, the effects might extend well beyond sales of superyachts, mansions and private jets. The windfall would probably also add to the flurry of private investments and philanthropic donations from tech-savvy entrepreneurs who are eager to jump-start their favoured areas of biomedical research, such as cancer biology, longevity and reproductive technologies. “It’s a very exciting time,” says Andrew Lo, who studies entrepreneurship at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge. “We’re going to see the creative energy of the tech sector unlocked.”

Wealthy technology entrepreneurs have long put their cash and creative energy into medical research. And as their fortunes have grown, so has the scale of their investments, and the variety of ways in which their funds are doled out. One major player is Altos Labs, a longevity-focused company in Redwood City, California, which launched in 2022 with $3 billion in funds raised from tech titans Yuri Milner and Jeff Bezos, among others — an unprecedented sum for a fledgling biotechnology company with no drug candidates. The Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (CZI) , founded by Facebook co-founder Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, physician Priscilla Chan, has spent about $4 billion on basic scientific research and other causes, and plans to spend up to $10 billion more over the next decade.

Ultra-wealthy research investors follow a different strategy than do government funding agencies such as the US National Institutes of Health (NIH). Organizations such as the CZI and Altos Labs boast a commitment to high-risk, long-term research. Tech entrepreneurs are also often keen to invest in new technology, and to harness the power of AI for biomedicine. In April, for example, the CZI announced that it would spend $500 million on funding predictive AI models of human cells. Last year, OpenAI Foundation, the non-profit arm of OpenAI in San Francisco, California, pledged to spend $25 billion on health, disease cures and AI resilience. The foundation has announced more than $100 million for Alzheimer’s disease research and another $125 million for life-sciences data projects this year.

But this investment comes at a time when the public is suspicious of the tech elite and its political influence. It is difficult to assess the success of philanthropic programmes, and many are geared towards encouraging the use of the same technology the philanthropists profited from developing. Meanwhile, high-profile private investment in firms that study longevity or controversial reproductive technologies, such as gene editing in human embryos, raises questions about whether tech entrepreneurs will skew research towards applications that benefit the wealthy, rather than helping a broader swathe of society. “In philanthropy, no one gets elected,” says Rob Reich, a political scientist at Stanford University in California. “There’s no way of holding them accountable.”

US philanthropists have a long history of influencing what research gets done, and how. In the early twentieth century, grants from industrialists such as Andrew Carnegie and John D. Rockefeller helped to transform higher education and solidify the role of US universities in scientific research. Their giving focused on ensuring that the institutions they supported succeeded; today’s philanthropists are more likely to seek a particular outcome rather than support the long-term health of a university, says Eric John Abrahamson, a historian at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland. In 2024, non-profit organizations, including philanthropies, supported an estimated $25 billion in research and development — about 11% of total research funding in the United States, according to the Science Philanthropy Alliance (see ‘Support sources’).

It is difficult to track all donations from technology magnates comprehensively, but individual examples show that their influence has been sizeable. In 2000, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates established the Gates Foundation (formerly called the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation), which made massive investments in vaccine development and the study of infectious disease, among other fields. It remains an influential behemoth: last year, Gates announced that he would donate about US$200 billion over the next two decades.

Other large tech donors include Sergey Brin, a co-founder of Google, who has donated more than $1 billion to Parkinson’s disease research. Sean Parker, an early executive at Facebook, has given hundreds of millions to cancer-immunotherapy research. In 2021, several philanthropists, including tech entrepreneurs, donated $650 million to found the Arc Institute in Palo Alto, California, in the heart of Silicon Valley, to understand the root causes of complex diseases. And US software magnate Larry Ellison announced that he will spend billions of pounds over ten years on a new campus near the University of Oxford, UK. The campus will focus on health care, as well as agriculture, climate change and AI.

In addition to charitable donations, tech entrepreneurs have been fuelling biomedical innovation through private-sector investments, such as funding Altos Labs. Another company, Calico Life Sciences, was founded in 2013 with backing from Google. With a focus on combating ageing and curing disease, Calico, in South San Francisco, California, was conceived as a long-term ‘moonshot’ programme. Sam Altman, a co-founder and chief executive of OpenAI, has invested about $180 million in Retro Biosciences, another longevity-focused company, in Redwood City, California.

In some cases, the line between for-profit investments and philanthropic donations are becoming more blurred, says Louis Shekhtman, a network scientist at Bar-Ilan University in Ramat Gan, Israel. The CZI, for example, was set up as a limited liability company (LLC), rather than as a tax-exempt foundation. Doing so comes at a cost: depending on how they are constructed, LLCs might not be eligible for the tax breaks that more-conventional charities enjoy. But an LLC can be more flexible in how it spends its money, and has fewer requirements to publicly disclose its activities, says Joan Heminway, a business-law scholar at the University of Tennessee in Knoxville.

In a 2015 statement shortly after the launch of the CZI, Zuckerberg said the LLC structure would give the initiative “the flexibility to give to the organizations that do the best work — regardless of how they’re structured”. He also said that any net profits from CZI investments would be put towards furthering its philanthropic mission.

How to spend $25 billion on science: OpenAI’s staggeringly rich research charity gets under way

How to spend $25 billion on science: OpenAI’s staggeringly rich research charity gets under way

Favourable US tax policies and a high concentration of billionaires — many of them in the technology industry — mean that the United States is unmatched among wealthy nations for charitable giving, says Shekhtman. It is also a major hub for biomedical research, and home to nearly half of the world’s biopharmaceutical companies.

And US tech entrepreneurs have a penchant for experimentation in how they structure their investments, says Keith Yamamoto, vice-chancellor of science policy and strategy at the University of California, San Francisco. When it comes to philanthropy, private donors are more able to take risks with their investments than are government funding agencies, which are beholden to taxpayers to ensure that their money is spent wisely. “Public money limits your activities,” says Harold Varmus, a former director of the NIH, who has also been on advisory boards for the Gates Foundation and the CZI. “There is a freedom of motion that is associated with private money.”

Some tech titans have experimented with various ways of structuring their grants. The Arc Institute, for example, boasts a “no-strings-attached” funding system that gives its investigators more freedom than do standard government grants awarded to biomedical researchers.

Philanthropists are also able to fund long-term, interdisciplinary projects that can be difficult for government grants to take on. Convergent Research, a non-profit organization funded in part by Eric Schmidt, the former chief executive of Google, is forming ‘focused research organizations’ that bring teams together to solve important scientific or engineering challenges that could benefit a wide swathe of research. “We’re looking for the pieces of critical, fundamental infrastructure missing from a particular field,” says Anastasia Gamick, a co-founder and president of Convergent Research, which is headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

Projects include developing cheap ways to map the neurons in mammalian brains, and large-scale screening to catalogue the off-target effects of small-molecule drugs.

Meanwhile, Yamamoto points to the CZI’s Institute for Advanced Biological Imaging as another example of a long-term, high-risk project that aims to develop pivotal technology. He hopes that the team there — which has brought engineers, physicists and computer scientists together with biologists — will succeed in refining a difficult technique called cryo-electron tomography so that it can image processes in a cell at the level of individual proteins.

Nature Spotlight: Philanthropy and awards

Nature Spotlight: Philanthropy and awards

Tolerance for risk is also evident in some tech entrepreneurs’ investments in for-profit companies. Some investors hope to reshape how fundamental research is conducted. Arcadia Science in Emeryville, California, for example, was launched with backing from Altman and from Jed McCaleb, a cryptocurrency entrepreneur in the United States, and pledges to “rethink the entire research cycle” by branching out from the usual laboratory model systems, such as mice and the bacterium Escherichia coli, to study more diverse organisms. Like Calico Life Sciences, the company warned investors from the start: this will take time.

Arcadia has also taken an unusual step for a for-profit company and embraced open science to a degree not typically found in industry, says Yamamoto. Its lab protocols, computer code and data sets are published directly online.

Silicon Valley investors are also sometimes willing to wade into controversial territory. Last year, Brian Armstrong, chief executive of the cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase, helped to fund a company dedicated to developing methods to edit the genome in human embryos to prevent disease. The company, named Preventive and based in San Francisco, will first have to grapple with the fundamental science of heritable gene editing to learn whether and how it can be done safely, says Lucas Harrington, a co-founder of Preventive. Private investment will enable the company to do that research, which US legal restrictions prohibit government grants from funding.

#3158. Faktencheck: Wie Flávio Bolsonaro Zweifel an Brasiliens Demokratie sät

Hört man dem rechten Präsidentschaftskandidaten zu, könnte man glauben, der amtierende linke Präsident Lula habe Brasiliens Demokratie an den Rand des Abgrunds gebracht. Wie viel Wahrheit steckt hinter der Rhetorik?

Am 25. Oktober entscheiden die Wählerinnen und Wähler in Brasilien zwischen dem linken Präsidenten Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva und dem rechten Kandidaten Flávio Bolsonaro, Sohn des ehemaligen, inhaftierten Präsidenten Jair Bolsonaro.

Im stark polarisierten Wahlkampf in Südamerikas flächen- wie bevölkerungsmäßig größtem Land hat Flávio immer wiederein dunkles Bild von Brasiliens Demokratie unter Lula gezeichnet.

Behauptung: Bolsonaro zufolge hat die Lula-Regierung "ein institutionelles Ungleichgewicht geschaffen. Sie hat sich entschieden, gemeinsam mit einer Fraktion des Obersten Bundesgerichts zu regieren."

Vor Journalistinnen und Journalisten erklärteder 45-Jährige nach der ersten Wahlrunde Anfang Oktober: "Ist Brasilien eine vollwertige Demokratie? Nein." Lula stelle eine Gefahr für die Demokratie dar.

Unter Lula hat sich der Zustand von Brasiliens Demokratie nicht verschlechtert – sondern vielmehr verbessert im Vergleich zu seinem Vorgänger Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio Bolsonaros Vater.

Das zeigen Demokratie-Indizes wie Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem)und der Bertelsmann Transformation Index (BTI), die den Zustand demokratischer Institutionen weltweit vergleichen. Bei BTI heißt esetwa: " Nach den Herausforderungen und Bedrohungen für die brasilianische Demokratie durch die Regierung von Jair Bolsonaro hat sich die politische Lage seit 2023 etwas stabilisiert."

Die Indizes beschreiben Brasiliens demokratische Institutionen als allgemein funktionsfähig, das Wahlsystem des Landes und die unabhängige Justiz als widerstandsfähig.

Der rechtsextreme Jair Bolsonaro war von 2019 bis 2022 Präsident Brasiliens, der ehemalige Militäroffizier machte aus seiner Sympathie für Brasiliens Militärdiktatur keinen Hehl und hatte für die Spielregeln der Demokratie nicht gerade viel übrig.

Dies bestätigt auch die Politikwissenschaftlerin Marjorie Marona: "Mit der Bolsonaro-Regierung haben wir erlebt, wie eine Strategie systematischer Angriffe auf demokratische Institutionen in der Praxis aussieht. Er griff den Wahlprozess an und drohte, Entscheidungen des Obersten Bundesgerichts nicht umzusetzen. Er setzte die Presse und die Kontrollorgane unter Druck. Und all das mündete, wie wir wissen, in einen Putschversuch.“

Am 8. Januar 2023 stürmten Tausende Anhänger von Jair Bolsonaro Regierungsgebäude in der Hauptstadt Brasília, weil sie das Ergebnis der Präsidentschaftswahl 2022 nicht anerkennen wollten. Bolsonaro wurde später wegen der Vorbereitung eines Putsches zu mehr als 27 Jahren Haft verurteilt.

Mit Lula war dagegen laut Marona, die an der Bundesuniversität des Bundesstaates Rio de Janeiro (UNIRIO) lehrt, "eine Umkehr jenes Autokratisierungsprozesses" zu beobachten: "Die Angriffe auf das Wahlsystem hörten auf, und das Verhältnis zwischen den Staatsgewalten funktioniert wieder deutlich weniger konfrontativ.“

Flávio Bolsonaros Behauptungen, Brasiliens Demokratie stehe am Abgrund, zielen nicht nur auf den amtierenden Präsidenten ab, sondern auch auf den Obersten Gerichtshof STF und insbesondere STF-Richter Alexandre de Moraes.

Laut Bolsonaro habe dieser Brasiliens "Demokratie gekidnappt"und verfolge gezielt Politiker aus dem rechten Lager. Zwar kritisieren Expertinnen und Expertentatsächlich schon lange, dass der Oberste Gerichtshof Macht bei einzelnen Richterinnen und Richternkonzentriert.

Auch Marona sagt: "Der Oberste Gerichtshof hat durchaus strukturelle Probleme, die nach Reformen verlangen. Ein Richter am Obersten Gerichtshof kann eigenmächtig ein Gesetz per einstweiliger Verfügung wegen Verfassungswidrigkeit aussetzen. Er kann ein Verfahren bisweilen monatelang blockieren – indem er Akteneinsicht beantragt –, selbst, wenn es bereits eine klare Mehrheit gibt."

Aber was Bolsonaro tue, sei keine legitime Kritik, sondern eine ständige Darstellung von sich und seiner Familie als politisch Verfolgte – Moraes war der federführende Richter im Prozess gegen Ex-Präsident Jair Bolsonaro.

Viele aktuelle Vorwürfe Bolsonaros gegen Moraes beziehen sich auch auf den Banco-Master-Skandal. Gegen den früheren Eigentümer der Bank, Daniel Vorcaro, ermittelt die Bundespolizei wegen milliardenschwerer Finanzdelikte und Korruptionsvorwürfen.

Es wurden auch Nachrichten Vorcaros an STF-Richter Alexandre de Moraes bekannt sowie ein Vertrag von umgerechnet 24 Millionen Euro zwischen der Bank und der Anwaltskanzlei von Moraes' Ehefrau. Moraes weist Vorwürfe des Fehlverhaltens zurück.

Dass Flávio Bolsonaro selbst auch in den Fokus der Banco-Master-Ermittler geraten ist – es gab Treffen und er hat den mittlerweile festgenommenen Bänker um finanzielle Unterstützung für den Film "Dark Horse" über seinen Vater gebeten – hielt ihn nicht davon ab, Moraes lautstark zu kritisieren. Auch Flávio Bolsonaro bestreitet Unregelmäßigkeiten.

Der Banco-Master-Skandal ist ein Beispiel für weitreichende systemische Korruption – diese wird auch von den Demokratie-Indizes als großes Problem in Brasilien beschrieben, das die Bewertung verschlechtert. So wird das Land etwa beim Democracy Index der Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) in die Gruppe der "Mangelhaften Demokratien"eingeordnet.

Zu den chronischen Mängeln von Brasiliens Demokratie gehört unter anderem die extreme politische Polarisierung, zu der Flávio Bolsonaro paradoxerweise selbst mit seinen Behauptungen beiträgt.

Expertinnen und Experten warnen, dass Institutionen allein eine Demokratie nicht dauerhaft tragen können, wenn große Teile der Gesellschaft Angriffe auf demokratische Institutionen und Regelbrüche der Rechtsordnung normalisierten und Politiker anderer Parteien als Feind betrachteten.

Marco Antonio Carvalho Texeira, Politikprofessor an der Päpstlichen Katholischen Universität von São Paulo, meint: "Wir haben das Verständnis verloren, dass Politik etwas Konstruktives ist und nicht nur ein Schlagabtausch oder eine Strategie, um den anderen auszuschalten."

Misstrauen gegenüber demokratischen Institutionenzu säen ist eine Strategie, die auch Rechtspopulisten anderer Länder erfolgreich einsetzen. Sie dient nicht nur der Mobilisierung von Wählerschaft, sondern kann auch den Grundstein dafür legen, demokratische Kontrollmechanismen nach der Wahl zu schwächen.

Marona sagt: "Ich erkenne da ein Muster, man denke etwa Viktor Orban in Ungarn oder Donald Trump in den USA. Am Anfang steht immer das Narrativ, diese Institutionen seien korrupt oder marode, um genau darauf aufbauend eine Strategie zur Änderung der Spielregeln in Gang zu setzen."

Viele Brasilianerinnen und Brasilianer fürchten sich vor einem solchen Szenario nach der entscheidenden Stichwahl am 25. Oktober.

#3159. 9 Best Boutique Hotels in Nashville for Your Next Music City Getaway

The best thing about Nashville is that everybody sings to their own tune. It’s a town of creatives. As a Music City resident, I walk outside and never know who I might meet: a country musician, a rock star, a clothing designer, an entrepreneur, a bride on her bachelorette, or all of the above.

The best boutique hotels in Nashville reflect that creative chaos. Many of the properties are so distinct, it’s hard to believe they share the same zip code. But that’s the beauty of this anything-but-one-note town. One day you could be checking into a 425-acre sustainable resort, looking at citrus trees grown inside a custom orangerie; the next, you could be bedding down at a hotel overlooking the football stadium after pre-gaming on the rooftop.

While each of the intimate hotels on this list is completely different, they all provide an authentic Nashville experience, whether you're looking to be blocks from Broadway or in a suburb where you can live like a local. Here are the nine boutique hotels in Nashville I recommend to my friends and family when they come to town.

Sometimes you want guests to stay close by, but not on your couch. Sylvan Boarding House, opened in 2026, was designed exactly for that scenario: The century-old former boarding house was carefully restored into a B&B by Sylvan Park residents who wanted folks to be able to stay in—and get a real feel for—their residential West Nashville neighborhood. With eight individually designed rooms named after famous Nashville families, the inn offers guests a homey breakfast, a restful night’s sleep, and a taste of what it's really like to live in Tennessee's capital, far from the neon of Broadway.

Nashville has a reputation as being a place to party with your friends, and if that’s on your itinerary, few places are better to hole up than Waymore’s. This East Nashville hotel is a friendly, funky stop with lots of communal space—plus a lobby photo booth—built for hanging out, making plans, and decompressing. The rooftop bar is well-designed as a cozy but bustling spot for groups, and Short Stories Café, the lobby restaurant, is the place for breakfast and lunch. The hotel's Main Street location is convenient to downtown, Nissan Stadium, and East Nashville’s Five Points neighborhood.

When training his staff at The Chloe, owner Ro Leblanc instills the golden rule. The result is a buzzy, friendly environment where people really feel welcomed—and it’s not just hotel guests. Located in Hillsboro Village, in the former home of Asylum Records, The Chloe is a hangout for locals too. Neighbors have pool memberships, and the bar is a go-to for a nightcap. Each of the hotel’s 19 rooms has different decor, contributing to the feeling that this is a place to live in, not just visit. Insider tip: Don’t skip the praline ice cream sandwich (served at the bar, in the restaurant, or by the pool).

Check Availability at The Chloe Nashville

The 1965 building that houses the Drift Hotel has lived a lot of lives since Elvis Presley reportedly stayed there in his heyday. The most recent incarnation features 87 rooms designed with impeccable midcentury-modern style and remarkable attention to detail, such as room numbers made from custom tapestries. The Sun Room and Poolside at Drift bars have become destination waterholes for locals, and the rooftop penthouses (where Elvis stayed) are the big-money picks for a pre-game party, offering views of Nissan Stadium.

I'm a fan of all the hotels on this list (that’s why I chose them), but if I were Eloise and got to live in one day in and day out, I’d choose the Fairlane. I love the terrazzo floors in the lobby, the plush headboards in the guest rooms (they have cup holders, so you can sip your wine, water, or coffee while you sit in bed), and the floor-to-ceiling windows providing some of the city’s best people-watching. All-day brunch at Modern Love, the lobby restaurant, is a draw for the sleep-in-late crowd.

As the city’s oldest and most historic hotel, The Hermitage is full of city lore. A member of the hotel’s staff serves as its historian, continuing to show how the property connects to Nashville’s past, present, and future—be sure to ask them about the lobby-level displays of historic ephemera. The 122-room hotel was completely renovated in 2022, so its large guest rooms feature modern amenities alongside old-school touches, like a sheet of stationery with your name on it waiting in your room. In 2021, celebrity chef Jean-Georges Vongerichten opened his first restaurant in the South in the Hermitage, a place that is at once refined and friendly, like the hotel itself.

Southall’s name isn’t just a clever marketing ploy. This 62-room resort is a working farm 25 miles south of downtown Nashville, with citrus trees, hydroponic greenhouses, an orchard, and sustainable farming practices. The fruits of the land are part of the experience, served in restaurant dishes and lining the walkways as you stroll the verdant acreage. Southall is a true resort experience, with options for traditional inn rooms or freestanding cottages with screened-in porches, deep soaking tubs, and firepits. The spa features a soaking pool with pond views and a lineup of wellness classes.

Housed in a former church in East Nashville, the Russell remains connected to its roots. The magnificently restored stained-glass windows boast bright colors that provide not just a color palette, but an aesthetic direction throughout the 23-room hotel. Local firm Mission Hotels (which also owns The Gallatin and 506 Lofts) donates 100% of the profits from each stay to people experiencing homelessness in the city.

This 10-room oasis stands in the heart of Germantown, and the building itself has been here since 1865. It offers a quiet and refined bed-and-breakfast experience just blocks from Nashville’s hubbub, including the minor league baseball stadium and the hip and happening Neuhoff District. A walled-in garden (and a glassed-in sitting room overlooking it) offers a compelling spot to sit, read, and decompress before or after visiting Music City’s most popular sites.

What is the difference between a hotel and a boutique hotel?

Boutique hotels are a category of hotel. They typically have fewer than 100 guest rooms and offer a one-of-a-kind vibe that makes the property stand out. They are often independently owned, but some major hotel chains have created unique boutique properties that show off the best of a particular city or neighborhood.

What is the most luxurious hotel in Nashville?

Luxury is in the eye of the beholder, of course, but the non-boutique 1 Hotel Nashville checks all the boxes, with impeccable service, enveloping scents from Bamford Wellness Spa, and design that provides an oasis from Nashville’s energy right outside the door. Every room in the pet-friendly hotel has live green plants, providing oxygen as you sleep.

Where should I avoid staying in Nashville?

Nashville’s core neighborhoods, including downtown, SoBro, and The Gulch, are quite walkable, but the further afield you go, the less you'll be able to walk, and public transportation options may become sparse. Budget hotels on and near Murfreesboro Pike are not close to many attractions, so any savings on room rates may be spent on parking and transportation. As in any city, visitors to Nashville should stay aware of their surroundings wherever they stay.

How we choose the best boutique hotels in Nashville

Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#3160. The World Adds a Third Terawatt of Solar Power

In March, the world passed a major energy milestone, adding its third terawatt of solar power. Increasingly, poorer countries are leading the shift to solar, analysts say.

It took nearly seven decades, after the invention of the silicon solar cell in 1954, for the world to install 1 terawatt of solar capacity, conceivably enough to power the entire United States. After passing that milestone in 2022, the world added its second terawatt in 2024 and its third in 2026, Bloomberg reports.

BloombergNEF expects installations will continue apace, with the world hitting 9 terawatts of solar power by 2036. Analysts project that, by that date, poor countries will have installed more solar power than rich countries, China notwithstanding.

The first terawatt of solar was installed largely in wealthy nations, as governments subsidized renewable energy, Bloomberg reports. But since then, China has emerged as the global solar leader, installing huge amounts of solar while exporting inexpensive panels across the developing world.

The dynamic is most evident in countries hard hit by energy shocks, such as Pakistan, Nigeria, and Cuba. In the face of soaring fossil fuel prices, homeowners have begun snapping up imported solar panels.

The global solar boom is now spurring a push to build out transmission lines that can ferry energy from where it is produced to where it is needed, and fueling demand for batteries that can store up surplus power. Countries such as Pakistan, where energy shocks have spurred a solar buildout, have seen a surge in battery sales.

China, which is responsible for more than half of all solar installations globally, doubled its battery storage capacity last year, according to data from energy think tank Ember. And in its latest Five-Year Plan, it set a goal to ramp up the use of renewable energy by deploying yet more storage.

A First Among Major Nations, India Is Industrializing With Solar

#3162. The Guardian view on Oxford Street’s pedestrianisation: cities should be designed around people, not cars | Editorial

The transformation of Europe’s busiest shopping street should be a case study in making cities greener, less congested and more inviting places to live

Sadiq Khan has been trying to pedestrianise Oxford Street since he first became the mayor of London in 2016. On Monday, after numerous setbacks, his plan will finally come to fruition. The busiest stretch of the nation’s famous shopping street will be closed to traffic in a scheme designed to improve the area and make it more attractive to pedestrians. It should be an emblematic case study in making cities greener, less congested, more inviting places to live and visit.

The Greater London Authority hopes it will rejuvenate a high street fallen on hard times. Since the pandemic, the number of vacant shops on Oxford Street has more than quadrupled. It estimates that the scheme will generate £82m of value a year in the area by increasing footfall and encouraging visitors to linger. This impact remains to be seen, but research from other cities suggests that shops experience higher sales once an area is pedestrianised. Given the prime minister’s focus on rejuvenating British high streets, whose dilapidation is correlated with support for Reform UK, he should be watching with interest.

The benefits of pedestrianisation are far greater than increased shopping. Domestic transport remains the largest contributor to greenhouse-gas emissions in Britain. This sector’s emissions have fallen more slowly than others largely because too many people still rely on cars. Mr Khan’s city is an outlier: 59% of all journeys in Britain were made by car in 2024, while in London cars accounted for 34%. This is hardly surprising when the Treasury spends twice as much on London’s transport system as it does on other regions in England, and the capital’s bus fares are cheaper. In Leeds, which has no mass-transit system, nearly half of people drive to work. Car use cannot be reduced without simultaneously improving public transport.

The critics of pedestrianisation – including Westminster council – suggest it merely displaces traffic elsewhere. But the evidence on this is more nuanced. One study from the University of the West of England suggests the closure of strategic roads causes some traffic to disappear permanently, as people switch to public transport or walk. Low-traffic neighbourhoods (LTNs), the pedestrianisation schemes that were rushed through in the capital during Covid-19 and have since been introduced in Manchester and Birmingham, were fiercely criticised for causing a buildup of road traffic elsewhere. Yet one study of 46 LTNs in London suggested their impact on traffic elsewhere was minimal.

Car-free areas should be accompanied by other policies that reduce pollution on surrounding roads, such as the low-emissions zones introduced in London and Oxford. Mr Khan was criticised by the then leader of the opposition, Keir Starmer, for the expansion of Ulez in 2023, and also suffered racial abuse. He has since been vindicated by research from Imperial College suggesting Ulez has significantly improved the health of primary school children in the capital, whose lung growth had been stunted by pollution.

That Transport for London estimates the pedestrianisation of Oxford Street will have only a minimal impact on nitrogen dioxide emissions, which were already decreasing as a result of Ulez, is testimony to the policy’s success. In 2014, Oxford Street had the highest concentration of nitrogen dioxide pollution in the world. Its pedestrianisation should be an inspiration to other cities to embrace policies that work for people, not cars.

Things started well enough, with the sun shining through the windows of my small studio apartment in Mindelo, Cape Verde, Africa. Then that idea returned for me to remove my passport from where I keep it when on flights and moving from place to place, and to put it somewhere safe so Iâm not walking around with it unnecessarily. I donât usually walk about with my passport unless I know Iâm going to need it, as thatâs just asking for something to happen to it.

I feel like you know where this is going.You seem like you understand foreshadowing…

READ NEXT: Traveling Tips For NewbiesâKeep Yourself Safe & Reduce Travel AnxietyWhat Do You Want To Be When You âGrow Up?â â Be Encourageous.

This site participates in the Amazon Services LLC Associates Program and other affiliate programs and may earn from qualifying purchases.

I reached my hand in the only place my passport should have been only to find it empty. The immediate, audible âFuuuuuuuu…where is my passport!?â blurted loud enough for the next apartment to hear. Then the next 45 minutes repeatedly emptying everything and searching every possible spot in my belongings. You know, all the places where I already knew I hadnât put my lost passport.

Iâve only been in Cape Verde for 4 nights now, and had to use my passport to get out of the airport on arrival. Therefore somewhere between scanning it at the terminal and now, it has vanished.

Did I drop it in the airport when I was putting it back in my secret spot?Â Did it fall out in the cab?Â Did the cab driverâwho knowingly double-charged our fareâmake off with it?Â Did someone lift it from my bag between then and now?Â Is it still hiding somewhere “safe” that I may have put it and forgotten?

At this point my insulin pump screamed at me to tell me that my insulin was still stopped and that I hadnât told it to resume insulin. Alarm fatigue is real my friend. Really felt like it was turning into one of those days at this point…

READ NEXT: Traveling Tips For NewbiesâKeep Yourself Safe & Reducing Travel AnxietyTravel Medical Insurance, Pre-Existing Conditions, & Type 1 Diabetes

Especially since I still feel Iâm very new to travel. I canât think of a time Iâve left my bag out of my sight or off my back in public spaces in the past few days, other than at the coworking space for a moment here and there.

So there I was pacing my apartment, boiling over the reality of facing âwhatâs next…â and knowing it probably wonât be a simple task to replace my lost passport before I leave the island in a couple of weeks. The US embassy is on another island in the country, so Iâm guessing Iâll need to spend a day going there and back somehow.

At this point I decided to stop searching the apartment for my lost passport and to just try again later. Then I headed off to coworking to get some work done.

I chose to dodge the normal spot where I get coffee as I just didnât feel like dealing with the crowd. Got into coworkingâfirst one here…since itâs Saturdayâand opened all the doors and windows to set it up for the day and get the air moving.

Then sat down at my desk, pulled out my computer and cords, reached for my international adapter so I could plug in and….I left it sitting back on the bed at the apartment. Blerg.

READ NEXT: Books for Inspiration, Motivation, & Generally Slaying it at Adulting

At that point, I had many choices, but the one I wanted (want?) to go with is to feel sorry for myself, be frustrated, and begin to give up on the day. At 8:30 in the morning no less. Of course, I could have packed up and made the roundtrip back and been working in 25 minutes.

Instead I chose to sit down and write this out. My computer has plenty of charge for that, and writing helps me vent and re-align my thoughts. Lost passport be damned, I needed to write.

Real talk time: I really do struggle with that âI just want to give upâ soundtrack often. Much more often than I want to admit, honestly. If Iâm not carefulâbetween traveling with Type 1 diabetes, other health stuff, and the overwhelm of learning-while-doing this whole location-independent nomad thingâI can easily lose a day or two to mental and emotional exhaustion if I’m not careful.

But what Iâm choosing to do this time is something that I know is right. Stop and breathe. Slowly and deeply.

READ NEXT: The Learn To Travel Series: A Brief Apology To FearFear & Loathing in Las Nomad: Admissions Of A Wannabe Nomad

Realize that these are small things, and that my overall picture is quite bountiful, especially compared to many in the place Iâm at right now. Put the music in my ear that will calm me. Then just take the day slowly and try to be thankful for all the things that are going right instead of the relatively few that are going wrong. Even a lost passport is something that has steps to correct. That’s what US embassies are for.

Not an easy task when it would be easier to just day drink myself into oblivion, taking two or three siestas between binges, or to just eat my way through the day and feel gluttonous and slovenly.

But the reality is that those escapes would only make things worse. Iâll feel better if Iâm productive for a while. Then if I choose to be relaxed and enjoy where Iâm at and the amazing people I have the opportunity to spend my time with.

So I guess the point of this whole story was to put out there for you and me the intention to make lemonade out of lemons whenever possible.

Make sure a friend or partner knows what those are as well, since we tend to forget when in the thick of it. For me, itâs a specific album by a certain artist. It almost always gets me right as rain in no time. Stop and breathe, then repeat. And realize you’re probably much better off than this moment is leading you to feel.

It’s about 11am now. Having gotten this down in writing, I already feel accomplished, and the rest of the day is still ahead.

#3164. Systolic style: meet the medical-grade smartwatch revolutionising blood pressure monitoring

Paid content is paid for and controlled by an advertiser and produced by the Guardian Labs team.

An estimated one-third of adults in England have high blood pressure, with research showing that many are unaware of their condition. But thanks to the new Huawei Watch D3, monitoring blood pressure is easier, accurate and more stylish than ever

Wearable technology has come a long way in the past decade. Take a look around at your colleagues, friends and family, and you’ll be hard pushed to find anyone not wearing some kind of health monitoring ring, watch or band – there are even tracking insoles and patches, too.

These gadgets have myriad benefits – not least, allowing us more control and insight over our health and wellbeing than ever before. We’re able to monitor everything from sleep and stress to heart health and more, and the technology is becoming more refined and intuitive seemingly by the day.

It’s no surprise, then, that companies are laser focused on developing ever more advanced gadgets. But in a saturated wearables market, Huawei is leading the charge when it comes to stylish, performance-led devices.

Its newest bit of tech enables medical-grade* blood pressure tracking. Also known as hypertension, high blood pressure is a global health concern, and one of the leading causes of cardiovascular disease and premature death worldwide.

But the good news is that adequate monitoring and treatment renders these risks largely preventable. So, instead of (or perhaps as well as) tracking our sleep scores and steps, experts are advocating that we all take note of our blood pressure numbers, regardless of our age.

“Although hypertension becomes more common as we get older, one of the biggest mistakes we can make is thinking that we only need to start worrying about blood pressure and cardiovascular disease from middle age,” says Dr Lucy Hooper, GP and co-founder of Coyne Medical. “We increasingly know that cardiovascular disease is something that develops over someone’s whole life course.”

While there are now plenty of devices offering some kind of blood pressure monitoring, the new Huawei Watch D3 goes beyond the capabilities of a single, one-off reading, more closely resembling medical-grade instruments, for a detailed and reliable look at the whole picture, rather than a single snapshot.

Featuring an innovative first-of-its-kind wrist-worn mechanical airbag, the watch delivers effective yet comfortable compression and precise sensing across a minimal skin-contact area for all-day comfort and wearability.

This combination enables both real-time data and longer-term measurements, allowing you to track your personal blood pressure trends throughout the day and night (even while sleeping) via 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM).

Perfect for those wanting a deeper, more comprehensive understanding of their blood pressure, the ABPM data syncs to tailored reports available in the Huawei Health app, which is recognised and endorsed by healthcare professionals, too. In fact, the findings can be shared directly with your healthcare provider.

“Blood pressure is actually a great example of a measurement that can be potentially really useful and have a profound impact on someone’s health and longevity,” says Hooper. “That said, lots of things affect a blood pressure reading, from stress, caffeine, sleep, pain and alcohol, and we also know it is highly affected by the way the measurement is taken.

“Since it is so variable, just checking it as a one-off at the doctor’s surgery or pharmacy isn’t actually ideal. Having access to a 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitor gives us a much better overall picture of blood pressure.”

One thing we know helps keep blood pressure at a healthy level is exercise. However, this is also a physiological stressor in and of itself – if you’ve ever taken an intense Hiit class after a night out, you’ll likely have noticed that it felt tougher than usual.

The good news is that the Huawei Watch D3 can help you tailor those all-important workouts depending on how your body is faring, with its dedicated feature for pre- and post-exercise blood pressure measurements.

“The Huawei Watch D3 represents an evolution in blood pressure monitoring and management,” says Dr Jamie Edwards, senior lecturer in cardiovascular science, University of East London. “Exercise blood pressure responses and ambulatory blood pressure monitoring have long been recognised as providing valuable additional insight into cardiovascular health.”

“However, their application has traditionally been limited by the accuracy, practicality and convenience of conventional measurement approaches,” he says. “The D3 provides a gamechanging approach to accurately and conveniently assess these measures without the need for often cumbersome devices.”

But it’s not just about blood pressure: the watch has a range of other intelligent key health indicators in its Health Glance feature, from sleep tracking and physical readiness to heart rate and rhythm. All of which can be shared with your loved ones via the community function in the Huawei Health app.

If you’re concerned about how technological medical capability marries luxury aesthetics, don’t be. The Huawei Watch D3 delivers stylish and sleek curves, so you’re not compromising on style or substance. The slim, lightweight design offers all-day comfort, and doubles as a stylish accessory. Drawing inspiration from the colours found in nature, the watch is available in a choice of chic neutral colourways (black, white or mocha gold) meaning it’ll always blend seamlessly with your outfit of choice.

Other standout features include those nice-to-haves that make life that little bit easier in daily terms: contactless payments, a carefully selected suite of fitness and wellness apps, more than 100 sport modes, an impressive six-day battery life and compatibility with both Android and iOS.

Put simply, the Huawei Watch D3 is the most comprehensive, medically-certified wearable for people looking to proactively prioritise their health safely, effortlessly and in style, making those health goals simpler to achieve than ever, because wellness doesn’t have to be complicated.

The HUAWEI WATCH D3 is available from the HUAWEI Store from £399.99 and includes a complimentary 10-month Bupa Well+ Silver digital health subscription (worth £200). Plus, until 3 November, readers of the Guardian can claim £20 off the HUAWEI WATCH D3 with the code AGUARDIAN20.

*The HUAWEI WATCH D3 is CE-certified as a medical device under the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR)

#3166. Elf Basketball STEM Challenge

This fun elf-themed basketball STEM challenge is a great hands-on science activity for learning about transfer of energy. The idea is to build a lolly stick catapult and a basketball net for an elf!

You could set this up as a ready made activity and encourage children to experiment using different projectiles on the catapult. Small pom pom balls and ping pong balls work well! Or, another idea is to leave instructions and materials out so children can build their own creations!

If you want to make the activity more structured, use my FREE instructions and template at the bottom of the post.

Follow my easy lolly stick catapult instructions or watch the video below.

Build a mini basketball hoop. Use our design for inspiration.

Try pushing the catapult arm all the way down, then halfway, to see how that affects the ball’s flight.

Experiment with a table tennis ball, pom poms or even marshmallows.

When the catapult arm is pushed down, it stores potential energy, which is transferred to the ball as kinetic energy when the arm is released.

As the ball flies higher, it starts to slow down. The ball’s kinetic energy is temporarily converted to potential energy as it gains height. As the ball starts to fall, it speeds up again, and the stored potential energy is turned back into kinetic energy. Gravity acting on the ball gives it a curved path through the air.

The amount of stored energy – the further the catapult arm is pushed down, the more elastic potential energy is stored, so the ball flies further.

The angle of the launch – for maximum horizontal distance of flight, the launch angle should be about 45 degrees.

The weight of the ball—lighter projectiles usually fly further than heavier balls when the same amount of force is used, as less force is needed to accelerate them.

Flexibility of the sticks and elastic bands – more flexible materials can store more energy.

This free pack includes a simple one-page worksheet and a more detailed three-page design and evaluation pack.

If you like this idea, take a look at my 24 days of FREE elf activity ideas!!

#3167. Mehr als 100 Festnahmen bei Protesten in Frankreich

Französische Sicherheitskräfte sind mit einem Großaufgebot im Einsatz. Wieder gibt es Ausschreitungen. Doch die Eskalation vor einer Woche wiederholt sich bisher nicht.

Unter massiver Polizeipräsenz haben in Frankreich Zehntausende Menschen gegen die Regierung demonstriert. Während es in mehreren Städten zu Ausschreitungen kam, fielen die Proteste insgesamt deutlich weniger heftig aus als vor einer Woche.

In Paris blieb es bei der Hauptkundgebung weitgehend friedlich. In Marseille und ‌Lyon lieferten sich ⁠vermummte ⁠Jugendliche Auseinandersetzungen mit der Polizei. In Clermont-Ferrand, Grenoble, Lille und Nizza setzten die Beamten Tränengas ein. In Nizza kam zudem ein Wasserwerfer zum Einsatz, nachdem Demonstranten eine Aufforderung zur Räumung ignoriert hatten.

Innenminister Laurent Nuñez​hatte landesweit 70.000 Polizisten mobilisiert, 10.000 mehr als vor einer Woche. Bis zum frühen Nachmittag seien 135 Menschen festgenommen worden, ​teilte er mit. Vielen Festnahmen seien präventive Durchsuchungen vorausgegangen, bei denen Feuerwerkskörper, Kugellager und andere ​potenzielle Waffen ‌gefunden worden seien.

Wegen befürchteter Ausschreitungen und Plünderungen, wie sie am vergangenen Wochenende stattgefunden hatten, gab es in mehreren Städten Versammlungsverbote für bestimmte Zonen sowie Ausgangssperren. In Paris wurde nur eine Demonstration genehmigt: ein von den Gewerkschaften organisierter Marsch.

Die Pariser Polizei ordnete in letzter Minute an, den Demonstrationszug von der Bastille im Zentrum an die weiter abgelegene Porte d'Italie am südöstlichen Stadtrand zu verlegen. In einer Eilentscheidung bestätigte das Verwaltungsgericht die Route.

Gewerkschaftsvertreterin Murielle Guilbert sagte dazu, es sei "skandalös", dass Präsident Emmanuel Macron den Demonstranten verboten habe, "dort zu demonstrieren, wo wir demonstrieren wollen".

"Wir sind heute ganz offensichtlich hier, weil in diesem Land immense soziale Wut herrscht und weil die Löhne immer noch nicht auf das Niveau angehoben wurden, auf dem sie sein sollten", fügte Guilbert hinzu.

Ursprünglich ging es bei den seit Wochen laufenden Protesten um Verbesserungen im Bildungswesen. Zunächst waren junge Leute auf die Straße gegangen, um für eine bessere Ausstattung von Schulen zu demonstrieren. Inzwischen haben sich weitere Gruppen angeschlossen, unter anderem, um gegen zu hohe Lebenshaltungskosten zu protestieren. Auch die sogenannten "Gelbwesten" sind wieder aktiv.

#3168. In an Already Broiling Summer, El Niño Is About to Turn Up the Heat

Temperatures forecasted between August and October of this year. Red areas are projected to be far warmer than normal. World Meteorological Organization

El Niño is expected to intensify in the weeks ahead, fueling more severe heat across the globe, according to the U.N. World Meteorological Organization. The forecast comes as blistering heat shatters temperature records from Europe to Asia.

During El Niño, warm waters pool in the eastern Pacific, driving hotter weather around the world, amplifying the impact of warming. El Niño drove record heat in 2023 and 2024, the hottest years ever recorded. This year, forecasters say a strong El Niño will take shape between August and October.

“El Niño is not just on our doorstep — it is inside the house and turning up the heat,” said U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres. “And this is only a warm-up act. El Niño is strengthening — adding fuel to a planet already on fire with scorching heat domes, apocalyptic wildfires, and record hot seas.”

On Sunday, South Korea saw the mercury reach 108.5 degrees F (42.5 degrees C), its highest temperature on record. The South Korean weather agency urged people to “immediately stop all outdoor activities,” warning that even “indoor spaces without air conditioning are dangerous.”

The unprecedented heat came on the heels of a record hot spell in Western Europe, which endured its hottest June on record. France experienced its hottest day ever, while weather stations in Denmark, Germany, and Poland recorded new all-time highs. The heat persisted in July, with Barcelona seeing heat of 105.3 degrees F (40.7 degrees C), the hottest on record.

Hot spells combined with dry conditions to fuel massive wildfires across France, Spain, and now Greece. More than 200,000 people in France were forced to flee their homes in what French President Emmanuel Macron called the worst fire-related crisis since World War II.

In the U.S. last month, scorching heat blanketed much of the country, and Salt Lake City recorded a temperature of 109 degrees F (42.8 degrees C), its highest on record. Climate scientist Brian Brettschneider, of the University of Alaska Fairbanks, said, “It’s going to be a close call, but it now appears more likely than not that July 2026 will be the warmest month on record in the Contiguous U.S.”

Overshoot: The World Is Hitting Point of No Return on Climate
