#3170. 17 Dreamy Hotels in Madrid Quietly Redefining Spanish Luxury

Madrid is one of our favorite city breaks in Europe, beloved for its cultural landmarks, vivacious art scene, and beautiful restaurants. These elements are also present within some of the best hotels in Madrid, where you can stay in historic palaces, art-gallery-meets-hotel hybrids, and unassuming addresses with Michelin-starred restaurants.

Then there are the low-key stays, from new-gen hostels to apartment-style setups. And the scene is still growing—the Four Seasons and Mandarin Oriental mark two of the newer luxury addresses in the Spanish capital. For the places to note ahead of your next visit, we’ve rounded up the best hotels in Madrid below.

The iconic Palace hotel in Madrid returned to its grande dame status in 2025 following a complete renovation by Ruiz Larrea Arquitectura, with Lázaro Rosa-Violán entrusted with the interiors. The end result is a beautiful love letter to Madrid. With 470 rooms and suites, The Palace is the largest luxury hotel in Madrid. The Neptuno Suite feels like stepping inside an elegant bourgeois Madrid house from the mid-20th century with its restored marble fireplace, wood paneling, Art Deco–inspired furniture, beautiful wallpaper above the headboards, and luxuries like Frette sheets and Le Chemin by Byredo bathroom amenities. Portuguese chef Nuno Matos has the task of breathing new life into La Cúpula, which now more than ever is the social epicenter of the hotel. The menu is defined by its use of local produce, simple preparations, and embrace of tradition. Pork tenderloin with clam sauce, excellent cuts of meat, and a beef Wellington intended to be shared are classic dishes befitting a classic hotel. Cocktails were central to life at the original Palace, and the hotel’s bars remain committed to the classics, with some updates; drinks can be enjoyed not only at the bar in La Cúpula, but also in the renovated and legendary bar, now called 27 Club. —D.M.

One of the city's icons and a pioneer in luxury hospitality when it opened in 1886, the Gran Hotel Inglés was the first hotel in Madrid to have a restaurant and electric lighting, as well as telephones and toilets with running water on each of its floors—an extravagance for the time. Its 48 rooms and suites, designed with a nod to the Art Deco style, have bathtubs that were flown in from Canada and are custom-made for each room. The beds, meanwhile, come with 500-thread-count Egyptian cotton sheets and an extensive pillow menu. In addition to its signature cocktail and gastronomic offerings at Lobbyto, which serves Madrid cuisine with an avant-garde twist (don’t miss the cocido madrileño!), the hotel has a brunch show with live music, an English tea service, and swing and rock-and-roll nights for the more lively. Le Max Club, the hotel's spa, includes a high-tech gym, spa cabins set up in collaboration with French brand Sisley (its botanical treatment menu is a delight, I promise), and a hot tub. —C.L.

Mandarin Oriental knows that its Madrid outpost will forever be known simply as “The Ritz”—the one inaugurated with pomp by King Alfonso XIII in 1910; the one that welcomed Grace Kelly and Rainier of Monaco during their honeymoon; and the one where Mata Hari, Salvador Dalí, and countless other stars caroused. After its remodeling and reopening in 2021, The Ritz is now even more Ritz-like than ever, thanks to Mandarin Oriental. Storied Madrid architecture firm Rafael de La-Hoz and French interior designers Gilles & Boissier (whose touch graced the Baccarat Hotel New York) had the challenging task of reinventing the hotel while holding onto a certain spirit. The most striking detail was the recovery of the great glass vault of the Palm Court, the social heart of the building, which had been concealed for 80 years, and the opening of the enormous doors that connect, physically—and emotionally—to the Museo del Prado (the great art gallery is so close you can almost touch it). But other magical corners abound. My favorites include The Beauty Concept spa, with its spectacular indoor pool, treatment cabins, and fitness trainers; the timeless counter of the Pictura cocktail bar, where I’ve spent endless hours watched over by gilt-framed oils; Deessa, chef Quique Dacosta’s artistic restaurant, which gained two Michelin stars in two years; and the rare oasis that is the hotel garden. To eat Dacosta’s paella here, under the city’s eternal blue sky, has become a defining Madrid experience at what remains a quintessential hotel. —D.M.

Smack dab in the middle of Gran Vía, Evok Collection’s second opening outside France is leading the third hotel wave in the Spanish capital—unsurprising given that one of the men who invented the boutique hotel helmed the design: Philippe Starck. The elegant, belvedere-topped seven-story building was finished in 1922. With the reception upstairs, the ground floor houses the bar, restaurant, and patisserie, which segue into each other, fostering a brasserie feel. The low-lit restaurant has woven-leather ceilings hung with double lampshades and mahogany-paneled walls. Chef Adam Bentalha’s recipes roam the Med, from the Middle East (croissant-like challah; za’atar-drenched suckling lamb shoulder) to the Iberian peninsula with Spanish produce (red tuna, Bellota ham). The 57 rooms and suites, a few with sun-trap terraces, have jatoba-wood joinery and are warmed by pinks and oranges, terra-cottas, and flashes of moss green. The La Capsule spa is decked with white and floaty curtains (very Delano Miami à la 1990s) and has a 65-foot pool clad in cream marble, a suite of biohacking gadgetry that includes a hyperbaric chamber, and a menu ranging from facial electrostimulation to Chinese massage. —Lydia Bell

Designed as a kind of contemporary bohemian retreat, Nômade Temple Madrid is structured around the idea of ​​"Halfway to Somewhere," which can be translated into a desire to foster encounters between travelers, artists, neighbors, creators, and the local community. There are 93 rooms and suites—including two penthouses—within the hotel, all decorated with plenty of personality. Forget rustic minimalism: you'll find wallpaper, mirrors, brightly colored sheets, and vintage-inspired pieces mixed with bold contemporary silhouettes. The property is more than its rooms, though—guests can enjoy the rooftop bar and pool, a speakeasy and a nightclub, and carefully curated cultural programming at Monopol of the People, a versatile wellness and gathering space. In the basement, GÖN House of Healing spa is the picture of understated elegance and staffed by an outstanding team of therapists who will make you forget you’re in the heart of one of the world’s most bustling cities. Café Libre, next to the eclectic and cozy lobby, is a space designed to make guests and visitors feel right at home. It’s the perfect spot to enjoy some tapas, a few beers, or a light bite, right on the street level. —Clara Laguna

For over a century, the Edificio Metrópolis—much photographed and admired but for years elusively inaccessible—has defined Madrid’s skyline. Now, a distinct and ambitious renovation project, stewarded by Marta Seco and Sandro Silva’s Grupo Paraguas, has restored not only its architectural splendor but also its vital pulse. Reborn as Club Metrópolis, the landmark building’s eight floors now house an international private members club, a 19-room boutique hotel, and seven restaurants, and are set to host a roster of twice-weekly experiences. Hotel guests enjoy club membership and all-area access for the duration of their stay. Lázaro Rosa-Violán’s design brings coherence to the interiors, shaping the building as a single contemporary house where luxury lies in discretion and a sense of belonging and time shared. From the surprising Spa de Langostas restaurant to the rooftop overlooking the city, and from the intimacy of the rooms to La Galería’s languid mood, Club Metrópolis comes together as a new way to experience Madrid. —María Casbas

Hôtel du Temps Madrid is born of Yoan and Jen Marciano, creators of the legendary Hôtel du Temps in Paris, who decided to start a new life in the Spanish capital with their children. It was love at first sight with this building in Malasaña, and after eight months of renovating a former hotel right on Calle Barco, almost at the corner of Gran Vía and with the Telefónica building watching over it, the Marcianos opened Hôtel du Temps Madrid. There are 31 rooms in total, 7 of them suites with living rooms and large windows or even small terraces overlooking the street. The jewel of the house is the rooftop suite, a kind of detached cottage with a private terrace where the silence is resounding, even though you are just steps away from Gran Vía, the second busiest shopping street in Europe. All rooms feature amenities created for the hotel by perfumer Francisca Manzini in collaboration with the Marciano family. Comfort and warmth abound, with a retro atmosphere that permeates everything. On the rooftop is a plunge pool where guests can cool off and enjoy a drink while soaking during Madrid’s sweltering summer months. —David Moralejo

Tucked away in the refined Chamberí neighbourhood, Hotel Orfila is a 19th-century palace radiating old Spanish glamour. With just 32 rooms and suites, this intimate Relais & Châteaux property feels more like a private residence than a hotel, with its aristocratic wallpapers, shiny silverware, portrait-lined corridors, and the gentle scent of fine soap drifting through the halls. The undisputed highlight is breakfast: an exceptional spread of cured meats, quince paste, and sourdough, elevated further by churros con chocolate served à la carte. In warmer months, the tiered garden terrace transforms this into one of Madrid's most civilized morning rituals. Service is impeccably formal yet quietly warm, with a concierge well-versed in securing restaurant reservations, museum tickets, and local experiences. The location is perfectly placed for access to the Prado, Retiro Park, and the unmissable Sorolla Museum. And with violet sweets left on the pillow each evening, Orfila feels unapologetically, gloriously old-school. —Stuart Brumfitt

Perfectly positioned between the vibrant Madrid neighborhoods of Malasaña and Chueca, 7 Islas is a quietly cool boutique hotel just two blocks from the Gran Vía. The hotel has a minimalist aesthetic, with polished concrete floors, rotating contemporary artwork, and considered design details, but it’s totally relaxed and welcoming. The best rooms here are the spacious loft-style Ático rooms with private terraces and sweeping rooftop views, ideal for warm Madrid evenings. Expect Malin+Goetz toiletries, Technogym fitness facilities, and welcome daiquiris on arrival. A comprehensive morning breakfast buffet and quiet cocktail bar complete the in-house offerings. The real strength here is the service: a well-connected team able to secure hard-to-book restaurant reservations, sold-out football tickets, and bespoke experiences, from exclusive cigar clubs to private cultural encounters. Family-friendly, eco-conscious, and genuinely characterful, 7 Islas punches well above its price point. —S.B.

The Meliá Collection opened its first hotel in Madrid, Casa de las Artes, with the aim of redefining luxury through a focus on modernity, art, and culture. Located in the Barrio de las Letras, the hotel is in a Beaux Arts–style building that once housed the General Association of Railway Employees. Inside, original Dalí lithographs decorate the walls, and a midcentury corridor leads to an indoor swimming pool and creatively designed meeting rooms. The 137 rooms include unique illustrations of Don Quixote, warm furnishings, Nespresso machines, and luxury bath products by Carner. The hotel's restaurant, Maché, serves classic Madrid tapas alongside a variety of fish and meats, while a cozy cinema named Miró pays tribute to the private projection rooms of Hollywood’s Golden Age. —D.M.

For years, Madrileños avoided the streets around Puerta del Sol, complaining about the decay of a once-grand downtown barrio that had also become a monstrous building site. But since the Four Seasons opened its doors in September 2020, those complaints have turned to compliments. Standing proudly on the corner of calles Sevilla and Alcalá, the Canadian group’s first Spanish property has sailed onto the Madrid hotel scene with all guns blazing, promising to grant the neighborhood a new lease on life. Part of a large project including private residences, a retail "gallery," and a gastro-market, the hotel has preserved the building’s ornate 19th-century stone façade (check out the elephant heads) and grand interiors such as the double-height lobby with its ivy-green marble columns, Alpujarra carpets, and stained-glass roof. You won’t find cutting-edge here, but there are no rough edges either: this is grown-up stuff. Everything breathes quality, from the solid walnut floors and gray-flecked Volakas marble of the rooms to the faultless soundproofing and refreshingly user-friendly lighting systems. Service manages the deft trick of being both briskly efficient and charmingly Spanish. In the top-floor restaurant, chef Dani Garcia does his New Andalusian thing to fabulous backdrop views of monumental Madrid. The Four Seasons sets the bar high, but clears it without breaking a sweat. —P.R.

The drama of the Madrid Edition building—cunningly repurposed from a boxy former bank HQ on the old-town Plaza de Celenque—begins with the ornate 18th-century granite doorway by Pedro de Rivera (one of the few historic elements remaining from the original site) and continues into a vast spiral staircase in pearly-white stone, curving spectacularly upwards like a giant seashell. The public spaces have a low-lit calm but go all-out for contrast: An antique tapestry hangs behind an all-white pool table lined with electric-blue baize, and you might find a minimalist bench artfully draped with a traditional Spanish shawl. On the ground floor, chef Enrique Olvera disembarks from Mexico City with a restaurant (Jerónimo) that eschews fancy fine dining for a streamlined modern interpretation of traditional Mexican cuisine; if budgetary restrictions apply, an evening in the Edition's rooftop wonderland is another great way of catching the hotel’s hedonistic vibe. —Paul Richardson

The raison d'être of JW Marriott Hotel Madrid comes from the founder of the brand (as well as the larger Marriott Corporation), J. Willard Marriott, who firmly believed in the importance of personalized service. Wherever you look and wherever you go on the property, there's the opportunity to check out of real life and embrace the present. A carpe diem attitude is expressed in elegantly pared-back rooms in neutral colors and attentive staff. The hotel’s restaurant is its crown jewel, the creation of the celebrated Sandoval brothers. Expect local produce and traditional meets cutting-edge cooking (plus, I'd say, the best breakfast in Europe). Service is endearingly enthusiastic, and the public spaces (cocktail bar, lobby, bookstore) make this the capital's trendiest spot right now.—María Ángeles Cano

Basing yourself at Rosewood’s first Spanish property in Madrid’s upscale Salamanca quarter is like staying just off Fifth Avenue in New York—you’ll think the city is all designer boutiques and people in gilets if you don’t wander further afield. The vibe inside is very local and knowing—black-framed floor-to-ceiling glass doors, tongue-in-cheek artworks smuggled among more serious pieces, and smart lounges you no longer have to book a table at. Regular restaurant pop-ups are intricate and designed to entice Madrid’s curious foodies, while the on-site patisserie Flor y Nata casts intoxicating smells. All-day dining destination Las Brasas de Castellana serves wonderful traditional dishes, and flagship Amós, run by three-Michelin-star-winning Jesús Sánchez, does skillful creative turns on Northern Spanish cuisine. Underground, there’s a small, stylish spa with a uniquely shaped hot tub, plus a sauna and steam room; up top is the last piece of the puzzle—the show-stopping Houses opened in 2022. Ask for Royal Anglada House for a seemingly endless space stretching over a long dining room, circular office, and both indoor and outdoor kitchens, the latter on a wow-worthy terrace with views out to the mountains beyond the cityscape. —Becky Lucas

Which part of Madrid is the best to stay in?

Many of Madrid's hotels are conveniently scattered around Centro, the city's central area. To be smack-dab in the thick of it, look to addresses surrounding the busy Gran Vía or the Literary Quarter of Barrio de las Letras. For a stay that's outside the hustle and bustle, head to the glamorous and grand boulevards of Salamanca where you'll find smart yet unassuming boltholes like Rosewood Villa Magna and Hotel Único Madrid.

Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. It was originally published on Condé Nast Traveller UK.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#3171. What essentials to keep, what rubbish to get rid of? Burnham, Badenoch, Farage don’t know either | Robert Hutton

After a fractious week, they probably agree that no one at all needs Liz Truss’s new book, but then the political housekeeping decisions get much harder

What are you stockpiling? Wes Streeting says we need water and food to last 72 hours in case of national emergency, as well as wind-up radios so that we can check in on how the apocalypse is developing in Ambridge. Personally, I have a two-week supply of jokes about the government that I can draw upon even as the zombies break down my front door.

Andy Burnham, far from stockpiling, is busy chucking stuff out. This week Labour’s much cherished commitment not to allow new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea went into the skip round the back of Downing Street, where it lies next to a complete set of European Union red lines, a plan for digital ID and a signed photograph of Peter Mandelson.

Tory frontbenchers waved their hands in amazement as the prime minister explained that the government is now in favour of dashing for gas. The argument Burnham was using about security of supply was exactly the one they’d been throwing at the government for months.

To Kemi Badenoch, it’s a sign that she’s winning the argument. But then the Tory leader’s self-confidence is so total that she sees the rising of the sun each morning as a sign that she’s winning the argument. A more thoughtful opposition leader might wonder what she will have left to throw at Burnham after he’s finished jettisoning the unpopular and hard-to-explain bits of policy that Keir Starmer left cluttering up Downing Street.

Badenoch is having her own clear-out. All of us do this when we move into a new place and find that the previous occupant left something hideous behind: a phallic ornament in the garden, for instance, or a list of approved candidates featuring Grant Shapps.

Of course, as anyone who’s spent a weekend driving to the local tip knows, there’s always something so toxic the council simply refuses to take it off your hands. In Badenoch’s case, it’s Liz Truss, who has a new book out next week on how everything was someone else’s fault.

That’s a line that the Tory leader has decided to recycle, as she bags up any sense of responsibility for the government in which she was a cabinet minister and leaves it out for the binmen along with a pile of “Mel Stride for chancellor” posters.

On Tuesday she was asked why, if cutting taxes and welfare spending is so easy, her party didn’t do either when it was last in power. “Well, I didn’t raise those taxes,” she replied, explaining that she had disagreed with the government she was part of, but had decided to keep this to herself. Courage takes many forms.

The effect of all these unwanted old positions hitting the Westminster landfill is that the electoral battleground is clearing nicely. We find ourselves in the unusual situation that both Burnham and Badenoch agree on the argument they want to have: was Margaret Thatcher right?

One party that is definitely stockpiling is Reform, which continues to lay in supplies of nasty ideas about race, as though there was the slightest danger they might run out. The party’s headquarters has now been so thoroughly turned over that it’s an open question whether there’s anyone on the staff who isn’t an undercover reporter. But if you want to know what Reform thinks, you really don’t need to spend six months hiding a camera inside your lapel. Just listen to what the party’s MPs are saying.

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

Danny Kruger, who defected from the Tories last year, has usually been seen as a genial soul, certainly relative to the Slytherin tendency that is Robert Jenrick and Andrew Rosindell. But introducing Nigel Farage on Tuesday, he made a determined effort to prove that his “nice but dim” image is only half right. “The problem isn’t with individual Muslims,” he told his audience. No, the problem is Muslims as a group, “who are taught by their clerics that their loyalty isn’t to the United Kingdom, but to the global Islamic community”. It’s an argument that was applied to Catholics 200 years ago and to Jews 100 years ago: you just can’t trust them.

Farage is too canny to say this stuff himself, and as an election approaches, he may find himself disavowing it, just as he’s distanced himself from his great buddy Donald Trump. But the trouble with stockpiles of the wrong stuff is that they can be hard to clear out at short notice. Just ask the Liberal Democrats: it’s weeks since they put Ed Davey on Freecycle, and they haven’t had even a nibble of interest.

Robert Hutton is an author and journalist

#3172. Intuitive living is the latest wellness trend – meet the new tech making it work

Paid content is paid for and controlled by an advertiser and produced by the Guardian Labs team.

Wellness culture can be overwhelming, but a more fluid approach is emerging. Smart devices such as the Huawei Watch Fit 5 perfectly embody this shift in direction – whether you’re regularly sleep tracking or just occasionally using data to support your lifestyle

When it comes to the world of health and wellness, it’s easy to suffer from information overwhelm. We’ve never had more access to data, research and expertise which, while valuable, isn’t always applicable to our own lives. What’s more, few of us have time to spend hours sifting through content to devise a personalised health routine, let alone work out if a “routine” is necessary at all.

All this information and expectation can come at a cost: emotional strain, guilt and confusion about where to turn. Health and fitness then start to feel like abstract milestones that we’re blindly chasing rather than important components of our lives.

So in a world where our plans, priorities and interests are constantly evolving, developing the ability to live fluidly and to better tune in to our bodies and minds feels more valuable than ever.

In some areas, the gap between “health” and our contemporary lifestyles is starting to narrow. Smart devices have evolved from clunky accessories reserved for the disciplined athletic elite, to everyday companions for modern living. The new Huawei Watch Fit 5 series embodies a more fluid, perceptive approach to fitness that seems to be emerging as the antithesis to “lock-in” culture and extreme regimens that have flooded social media over recent years.

Aesthetically, there’s a colourway to suit every vibe. The Fit 5 Pro comes in orange, white and black while the Fit 5 is available in silver, purple, white, black and green. Style-wise, there are options to stand out or blend in. But these watches aren’t here to steal your valuable attention. Nor will they be loud and pushy about what you should be doing. The Watch Fit 5 series works alongside you to support and enable.

A standout feature is undoubtedly the contactless payment support via Curve Pay. On-the-fly purchases become both practical and seamless – because why scramble through pockets for your phone when your wallet can live on your wrist.

While your focus is elsewhere, the Watch Fit 5 remains proactive. The 10-day battery life means you can strap it to your wrist and move on with your day (or week), leaving it to monitor your wellbeing in the background. Cardio tracking keeps tabs on your heart health, detecting irregularities and flagging if there’s anything you need to know. Huawei’s latest generation of smartwatches also come with enhanced sleep tracking, offering an overview of your recovery levels and insight into when you’re best placed to tackle a long-distance run or advanced pilates class without putting yourself at risk of injury or illness.

Intuitive wellness is not about ignoring the breadth of information at our fingertips, but about editing our exposure to the noise. “Taking an intuitive approach to health and wellness is ultimately about allowing yourself to connect to what you really need as an individual, rather than changing parts of yourself to follow a regime that may not be suitable for you,” says Amber Fieldgate, a psychotherapist registered with the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy. “An intuitive approach asks you to take responsibility for yourself in a meaningful way. It also challenges you to check in and connect with yourself by asking: ‘What do I really need right now? What is best for me right now?’”

In the past, living life intuitively was typically interpreted as “trusting your gut”. Now, it’s more about identifying trusted tools and information sources and using that data to work out what you need, rather than letting alerts dictate your every move. That’s where something like Huawei’s TruSense System can become your best friend. This next-gen tech will monitor crucial health components such as blood oxygen, stress, heart rate and sleep with 15% better accuracy than previous models. Sure, the intricacy of some of this data isn’t going to be an everyday necessity for many of us, but knowing it’s there ready to explore only makes fluid living easier: the insights are there for you to examine on your own terms.

“Things like your sleep, heart rate and recovery can highlight how ready your body actually is to train,” says personal trainer Aimee Victoria Long. “Instead of relying purely on guesswork, you have something to guide your decisions. The key is using that information to support how you feel, not override it, so it becomes a tool that helps you tune in.”

Chartered physiotherapist and sleep expert Sammy Margo emphasises that sleep is an invaluable part of recovery, and making sure you feel your best throughout the day. “Deep sleep (also known as slow-wave sleep) is vital for physical recovery, immune function, and memory consolidation. Aim for 13-23% of your total sleep time in deep sleep,” she says. If you’re getting eight hours a night, that works out at roughly one to two hours. “REM sleep is where emotional processing, creativity, and long-term memory occur. You should aim for 20-25% of total sleep time in REM, approximately one and a half to two hours per night.”

“Tracking your sleep with a wearable gives you a clear picture of how much of each stage you are actually getting,” Margo adds. And for those days when you need to take some extra time out in the day, the watch’s nap tracking feature is super handy. It can identify short periods of sleep and incorporate them into your broader sleep score and recovery data. These moments can get lost in the big picture of what your body needs and where you are mentally, but being able to review your naps allows you to decide what type of daytime rest helps you feel your best: if napping for too long leaves you feeling groggy, for example, you can make a change.

The emphasis on flexibility releases us from the “all or nothing” mindset. It also makes wellness more engaging. The Mini-Workout assistant built into the Huawei Watch Fit 5 series makes embracing this flexibility simple. The fact that this assistant takes the form of a virtual panda (undoubtedly the cutest PT known to remind anyone to do a few stretches) only adds a cute, nonchalant appeal to personal fitness. Whether you’re feeling sluggish after an afternoon sitting at a desk, are holding tension in your back after a stressful day, or want to shake off nervous energy before an important meeting, you’ll find short, guided exercises lasting from 30 seconds to a few minutes available on your wrist. The panda assistant can even offer exercise prompts based on your surroundings, so all you need to focus on is what your body needs in the moment.

Technology gets a bad rap for stealing our attention, but the Huawei Watch Fit 5 series demonstrates that so much of it comes down to design. Living intuitively doesn’t need to be a complicated lifestyle shift, and the right smart devices can make that step even easier.

The HUAWEI WATCH FIT 5 Series is compatible with both iOS and Android and is available from the Huawei Store for £249.99 (WATCH FIT 5 Pro) and £159.99 (WATCH FIT 5). #3174. The Best Hostels I’ve Stayed At…& More Importantly Why They Make The List

I’ve now stayed at dozens and dozens of hostels in the US and internationally. And while this list of the best hostels I’ve stayed at will continue to flex and grow, it’s important that I give love to the ones that currently rank as my favorite hostel stays! And more importantly, why they rank.

If you’ve stayed at hostels, I likely don’t have to convince you of their merit. If you’re still on the fence, and looking to try your first hostel, this article should be a great place to get a feel for all the different types of hostels and experiences you could have.

This site participates in the Amazon Services LLC Associates Program and other affiliate programs and may earn from qualifying purchases.

Hostels around the world have pretty much any amenity you could wish for. From basic, backpacker hostels to trendy, boutique hostels, it really is up to you what you prefer. I’ve stayed at many hostels with onsite barsâincluding rooftop bars, swimming pools, pool tables, lounges, private rooms, surf lessons, free happy hours, ensuite bathrooms, and dorms with 3-story bunkbed rooms with like 15-20′ ceilings…in a train station! (See that one here.)

I’m primarily a solo traveler, and I have to remote work while traveling. For those reasons and more, I have some pretty specific things I look for when booking a hostel. I want to book a hostel where I feel my belongings are safe while I’m out exploring, and one that has good, quiet workspaces.

I prefer hostels that have free breakfast or an occasional free meal to make my budget go further. Small dorm rooms with beds with curtains for privacy. And the best hostels for me have active social calendars and plan events to help this solo traveler meet other travelers!

These reasons why I may or may not book a hostel are in order from most important to less important…but it is a toss-up as to which is the most important when I book a hostel. Mostly because there’s always some give-and-take, and just like booking a hotel, Airbnb, or VRBO, no property is “perfect.” Just keep that in mind!

If you travel with a lot of expensive technology that literally makes travel feasible (like…pays the bills), then keeping your belongings safe has to be high on your list of reasons to book a hostel or not. The best hostels have strong lockers in the rooms where you can store everything you travel with…not just a handful of electronics.

All entry doors and dorm rooms should have locks. And the best hostels have 24-hour reception and some cameras throughout the common areas to give some added security.

Yes, I’ve literally walked out of a hostel when they didn’t have strong, secure lockers as described in their descriptions. Always have a backup plan…or at least know that there’s always a chance you’ll need to pull an audible!

READ NEXT: UPDATED: 18 Safe Traveling Tips For NewbiesâKeep Yourself Safe & Reduce Your Travel Anxiety

Let’s not be naive; when you stay at a hostel you’re passing on at least some of the personal comforts of having your own place to stay. Accommodations with others, whether within the same dorm room or in a hostel where you have a private room still require common space and personal space to be compromised a little bit.

The difference between staying in a 3- or 4-bed dorm and an 8- to 12+ bed dorm will make a difference in your ability to get a good night’s sleep and feel secure.

The best hostels have a privacy curtain on every bedâeven the upper bunksâand invest a little more into their mattresses and pillows.

My suggestion is to look very closely at the pictures in hostel descriptions and booking sites and let this weigh heavily on whether or not you book a particular hostel! There are also plenty of clues on this topic in online hostel reviews, so don’t forget to look there.

If you’ll need to work while traveling, it’s a good idea to pay close attention to the common areas when booking a hostel. You may even go so far as emailing the hostel to ask if they have fast internet if you know you’ll need to be on meetings or uploading/downloading a lot.

I look for at least 2-3 potential places to work in the hostel. That while still knowing that I can always go out to a coffee shop or even find a bonafide coworking space to pay for. But the best hostels will have plenty of room for this, and plenty of people remote working at all hours of the day.

Hostel cost and value don’t end simply with the cost of a night of sleep. It’s tricky. One hostel may cost $4 more a night but give free breakfast, whereas the one you’re comparing it to is $4 cheaper and you’ll need to get your own breakfast…which may cost $5-6 a day. It adds up, but it’s not a black-and-white dealbreaker!

Some hostels have free happy hours where they supply drinks to help open the conversations and get solo travelers and group travelers all mixed up and friendly. And free tours, snacks, coffee, pool access, etc., can all add to the value of a hostel well beyond the cost.

Oh, and I definitely prefer a hostel that has a good kitchen that travelers can cook in and store groceries. This is a serious budget saver and a great place to meet fellow travelers! (I also need a refrigerator to store my insulin!)

I’m a solo traveler most of the time, and a shy introvert at that. For that reason, my experience staying at a hostel can be seriously impacted by the level of community that a hostel creates for travelers.

The best hostels in the world will have friendly staff encouraging you to engage with planned events and get-togethers meant to help everyone meet fellow travelers. Yes, you could skip all of this if your itinerary is completely full, but it’s always nice to have the option.

Also, I find that the best hostels with lots of programming employ more outgoing and kind staff and volunteers. They go hand-in-hand!

I’ve also stayed at many expensive hostels that had great amenities and working conditions but no community vibes or programming whatsoever. I tend to really get bummed in those types of hostels and it reminds me why community is so important when booking a hostel!

CHECK OUT: Carry-On Only / Theft-Deterrent Packing Recommendations

Be careful to look closely at where a hostel is located not only in relation to the sights and tourist attractions but also with regard to public transit, airports, bus and train stations. If you’re using these types of travel, it will play into your trip and your budget.

READ NEXT: UPDATED: 18 Safe Traveling Tips For NewbiesMexico Travel By Bus; They Could Straight-Up Leave Your Ass Behind

This is another category where an inexpensive or cheap hostel can get really expensive, especially if you choose to spend money on more expensive transit options like rideshares every time you go out.

Know where you’ll spend your time outside the hostel, then book a hostel that is within walking distance of those places.

Yes, that’s the actual name of the hostel; “We Love F. Tourists.” And as a branding consultant, I still find it a bit questionable. But it’s also laughable and unforgettable for sure, so I guess the name is working!

We Love F. Tourists tops my list of the best hostels I’ve stayed at for so many reasons. It started with the welcoming staff and the check-in process.

IagoâI really hope you get to meet Iago (he’s in the holiday hat above)âoffered up some cucumber water while I waited. Then after a couple of other new guests arrived, spent 20 minutes going over the hostel details, city maps, and everything else we needed to know about our stay.

When we were done, I was shown to my room…where someone had already delivered my luggage! (And this place had like 4-stories, so that’s a big deal!)

Every evening We Love F. Tourists hostel gives the option of an inexpensive home-cooked dinnerâwith bottomless wine and endless conversationâin their upper floor lounge area. These dinners were literally my favorite part and the reason I came back to stay at this hostel repeatedly during my 6-weeks in Lisbon.

There were also Fado music bar tours, Christmas decorations, and an evening Christmas walk around the city. (Did I mention I stayed there over Christmas?) Someone would randomly come around in the afternoon with a tray of hot tea.

I also stayed in a 3-bed dorm, which is about the smallest dorm you find when searching for hostels. Yes, one less person potentially snoring through the night is a big deal!

I can’t say enough about this hostel, which is why it’s at the top of my list of favorite hostels I’ve ever stayed at. And for around $20/night for a 3-bed dorm, it’s a steal.

Another amazing hostel with such a good vibe and many events to get people together if needed. Yeah! hostel in Barcelona balances the chill, family vibe while straddling the line between being a party hostel.

I’m usually not a big fan of party hostels and avoid them like the plague. But Yeah! Hostel Barcelona has a perfect balance.

There are tons of common areas, including a lounge with tables for working and a spacious king-size bed to chill on, a 7th-floor terrace with a rooftop pool, a huge kitchen with tons of fridge space, and a bar and dining room that can sit about 40-50 people. Dorm rooms have huge lockers for luggage and even another in the bunk for small things.

The first floor bar and dining room is where Yeah! Hostel Barcelona hosts a 3-course dinnerâwhich includes 3 large sangrias or draft beersâevery night cooked by a full-time chef. All for about $10.

The food here was amazing! Literally the best dinners I’ve had at any hostel I’ve ever booked. And they make special dishes for anyone that eats vegetarian or even vegan.

Combine these things with an extremely welcoming staff and nightly pub crawls. Daily walking tours, happy hour at the rooftop bar with $2 sangrias or drafts, huge lockers, and electronic locks on room and hostel doors. It’s easy to see why Yeah! Hostel has repeatedly been named one of the top hostels in Barcelona.

They’ve also been named one of the best hostels in Europe and one of the best hostels for solo travelers many times over the years. Popular hostels in Barcelona aren’t cheap, but at around $30-40/night for all of this in a 6-bed hostel dorm room, it is one of the best options in town.

This is a tricky one, and unfortunately this hostel is most likely to eventually drop out of my top 3 favorite hostels I’ve stayed at around the world. Sometimes the best hostel doesn’t include amazing programming or community building, or many other amenities. They’re just OK.

But if a said hostel is located in one of the most beautiful and interesting places you’ve ever visitedâduring a time when nobody else is visitingâthen it has a chance to make the list.

That’s why Kilronan Hostel on the Aran Isle of Inis MÃ³r (Inishmore) is here. Inis MÃ³r is f*cking epic and exactly what the romantic voice in the back of your head thinks Ireland is like.

Backstory: Shoulder season travel, typically Oct-Dec and Mar-May (give or take), almost always has smaller crowds and cheaper accommodations and tourist attractions. I traveled to Inis MÃ³r (Inishmore) in early October when the typical ferries of travelers were carrying a couple of hundred people daily to the island as opposed to a couple thousand during the high season.

By staying for 3 nights on the island I had the mornings and evenings to myself to explore.

The hostel was small, quaint, and pretty bare. The 5-bed hostel dorm roomâthat I had to myself every nightâwas small and would be cramped if full. The free breakfast was minimal but adequate. But this is one time when location, location, location was everything.

Kilronan hostel is an inexpensive gem of a hostel located in an absolutely stunning setting.

I truly hope this hostel can weather the storm of pandemics and slow seasons so you can experience everything that the Aran Isles has to offerâfor under $25/night. Protip: You can rent a bike nearby to get around the island early and late before and after the ferries drop off so that you can have these stunning places all to yourself!

Oaxaca, Mexico is blowing up recently as a very trendy travel destination. So it should come as no shock that they have some great hostels. Azul Cielo hostel in Oaxaca is another hostel that has a great vibe that overcomes some of its potential deficiencies. No huge programming calendar, and the dorm rooms had more beds than I typically tend to preferâand with no privacy curtains.

But friendly spaces, a tiny…and adorable…second-story bar, freshly-prepared breakfasts, and the kind and helpful staff and owner elevate Azul Cielo Hostel. The huge plants in the garden courtyard area didn’t hurt!

READ NEXT: Mexico: Murals & Street Art of Oaxaca, Mexico: The Colors of Oaxaca Full Hostel Review: Oaxaca, Mexico â Azul Cielo Hostel

Combine those things with the fact that Oaxaca, Mexico is an absolutely quaint and welcoming Mexican city, and it deserves a place on this list. Having met 6-7 people in the morning at the freshly prepared breakfast, then exploring together for a few days, we all decided to travel 6 hours south to Puerto Escondido to meet up again. Over 2-3 days we all met back at another hostel and continued to make memories.

Those types of things seem to happen at good hostels, and those are the memories that keep me wanting to stay at hostels over hotels and VRBOs whenever it’s an option.

Oh, and Azul Cielo hostel is about $10/night but also has options for private rooms for a little more. One of the best budget hostel options on this list.

I’ve stayed at the HI Portland Northwest hostel on three different occasions over the past 5 or so years. Every time I’m amazed by this massive hostel property, full of hidden little spaces to get away, have a beer, or even smoke a little…you know.

This hostel is made up of like 2-3 buildings and can hold a lot of travelers, but it never felt too crowded in the common areas.

The rooms were clean and secure, with really nice bathrooms and shower areas. There are at least 2-3 patio areasâmake sure you find the “secret garden”âand a small coffee shop/bakery shopfront that welcomes people that live in the neighborhood to patronize.

The HI Portland hostel has beers on tap for the evening and plenty of live music programming throughout the warmer months.

I chilled at an amazing open mic the last time I was at the HI Portland Northwest hostel and met amazing people.

While $40/night for a 4-bed dorm may not sound inexpensive, it’s on par for hostels in the US.

The Apple Hostel in Philadelphia was a very pleasant surprise. Partly because everyone around me was kind of a d*ck about my choice to go to Philly, and partly because USA hostels can be pretty hit or miss.

But the clean digs, welcoming atmosphere, free happy hour, and nightly ghost tour of the cobblestone streets and alleys of Philly made this hostel rank.

Apple Hostel has a huge remodeled kitchen to cook in, but they hosted dinners some nights so that you didn’t have to worry about a thing.

And I still remember the first night when someone who worked at the hostel came in and dropped two cases of beer in the middle of the room, by the pool table, and told us all to get to know each other. Then we hit the town to talk about ghosts, beer makers past, and of revolutions.

Spoiler alert: It worked. Many great conversations were had and memories were made.

4-bed hostel dorm rooms at the Apple Hostel in Philly start at around $45, or you can get a dorm bed with 17 other people in a room for $35. I suggest you go with the first option.

So I accidentally ended up at the Ballyhoura Luxury Hostel when on a 2-week stopover in Ireland. I say accidentally because as a fairly new traveler, I didn’t realize that county Limerick means something quite different than city Limerick. And by not paying attention, I actually ended up in Kilfinane Ireland…in county Limerick instead of the city of Limerick.

And to be honest, there ain’t much in Kilfinane. But…

…what did work out was that the Balyhoura Luxury Hostel ended up being the bomb. (Pretty sure nobody says “the bomb” anymore, but Ima try to bring it back.) It was the offseason and the hostel was fairly empty, so my luxury bed, pillows, and 8-bed dorm room all to myself was a treat.

The owners (Seamus & Teresa) and I talked nerdy about how they designed and had everything in the hostel built custom. From the dorm beds to the massive 20’+ wood slab dining table, to the sauna and the fireplace room.

Being forced to slow down and simply enjoy super small-town Ireland and the countryside was also a nice value-add.

The Ballyhoura Luxury Hostel dorm bed I stayed in was only $25/night during the travel shoulder season in October.

WATCH NEXT: Lost in Limerick, Ireland. Thinking About The Little Adventures In LifeThe WORMHOLEâ¦Epic Ireland: 3 days on the Aran Islands / Inis Mor

Since I spent about 3 months hopping around Portugal, I stayed at a lot of different hostels. Here are a couple more that I absolutely loved. That said, these hostels are all completely different from each other!

Porto Travel Guide | Sintra Travel Guide | Guimaraes Travel Guide | Aveiro Travel Guide

The Porto Wine Hostel is another one of those great hostels that gets much of its charm because of the visible love and dedication put into it by the owners. The owners (she was Serbian, and he Portuguese I believe) were always milling about smiles on their faces, making sure guests were happy.

There was a small but adequate communal gathering level which had a kitchen for cooking and a large common room with a wine bar. The stairwells and colors in this hostel were gorgeous. The rooms were modest, but I believe they were all ensuite, which was nice.

Guitars, a piano, and other instruments were available for anyone to play, along with games. Guests are also welcomed during check-in with a small glass of Port Wine; a perfect start to a trip to Porto.

The Portuguese people are late-night partiers, so the big, beautiful city square in front of the hostel was loud late into the morning. But that just added to the atmosphere. My bed in a 6-bed hostel dorm room at The Porto Wine Hostel was about $20/night.

This hostel was anything but homey and quaint. The Gallery Hostel was exactly the opposite; more like a hotel than a hostel, complete with a baller restaurant on the lower level and a small but swanky bar right off the street.

But because I work remotely, and I had a lot of work to do, it was exactly what I needed at the time.

The hostel vibe was…well…kind of sterile, but the people running the hostel and restaurant were super friendly. Had one of the most epic dinners with friends in the restaurant…when the power went out. Story for another time.

The wifi was fast, and the small but capable kitchen had huge tables for working at…all day if necessary. The beds were crazy comfortable and tucked and made “like new” every day at cleaning. The ensuite bathrooms were pristine, along with mechanical, code lockers to keep things safe.

This Gallery Hostel was literally in an artsy part of the city. From a clean-line, art-infused aesthetic, actually one of the coolest hostels I’ve stayed in.

I stayed in dorm rooms at times, and another stay booked a 3-bed dorm with 2 friends, so we had it to ourselves. Highly recommend you bring friends or be outgoing, because there isn’t much programming or community-building here.

My bed in a 6-bed ensuite dorm at The Gallery Hostel in Porto was about $24/night. That’s not cheap for Portugal, but given the level of this hostel, it’s way more bang for the buck than most backpacker hostels or more standard hostels.

READ NEXT: UPDATED: 18 Safe Traveling Tips For Newbies

The Lost Inn Lisbon (and many other Lisbon hostels) was at home in an absolutely beautiful old building with easily 14-footâoften vaultedâceilings throughout. Beautiful stairwells, hallways and dorm rooms. While the dorms were simple (hence no pics) most had curtains and they were filtered from street noise since it’s on a side street away from the crowds.

The bathrooms and showers were huge and never packed with people, since there were plenty.

Each night there was free sangria for two hours at the small first-floor bar/check-in common area. After that, there was typically a soup dinner. Free breakfast each morning got the day started with a full stomach.

While it definitely catered to those looking to pregame and go out to clubs later, it still had a fairly chill, family vibe. And the fact that all of the rooms were on the upper floors, well away from the ruckus, kept things quiet. One of the best party hostels I’ve stayed at…since the party vibe was pretty chill.

And no. Don’t ask me to describe the ruckus. All things considered, The Lost In Lisbon was a really great hostel. Beds in a fairly basic 4-bed mixed hostel dorm room (with privacy curtains) start around $20/night.

Jason is the author of “The Beginner Traveler’s Guide” as well as the voice behind the words and the eye behind the lens for The Nomad Experiment. “Planning to travel at some point” wasn’t actually getting the job done, so nearing 40 he decided to make it a priority, nomatter how scary that was. A few years laterâthrough the pandemic and a type 1 diabetes diagnosis at age 42ânow living a life of nomadic travel, he’s speaking out to encourage others of any age, or with any serious medical diagnosis, to live an unconventional life.

Want to travel more but donât really know where to start? Have a friend or family member that keeps talking about travelâbut clearly needs a little help actually getting off go and making it happen? This is the no-fluff, hands-on guide to finally getting unstuck and on a travel pathâwith confidence, intention, and zero shame.

#3176. How a new wave of science philanthropists can have the greatest impact

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Priscilla Chan (centre) is the co-founder of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, which is taking an interdisciplinary approach to tackling disease.Credit: Mike Windle/Getty for Vanity Fair

Some of the richest people in history are using charitable donations to explore fresh approaches to funding scientific research. Their ranks could soon grow: in the next year or so, initial public offerings by some of the biggest artificial-intelligence companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, both in San Francisco, California, could see the companies valued at more than US$1 trillion apiece, making hundreds of their employees millionaires in the process.

How tech billionaires are disrupting biomedical science

How tech billionaires are disrupting biomedical science

Many of the new philanthropists are adopting an engineering mindset, focusing their donations on technological approaches to solving societal problems. As Nature reports in a News feature, they are also bringing many of their own ideas about how this research should be prioritized, funded and executed.

These donors speak of high-risk, long-term and interdisciplinary research. Their goals include finding ways to make research faster and more efficient by encouraging data sharing and speeding up grant approvals, with solutions that include incorporating AI into the processes.

But there’s a disparity when you compare how these funders and those in the public sector operate. Like much of the research that takes place in companies, the results of projects funded by philanthropy won’t necessarily be published. Private organizations are not always obliged to collect and report data on how well their projects have worked — by publishing in peer-reviewed journals, for example — or to make other details about their grants public. At Nature, we think they should be more transparent. Transparency in science funding is a component of transparency in science itself: a non-negotiable principle. Research that is not transparent cannot be verified or built on by others, who might then improve it or find new applications.

An increasing number of examples of science philanthropy can be found around the world. In China, tech entrepreneurs have launched awards such as the Xplorer Prize for young researchers, which is funded mainly by the company Tencent in Shenzhen. New philanthropic foundations are emerging, including the Beijing-based Xiaomi Foundation, which supports universities and provides grants to teachers and researchers. And in Brazil, the Serrapilheira Institute in Rio de Janeiro was established in 2017 by private donors to fund fundamental research, which is usually supported by governments.

When the best decision is no decision: the rise of randomization in grant funding

When the best decision is no decision: the rise of randomization in grant funding

But it is in the United States that philanthropists have one of the longest histories of shaping the direction and structure of the scientific enterprise, from the industrialists of the early twentieth century to today’s tech entrepreneurs.

In 2015, Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg and his wife, paediatrician Priscilla Chan, pledged to donate 99% of Facebook shares, then valued at US$45 billion, to the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative. One of the initiative’s ambitions is to build interdisciplinary research infrastructure to allow the study of complex biology, to take research beyond the study of individual diseases. By 2025, Bill Gates and Melinda French Gates had donated nearly $64 billion of their wealth to the Gates Foundation (formerly the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation) in Seattle, Washington, which is focused on projects to improve public health and alleviate poverty in some 140 countries.

These and newer donors are keen to fill some of the perceived gaps in publicly funded research. Some, such as those financing the Arc Institute in Palo Alto, California, have created funding schemes to allow investigators to rapidly change direction in response to research results — something that is difficult, if not impossible, to do with conventional grants. Others, including former Google chief executive Eric Schmidt, are investing in technologies to speed up research. The Astera Institute, co-founded by cryptocurrency entrepreneur Jed McCaleb and based in the San Francisco Bay Area, is focused on using AI and developing infrastructure to tackle what it describes as “neglected ideas that aren’t supported well through existing institutions”.

The ‘Bill Gates problem’: do billionaire philanthropists skew global health research?

The ‘Bill Gates problem’: do billionaire philanthropists skew global health research?

Philanthropic foundations do not have the same reporting requirements as government funding agencies, which must publicly document their investments and the outcomes of their spending choices. It can be argued that freedom from such requirements is liberating. Without the fear of being called before lawmakers to explain the value of specific research projects, philanthropists are free to be more adventurous with their money. They can invest in long-term and high-risk projects. And with fewer bureaucratic obligations, charities can be better positioned to pivot rapidly when new technologies emerge, and to bridge disciplinary divisions to assemble teams with diverse expertise.

That said, science supported by philanthropy still relies on a foundation of public funding. Privately funded science and technology builds on published findings, many of which have been achieved through research funded by the public purse (M. Mazzucato and G. Semieniuk Oxford Rev. Econ. Policy 33, 24–48; 2017). If privately funded science is to achieve its ambition to benefit the world, philanthropists need to coordinate with and support the public sector. There are pragmatic reasons for doing so. Any new technologies that tech philanthropists want to roll out to the public will need to be compatible with existing ethical and safety frameworks.

New peer-review trial lets grant applicants evaluate each other’s proposals

New peer-review trial lets grant applicants evaluate each other’s proposals

Philanthropists should also bear in mind that in science, the line between an idea and a result is rarely straight or predictable. Those still relatively new to philanthropy would be wise to study the experiences of the Gates Foundation. In 2003, the organization, working with academic researchers, announced that it would fund up to 14 Grand Challenges in Global Health (H. Varmus et al. Science 302, 398–399; 2003). This was a set of ambitious goals to harness science to improve public health, ranging from developing vaccines that require no refrigeration to creating new treatments for infectious diseases. Some of the work, such as the use of gene editing in mosquitoes to control malaria, is paying off. But it has taken time. A decade after the launch of the challenges, Gates acknowledged that he had been “pretty naive” about how quickly the objectives could be achieved — a salutary lesson for his successors.

In countries around the world, public funding for scientific research is being cut or is at risk of being cut. That makes philanthropy an even more important source of finance. Without greater transparency about the results of philanthropic grant-making, however, there is no way of knowing what approaches have been successful or which might be instructive for guiding future science funding.

The engineer’s drive for efficiency and constant improvement, combined with the philanthropist’s freedom from constraint promise to bring fresh perspectives to science and innovation. Open science offers the best bet for ensuring that the resulting research delivers on its lofty goals.

#3178. Abandoned Study of Australian Ash Trees Challenges Case for Clearcutting

A landmark study of the towering ash trees that grow in the mountains of Victoria, Australia, which was launched in the 1980s, boosted arguments for clearcutting the iconic trees. But when scientists returned to the site years later, they came to a much different conclusion.

Australian conservationists have long contended that clearcutting imperiled koalas and other native wildlife. Foresters, on the other hand, argued that mountain ash trees, which can grow taller than 300 feet and live for more than 400 years, were adapted to catastrophic bushfires that cleared the forest, leaving nothing behind. They pointed to stands of ash trees that were essentially uniform in age — evidence that the forest had been leveled and then regrew — and said that by clearcutting ash and burning any detritus that remained, they were recreating the effects of the most intense fires.

To settle the argument between conservationists and foresters, scientists launched a landmark experiment in Victoria’s Central Highlands in 1987. They compared large clearcuts, which could be more than 1,000 feet wide; small clearcuts, some less than 200 feet across; and plots that had been heavily thinned, with at least half of trees removed.

By the early 2000s, it was clear that mountain ash regrew best in the footprints of large clearcuts, giving credence to the foresters’ argument. In the smaller clearcuts and thinned plots, the study found, shorter acacia trees dominated. The results were published and the experiment abandoned.

However, when scientists returned to the site in 2014, they noticed something surprising: While mountain ash were abundant in the clearcuts, both large and small, in the thinned plots, ash trees had grown at a startling pace.

Monitoring showed that, with few competitors, the biggest trees in the thinned plots were 20 percent larger in diameter than trees in areas that had never been harvested. They also stored at least as much carbon, meaning that, in just a few decades, the surviving ash in the thinned plots had recovered all the carbon lost to logging, and then some. The findings were recently published in Forest Science.

The study authors say that bigger trees are more resistant to fire and more likely to form the hollows where greater gliders and Leadbeater’s possums make their homes. Thinning, they say, offers a way to supply timber while also preserving vital woodlands and their stores of carbon.

“Our findings show this for mountain ash, and other studies in North America have shown this for conifer forests,” they said, writing in The Conversation. “It is a win-win-win outcome that challenges the false dichotomy of conservation versus production that has dominated public debate for decades.”

#3179. "Tinubu muss weg": Regierungskritiker in Nigeria unter Druck

Die Festnahme junger Männer wegen regierungskritischer T-Shirts und die Verhinderung eines politischen Treffens haben die Debatte über Meinungsfreiheit und das Recht auf Protest in Nigeria neu entfacht.

T-Shirts mit dem Slogan "Tinubu Must Go" ("Tinubu muss weg") stehen im Norden Nigerias im Zentrum eines zunehmend harten Vorgehens gegen Regierungskritiker. Der Schriftzug richtet sich gegen den nigerianischen Präsidenten Bola Tinubu.

Im vergangenen Monat nahm die Polizei im nordöstlichen Bundesstaat Borno fünf Männer fest, weil sie solche T-Shirts trugen.

Die Behörden warfen ihnen vor, sich verschworen zu haben, die Shirts herzustellen und zu tragen, um den öffentlichen Frieden zu stören. Anschließend wurden die Männer unter anderem wegen krimineller Verschwörung, Anstiftung, Störung der öffentlichen Ordnung und Rowdytums angeklagt.

Menschenrechtsorganisationen und Aktivisten kritisierten das Vorgehen scharf. Die Polizei erklärte später, die Festnahmen seien im Rahmen einer routinemäßigen Streife erfolgt. Dabei hätten die Beamten mutmaßlich illegale Drogen und weitere Gegenstände bei den Männern gefunden. Die Männer würden nicht wegen ihrer politischen Ansichten strafrechtlich verfolgt, betonte die Polizei.

Doch nur zwei Wochen später verhinderte die Polizei im nördlichen Bundesstaat Kano den Zugang zu einem Veranstaltungsort, an dem Mitglieder derselben Bewegung ein Treffen abhalten wollten. Zur Begründung verwies sie auf Bedenken hinsichtlich der öffentlichen Sicherheit.

Die beiden Vorfälle werfen die Frage auf, wo die Grenze zwischen legitimen Sicherheitsmaßnahmen und der Einschränkung abweichender politischer Meinungen verläuft. Viele fragen sich, ob Nigerias Demokratie den Bürgerinnen und Bürgern genügend Raum lässt, die Machthaber zu kritisieren.

Hassana Maina, Anwältin und Aktivistin, bezeichnete das Vorgehen der Polizei gegen die Träger der T-Shirts als "verabscheuungswürdig".

"Das ist bestenfalls zutiefst unehrlich. Die Probleme, mit denen wir zu kämpfen haben, und die Unsicherheit, die dadurch entstanden ist, lassen sich nicht lösen, indem man ein System schafft, das auf Faschismus beruht und in dem abweichende Stimmen nicht existieren dürfen. Menschen dürfen nicht gezwungen werden, auf eine bestimmte Weise zu denken. Das wäre an sich schon ein Angriff auf ihre Freiheit", sagte Maina der DW.

Es ist nicht das erste Mal, dass Behörden gegen Menschen vorgehen, die Ansichten äußern, die als regierungskritisch gelten.

Abubakar Idris, ein bekannter Kritiker in den sozialen Medien, der unter dem Namen Dadiyata bekannt ist, verschwand im August 2019. Zuvor hatten bewaffnete Männer ihn aus seiner Wohnung im Bundesstaat Kaduna verschleppt.

Dadiyata hatte die damalige regionale Regierung unter Umar Ganduje im Bundesstaat Kano wiederholt kritisiert. Seit seiner Verschleppung fehlt von ihm jede Spur. Im August 2026, sieben Jahre nach seinem Verschwinden, berichteten nigerianische Medien, er werde nach nigerianischem Recht als mutmaßlich verstorben betrachtet.

In einem weiteren Fall wurde die damals 18-jährige Hamdiyya Sharif festgenommen, nachdem sie auf TikTok ein Video veröffentlicht hatte, in dem sie den Umgang des Gouverneurs des Bundesstaates Sokoto mit der Sicherheitslage im Nordwesten Nigerias kritisierte. In dem Video schilderte Sharif, wie kriminelle Banden, die vor Ort als "Banditen" bezeichnet werden, Dörfer überfielen und plünderten. Außerdem sprach sie über die schwierige Lage vertriebener Frauen in dem Bundesstaat.

Nach der Veröffentlichung des Videos wurde Sharif am 9. November 2024 festgenommen und später wieder freigelassen. Wenige Tage darauf wurde sie von bewaffneten Männern verschleppt und schwer misshandelt. Im weiteren Verlauf wurde sie erneut festgenommen und vor einem Scharia-Gericht angeklagt. Die Vorwürfe lauteten, sie habe den Gouverneur Ahmed Aliyu beleidigt und zu "Unruhen angestiftet". Im Mai 2025 berichteten Medien erneut über ihre Verschleppung und anschließende Festnahme durch die Polizei.

Die Bewegung "Tinubu Must Go" richtet sich gegen die Regierung von Präsident Bola Tinubu. Nach eigenen Angaben will sie die Bevölkerung im Vorfeld der für 2027 geplanten allgemeinen Wahlen mobilisieren.

Doch hinter dem Protest steckt mehr als die Forderung nach einem Machtwechsel.

Nigeria steckt in einer schweren Wirtschaftskrise. Die Lebensmittelpreise sind stark gestiegen, die hohe Inflation und die deutlich gestiegenen Transportkosten verschärfen die Belastungen für die Bevölkerung.

Im Norden des Landes bleibt die Sicherheitslage vielerorts angespannt, insbesondere in ländlichen Gebieten.

Seit mehr als einem Jahrzehnt führt die islamistische Miliz Boko Haram gemeinsam mit verschiedenen Splittergruppen einen bewaffneten Aufstand gegen den nigerianischen Staat.

Der Konflikt hat Zehntausende Menschen das Leben gekostet und Millionen aus ihrer Heimat vertrieben. Trotz jahrelanger Militäreinsätze beeinträchtigen die Kämpfe weiterhin die Lebensgrundlagen der Menschen und die wirtschaftlichen Aktivitäten in der Region.

Isa Sanusi, Geschäftsführer von Amnesty International in Nigeria, sieht in den Maßnahmen gegen Menschen, die T-Shirts mit dem Aufdruck "Tinubu Must Go!" tragen, ein besorgniserregendes Muster. Sie seien Ausdruck einer zunehmenden Einschränkung des Rechts auf Vereinigungsfreiheit und freie Meinungsäußerung.

"Die Menschen dürfen eine politische Partei oder einen Kandidaten unterstützen oder ablehnen. Es ist inakzeptabel, dass schon das Tragen eines T-Shirts zum Grund für eine Festnahme und Inhaftierung werden kann", sagte er der DW. "Diese Maßnahmen der Polizei sind ein Angriff auf die Demokratie selbst."

Während sich Nigeria auf die nächsten allgemeinen Wahlen vorbereitet, betont Sanusi, dass Wahlen zwar ein zentraler Bestandteil der Demokratie seien, aber nicht deren einziges Kriterium.

Der Zustand der Demokratie in Nigeria müsse auch daran gemessen werden, wie es um die Freiheit und den Schutz der Grundrechte bestellt sei, sagte er.

"Die Bilanz ist ernüchternd: Menschen werden angegriffen und festgenommen, nur weil sie ihre politische Haltung oder Meinung äußern", sagte Sanusi der DW. "Oppositionspolitikern wird der Raum genommen, politische Versammlungen abzuhalten. Hotels werden unter Druck gesetzt, damit sie der Opposition ihre Räumlichkeiten nicht zur Verfügung stellen."

Erst kürzlich zog die Leitung des Arewa House in Kaduna ihre Genehmigung für die Vorstellung eines Buches zurück, das als regierungskritisch galt. Das Arewa House ist ein Forschungszentrum, das sich der historischen Dokumentation widmet. Zur Begründung der Absage verwies die Leitung auf betriebliche Gründe.

Eine lebendige Demokratie ohne starke Opposition sei eine Farce, betonte die Anwältin und Aktivistin Hassan Maina.

Nigeria müsse insbesondere die Vorstellung zurückweisen, Kritik an der Regierung, ihrer Politik oder dem Staat stelle die Vaterlandsliebe der Kritiker infrage. Die Regierung versuche, genau diesen Eindruck zu vermitteln, sagte Maina. Dabei gebe es nicht nur eine einzige Art, patriotisch zu sein.

"Sich gegen politische Maßnahmen zu stellen, von denen man glaubt, dass sie der Entwicklung des eigenen Landes schaden, ist meiner Meinung nach Patriotismus in seiner reinsten Form", sagte sie der DW.

#3180. Fine ‘headphone dodgers’ if you will, but to really tackle antisocial behaviour, Britain should look to Japan | Emily Bratt

Working in Japanese schools, I saw how teaching young people civic pride creates adults with consideration for others

There are two types of people who listen to music in public: those who wear headphones and those who … are a word I probably can’t use here. “Loudcasting” – playing audio, watching videos or talking on speakerphone in public spaces – is a form of antisocial behaviour that drives eight in 10 of people in the UK crazy, and I’m glad Andy Burnham is one of those eight. But while I welcome his policy to fine “headphone dodgers”, I’m not convinced it will solve the problem.

This behaviour isn’t only a nuisance, but a grave indicator of a deeper societal issue: the erosion of empathy. You can’t legislate civic pride into an individualistic culture where feelings of social disconnection are widespread.

From 2019 to 2021 I lived in Japan, where keeping the peace is paramount and you can be reprimanded just for talking on the bus. When I returned to England, I felt shock and shame at how we treat one another and our public spaces. I still do. We watch our dogs defecate in the street and walk away. We use public bathrooms as if we’re feral two-year-olds. We inflict the soundtrack of our mindless social-media scrolling on an entire train carriage.

Japanese society is not without its flaws; I often chafed at the level of deference I witnessed. But living there also highlighted to me just how selfish we can be in Britain. Last week, I saw someone had smeared dog poo into the communal carpeted entrance of their own block of flats. Some on the far right love to cast other cultures as primitive, but I think we need to look at ourselves.

We could learn from Japan. As a broadly collectivist society, it favours social harmony and group responsibility. One guiding principle is meiwaku wo kakenai: the idea that you should avoid inconveniencing others.

I worked in Japanese state schools and was astonished when students as young as five diligently began stacking chairs and clearing apparatus as sports day wrapped up. Nobody told them to. Additionally, Japanese schools don’t completely rely on cleaners: the students sweep the halls, wipe down desks, empty bins and even disinfect and scrub the bathrooms. This cleaning practice, a component of tokkatsu (special activities), forms part of a wider approach to holistic education and teaches children personal responsibility for, and pride in, their environment.

It’s important to add that a teenager is still a teenager, no matter the country. It’s a myth that all Japanese children are innately disciplined perfect little angels. But the wider impact of these social ethics is obvious. Crime rates in Japan are (comparatively) low, public spaces are meticulously maintained and litter is a rarity. It’s not a myth that Japanese streets are so clean you could lick them. Lick an English street and, bam! Dysentery.

The UK government’s crackdown on content-blaring can only work in conjunction with a wider effort. First, fines have to actually be imposed by those in authority – and they need to feel safe and incentivised to do so. Train managers have been hot on calling out fare dodgers for years (one made me cry when I was 19 for not having my student railcard, such was his wrath). Now they need to bring the same resolve to headphone dodgers. Burnham’s policy states that drivers would not be expected to enforce such rules – it’s a job for safety officers or the police. But unless someone is there to enforce the rules in the moment, the policy becomes little more than an empty threat.

Second, we need to rebuild social norms so that consideration for others is instinctive. The word etiquette seems antiquated, but given that almost half of us in the UK play content from our phones without headphones – and that this behaviour bothers most of us – etiquette education is still necessary. Maybe, so we don’t feel we’re in a Jane Austen novel, we call it something else. Perhaps in schools, it’s civic responsibility class, or lessons in caring about others, or simply learning how to not be a twat. It doesn’t require major educational reform. Copying Japan’s approach to school-cleaning, for example, could be a good (and easy) place to start.

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

The onus, of course, isn’t only on schools – parents have to lead by example. But imagine the ripple effect if British schoolchildren were given the responsibility of caring for their classrooms and corridors.

Unfortunately, there’s also a deeper issue. Some loudcasters are simply oblivious, but others are deliberately rage-baiting. The latter is a product of a disaffected society, which Burnham’s fines by themselves could exacerbate. Nobody likes being told off, but especially not angry people.

We don’t need to become Japan. But in an increasingly divided world, consideration for others and respect for our surroundings are what can still hold us together.

#3181. Easy Thanksgiving STEM Challenges

Keep the kids busy over Thanksgiving with these easy STEM Challenges. Science activities and challenges are a great way for kids to learn without realising. I’ve made these challenges simple, inexpensive and great fun to do with family and friends!

Learn about strong shapes with a turkey tower, find out why calcium is so important for bone health with a bendy bone challenge and lots more!

Use toothpicks and marshmallows to build a tower tall enough to hold a small turkey toy. If you don’t have toothpicks, spaghetti is a fun alternative.

Shapes are important to think about when building toothpick towers. Triangles, arches, and domes are all strong shapes used by engineers to make structures stronger. Experiment with square shapes and triangles as you build your toothpick tower.

Soaking cooked turkey or chicken bones in vinegar is a great way to learn about the importance of calcium. The vinegar dissolves the calcium, making the bone bendy!

Cranberries float because they have lots of air pockets. This makes them less dense than water, so they float! Add toothpicks to cranberries to make a raft or boat shape.

Making a parachute is a great way to learn about forces. The parachute slows the pumpkin pie’s fall because it has a larger surface area than just the pie itself, increasing air resistance and slowing the pie’s descent.

I have two free options available if you want to print out my challenges. The first option is the basic challenges on one page. Option two is the basic challenges and investigation worksheets for the Turkey Tower, Cranberry Boats and Pumpkin Pie Parachute.

Learn about filters with a delicious apple cider recipe.

Learn about circuits with a potato battery. This is much easier than you think, but it does require some special materials.

Make a mini basketball hoop and catapult to learn about forces.

Let us know if you have any more ideas for Thanksgiving STEM Challenges.
