#3182. The story of ‘earvolution’: from ceremonial piercings to fashion-statement earbuds

Paid content is paid for and controlled by an advertiser and produced by the Guardian Labs team.

For millennia, humans have been captivated by ear decorations. Now, earbuds not only connect us to the digital world, they also showcase our personal sense of style – and the HUAWEI FreeClip 2 is at the forefront of that development

When we are born, a cry can let the world know that we are healthy and OK. When we first begin to talk, we learn to express our needs and understand the needs of others. As we grow older, we learn that the sound of a siren denotes danger, that certain notes swelling together create the sound of a favourite song which lifts our spirits, or that a warm familiar voice on the other end of the phone means our best friend has our back.

Our ears give us grounding and clues: they are our maps of the world, guiding us towards truth, keeping us from harm, giving us a constant stream of sensory information.

So it makes sense that humans have been highlighting this particular part of their anatomies for millennia. The power of the ear, as a portal through which good and bad could traverse was something that was clocked by ancient cultures who believed that evil spirits could enter through the ear canals. Metal earrings were thought to repel the malevolent forces.

In other cultures, ceremonial ear piercing would mark a rite of passage – such as coming of age or the ascension of a person to a particular status in the community. In some belief systems, certain parts of the outer ear were believed to be connected to other organs. And by piercing those parts of the ear it would lead to healing in the body. Meanwhile sailors wore gold loops in their ears as a sort of maritime life insurance, making sure they would get a respectful burial if they washed up ashore after being lost at sea. When the church banned the practice of ear piercing in the 13th century, it became subversive.

Of course, in different times, the wearing of ear jewellery also indicated wealth in societies, with gold and gemstones being worn to indicate status.

Currently, there are trends for multiple piercings throughout the ear – an aesthetic flex that’s as much an act of quiet-fashion rebellion as it is a visual insight into your unique style.

But there’s a revolution happening in ear adornments too. The act of listening has become increasingly crucial in today’s age of digital audio experiences, podcasts, personal assistants – as well as the need to maintain human connection and situational awareness as we move through our hybrid digital-IRL worlds.

We spend a great deal of time ingesting information through our ears, whether that’s having conversations with colleagues, listening to content or checking out a new band recommended by a trusted friend.

We spend so much of our waking day “plugged in” that it is increasingly important that our wearables work for us, mirroring our lifestyles. In this attention economy, we’re multi-tasking audio information the whole time so it’s important to have earbuds that meet us where our real lived experience is. Our listening habits – how we listen and what we listen to – are reflected through what we are listening on.

In 2023, Huawei changed the wearable tech game with its HUAWEI FreeClip: an open-ear earbud that clipped around the middle of the ear, resting outside a person’s ear canal in contrast with in-ear earbuds – marking a new stage in the history of ear adornments.

So lightweight and comfortable you forget you are wearing them, they offer crisp and clear audio that allows you to converse with ease. Now Huawei is launching a new iteration: the HUAWEI FreeClip 2, which elevates fashion, functionality, design nous and audio excellence even further.

Audio wise, the HUAWEI FreeClip 2 has had a multifaceted upgrade. The bass has improved thanks to a dual-diaphragm driver, offering a deeper low-end sound and more elasticity and richness in the lower frequencies, giving you more sonic details in the music you love. There are also “smart” features, where the buds automatically adjust the volume to match your surroundings, from a busy commuter train to your office. Not only that, the vocal content of what you’re listening to is then enhanced so the delivery is as audio perfect as can be.

And if you are taking an important call while you are listening to a new audiobook, you don’t have to worry about levels. The earbuds contain an advanced noise cancellation system that will kick in. It also identifies ambient noise in public spaces, so you will be able to be heard clearly and plainly even if you are in the middle of a busy coffee shop or restaurant.

With their hybrid ear-cuff design, the HUAWEI FreeClip 2 will be loved by the fashion set. The buds come in a range of colour schemes (black, white and blue, with rose-gold coming soon) and the blue and white editions feature a charging case with a denim texture produced through high-precision infrared scanning of real denim fabric. They’re also dust and water resistant, so they’re ready for any change in season (weather and fashion wise!).

The fashion set will also love that Huawei has announced its partnership with French jewellery designer, Les Néréides, which has created a series of three stylish, FreeClip 2 clip-on accessories which mirror the brands iconic pieces, so you can accessorise your tech with a perfect blend of tech and fashion.

Ergonomically, the HUAWEI FreeClip 2 is made with skin-friendly silicon and a shape-memory alloy, which enables it to hold its “C” shape while remaining flexible. The effortless fit makes the buds ideal for active users who want to incorporate them into their exercise activities such as running, yoga or dancing. Weighing just 5.1 grams, the earbuds themselves are also lighter than the first generation.

And don’t worry about running out of juice, the design team is on top of that too. Fast wireless charging offers three hours of playback after only a 10-minute charge, and you get nine hours of continuous playback after a full charge (38 hours with a fully charged charging case).

The HUAWEI FreeClip 2 is the next stage of human “earvolution” and we’re here for it.

#3186. ‘Wastelands’ No More: India Charts a Future for Its Grasslands

A wolf looks out over grasslands in the Indian state of Maharashtra. Mihir Godbole / The Grasslands Trust

Since the colonial era, India has regarded its native savannas as little more than degraded forests. Now, amid a growing recognition of rangelands globally, officials are working to map the nation’s ailing grasslands, with a view to restoring these vital ecosystems.

By Vaishnavi Chandrashekhar • July 30, 2026

It’s almost noon, and the sun is high over Gulunche, a village in the western Indian state of Maharashtra that is surrounded by sugarcane fields, grassy pastures, and short trees. The landscape appears verdant, but it belies an ecological precarity. The sugarcane guzzles water in the semi-arid terrain; a dominant tree species is a South American mesquite, introduced decades ago to fight desertification and provide firewood; and the grass itself has been overrun by a single species that provides poor fodder for the wild herbivores and sheep that depend on these pastures.

Standing on the edge of a small nursery off the highway, conservationist Mihir Godbole points to rows of tall green grasses growing at the edge of a trench. The grass is one of several indigenous species thought to have vanished from the land years ago and that his organization, the nonprofit Grasslands Trust, is trying to revive in one corner of this 50-acre site. The blades have survived two summers now without irrigation or fertilizer. “It can grow without a lot of external inputs,” says Godbole. “That tells us that this is the right grass for this region.”

Godbole’s experiment is a small step in an ambitious effort to restore the region’s native grasslands — part of a new conservation agenda in a country better known for tiger-filled forests than open savannas. Such efforts are showing early signs of success: In the arid northwestern state of Rajasthan, grassland restoration efforts in the Tal Chhapar Wildlife Sanctuary have brought a resurgence of wildlife and birds. In Gujarat’s Banni grasslands, pastoralists have helped remove invasives and restored around 7,000 acres of land.

And in an important policy move, India’s National Board for Wildlife in April directed government agencies to map, for the first time, the extent and biodiversity of these ecosystems nationwide. The findings will eventually be published in an “Atlas of Grasslands,” with a view to creating a national policy framework to protect and manage these lands. “It’s a long overdue recognition,” says Abi Vanak, an advisor to the Grasslands Trust and the director of the Centre for Policy Design at the Ashoka Trust for Research in Ecology and the Environment. “[The move] signals an important shift in government thinking about these ecosystems.”

The shift is not restricted to India. International attention on grasslands and other scrub landscapes has grown in recent years. A key policy moment, says Chetan Kumar, global head of forests and grasslands at the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), was the publication of the United Nations’ 2024 Global Land Outlook report, which highlighted the untapped potential of rangelands and pastoralism to bolster climate resilience, biodiversity, and rural development. This year is also the U.N. International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists — an attempt, says Susan Gardner, director of the ecosystems division of the U.N. Environment Programme (UNEP), to “recognize rangelands as core infrastructure… and to recognize pastoralists as essential partners in protecting, managing, and restoring them.”

In the northern Great Plains of the United States, the National Audubon Society has restored more than 20,000 acres of grassland through a program that works with farmers and ranchers. In Kazakhstan, the Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative has helped protect around 12 million acres of grassland across the Central Asian steppe, increased the population of native saiga antelope, and reintroduced wild horses. Between 2021 and 2025, China restored an average of about 7.7 million acres of degraded grassland each year.

A herder grazes his sheep in the state of Rajasthan. Sandeep Bisht / Alamy

Savannas, steppes, grasslands, and scrub are open lands marked by grass or shrubby vegetation and sparse tree cover. These ecosystems may look desolate, but they contain extensive root systems that stabilize soil, increase rainwater infiltration, and store carbon long term. These habitats are also vital for migratory birds, native bees and butterflies, and diverse wildlife. Many of these landscapes also function as rangelands, supporting livestock and pastoralist communities. According to the UNEP, these lands cover more than half of Earth’s surface, support 2 billion people, provide 16 percent of global food production, and store up to 30 percent of terrestrial carbon.

Yet their importance has not, until recently, been reflected in policy or investment, says Gardner. Much of this landscape has already been lost to farming, industry, and invasive species. The U.S. has lost more than half its historic prairies, primarily to industrial agriculture. India has seen its grasslands shrink from roughly 110 million acres in 1880 to 60 million in 2010, according to one estimate.

In India, this loss has historical causes. Conservation policy has historically focused on forests, in part due to a legacy of colonialism. British officials in India viewed forests primarily in economic terms, as resources that could be converted to timber plantations and cropland or conserved for game animals. Vanak, of the Ashoka Trust, argues that the British recognized savannas as distinct ecosystems in Africa but not in India partly because India’s large game animals, especially its tigers, were concentrated in forests. Apart from the cheetah, which was hunted to extinction, grassland species like wolves weren’t as valued.

The British classified many grasslands as forests, where grazing was prohibited, while others were labeled as degraded forests or “wastelands,” making them easier to convert to other uses. More recently, says Gardner, farming has shaped assumptions about what “productive” or well-managed land should look like, privileging stationary agriculture over pastoralism.

The wasteland classification persisted in independent India. For a long time, scientists continued to believe India had no natural savannas and that grassy or shrubby areas were merely deforested land. But paleoclimate research has shown otherwise: A 2021 study of lake sediment in western India found evidence that a weakening monsoon 6,000 years ago drove the expansion of savannas in peninsular India.

Misperceptions about baseline conditions have made some areas vulnerable to change. In the 1980s, the government set up a National Wasteland Development Board with the aim of turning these lands to “productive use,” promoting their conversion to farming, plantations, and other uses.

A first among major nations, India is industrializing with solar. Read more.

A 2023 study led by Vanak found that less than 5 percent of India’s semi-arid open natural ecosystems are protected — and that nearly 70 percent of those open systems overlapped with officially designated wastelands. More recently, these seemingly empty landscapes have been targeted for solar and wind power projects — to the detriment of local wildlife and pastoralists — as well as for more tree plantations. In 2024, a new policy opened degraded land, including scrubland and pasture commons, to private plantations for the generation of carbon credits or to fulfill national afforestation goals.

Left to right: An Indian gazelle, Indian wolf, and Indian courser. All three species have been harmed by the loss of grasslands. The Grasslands Trust; Tisha Mukherjee via Wikipedia; Rushikesh Deshmukh via Wikipedia

Conservationists hope that the new effort to map grasslands will help avert further losses. The official Atlas project is still in early stages: Since the April directive, the government-funded Wildlife Institute of India has put together a comprehensive plan, in partnership with two other forest research agencies, to map existing grasslands, document biodiversity, and highlight areas under threat. Based on the findings, agencies will suggest restoration and management strategies, according to a government researcher with knowledge of the project.

State governments are also beginning to shift their approach to land use. In May, the state of Maharashtra issued guidelines for afforestation that recognized grasslands as distinct ecosystems that need locally tailored restoration, rather than blanket tree plantation. “Government attitudes are slowly changing,” says Godbole of the Grasslands Trust. “But things need to move faster on the ground.”

The challenges of conservation are apparent on the newly widened road to Gulunche. The restoration site lies less than 60 miles southeast of Pune, a once-small town that has tripled in size over the past three decades. The semi-arid landscape is a patchwork of privately owned farms, state-owned forest land, and commons, known as “gairans,” which are also state-owned. An irrigation scheme introduced 10 years ago helped expand the farming of sugarcane, a water-intensive cash crop. With an international airport planned in the area, land prices have risen and owners have begun to fence off their plots, blocking the passage of sheep and wild deer.

As Pune’s native habitat has shrunk, so has its wildlife. Some of India’s fastest-declining bird species, according to the IUCN Red List, are scrubland species that don’t perch on trees. Populations of the Indian courser, for example, have declined by more than 70 percent due to habitat loss. Gazelle numbers have also declined, and Indian gray wolves survive in these habitats partly by feeding on waste dumped by poultry farms, says Godbole. One major conservation challenge, notes his colleague and cofounder Vishwatej Pawar, is that “the species is protected but the habitat is not.”

Local and nomadic pastoralists, who graze their flocks of sheep on this open land, have also been affected by habitat loss. Sadashiv Mote, a local shepherd, says he’s reduced his flock because farms, buildings, and fences have taken over grazing land. “Water is also scarcer now,” he says as he herds his roughly 100 sheep toward a patch along the highway where he spotted new grass growing.

While pastoralists have traditional rights on grazing commons — according to one estimate, India has some 13 million practicing pastoralists — the practice has often been viewed by economists as inefficient and by conservationists as environmentally destructive, says the UNEP’s Gardner. But such attitudes are starting to change. Last year, for the very first time, India’s five-year livestock census counted the animals held by nomadic pastoralists, not just animals on farms — a sign of expanding recognition for pastoralists. “The shepherd is as much a part of the grassland landscape as the wolf,” says Godbole.

Locals plant native grasses at a restoration site in the village of Gulunche. The Grasslands Trust

That philosophy underpins the work of the Grasslands Trust, which partners with local communities as well as the forest department. The Gulunche restoration site sits on commons land where, with the consent of the village, grazing is temporarily banned. “We were not using the area much, and we wanted to support a project that could benefit us,” says Samradnee Nigade, the young head of the village council. Those benefits include employment for locals and the production of a high-quality fodder made of fermented native grasses, sugarcane, and corn, as well as biochar made from invasive trees removed from the site. The trust is also figuring out how to revive ancient water courses that may have shrunk due to human activities.

Heat stress is a major driver of India’s kidney disease epidemic. Read more.

The challenges at Gulunche mirror those of larger restoration projects. Scientists know much less about restoring grasslands than conserving forests — one review found that 89 of the 206 endemic Indian savanna species had been described only in the last two decades. Traditional knowledge is critical for managing many of these landscapes, says the IUCN’s Kumar, but research is especially important in areas changing rapidly due to development and climate change. Unfortunately, conservationists say, funding to run restoration experiments is not nearly as abundant as funding for forests, in part because donors prefer to support projects with highly visible outcomes.

“We need to provide alternative models to afforestation for dryland areas,” Vanak says. It shouldn’t be that hard: As Godbole likes to point out, trees are difficult to grow in dry landscapes. Grassland restoration, he says, “is cheaper and more ecologically responsible.”

Mumbai-based Vaishnavi Chandrashekhar has worked as a reporter and editor at The Times of India and at The Christian Science Monitor. Her work also has appeared in The Daily Beast, The Guardian, and The New York Times. More about Vaishnavi Chandrashekhar →

#3188. No unions, low taxes: why some of Britain’s top chefs are opening outposts in Gulf states

Leading restaurateur says Gulf countries actively help businesses set up, while east Asia has a better work ethic

Some of London’s top restaurants are opening branches in Dubai because of a “tax tsunami” in the UK and better work ethic abroad, according to a leading restaurateur.

James Robson, a co-owner of Fallow in St James’s Market, regarded as the capital’s hottest restaurant, serving 1,000 people a day, has just signed a deal to open an outpost in the Gulf.

Other restaurants have opened in Dubai, including the celebrity hotspot Scott’s in Mayfair, the two Michelin-starred Indian venue Gymkhana, and the upmarket Chinese restaurant Park Chinois. Isabel’s, a Mayfair institution enjoyed by politicians, has opened in Abu Dhabi. And the trendy Borough Market bakery Bread Ahead has branched out in Dubai.

Despite conflicts in the Middle East, including the US-Israeli war in Iran which caused Dubai to face bombardment and an exodus of expats earlier this year, restaurants continue to open in the emirate.

Speaking from Hong Kong, where he is looking at opportunities in Asia, Robson said: “East Asia, the States and the Gulf are key growth targets for us. America champions business, the Gulf actively encourages and assists, whilst east Asia has a work ethic and taxation system that puts the UK to shame. I’m incredibly keen to start working in these regions over the next few years.”

Fallow has risen to fame partially through Instagram, where it has 650,000 followers, and its striking dishes including a whole cod’s head drenched in a spicy butter sauce.

Restaurateurs have complained of the VAT rate for hospitality in the UK, which at 20% is one of the highest rates in Europe. The European average for restaurants is about 12%. In Italy, it is set at 10% for food sold in restaurants. Chefs are calling for Andy Burnham to use next week’s budget to cut the VAT rate.

“We have had a tsunami of taxes that have got to the point where taking business risk simply does not make sense in the UK,” Robson said, “Sadly the country has sleepwalked into multiple anti-growth taxations the last two budgets and likely more will be forthcoming next week.”

The entrepreneur has asked for VAT to be put more in line with Europe. “Add 25% corporation tax and 40%-plus dividend tax, then you start to question why do businesses any more.”

Jason Atherton, a Michelin-starred chef, spends a third of his time at his Dubai restaurant now and says it is easier to make a profit abroad than in London.

But human rights experts have warned of exploitation and poor worker protections in the Gulf. Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK’s director of campaigns, said: “Dubai might look like an attractive place to do business, but the UAE has a very poor record on workers’ rights and protection from labour exploitation. The UAE has spent heavily on polishing its image in the UK, not least through Manchester City, but that glamour shouldn’t distract from how the people who keep its economy running are treated.

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

“Migrant workers, who make up the majority of the UAE’s population, remain bound by a sponsorship system that ties them to their employers and exposes them to labour abuse. They are denied the right to form trade unions, leaving them few ways to challenge unfair treatment.

“Any UK business expanding into the Gulf has a responsibility to carry out proper human rights due diligence, to make sure the people working in its kitchens are treated fairly, paid properly and able to raise concerns without fear of losing their job or visa.”

Some restaurants in Dubai are struggling: Dinner by Heston is temporarily closed and has been since the fallout from the war in the Middle East. The Michelin guide came under fire earlier this month because it included 16 restaurants that were either permanently or temporarily closed. It appears that some visits were undertaken by inspectors at the beginning of the year, before the war started.

Robson said he had no resentment paying UK tax. “I am incredibly proud of the taxes I pay and feel privileged that I can contribute to our country’s deficit and will continue to do so,” he said. “My point is UK growth simply does not have any risk-reward balance any more, therefore it’s play incredibly safe here and focus overseas.”

#3189. Tschechien: Umstrittenes Rundfunkgebühren-Aus nimmt erste Hürde

Wird der tschechische Rundfunk bald vom Wohlwollen der Regierung abhängig sein? Die Finanzierung soll sich ändern. Der Widerstand wächst.

Trotz Protesten, Kritik der Opposition und Vorwürfen der Einschränkung der Pressefreiheit: Tschechiens Parlament hat einen Gesetzentwurf zur Änderung des Finanzierungssystems für das öffentlich-rechtliche Fernsehen und Radio im Eilverfahren verabschiedet.

Hintergrund: Die Regierungskoalition in Prag - geführt vom rechtspopulistischen Ministerpräsidenten Andrej Babiš - will die Finanzierung des öffentlich-rechtlichen Radios und Fernsehens auf eine neue Basis stellen. Statt durch Rundfunkgebühren sollen sie direkt aus dem Staatshaushalt finanziert werden. Die Regierung erklärt, sie wolle die monatliche Gebühr von 205 Kronen (8,42 Euro) pro Haushalt abschaffen, um die Kosten für die Verbraucher zu senken.

Kritiker befürchten, dass damit das Tschechische Fernsehen ČC und der Tschechische Rundfunk ČRo direkt von der Regierungsmacht abhängig und zu deren Sprachrohr gemacht würden. Setzt sich die Regierung durch, könnten die Mittel für die öffentlich-rechtlichen Medien ab kommendem Jahr um rund 15 Prozent gekürzt werden.

Politiker von Babiš' Dreier-Bündnis, dem auch zwei rechtsextreme Parteien angehören, haben Tschechiens öffentlich-rechtlichen Medien wiederholt Voreingenommenheit vorgeworfen. Bei der Regierungsübernahme im Dezember versprach die Koalition, die Reform durchzuziehen.

Nun hat der Plan in Prag die erste Hürde genommen. Trotz heftiger Kritik der Opposition setzte die Regierungsmehrheit durch, dass das Parlament bis weit in die Nacht auf diesen Samstag tagte. "Es ist unmoralisch und beschämend, für etwas zu bezahlen, das meinen Interessen, den Interessen meines Landes und meines Volkes zuwiderläuft", sagte Tomio Okamura, Vorsitzender der rechtsextremen SPD, während der nächtlichen Debatte.

Die tschechische SPD (Svoboda a přímá demokracie, deutsch: Freiheit und direkte Demokratie) ist nicht zu verwechseln mit der deutschen sozialdemokratischen Partei, die unter gleicher Abkürzung firmiert.

Nach der ersten Lesung gab es am frühen Morgen eine Abstimmung. Um 4.36 Uhr machte eine Mehrheit der Abgeordneten den Weg dafür frei, dass der Regierungsvorschlag an die zuständigen Ausschüsse weitergeleitet wurde, damit dann endgültig darüber abgestimmt werden kann.

Mit der Nachtsitzung habe die Regierungskoalition "alle bisherigen Regeln gebrochen" und "gegen alle demokratischen Prinzipien verstoßen", beklagten Oppositionspolitiker. "Wir halten unsere Versprechen", ließ hingegen Ministerpräsident Babiš nach der Abstimmung verlauten.

Die Koalition argumentiert, dass beide öffentlich-rechtlichen Sender Einsparungen vornehmen müssten. Die Änderung des Finanzierungsmodells würde aber keine Auswirkungen auf die redaktionelle Unabhängigkeit oder die Programminhalte haben.

Babiš und der direkt für die Medien verantwortliche Kulturminister Oto Klempíř versicherten wiederholt, es werde keinerlei politische Einflussnahme auf die Berichterstattung geben. In dem Gesetzentwurf heißt es, dass die Regierung mit der Abschaffung der Rundfunkgebühr "einem europäischen Trend folgt, da sich immer mehr Länder vom Prinzip der Finanzierung durch Rundfunkgebühren abwenden".

Zdeněk Hřib, Vorsitzender der oppositionellen Piratenpartei, verglich die Strategie der tschechischen Regierung mit der des ehemaligen ungarischen Ministerpräsidenten Viktor Orbán. Dessen Amtszeit war von Auseinandersetzungen um Medienfreiheit und Rechtsstaatlichkeit geprägt. Die Opposition will bei einer Änderung der Rundfunkfinanzierung vor das tschechische Verfassungsgericht in Brünn (Brno) ziehen.

Oppositionsparteien, Bürgerinitiativen und Medienvertreter kündigten nach der Abstimmung an, weiter gegen die Regierungspläne anzukämpfen. Kritik kommt auch von Institutionen wie Universitäten und der katholischen Kirche.

Der Europäische Journalistenverband EFJ bezog ebenfalls Stellung: "Der Gesetzentwurf verstößt gegen das Europäische Medienfreiheitsgesetz (EMFA), das eine angemessene, stabile und vorhersehbare Finanzierung der öffentlich-rechtlichen Medien vorschreibt." Die EFJ fordert die EU-Kommission auf, unverzüglich Maßnahmen dagegen zu ergreifen.

Schon in den vergangenen Monaten hatte es zahlreiche Demonstrationen in Prag und anderen tschechischen Städten gegeben. Nach einer Protestkundgebung am Freitag in der Prager Innenstadt harrten einige Hundert Demonstranten auch während der Nacht auf Samstag vor dem Gebäude des Abgeordnetenhauses aus. Die Initiative Milion chvilek pro demokracii (Eine Million Momente für die Demokratie) will am Sonntag eine große Demonstration organisieren.

Und die Mitarbeiter von ČT und ČRo kündigten für Dienstag einen ganztägigen Streik an. Sie schlossen auch weitere Kampfmaßnahmen nicht aus.

Redaktionsschluss: 17.30 Uhr (MESZ) - dieser Artikel wird nicht weiter aktualisiert.

#3191. Is a job guarantee the solution to mass AI unemployment?

An old idea springs anew as a chorus of influential voices predicts that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude

In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream.

“Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes.

A chorus of influential voices is now predicting that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude. Bill Gates has declared that AI will advance so rapidly that within a decade, humans will not be needed “for most things”. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has warned that the technology could cause widespread unemployment within one to five years, eliminating many positions in law, tech, finance and other white-collar professions. Even if these predictions are wrong, investors who bet heavily on the technology may conclude that AI is a bubble, and this in itself could cause a recession and widespread job loss.

Whether a crisis of mass AI-related job loss turns out to be actual or perceived, one policy idea that is attracting growing attention and support could directly mitigate this problem: a job guarantee.

In its most ambitious form, such a program would ensure that anyone who wants work is guaranteed a meaningful, decently paid job. By creating a public option for employment, its supporters argue, a job guarantee could protect millions of people from the financial and psychological damage of joblessness and mobilize a vast labor force to tackle urgent societal problems, from infrastructure and climate adaptation to elder care and childcare.

The concept of a job guarantee has a long history, both as an ideal and an actual policy. Article 23 of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights states: “Everyone has the right to work, to free choice of employment, to just and favourable conditions of work and to protection against unemployment.” During the Great Depression in the 1930s, Franklin D Roosevelt established the Works Progress Administration (WPA), which employed millions of Americans in ambitious public works projects that constructed roads, bridges, sewers, playing fields and much more. More recently, France, India and Argentina are among the countries that have launched versions of a job guarantee.

Though a job guarantee and universal basic income (UBI) are often grouped together, a recent global survey found greater support for job guarantees than UBIs. Polling of Americans by the Democratic strategist David Shor also shows the same pattern, with greater support for the creation of well-paid jobs than for direct income support. This makes sense, the venture capitalist and civic activist Nick Hanauer said, because “jobs represent so much more than income in human societies. They represent connection and dignity and enfranchisement and participation.”

Algernon Austin, director for race and economic justice at the Center for Economic and Policy Research, agreed: “A job guarantee is significantly preferable to UBI because work is more than just income. When you have a job, you gain work experience and you gain skills and you gain a network.”

Calculating the cost of a job guarantee depends on a holistic assessment of its impacts. During a US Senate hearing on affordability in June, John Kennedy, a Republican senator for Louisiana, suggested that a job guarantee would cost trillions of dollars and was impossible. When Dr Julie Margetta Morgan, president of the public policy thinktank the Century Foundation, told Kennedy that she supported a federal job guarantee, he replied: “Do you believe in the Easter bunny?”

Economists who study job guarantees see the calculation of costs and benefits differently. Max Kasy, a professor of economics at Oxford who has studied a recent job guarantee experiment in Austria, said that while the wages a job guarantee pays participants comprise a cost, such programs also save money in multiple ways.

“The cost saving comes from the fact that you don’t have to pay unemployment benefits, or maybe disability benefits or early retirement benefits. Then people who are working pay taxes and make social insurance contributions, so that’s additional revenue for the state. And then they hopefully do something that’s actually useful for society,” he said.

Participants in the job guarantee experiment in Austria also experienced social and psychological benefits. While the monetary value of greater wellbeing may be hard to quantify, such intangibles are crucial, according to Pavlina Tcherneva, a professor of economics at Bard College.

“Providing a good job to a person is absolutely transformative,” she said. Factoring in the costs of health problems that come from precarious unemployment and long-term unemployment, she added, makes the policy even more attractive, saying: “It’s not only affordable, it’s an investment.”

In September, the US representative Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat from Massachusetts, reintroduced a congressional resolution calling for the creation of a federal job guarantee, something she first proposed in 2021. Her proposal would create a federally funded but locally administered job guarantee that pays participants at least $25 an hour, with regular adjustments to reflect the rising cost of living. The jobs would include a range of sectors, such as emergency preparedness, relief and recovery after natural disasters, care for children and seniors, and public art projects modelled on the WPA’s popular Federal Art Project.

Another recent proposal would directly tax AI companies to fund a federal job guarantee. The plan, which is supported by Democratic US representatives Greg Casar of Texas, Valerie Foushee of North Carolina and Sara Jacobs of California, would tax large AI companies on whatever was higher: the value of their “tokens” – units of data used in AI models – or their revenue from AI products.

If the unemployment rate rose, the tax rate would increase. “AI CEOs are openly predicting their technology could put millions of Americans out of work, and our government is doing nothing to save jobs and protect working people,” Casar said in a written statement.

In Cleveland, Ohio, a non-profit called Universal Basic Employment (UBE) is launching a small pilot study with a cohort of five workers who drive vans at a transportation company. Rather than create new jobs from scratch, the program subsidizes the wages of existing private-sector jobs in a way that benefits both workers and employers, according to Devin Cotten, founder and CEO of UBE.

Cotten and his team wanted workers to make what they call an autonomous wage – the pay level at which people are no longer eligible for most social safety net benefits. In Cleveland, that was just over $27 per hour. At a cost of almost half a million dollars for one year, UBE’s pilot will split that $27 figure with employers. The drivers currently make about $15 an hour, so the employer will save money, and the workers will get a sizable raise.

The program is not meant to replace other forms of assistance such as housing vouchers, Cotten said. But workers receiving more money as wages, rather than as a siloed benefit, can build their credit, perhaps qualify for a mortgage and also keep dollars circulating in the local economy, helping to revitalize poor neighborhoods.

Such a model may even attract a broader base of political support. “Work is a shared value across political lines,” Cotten said. “I think crafting a solution based on work allows us to be a bipartisan solution.”

#3192. The Best Bouncy Jumping Bean

Have you ever seen a jumping bean toy? They bounce, flip and jump as if they’re magic, but the real magic is that you can make your own jumping bean with just a marble and kitchen foil! You might be wondering how a foil and a marble can flip and jump. The answer is physics! When the marble rolls inside the foil and hits the end, the sudden change in centre of mass and momentum causes the foil tube to lift and flip!

Follow the instructions below to make your own jumpy, bouncy bean!

Roll the foil carefully into a tube shape slightly wider than the marble.

Use a small amount of tape to secure the foil in place and insert the marble into the tube.

Fold and press both ends carefully to seal them. The marble should be able to move freely inside the foil.

Put the foil covered marble into the plastic container and shake it around until both ends are round and smooth.

As the jumping bean moves, the marble rolls in the foil until it hits the end of the tube. This makes the bean flip over, the marble then rolls to the other end, and the bean flips again. This is why the movement of the bean seems so strange. The foil and marble are moving independently of each other.

Roll the bean down a ramp with different surfaces.

Experiment with different sizes of marble and foil tubes to see how the movement of the bean changes.

#3196. Fatal Detonation of WWII Explosive in Indonesia Linked to Illicit Fishing

Wreckage from the detonation of a World War II shell in Biak, Indonesia, in May. Indonesian National Police

In May, a group of fishers on the Indonesian island of Biak were dismantling an unexploded shell left over from World War II when the device went off, reportedly killing seven people and injuring 19 others. Officials have concluded that the fishers were harvesting materials from the shell for use in blast fishing.

Biak, a small island, lies off the coast of New Guinea, which was the site of intense fighting between Allied forces and Imperial Japan. Heavy bombing and naval battles left behind a host of unexploded bombs and artillery shells, which are still being uncovered by fishers, farmers, and construction workers.

On nearby Wakde Island, bombs may emerge from the ocean at low tide or explode in the forest during heat waves, according to Sonya Martha Kawer, an archaeologist with the National Research Center for Archaeology in Indonesia. “People there can’t just burn the forests indiscriminately,” she told Mongabay. “They do burn them, but usually with caution, because the fires often trigger bullets or bombs to explode.”

Fishers in the region are known to recover wartime munitions to extract TNT to produce their own explosives for blast fishing. A 2004 report commissioned by the U.S. government noted that in Indonesia, Papua New Guinea, and the Philippines, people had “fished with explosives since World War II when ordnance and explosives left behind provided the basis for a new and effective method of harvesting reef fish.”

Cliff Marlessy, a director with the Indonesia Locally-Managed Marine Area Network, said there is evidence that, on Biak, explosives are now being traded. “Apparently, it has grown into a market,” he told Mongabay.

But the harvesting of bombs poses clear risks for fishers. Just last year, a fisher named Agus Drunyi died in his home on Papua while assembling a bomb from a salvaged explosive, Mongabay reports.

Unexploded bombs can also leak harmful chemicals into soil and water, and the risks from aging munitions may be growing over time. A 2024 study, published in Royal Society Open Science, warned that the changing chemistry of unexploded World War II bombs may be making them more volatile.

Even when fishers are spared harm from explosives, blast fishing can wreak havoc on marine life. According to a 2021 paper published in the journal Biological Conservation, the practice has led to the “large-scale destruction of coral reefs in much of Southeast Asia.” The paper found that a lack of enforcement is driving blasting globally.

#3197. Tinned food, loo roll and power banks: the Brits following advice to stockpile

Government campaign recommends three days’ worth of stores for emergencies, but some are ahead of the game

Dried foods, bottled water, medicine stocks and backup power banks: it could be the props cupboard on a disaster movie, but instead it is precisely what some UK residents are stockpiling amid official warnings about Russian “state-sponsored terrorism” and the impact of the climate crisis.

The government launched a campaign on Thursday advising people to set aside three days’ worth of stores to deal with a whole range of eventualities, and some are already well under way.

“I’m adding a few extra tinned foods and dried foods to each weekly shop to build up a stockpile over time,” said Lawrence Barratt, from Hythe in Hampshire. “Tinned beans, soups, chilli con carne. Dried noodles, pot noodles, rice. Foods I can cook with bottled water, which I’m also buying gradually – aiming to have enough for two people for three days.”

He added that he was also putting aside a first aid kit, a battery-powered FM radio and a torch. “I have a portable power bank that I’ve used when camping; that should give enough electricity to charge phones, run the TV, even a small fan heater.”

Barratt is not alone. Marco Camurri, from Greenwich in London, said he was collecting pasta, passata and stock cubes as well as tinned foods, bottled water and medicines. And toilet paper, he added. “We remember Covid.”

Camurri said that, with relatives in continental Europe, he and his family could flee temporarily if the UK “entered war and if there was a risk of direct attacks to London”, or if there were “extreme infrastructure failure that would put our jobs at risk”.

He said: “Although I live in London, I have some wood set aside in the back of our small garden in case we need to make fire on the barbecue to boil water. We have power banks that we keep charged, USB rechargeable flashlights, matches and lighters. Although gasoline is expensive, we try to keep the tank over 50% – about 300 miles.”

While the government launched its PR campaign on Thursday, ministers have been making similar noises for several months now – and it had already prompted some to start preparing.

Barratt said a combination of noticing government advice to stockpile online and having been in situations in the past where it would have been useful prompted him to begin about a fortnight ago.

“I took action, I suppose, because I thought back to how scary the initial few days just before and after the first lockdown in 2020 were – remember when you went to the shops and all the pasta, loo roll and tinned stuff would be gone.”

He said he had put that period out of his mind but the government’s Be Ready campaign website made him realise: “I’d be completely unprepared for anything. So I thought I’d better get started.”

Camurri has been setting things aside for himself and his family for much longer. “We started preparing a few months ago when news about potential disruptions to the supply chain caused by El Niño made it into the news. It was an easy decision as we usually eat everything we stocked up, so it was just like doing one extra week of shopping for staples. We are now starting a spreadsheet with the expiry date of all our ‘Doomsday Stash’ items so we can eat them and replace them before they go bad.”

Jack Davenport, from North Shields on the River Tyne, also cited El Niño as a motivation for beginning to stockpile. But he said it was “hard to judge the size” of the multiple threats facing the country.

“From El Niño and other climate-related disasters to Russian shadow threats and AI, as well as interest rate hikes due to energy insecurity. The fact is our physical and technological infrastructure is creaking and outdated.”

He said he thought the government’s goal in highlighting this advice now was to “reduce long-term panic by rolling the pitch that these events are a possibility, and that just because several generations in our country haven’t faced hardship that was common prewar doesn’t mean we won’t”.

But Deirdre O’Sullivan, from Leicester, was less convinced. “This daft advice takes me back to the 1970s when I recall being instructed to hide under the table in the event of a nuclear attack. I didn’t have a table, but somehow made it through.

“In the event of a real emergency, the advice seems totally inadequate. For example, if our drinking water becomes dangerous, I would hope that this could be anticipated a bit more precisely. And we would surely become aware of extreme food shortage within a much longer timeframe.

“The guidance looks like something Yes Minister would come up with to demonstrate that they have a policy in place, even if that policy is clearly totally useless.”

#3199. Türkei und Griechenland: Neuer Seerechtsstreit im Mittelmeer

Die Türkei will zusammen mit Libyen die Seegrenzen im Mittelmeer verändern und einen gemeinsamen Wirtschaftskorridor schaffen. Das sorgt für scharfen Protest aus Griechenland – und ruft auch die EU auf den Plan.

Die Entscheidung kam überraschend, und sie war überraschend eindeutig: Einstimmig billigte das libysche Parlament in Tobruk am Dienstag ein Seerechtsabkommen mit der Türkei, das eigentlich seit Jahren auf Eis gelegen hatte.

Infolge eines jahrelangen Bürgerkriegs ist Libyen zweigeteilt. Mit der von den UN anerkannten Einheitsregierung im Westteil Libyens hatte die Türkei schon im Jahr 2019 Einigkeit erzielt. Die Ratifizierung scheiterte jedoch am jahrelangen Widerstand des libyschen Ostteils. Doch nun machte dessen Regierung den Weg frei.

Die Entscheidung, die vom türkischen Außenministerium begrüßt wurde, dürfte die Spannungen mit den anderen Anrainerstaaten des östlichen Mittelmeeres neu entfachen.

Das Abkommen sieht vor, einen direkten maritimen Wirtschaftskorridor zwischen der türkischen Süd- und der libyschen Nordküste zu errichten. In der betroffenen Region wurden zuletzt große Öl- und Gasvorkommen entdeckt - Schätzungen zufolge könnten unter dem Meeresboden mehrere hundert Milliarden US-Dollar an Erdgasreserven liegen. Beide Länder wollen ihre wirtschaftlichen Rechte an diesen Rohstoffen sichern und streben eine gemeinsame Förderung der Ressourcen an.

Der geplante Korridor ignoriert jedoch wissentlich in unmittelbarer Nähe liegende griechische Inseln wie Kreta, Karpathos oder Rhodos. Die Regierung in Athen pocht darauf, selbst eine umfassende ausschließliche Wirtschaftszone (AWZ) um diese Inseln herum zu besitzen und hat bereits erbitterten Widerstand angekündigt.

Binnen kürzester Zeit reagierte das griechische Außenministerium auf X: Griechenland lehne das Votum des libyschen Parlaments entschieden ab. "Diese Entscheidung ändert nichts daran: Das Memorandum bleibt illegal, null und nichtig!"

Auch die Europäische Union reagierte alarmiert. "Die EU hat ein strategisches Interesse an einem stabilen und sicheren Umfeld im östlichen Mittelmeer und fordert alle Länder auf, die souveränen Rechte aller Mitgliedstaaten gemäß EU- und Völkerrecht zu respektieren, einschließlich der UN-Seerechtskonvention", heißt es in einem Statement der EU-Außenbeauftragten Kaja Kallas.

Die Frage, wessen Ansprüche legitim sind, ist das zentrale juristische Streitthema im östlichen Mittelmeer.

Griechenland beruft sich vor allem auf das UN-Seerechtsübereinkommen (UNCLOS). Dessen Artikel 121 besagt, dass bewohnbare Inseln, die "ein eigenes Wirtschaftsleben zulassen", die gleichen Rechte auf eine AWZ besitzen wie das Festland selbst. Dies gelte auch für Kreta, Rhodos oder Lesbos.

Athen beruft sich dabei auf Präzedenzfälle wie den Streit zwischen Nicaragua und Kolumbien vor dem Internationalen Gerichtshof. Dort wurde diese Auslegung des Seerechts im Prinzip bestätigt - auch wenn bei sich überlappenden Interessen eine gerechte Abgrenzung gefunden werden muss. Diese muss die Küstenverläufe, die geografischen Verhältnisse und die Auswirkungen einer möglichen Grenzziehung berücksichtigen.

Genau darauf wiederum beruft sich die Türkei. Ankara argumentiert, dass die Geografie des Mittelmeers eine Sonderrolle einnimmt: Würde man jeder kleinen griechischen Insel vor der türkischen Küste (und Zypern) eine vollständige AWZ zusprechen, wäre die Türkei größtenteils vom offenen Meereszugang abgeschnitten. Dies müsse bei der Grenzziehung stärker berücksichtigt werden.

Anders als Griechenland hat die Türkei UNCLOS nie unterzeichnet. Aus diesem Grund will sie den Streit auch nicht vor einem UN-Schiedsgericht verhandeln lassen. In der Frage, wie eine "gerechte Aufteilung" in diesem Fall konkret aussehen könnte, sind aber auch internationale Seerechtsexperten uneins.

Als die Türkei das Abkommen 2019 forcierte, herrschte in Libyen noch ein erbitterter Bürgerkrieg. Damals intervenierte die Türkei militärisch im Westen, um die Regierung in Tripolis zu retten, und schlug damit die Offensive des ostlibyschen Generals Khalifa Haftar zurück.

Inzwischen hat sich das Verhältnis jedoch grundlegend gewandelt: Ankara betreibt seit geraumer Zeit eine aktive Charmeoffensive gegenüber dem Haftar-Lager, was zu einer politischen Annäherung führte.

Mittlerweile besitzt Ankara ein gutes Verhältnis zu beiden Teilen Libyens - zum eigenen Vorteil: Neben dem Plan, gemeinsam mit dem nordafrikanischen Land die Energieressourcen im Mittelmeer zu fördern, haben türkische Baukonzerne in den vergangenen Jahren milliardenschwere Aufträge für den Wiederaufbau des kriegszerstörten Landes erhalten. Zudem arbeiten die staatliche türkische Erdölgesellschaft TPAO und die libysche National Oil Corporation bereits an gemeinsamen Plänen für seismische Untersuchungen vor der libyschen Küste.

Außerdem hat Ankara sich als neuer militärischer Partner für Haftars Streitkräfte etabliert, liefert Waffen und bietet Trainingsprogramme an. Damit drängt die Türkei den Einfluss Ägyptens und Russlands in Ostlibyen zurück und stärkt seine eigene Rolle als geopolitischer Player in der Region.

Durch die nun erfolgte Ratifizierung will sich auch der Osten Libyens seinen Anteil an den lukrativen Rohstoffen sichern. Und auch General Haftar erhofft sich dadurch in Zukunft mehr internationales Gewicht.

Die Spannungen im östlichen Mittelmeerraum dürften sich durch die Vereinbarung weiter erhöhen - insbesondere dann, wenn die Türkei und Libyen tatsächlich mit der Förderung der Öl- und Gasvorkommen im umstrittenen Seegebiet beginnen sollten.

Zudem gefährdet das Abkommen ein anderes Großprojekt, das sich derzeit noch in Planung befindet: die EastMed-Pipeline. Sie soll eigentlich in Zukunft Erdgas von Israel und Zypern aus über Griechenland nach Europa transportieren und so auch einen wichtigen Beitrag zur Energiesicherheit in der EU leisten. Der neue türkisch-libysche Korridor durchschneidet jedoch nicht nur den geplanten Verlauf der Pipeline, die Türkei beansprucht zudem das Recht für sich, Kabel- oder Pipeline-Projekte durch diese Zone kontrollieren oder blockieren zu können.

Langfristig könnte es so zu einer zunehmenden Spaltung des östlichen Mittelmeerraums in zwei konkurrierende Energie- und Verteidigungsblöcke kommen: Der Achse Türkei-Libyen stünde womöglich eine Allianz aus Griechenland, Zypern, Ägypten und Israel gegenüber, die auch von der EU unterstützt wird.

#3200. Multimodal precision diagnostics in clinical xenotransplantation

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature volume 658, pages 883–896 (2026) Cite this article

Recent breakthroughs in pig-to-human xenotransplantation have successfully prevented hyperacute rejection of kidney, heart, liver and lung xenografts, marking a milestone long considered a critical barrier. However, these major advances also brought new challenges into focus, as immune-mediated graft injuries including antibody-mediated rejection, T cell-mediated rejection and innate immune activation have been observed in most xenotransplantation procedures to date. Detection and management of these injuries remain a critical bottleneck, as conventional histopathology and standard clinical monitoring lack the sensitivity required to identify subclinical injury early enough to guide timely intervention. This diagnostic gap underscores an urgent need for the development of advanced, multimodal precision diagnostic frameworks to enhance immune surveillance, which will be essential for standardizing clinical protocols and enabling pathogenesis-driven therapeutic intervention. This approach will inform both immunosuppressive regimens and future gene editing strategies aimed at engineering rejection-resistant porcine organs, ultimately prolonging graft survival. Broad adoption of such an integrative strategy will be essential to transition xenotransplantation from an experimental intervention into a safe, scalable and patient-centred clinical therapy. In this Review, we synthesize recent progress in xenotransplantation and position multimodal precision diagnostics as a pivotal strategy to address the remaining immunological and clinical barriers to widespread clinical implementation.

#3201. Labor and the Coalition are poised to take a reckless gamble on AI. Haven’t they realised community support has collapsed? | Edward Santow and Sarah Sacher

Australian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at hand

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

Australia’s major political parties are edging towards rare consensus. Labor and the Coalition increasingly want to take a major bet on artificial intelligence. Yet, just as the parties are coming together, the Australian community is running the other way.

Last year, only 30% of Australians believed the benefits of AI outweighed the risks. In 2026, community trust in AI appears to be falling even further.

It was an unusual step for our parliament to form a joint select committee on AI. It signalled that the decisions being made now on datacentres and how we adopt AI could define our economy, environment and society for generations.

As a fresh round of hearings starts this week, the committee members must confront the gulf between the politics of AI and the stark reality on the ground. Some parts of the business sector are urging us to prioritise innovation and AI adoption, which is often another way of saying: “Do a better job of selling the upside of AI.”

Whether you’re an AI optimist or a sceptic, this is a terrible idea. Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and the other titans of Silicon Valley have a golden megaphone to spruik the benefits of their technology. Australians don’t want our elected representatives to do the same thing – especially when the technology is already bringing both opportunity and harm.

This doesn’t mean being blind to the benefits of AI. On the contrary, Australia is among the highest users per capita of Anthropic’s Claude and other generative AI applications. But we must also be clear-eyed about potential risks. And, crucially, we don’t see a compelling response to our concerns from government or the AI companies themselves.

Take the impact of AI on work. Our community is asking practical questions. How will AI impact our jobs and the jobs of our children? What is the government doing to ensure the AI systems used in Australian workplaces are safe?

Our new report, Drawing the Line, lays out how AI is propelling the rise of harmful tech-enabled worker surveillance. Often workers are unaware of the extent to which they are being monitored – including through their work devices and phones, and via software such as Microsoft Teams.

Unlike some of the hypothetical (and frankly terrifying) risks that the joint select committee on AI has already covered, such as AI-enabled biological weapons and engineered pandemics, this is happening today.

Australian supermarket workers are already being pushed to meet AI-generated productivity metrics that force them to work harder and faster under the threat of punitive repercussions – putting them at risk of injury and workplace accidents.

Remote workers are already being subjected to intrusive surveillance software capable of watching everything they do on their screen – including audio recording conversations they have with their families.

Rideshare drivers are already being penalised for road conditions and customer complaints that are unrelated to their performance, which can result in their account being deactivated and days of work lost.

Workers are being quietly crushed by commonplace AI-powered surveillance tools that have crept into our workplaces and home offices. And the impact is real. Think, for example, of the young woman who reported being sexually harassed by a boss that required her to be on video at all times. Or warehouse workers driven to suicidal ideation due to relentless micromanagement by machine.

Our workplace laws don’t protect workers from unreasonable surveillance. Nor do they give employers clarity about what types of monitoring are lawful.

Unlike existential risks from AI, which are outside the Australian government’s direct control, this problem could be addressed through straightforward law reform.

We urge the government to update the Fair Work Act to require any worker monitoring be “fair and reasonable”. This builds on the government’s commitment to require all personal information covered by the Privacy Act to be handled fairly and reasonably.

Australian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at hand. This is not a hypothetical future risk – let’s address it now.

Prof Edward Santow is co-director of the UTS Human Technology Institute and served as human rights commissioner from 2016-2021. Sarah Sacher is HTI’s senior responsible technology policy specialist

#3202. SIX, SEVEN – Fun Facts

If you’ve spent any time with kids recently, you’ve probably heard the slang term “six – seven“. It seems to have no meaning, just a general playful, in with the joke type phrase. Six – Seven is often accompanied by a palm up, hands moving up and down action. The slang term 6-7 is fairly unique as it is deliberately nonsensical!

6-7 is thought to trace back to the rap song “Doot Doot 6 7” by Skrilla, released in 2024, which was later used in TikTok videos featuring basketball player LaMelo Ball, who is 6 ft 7 inches tall.

Did you know 6-7 is Dictionary.com’s word of the year for 2025!

Some people think 6-7 means “maybe this, maybe that” or is a general term of agreement.

An older phrase, “at sixes and sevens,” means not knowing what to do, or being in disarray.

Did you know that if people are asked to choose a random number between 1 and 10, 7 is the number most often chosen!

There were 7 Wonders of the Ancient World.

Visible light can be split into seven different colours.

6 is the smallest perfect number. A perfect number is one that is equal to the sum of its divisors. For 6, these are 1, 2 and 3.

A dice ( and a standard cube ) has six faces.

#3206. In Germany, Wind and Solar Overtake Fossil Power

In a first, Germany drew more power from wind and solar than from fossil fuels last year.

Together, wind and solar generated 44 percent of Germany’s electricity, while fossil fuels generated roughly 43 percent, according to data from the Energy Institute, a think tank based in London. The figures represent a major milestone for the German “Energiewende,” or “energy turnaround,” a national push to ramp up renewable energy and phase out gas, coal, and nuclear power.

Germany shut down its last remaining nuclear power plants in 2023. It is aiming to wean off of coal power by 2038, though experts say it will likely achieve that goal much sooner. By 2045, its target date for net zero emissions, Germany plans to convert any remaining gas-fired power plants to green hydrogen.

Aiding the buildout of wind and solar is an effort to simplify permitting for renewable energy projects. German officials have digitized permitting, streamlined approvals, and declared clean energy to be of “overriding public interest,” a designation that lends projects protection from legal challenges.

Germany has the third largest economy in the world, after the U.S. and China, and the largest economy in Europe. Its embrace of renewable energy has helped push the E.U. toward cleaner power. Last year, for the first time, the bloc saw wind and solar overtake fossil fuels, according to data from energy think tank Ember. Wind and solar generated 30 percent of E.U. power in 2025, while fossil fuels generated 29 percent, and nuclear and hydropower supplied most of the rest.

#3207. ‘Comfort in a bowl’: porridge hotter than ever as fibremaxxers get their oats

Humble breakfast staple at heart of trend stirred up by health concerns and hearty spoonfuls of nostalgia

The clocks may be going back in the UK this weekend, but the biggest sign winter is coming is a steaming bowl of porridge on a breakfast table.

A staple for centuries, porridge is traditionally made with oats, water and a pinch of salt or sugar. However, the humble dish is now experiencing its own renaissance, with the latest iterations transforming it from drab to decadent. The trend is being driven by a growing fibre-centric movement as well as by nostalgia.

On social media, recipe creators are experimenting with everything from miso versions to sour cherry and pistachio butter toppings. At 26 Grains, a central London restaurant that specialises in porridge, this month’s offering includes a five-grain porridge topped with fig and red grape jam and a dollop of whipped cream. Over at Oatis in west London, toppings range from caramelised banana and tahini to mushrooms and pesto.

Alex Hely-Hutchinson, the founder of 26 Grains, describes porridge as “comfort in a bowl”. Part of its appeal, she says, is that it allows a “moment for pause in a busy world” – plus most people know how to make it.

It is a trend that is affecting home store cupboards. Searches for organic jumbo oats at Ocado are up 98% year on year while sales of White’s jumbo oats are up 56%.

Hedié Rhodes, the founder of the UK’s first dedicated cereals bakery, Husk & Honey in south London, describes the “personalisation aspect” of porridge as an instigator of the trend. Her brand, which began in 2015 specialising in granola, now also sells dedicated porridge blends. Bestsellers include cinnamon bark and cranberry and a spiced apple version.

“Porridge is a great carrier for a lot of nice things,” Rhodes says. “You can make a big pan of it and everyone in the family can still have a different style. Some might want it just with honey, others might want to add really fancy toppings.”

Alex Hayes, a co-founder of the food innovation studio Harris and Hayes, compares porridge to salads and smoothies. “It’s a great canvas for adding specific toppings that suit specific taste and nutritional needs,” she says, pointing to nut butters alongside more functional additions such as psyllium husk.

While protein mania isn’t slowing down, the online nutrition trend of “fibremaxxing” is encouraging more people to up their fibre intake. The NHS recommends adults should eat 30g of fibre a day, but according to the British Dietetic Association the average intake is only 18g. Oats are a source of the soluble fibre that is essential for gut health and can also help reduce cholesterol levels. So rather than eating protein-rich eggs for breakfast, many people are now reverting to a bowl of porridge.

On the menu at Café Cùil on the Isle of Skye you’ll find a “wee porridge” featuring pinhead oats that are soaked in oat milk overnight. Its founder, the chef and writer Clare Coghill, then finishes it with seasonal toppings. At the moment it’s a hazelnut praline brittle and poached pears.

Coghill, who recently tasted 86 bowls of porridge in her role on the judging panel of the world porridge-making championship that takes place in the Scottish Highlands each year, says “porridge purists” prefer to use coarser pinhead oats, also known as steel-cut oats, rather than rolled oats which are softer. “Pinhead were the original oats, so it’s a way of celebrating Scottish heritage,” she says.

Hely-Hutchinson opts for a mixture including jumbo oats and rolled oats for “creaminess”, along with rye, barley and malted wheat for added texture and “a slight fermented note”. Other recipes have ditched the oats altogether for rice, amaranth or quinoa.

Recipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every week

To avoid a gloopy porridge, Coghill says stirring is key. “It’s all about slowly warming up the pot and constantly moving the spurtle [stirrer] around, which will create a really nice silky bowl of porridge.”

Hely-Hutchinson prefers hers “just right”, which for her is on the softer side. “Porridge is so nostalgic, I make it how my mum used to for me,” she says. “It all depends on the person. It’s like the same as how much Marmite someone puts on their toast or the amount of milk they put in their tea.”

Next, as porridge pivots from basic to bougie, is a move beyond the breakfast table. “People are increasingly busy and seem to be receptive to a more simple dish,” says Hely-Hutchinson, adding that customers get annoyed if porridge is not available on the menu past 3pm.

Hayes says we can expect to see more savoury options popping up on menus taking influence from Chinese congee, a traditional savoury rice pudding, and Indian kitchari, made with yellow split mung beans.

Rhodes points out that similar to how bakers experiment with wheat, people are now realising how much potential oats have. “It’s really interesting pushing the limits with oats. There are so many avenues to explore,” she says.

There is one downside to this new porridge passion, though: having to wash up the pan.

#3209. Anschlag auf Kirche in Jordanien: Fahndung nach Tätern läuft

Nach den tödlichen Schüssen bei einer Trauerfeier im Westen Jordaniens sind die Täter weiter auf der Flucht. Die Regierung in Amman stuft die Tat als Terrorakt ein.

Die Zeremonie in einer griechisch-orthodoxen Kirche im Westen Jordaniens lief gerade 15 Minuten, so ein Augenzeuge, da eröffneten am Freitag bewaffnete Männer das Feuer auf die Trauergemeinde. Sieben Menschen starben im Kugelhagel bei dem Angriff auf die griechisch-orthodoxe Sankt-Georgs-Kirche in dem Dorf Hamoud in der Provinz Karak.

Ein weiteres Opfer erlag seinen schweren Verletzungen, teilte Gesundheitsminister Ibrahim al-Bdour am Samstag mit. Weitere 26 Menschen befänden sich weiterhin im Krankenhaus, darunter einer in kritischem Zustand, sagte al-Bdour der Nachrichtenagentur AFP.

Der Generalstaatsanwalt von Amman untersagte laut der jordanischen Nachrichtenagentur Petra unter Androhung rechtlicher und strafrechtlicher Konsequenzen die Veröffentlichung von Details zu den Schüssen in der Kirche. Ausgenommen von der Nachrichtensperre sind offizielle Regierungsmedien. Sie stehen unter der Aufsicht des Ministeriums für Regierungskommunikation.

Aufnahmen, die offenbar von einer Überwachungskamera der Kirche stammen, zeigen drei Personen, die von einem Gehweg aus auf das Gebäude schießen. Anschließend liefen sie zur Eingangstür des Gotteshauses.

Zwei der Bewaffneten, die auf den Aufnahmen zu sehen sind, hielten offenbar Pistolen in der Hand, als sie sich der Kirche näherten und Schüsse abfeuerten. Ein dritter Mann, offenbar mit einem halbautomatischen Gewehr bewaffnet, eröffnete ebenfalls das Feuer. Von Zeugen aufgenommene Videos zeigen zerbrochenes Glas und Blutlachen auf dem Boden der Kirche.

Dorgham Halasa, der sich unter den Trauergästen befand, sagte der Nachrichtenagentur AP, dass die Menschen in der Kirche zu fliehen begannen, als die Schüsse fielen. Er habe die Bewaffneten nicht gesehen, aber andere hätten berichtet, vier von ihnen gesehen zu haben. Die Gesamtzahl der Angreifer lässt sich nicht unabhängig überprüfen.

Augenzeugenberichten zufolge sollen sich während der Trauerfeier zwischen 150 und 200 Menschen im Bereich der Kirche aufgehalten haben. Der Angriff soll etwa fünf Minuten gedauert haben. Anschließend seien die Täter geflüchtet.

Jordaniens Innenminister sprach von einem "Terroranschlag einer Gruppe von Extremisten". Es sei jedoch noch zu früh, um zu sagen, ob sie Verbindungen zu bekannten Gruppen im In- oder Ausland hätten.

Der jordanische König Abdullah besuchte Karak wenige Stunden nach dem Angriff und kündigte an, die Täter würden "mit eiserner Faust" bestraft. "Der Terroranschlag wird mit härtester Vergeltung beantwortet werden", heißt es in einer Erklärung des Königs.

Jordaniens Minister für ⁠islamische Angelegenheiten, Mohammad Chalajleh, und mehrere Abgeordnete verurteilten den Angriff. Laut Nachrichtenagentur Petra kündigte die Regierung in Amman drei Tage Staatstrauer an.

Angriffe dieser Art sind in dem Land im Nahen Osten äußerst selten. Die jordanischen Behörden haben nach eigenen Angaben in den vergangenen Jahren jedoch wiederholt Anschlagsversuche islamistischer Extremisten vereitelt.

Jordanien gilt als relativ stabil. Das Land im Nahen Osten ist in diesem Jahr jedoch zunehmend Ziel iranischer Angriffe geworden, nachdem die USA und Israel Ende Februar ihren Krieg gegen den Iran gestartet hatten.

Christen bilden eine Minderheit in dem mehrheitlich muslimisch geprägten Königreich. Sie machen zwischen zwei und drei Prozent der Bevölkerung aus. Jordanien beherbergt jedoch mehrere biblische Stätten, die christliche Pilger aus der ganzen Welt anziehen.

In der Provinz Karak verübten im Jahr 2016 Bewaffnete eine Reihe von Anschlägen auf Polizisten, unter anderem an einer bei Touristen beliebten Kreuzritterburg. Dabei wurden zehn Menschen getötet

#3210. I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka

AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment

Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal.

That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI.

People expect AI to lead to fewer jobs in 34 of the 37 countries surveyed by the Pew Research Center. In wealthy countries like the US, Australia and South Korea, about seven in 10 expect job losses over the next 20 years. And across countries, concern among young people is rising. While fears focus on job numbers, the bigger change will be what jobs become.

The nature of human work will move towards judgment. Experts refer to AI as “jagged”, superhuman at certain tasks but weak at others, with no clear boundary between the two. AI rapidly improves where work can be automatically checked and examples are endless. But it’s shaky where no automated test can determine whether the answer is right. Even if AI is correct a majority of the time on a task, it often doesn’t tell you when it’s inaccurate. If you’ve used AI, you’ve probably experienced how it can be confidently wrong.

Some of these errors will solve themselves as models get better. But jaggedness is a symptom of how these models learn. I see this often as a technology leader building with these systems.

A smarter model still needs a right answer to learn from. When one gap is closed, it shows up somewhere else no one thought to check. But many business decisions don’t immediately have a clear right answer. Whether a choice is good depends on a future no one can see and data no one has. That’s where judgment comes in. So AI will keep mastering tasks that have checkable results but struggle where a person has to decide what a good outcome looks like.

As a result, a new type of work is starting to appear. Someone tests whether the output of AI is correct based on real work, not just on benchmarks. Someone sets limits on what AI is allowed to do before it runs, so the worst mistakes are avoided. Someone runs and manages several agents the way a shift manager runs a crew. Picture an airport control tower. Radar and software track flight paths, with humans judging the few that matter to avoid collisions. No one is manually watching every screen. That would never scale.

Setting AI’s limits is harder than it sounds. In a 2026 study, after an agent was told to protect a secret, it destroyed its own email server, deleting every single email. It was given a goal, without any limits on what it could do. The researchers described it as the right values paired with terrible judgment. Deciding what is off limits and what a mistake would cost takes someone who knows the work and will answer for the result.

Here is the good news for people worried about their own jobs. The people best suited for doing this new type of work aren’t computer programmers. They are the ones who know how the real work is done. Catching what a confident AI left out or got wrong takes someone who knows the complete answer. That knowledge is uncheckable, unwritten and takes the form of judgment honed over years of doing the task and watching it break.

Ford recently learned the value of human expertise. In recent years, it leaned hard on automating its quality control, cutting thousands of jobs. But earlier this year, it had to rehire 350 veteran engineers to oversee the process and hunt for failure points before a part reached the factory floor. They brought the judgment of watching parts fail over years. With humans at the helm, Ford’s quality ranking then hit first among mainstream brands for the first time since 2010.

But we are making a serious mistake with the jobs we’re eliminating due to AI: the entry-level, routine ones. That routine work is how judgment gets built over time. Junior employees work under the supervision of senior experts until their experience turns into instinct. AI eliminates the friction related to learning how to do the job. But the demand for judgment did not go away. We are just destroying the path to developing it.

The real question is not whether machines will take over our work. It is whether we will have the people who can tell when the machines are wrong. Right now, we are automating the training ground where judgment is learned. If you have hard-earned expertise about anything, the next few years will only make you more valuable. And if you are just starting out, the old apprenticeship model will not hand it to you. You have to go and earn it, deliberately, on tasks the machines cannot yet judge.

Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software company

#3213. Apple Ramp STEM Challenge

This simple apple ramp STEM challenge is a brilliant, hands-on way to learn about the effect of gradient on speed and friction. We’ve made a friction ramp to test toy cars before, and this apple version is a fun twist for an autumn themed STEM activity.

The ramp is covered with bubble wrap to increase friction between the apple and the ramp surface, and then with kitchen foil to reduce the friction between the two.

Friction is the force that slows objects down when they try to slide past each other. If you run your hand over a smooth table, there’s not much friction; if you do the same on a carpet, there’s more friction. The rougher the surface, the more friction is created.

If you walk along a slippery surface barefoot, it’s much harder to slip than if you wear socks. There’s less friction between socks and the floor than between uneven, and sometimes damp bare feet and the floor.

A friction ramp is a ramp covered with different surfaces to investigate how the surface affects the time it takes for a moving object to travel down the ramp. The apple should not be pushed down the ramp with any force; instead, it should be held at the top and then released as the timer starts. The ramp surface is the variable, everything else must be kept the same.

Create a ramp using the cardboard and blocks.

Record how long the apple takes to roll down the cardboard. Repeat twice more, so you have three recordings.

Cover the ramp with bubble wrap and record how long it takes the apple to roll down the ramp three times.

Remove the bubble wrap and cover the ramp with kitchen foil, then record how long it takes the apple to roll down the ramp three times.

Repeat the investigation with a longer ramp and compare the times.

Use a ball or toy car instead of an apple.

Experiment with different materials covering the ramp.

Learn about friction with a teddy zip line.

Which surface allows the apple to move the fastest?

Which surface slows the apple down the most?

L'Éthiopie, un géant africain à l'histoire millénaire, mais un pays profondément divisé. Quatre ans après l'accord de Pretoria, les tensions persistent et les fractures politiques restent entières. Pourquoi est-il si difficile de construire un projet commun dans ce pays aux multiples peuples, langues et traditions ? Au pouvoir depuis 2018, le Premier ministre Abiy Ahmed porte une vision ambitieuse de l'Éthiopie. Mais sa conception du pouvoir, ses relations avec l'Érythrée et sa volonté d'obtenir un accès à la mer Rouge soulèvent de nombreuses questions. Comment comprendre les contradictions de l'Éthiopie ? Dans le Journal de l'Afrique, Fatimata Wane reçoit Éloi Ficquet, historien et anthropologue, maître de conférences à l'EHESS, spécialiste de l'Éthiopie et de la Corne de l'Afrique.
