#3228. iPhone 18 Pro Max review: Apple’s biggest, heaviest and longest-lasting superphone

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

A giant screen, big battery, rapid chip and top cameras push the great iPhone 18 Pro to the max with a price tag to match

Apple’s largest Pro iPhone gets its biggest battery upgrade yet to make it a true two-day phone with new Siri AI and a variable aperture camera.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max is the supersized sibling of the regular 18 Pro and, though it is no longer Apple’s most expensive phone thanks to the £2,000 iPhone Duo, it has a similarly large price tag to match costing from £1,299 (€1,599/$1,299/A$2,299).

The 18 Pro Max follows the familiar formula of its Pro Max predecessors: take everything that’s great about the 18 Pro and supersize the screen and the battery. That means it has a first-class camera, the fastest performance and very long software support.

But it also means the 18 Pro Max is hard to use with one hand and pretty big to fit in a pocket. It weighs 249g, which is really heavy for even a very large smartphone, 23g more than its nearest rival, 38g more than its smaller sibling and heavier still than folding phones. It made my hand hurt after 10 days of use and is a two-handed phone needing some sort of handle or strap.

The 6.9in screen is a joy to behold. Super bright, crisp, smooth and with a very effective anti-glare coating it’s great for films, TV or games, and offers a similar level of real estate for video to most folding phones. It also has the new, smaller camera cut out and bigger dynamic island of the regular 18 Pro.

Screen: 6.9in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (460ppi)

Camera: 48MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 4x, 18MP front-facing

Connectivity: 5G, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Satellite, UWB and GNSS

Water resistance: IP68 (6 metres for 30 mins)

The 18 Pro Max has the same new A20 Pro chip as the 18 Pro, which is one of the fastest chips you can get in a phone, plus a resigned cooling system that helps maintain peak performance during long gaming sessions.

It has the longest battery of any iPhone, lasting almost three days of light usage between charges, actively using the screen for seven hours for apps, browsing, messaging and photos. That is about four hours longer than its predecessor and almost a day longer than the 18 Pro. Even with heavy use, the 18 Pro Max still managed to end the day with about 50% left in the tank, meaning most people will have to charge it only every second or third day.

The 18 Pro Max runs the same iOS 27 as smartphones from the iPhone 11 onwards. The new software speeds up app launches and other parts of the system, refines the Liquid Glass redesign from last year and revamps Apple’s AI tools.

The new Siri AI chatbot is a significant step in the right direction, able to better understand you and perform tasks. It has its own app to review previous conversations and can see what is on your screen or through the camera. It can also suggest data from your various Apple apps, similar to Google’s proactive tools on the Pixels. But it relies on you using messages and mail, rather than third-party apps such as the WhatsApp or Gmail apps.

The battery will last in excess of 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity, and it can be replaced for £119. Out-of-warranty screen repairs cost £389. The specialists iFixit awarded the phone seven out of 10 for repairability.

It contains more than 40% recycled material. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.

The 18 Pro Max has the same camera system as its smaller sibling, which includes an 18 megapixel centre stage selfie camera in the screen and three 48MP cameras on the back.

The three rear cameras are some of the best on a phone, including a 4x/8x optical zoom and 0.5x ultra wide.

The big addition for the 18 Pro Max is a variable aperture on the main camera, allowing it to open wider than other iPhones for better low light performance or to narrow to preserve depth of field. But it also allows additional creative photography possibilities, including shooting starbursts.

The 18 Pro Max also has new AI-powered focus tracking, improved Photographic Styles for greater customisation, Apple’s new digital negative feature and automatic cinematic mode for video.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max costs from £1,299 (€1,599/$1,299/A$2,299).

For comparison, the iPhone 17 costs £899, the iPhone Air £1,099 and the iPhone 18 Pro £1,199; the Google Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,279 and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra £1,359.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max is Apple’s biggest, longest-lasting and most expensive slab phone for 2026.

It takes what is great about the regular 18 Pro and supersizes the screen and battery, giving it a run time of up to three days, which is a good half day more than its smaller sibling. That places it shoulder to shoulder with some of the longest-lasting phones available on any platform.

But similar to superphones from Google and Samsung, the 18 Pro Max is too big to use one-handed and tricky to pocket. It is also too heavy and made my hand hurt without using a Popsocket or a similar handle attached to it.

Otherwise, it is a fairly iterative upgrade on the 17 Pro Max, with the same design and feel. The screen is still one of the very best on a phone, and the improved dynamic island is a useful upgrade. The A20 Pro chip is seriously quick, the cameras are some of the best you can get on a phone and the variable aperture on the main camera opens up some new creative opportunities, even if its impact on image quality is fairly minor.

Pros: fabulous 6.9in screen, better dynamic island, very long battery life, great cameras with variable aperture, USB-C, top performance, long software support, Face ID, better AI.

Cons: very expensive, very heavy, hard to use one-handed, small upgrade on last year, AI tools still lag top competitors.

#3232. Polen: Historische Zeugnisse von NS-Verbrechen übergeben

Knapp ein Jahr nach der gestoppten Versteigerung von Dokumenten von NS-Opfern sind die Artefakte in Warschau an Gedenkstätten, Museen und Archive in Polen sowie anderen europäischen Staaten übergeben worden.

Polens Kulturministerin Marta Cienkowska sparte nicht mit großen Worten. "Das ist ein Ereignis von historischer Tragweite", sagte sie am Freitag (23.10.2026) in Warschau, kurz vor der feierlichen Übergabe von 289 Dokumenten - Zeugnissen der persönlichen Schicksale von Opfern des Nationalsozialismus.

Ein Auktionshaus im nordrhein-westfälischen Neuss hatte im November 2025 geplant, diese und weitere historische Gegenstände zu versteigern. Insgesamt standen mehr als 600 historische Dokumente und Objekte zum Verkauf. Darunter befanden sich etwa Briefe von Häftlingen in den deutschen Konzentrationslagern, persönliche Erinnerungsstücke von Holocaust-Opfern und Gestapo-Karteikarten, aber auch ein "Judenstern mit Gebrauchsspuren".

Der Vorfall hatte in Polen und Deutschland große Empörung hervorgerufen. Das Internationale Auschwitz-Komitee forderte das Auktionshaus auf, die Versteigerung abzusagen. Das Fritz Bauer Institut warnte: "Mit solchen Unterlagen dürfen keine Geschäfte gemacht werden." Der polnische Außenminister Radoslaw Sikorski forderte die Übergabe der Gegenstände an die Gedenkstätte Auschwitz und mahnte auf X: "Die Erinnerung an die Opfer des Holocaust ist keine Ware." Der deutsche Außenminister Johann Wadephul pflichtete seinem Amtskollegen bei und sprach von einem "ungeheuerlichen Vorgang".

Das Auktionshaus sagte die Versteigerung schließlich ab. "Hunderte historische Zeugnisse sollten in die Hände derer gelangen, die den höchsten Preis bieten", sagte Polens Kulturministerin Cienkowska am Freitag in Warschau. "Heute übergeben wir sie an Museen, Archive und Gedenkstätte. Dort werden sie geschützt, untersucht und den kommenden Generationen zur Verfügung gestellt", erklärte die Ministerin.

Sichtlich gerührt erinnerte Cienkowska an die Postkarte, die Jan Perkowski am 20.01.1940 aus dem Warschauer Gefängnis Pawiak an seine Mutter Maria schickte. Perkowski bedankte sich für Briefe, Tannenbaum und Oblaten, die er von den Eltern bekommen hatte. Er schrieb, dass er gesund sei und es ihm gut gehe und fragte, wie die Familie die schreckliche Kälte ertrage. "Es sind einige einfache Sätze. Gewöhnliche Sorge des Sohnes um seine Nächsten, festgehalten in einer Wirklichkeit, in der nichts gewöhnlich ist", sagte die Kulturministerin.

Für die Unterstützung bei den Bemühungen um die Rettung der Sammlung bedankte sich Cienkowska beim Europaminister von Nordrhein-Westfalen, Nathanael Liminski. Er saß bei der Feierlichkeit im Warschauer Kulturministerium als Ehrengast in der ersten Reihe. Der CDU-Politiker aus Nordrhein-Westfalen hatte sich als erster eingeschaltet, als die Versteigerung der persönlichen Dokumente und Gegenstände aus der NS-Zeit im November 2025 bekannt geworden war.

"Wenn Erinnerung zur Ware wird, gerät die Würde ins Wanken", sagte Limanski. "Es ist schwer zu ertragen, wenn Tagebücher von Verfolgten, Briefe aus Konzentrationslagern oder sogenannte 'Judensterne' als Devotionalien gehandelt werden", begründete er sein Engagement.

"Wir dürfen nicht zulassen, dass die Opfer der Nationalsozialisten durch die kommerzielle Verwertung ihres Nachlasses erneut zu Nummern werden, dieses Mal in den Katalogen von Auktionshäusern und in Listen von Kunsthändlern", betonte der Europaminister. "Hier geht es um historische Verantwortung, um Glaubwürdigkeit und um den respektvollen Umgang mit unseren europäischen Partnern, insbesondere mit Polen, dem Tatort der meisten dieser von Deutschen begangenen Verbrechen."

Als Reaktion auf die Auktion brachte NRW einen Gesetzentwurf in den Bundesrat ein, der den kommerziellen Handel mit Gegenständen verbietet, die einen unmittelbaren Bezug zu Opfern der nationalsozialistischen Gewaltherrschaft und ihrem Schicksal haben. Der Bundesrat beschloss den Gesetzentwurf im Juni einstimmig. Die konkrete rechtliche Ausgestaltung des Verbots wird aktuell noch vom Bundestag geprüft. Bei der Veranstaltung in Warschau sagte Liminski, er sei zuversichtlich, dass das Gesetz "zeitnah im Deutschen Bundestag verabschiedet werden wird".

Laut Liminski sollte als nächster Schritt ein europaweites Verbot des Handels mit NS-Dokumenten erwogen werden. Polens Kulturministerin Cienkowska hält einen gemeinsamen polnisch-deutschen Vorstoß in dieser Frage für "gut möglich". "Diese Idee ist ganz frisch. Die Gespräche haben noch nicht begonnen. Beim EU-Treffen im November plane ich ein Treffen mit Kultur-Staatsminister Wolfram Weimer - wir werden sehen. Ich bin zuversichtlich", sagte die Ministerin gegenüber der Deutschen Welle.

Die von der Versteigerung verschonten NS-Dokumente wurden im Januar von der Stiftung Auschwitz-Birkenau gekauft. Ein Teil wurde bereits im Sommer an die deutschen Gedenkstätten übergeben. Jetzt waren die polnischen und die europäischen Museen und Archive dran. 289 Dokumente und Gegenstände wurden an 18 Institutionen in Polen, Tschechien, Litauen, Dänemark, den Niederlanden und Ungarn übergeben.

Der Generaldirektor der Auschwitz-Birkenau-Stiftung, Wojciech Soczewica, hob die Spendenbereitschaft der deutschen Gesellschaft hervor, die den Kauf der Dokumente unterstützt habe. "Mehrere hundert Menschen haben uns finanziell unterstützt, mit Beiträgen zwischen 15 und 10.000 Euro. Am Ende haben wir 140.000 Euro gesammelt", sagte der Stiftungschef. "Die Spenden fließen weiter. Wir setzen unsere Suche nach NS-Dokumenten fort", kündigte er an. "Die Suche ist noch nicht beendet."

#3233. Flying Bats and Ghosts

This spooky science trick uses a magnet and a paper clip to make paper ghosts seem to fly through the air. It’s a fantastic way to learn about magnets and gravity with a fun Halloween twist!

You can either draw your own bats, ghosts and other Halloween images or use my FREE handy template!

Carefully cut around the images from the template, or draw your own.

Cut a piece of string about 10 cm long. Tape one end to a surface and one end to the bottom of one of the images.

Place a paper clip on top of one of the images.

Hold a magnet above the paperclip and watch the ghosts and bats fly.

It’s a bit tricky to get the distance between the paper clip and the magnet just right, but keep trying! You might need to tape the paper clip to the image so it doesn’t jump up to the magnet.

The magnetic force between the paperclip on the paper ghost and the magnet is stronger than the force of gravity pulling the ghost down. This means the ghost stays suspended in the air rather than falling to the ground.

Learn about static electricity with a jumping ghost. Tissue paper ghosts jump up to a balloon that’s been charged with static electricity.

#3235. Most levelling up projects still unfinished years after funding allocated

Data released under freedom of information laws reveals hundreds of projects unfinished despite Tory promises on regional equality

Can a £5.8bn scheme help revive Grimsby and other town centres?

Most levelling up projects are not finished, years after funds were allocated, highlighting how ambitious Conservative promises of quick progress on regional equality have faltered.

Data released under freedom of information laws and manually reviewed by the Guardian found 821 levelling up projects out of 1,347 were yet to be finalised as of May this year. Across the UK, 73 council areas that had a bid for a project accepted were yet to see a single one fully completed. The Guardian has identified 59 projects that were completed since the data was collected.

Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have seen slower delivery in their levelling up projects, despite having fewer overall. North-west England and Yorkshire also had low project completion rates, but they were also the two regions allocated the most projects to begin with.

Boris Johnson’s government swept to power in 2019 after promising to revive left-behind towns and spread opportunity as part of a levelling up agenda headed by Michael Gove. With 57% of projects still unfinished, the figures show many communities are still waiting for those ambitions to become reality.

The figures cover three of the main funds associated with the levelling up agenda: the Future High Streets Fund (launched in 2018), Town Deals (2019) and the Levelling Up Fund (2021).

The Future High Streets Fund was supposed to complete in March 2024, and the official deadline for spending all of the Towns Fund and Levelling Up Fund money was March 2026. The Levelling Up Fund and Town Deals were consolidated into the Local Regeneration Fund under Labour, with a new deadline of March 2028.

Labour has since also launched the Pride in Place programme. It gives places longer-term funding, with local boards deciding how it is spent, rather than making councils compete for grants.

Jack Shaw, the director of Groundwork Research, which supplied the data to the Guardian, said it showed a large gap between the intentions of levelling up and what had been delivered. He said: “Despite significant funding, too many one-off commitments have failed to translate into substantive improvements in communities or local economies.

“The Pride in Place programme is a step forward because it provides communities with £2m a year over 10 years, giving places the certainty and time to deliver visible, lasting improvements.

“But in future the government also needs to look at how investment can reach communities more quickly, so that funding announced at this budget can improve neighbourhoods over the course of this parliament, whether that be through new social infrastructure or a better public realm.”

Blackburn with Darwen council had eight projects funded through the Local Regeneration Fund, none of which have been fully completed.

Similarly, all eight projects funded in Leeds are yet to close. Five are in Morley: a refurbishment of Morley town hall, the establishment of a learning and skills centre, the station gateway transport scheme, a project to make the area greener and better connected, and the Heritage Investment Programme (which has only partly been completed).

Two projects in Holbeck – a green housing retrofit and a local centre scheme – also remain incomplete, as does the St Matthew’s community centre and Old Box Office project.

Part of the reason for the delays across the UK has been inflation, which meant councils had to scale back or pause projects due to increased costs eating into their awarded pots.

Zoë Billingham, the director of the IPPR North thinktank, said the Tories’ Town Fund failed because it had created a “begging bowl culture” where councils would need to approach Whitehall mandarins to access centrally controlled funding pots.

She said: “The levelling up – the ‘hanging baskets strategy’ as it was called – was short-term pots of money that could help clean up high streets and make tangible and important improvements. But that’s different to long-term support for what high streets are and should be. No one would dismiss it [levelling up funding], but you have to have a long-term plan rather than pots of money that run out.”

Andy Haldane, the former Bank of England chief economist who has advised Burnham, said the levelling up fund was “better than nothing” despite problems with it. He said: “It was in some ways the kind of worst of Whitehall. Because all the decisions were centralised. There looked to be degrees of pork barrel politics rolled into which places got it.

“It was all a bit sort of unsightly and pork barrelly.”

The national figures exclude 69 projects that were either cancelled or merged into another existing project. Some of the projects are broader programmes of funding, parts of which may have been completed.

Sarah Longlands, the chief executive of the Centre for Local Economic Strategies, warned Labour’s Pride in Place programme could face similar pitfalls to the Tories’ towns fund. She said: “It doesn’t surprise me the [Towns Fund] projects are not finished. Capital money takes time – you just can’t throw stuff up. This is my worry with the current programme of neighbourhood boards. We’re dealing with a lot of capital money, and it can’t be done quickly sometimes.”

You can look at the projects in your area and whether they have been completed or not using the map below. The government data may be missing some recent project completions. The Guardian has attempted to correct for this using published online announcements, but it is possible some completed projects may be missing from the data.

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: “We are committed to driving good growth in every postcode, giving local leaders stability through long-term targeted funding.

“That’s why we introduced our £5.8bn Pride in Place programme, giving the power to local people to decide how to invest this money to regenerate their own communities.

“And thanks to our Local Regeneration Fund, we’re seeing more money from previous funding programmes being delivered quicker.”

#3236. After Decades of Drought, Water Is Rising in the African Sahel

Dogondoutchi, Niger, is heavily reliant on groundwater, which is growing more abundant across the African Sahel. Sergey Mayorov / Zoonar

Warming has brought extreme rain to the parched Sahel, which is seeing aquifers refill as monsoons grow stronger. But heavier downpours alone cannot explain the groundwater revival, say hydrologists, who believe efforts to harvest rainfall may also be paying dividends.

Near-extinct oryx are returning. Farms are prospering as irrigation water reaches fields for the first time in decades. Farmers are even nurturing new trees on their land. Once a byword for drought and famine, the African Sahel region on the southern flank of the Sahara Desert now has more water than it has for decades. Wells are filling as water tables have risen by 13 feet or more in places. Lake Chad, which was one of Africa’s largest expanses of water before shriveling during the droughts, is recovering.

Over years of drought in the late 20th century, the sun hard baked the soils of the Sahel. Now, erratic but extreme rains are returning to this semi-arid region, causing lethal floods but also replenishing rivers, filling desert depressions, restoring water to dried riverbeds known as wadis, and sluicing rainwater off impermeable soils directly into aquifers. The process began in the 1990s but has accelerated in the past five years.

“Across the Sahel, from Ethiopia to Senegal, we have evidence of increased terrestrial water storage,” says Richard Taylor, a hydrogeologist at University College London who has led ground teams investigating the relationships between climate, land use, and groundwater recharge in the region.

But increased rainfall since the drought years of the 1970s and 1980s explains only some of the rewetting of the Sahel. It cannot fully account for the transformation, say researchers. Also driving the rewetting, they posit, are changes to the land surface, ranging from the internationally funded Great Green Wall project to the revival of traditional water harvesting methods and the chaos caused by jihadist militants, which has led to the abandonment of irrigation projects that once emptied rivers of their flows.

Much remains unclear in these remote lands on the edge of the Sahara Desert, but the trend seems set to be long-term, with climate scientists saying more — and more extreme — rainfall is on the way in the 21st century. As underground water reserves revive, some are forecasting an agricultural renaissance.

The Sahel is a band of semi-arid land around 500 miles wide that stretches across North Africa, from Senegal in the west to Ethiopia in the east, with a fast-growing population above 150 million. It is a transition zone between the Sahara Desert in the north and savanna grasslands and coastal forests to the south. Water is everything in the Sahel. Its rains are critical to human survival, but they have been sporadic and unpredictable since the close of a humid era around 5,000 years ago.

Shallow groundwater storage in February 2003 and February 2025, as compared to the average from 1948 to 2012. Source: NASA Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment. NASA / Adapted by Yale Environment 360

How much rain the Sahel gets depends on the West African monsoon, a wet wind that sweeps north from the Gulf of Guinea between June and September, and on how far the monsoon penetrates into the interior. Whether it reaches the 15th parallel north of the equator or stalls at the 10th parallel make the difference between a good year and a failed harvest, say hydrologists.

During the droughts of the late 20th century, as the monsoon repeatedly fell short, up to a million people died of hunger and disease. But now, with a strengthening monsoon, there is talk among scientists of the Sahel being on the verge of a new humid era.

That is good news for wildlife. With wadi systems reviving in Chad’s Ouadi Rimé-Ouadi Achim nature reserve, conservationists are documenting resurgent numbers of aardvarks, porcupines, badgers, and foxes, and the successful reintroduction of the scimitar-horned oryx, which was once declared extinct in the wild but now numbers more than 600 individuals. Elsewhere, West African giraffes are browsing on verdant vegetation in areas from which they had disappeared.

As Africa loses forest, its small farmers are bringing back trees. Read more.

As the rains return, farmers have boosted crop yields by nurturing the natural regrowth of some 200 million trees on formerly treeless fields in southern Niger, according to former World Resources Institute geographer Chris Reij. And, supported by new aid programs such as the World Bank’s regional recovery program PROLAC, they are re-establishing small-scale irrigation systems by tapping groundwater around resurgent oases in Chad, Niger, and Cameroon.

“In the past… there was not enough water to irrigate crops, and our harvests were meager. Now our lives have changed,” Achta, a farmer in Chad, said last year. She now has water to plant on four times as much land and has doubled her onion crop. The Bank says her story “reflects a broader transformation across the Lake Chad basin.”

Most places in the Sahel are seeing more rainfall. And that rain has become concentrated in extreme downpours from clusters of violent thunderstorms, known to meteorologists as Mesoscale Convective Systems, that occasionally bubble up during the monsoon season. Sahelian storm clusters are now rated as some of the most powerful on the planet, and they deliver most of the region’s rainfall. There has been a threefold increase in the frequency of extreme storms since the 1980s, according to a recent analysis.

Why the revival of the rains? An assessment published in 2021 by the U.N.’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change found “high confidence” among climate scientists that it is a result of strong warming in the North Atlantic, caused by a combination of global heating and a reduction, in Europe and North America, of sulphate aerosols from coal burning, which once created a thin haze that cooled the ocean. That cooling prevented the northward migration of the West African monsoon into the Sahel, resulting in drought. But the clean-up has warmed the ocean and pulled the monsoon back into the Sahel, strengthening its ability to produce deluges.

Flooding in Dakar, Senegal, following heavy monsoon rains in August 2022. John Wessels / AFP via Getty Images

The effects of these mega-storms are especially challenging in a region more used to disasters caused by the absence of rain. Niger, one of the world’s 10 poorest countries, saw tens of thousands die from famine during the late 20th century droughts. Now, it sees more deaths from floods than droughts. Fierce storms during the 2024 monsoon season inundated the capital, Niamey, and in rural areas washed away more than 150,000 mud-brick homes.

Sudden downpours are initially destructive, but they are a boon to underground water reserves. Falling onto compacted ground, the water does not initially infiltrate the soil but rushes into rivers and dry wadis, which speed the water’s flow into aquifers.

Hydrologists say that this indirect infiltration is most intense after heavy storms. “In some locations, rainfall intensity is more important than the annual rainfall amount in determining the magnitude of groundwater recharge,” says Taylor. This intensity, he says, is a major cause of the rapid rising of water tables — especially since, in the Sahel, most water drains not to the ocean but inland to depressions and lakes.

Not only are new ponds forming across the formerly arid lands; ancient networks of wadis are being restored. And Taylor’s network of researchers has found wells across the region refilling. Mean water tables in much of Niger have risen by some 13 feet, indicating a 15 percent increase in aquifer reserves.

This local data is now being corroborated by analysis from satellites that measure changes in land mass by tracking subtle changes in gravitational force from the land below. NASA’s Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment mission has found a sharp increase in gravitational force across the Sahel in the past two decades that hydrologists attribute to growing terrestrial water storage.

But rainfall and its intensity are only part of the story. Events on land also play a part.

Environmentalists have long held that the encroachment of agriculture into the Sahel during the 20th century caused “desertification” by removing natural vegetation, destroying soils, and allowing the advance of desert sands. But hydrologically, the effect may be the opposite because some crops can actually help the land retain water.

All vegetation absorbs moisture from the soil before transpiring it into the air. But shallow-rooted African grain crops such as millet and sorghum transpire less moisture than the deeper-rooted grasses they replace, leaving more moisture in the soil.

Dead trees in an arm of Lake Chad near Kiskawa, Chad, that was recently flooded. Joris Bolomey / AFP via Getty Images

An amplifying factor is the drought-driven crusting of soils, which has increased runoff by around 50 percent in the central Sahel in recent decades. Analysis by Christophe Peugeot, a hydrologist at the HydroSciences laboratory at the University of Montpellier in France, found that the droughts “have permanently transformed the region’s soils… fueling today’s floods.”

Much of this runoff ends up in Lake Chad, on the border between Nigeria, Cameroon, Chad, and Niger, which drains an area almost six times the size of California. The lake’s dramatic demise became a totemic image of the late 20th century hydrological decline of the Sahel. But less well known is that the lake is now recovering, as water inflows increase. Hydrogeologists at the University of N’Djamena in Chad report that in 2024 it swelled to a peak of more than 9,000 square miles, almost as big as in the 1960s and 10 times its size in the mid-1980s.

This growth is partly masked by large areas of saturated vegetation in the lake that do not show up in satellite images, say hydrologists. But as the lake grows, the aquifer beneath is also refilling.

Some researchers argue that deliberate efforts to capture rain in soils can also help explain the rising groundwaters across the region. One such effort is the Great Green Wall. Originally planned as a barrier of planted trees to prevent the advance of the Sahara, it has morphed into more grassroots efforts to control soil erosion by capturing rainfall and improving soil moisture, all of which can improve infiltration underground.

Many such projects revive traditional water-harvesting techniques, including the placement of stones along hill contours, digging small holes known as “zai pits” amid crops, and forming crescent-shaped mounds around trees.

Alpha Lo of the Climate Water Project, who highlighted the restored Sahelian groundwaters in a recent online analysis, argues that such techniques are “the primary reason.” But most researchers believe that, while locally effective in nurturing trees or crops, they are not happening at sufficient scale to explain the region-wide resurgence.

A final suggestion is that humans are extracting less water from rivers, leaving more to eventually infiltrate into aquifers. One driver of this trend is the decline of big irrigation projects that were constructed during the drought years to boost food production. For instance, Cameroon once largely emptied the River Logone, historically the biggest single source of water flowing into Lake Chad, to grow rice. But the SEMRY irrigation project reportedly diverts much less water now, due to poor management, aging infrastructure, and the outmigration of farmers.

Crescent-shaped mounds created to trap rainwater around gum acacia trees in Ninefouno, Niger. Rodrigo Ordonez / GLF

In areas around Lake Chad, farmers have also abandoned their irrigated fields because of Boko Haram, a militant jihadist group that continues to terrorize communities. Timmo Gaasbeek, food security policy officer at the Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affairs, says the chaos in northern Nigeria “means that the water in the rivers is not caught upstream, and continues to flow into Lake Chad, where it contributes to higher water levels and more groundwater recharge.”

Most climate models predict a further increase in annual rainfall in the coming decades, due to global heating and the banishing of cooling aerosols from the North Atlantic. Taylor predicts that “the Sahel will experience particularly marked increases in extreme rain” that will “serve to increase groundwater recharge.”

How a solar revolution in farming is depleting world’s groundwater. Read more.

Peugeot says that “the increased availability of water in valley bottoms could promote the development of irrigation, offering new prospects in several Sahelian regions.” Buoyed by such predictions, Nigeria is looking to restore the 165,000-acre South Chad Irrigation Project on the former shores of Lake Chad, which has long been abandoned for want of water.

But the road ahead will not be straightforward. Sahel rains will continue to be erratic on all timescales. Most immediately, climatologists are predicting that this year’s strong El Niño event could deliver drought in the eastern Sahel, but bumper rains and more floods further west.

Fred Pearce is a freelance author and journalist based in the U.K. He is a contributing writer for Yale Environment 360 and is the author of numerous books, including The Land Grabbers, Earth Then and Now: Amazing Images of Our Changing World, and The Climate Files: The Battle for the Truth About Global Warming. #3237. Apple iPhone 18 Pro review: big changes for small differences

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Longer battery life, better screen, upgraded Siri and new variable aperture camera in refreshed design from last year’s model

Apple’s smaller Pro iPhone gets the best kind of spec bump for 2026: longer battery life, faster chips and a fancy new variable aperture for the main camera.

The iPhone 18 Pro is one of a pair of slab phones launched alongside Apple’s first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, and is the cheapest of the new phones, with a regular iPhone 18 yet to be announced.

It isn’t exactly low cost, priced from £1,199 (€1,449/$1,199/A$2,099), with a £100 or equivalent rise over previous models courtesy of RAMageddon.

Having fully revamped the design of the body for the iPhone 17 Pro, the new model is a modest refinement. It is 7g heavier and the back glass now matches the colour of the aluminium body, which is available in a handful of new shades.

Apple has shrunk the amount of the screen taken up by the Face ID camera, allowing the dynamic island to show three continuing tasks, up from two on previous devices. It also now shows the 3/4/5G indicator next to the signal level when playing music, which is a most appreciated feature for public transport commuters sorely missed on previous models.

Otherwise, the 6.3in screen is one of the very best on a phone: super bright, crisp and smooth, while being big enough without making the phone enormous. An anti-glare coating makes it much easier to see outside, too.

Screen: 6.3in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (460ppi)

Camera: 48MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 4x, 18MP front-facing

Connectivity: 5G, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Satellite, UWB and GNSS

Water resistance: IP68 (6 metres for 30 mins)

The 18 Pro has Apple’s new A20 Pro chip, which is about 27% faster than the A19 Pro in last year’s model, with about 45% faster graphics performance. Since the A19 Pro was no slouch, that’s quite the leap and puts it miles ahead of the competition, ready to handle anything.

The phone has a redesigned cooling system for longer peak performance, too, which is especially useful for running games on top settings.

The battery lasts a solid six hours longer than the iPhone 17 Pro, managing to stretch to about two days between charges with more than six hours of active screen use across apps, browsing, messaging and photos. Even with the heaviest of use while out and about, the 18 Pro managed to end the day with 40% left in the tank. Most people will only need to charge it every other day.

The 18 Pro ships running iOS 27, which was released for the rest of the iPhone line on 14 September. It refines the relatively controversial Liquid Glass redesign from last year and speeds up the system, including app launches. But the big new addition is Apple’s revamped Siri, backed by Google’s AI technologies.

Siri AI, as the new system is called, is significantly more capable of understanding and answering questions than previous iterations. It is a chatbot like most other AI assistants, but it is less chatty and sycophantic than others, being more likely to just get the job done. As well as a choice of voices, there are sliders to control how fast it talks and how expressive its responses are. It has its own app where you can review previous interactions, but it is accessible anywhere on the phone via the side button, is built into Spotlight search and can see what’s on your screen, including when using the camera.

It can also offer suggestions, such as adding an event to your calendar from the messages or mail apps, and attempts to display relevant information from your emails in the phone app when you call a business. But Siri can only do so if you use Apple’s apps, so if you use WhatsApp for texting and Gmail for your email, none of it works.

The battery will last more than 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity and can be replaced for £119. Out-of-warranty screen repairs cost £349. The specialists iFixit awarded the phone a seven out of 10 for repairability.

It contains more than 40% recycled material. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.

The 18 Pro has a similar camera system to last year’s 17 Pro with one big addition, a variable aperture for the main camera.

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

That means it has a very good 18MP centre stage selfie camera on the front and three 48MP cameras on the rear: main, 0.5x ultrawide and 4x telephoto.

The ultrawide is one of the best on a phone, handy for landscapes and group shots. The 4x telephoto is very good too, full of detail and manages lower light settings well. It shoots excellent photos with a crop zoom to reach 8x before digital zoom is required, which is a little behind rivals with 5x/10x telephoto zooms.

The variable aperture on the main camera can be left on automatic or controlled manually. It allows the camera to open wider than previous models for better low light performance, speeding up night mode shots and reducing unwanted motion blur.

But it also enables a number of creative uses, such as making starbursts by narrowing the aperture when shooting lights, which is very fun, or controlling the depth of field in your photo. However, because the iPhone’s camera is tiny compared with an APS-C or full-frame camera, the difference in depth of field – where the foreground and background of the image are either in focus or blown out for a nice bokeh effect – is pretty minor. When shooting something up close, manually closing the aperture to f/4.0 can bring things in the foreground or background into focus, but otherwise the difference for most shots is small.

The 18 Pro’s camera has a number of other useful upgrades. My favourite is AI-powered focus tracking that keeps a subject in focus as it moves about or into and out of the frame, which has been one of the best features of a Pixel camera for years and is extremely handy for fast-moving children or pets.

Apple has also added texture and grain control to its Photographic Styles feature to customise how the camera shoots photos beyond what was introduced with the iPhone 16 Pro, including film simulation. Finally, the new Apple Reference Image feature can sign an image for authenticity, on a per pixel level directly on the sensor, to help later prove a shot is not AI-generated, similar to a digital negative.

The camera shoots some of the very best video on a phone, too. New for this year is the ability to convert a regular video to a cinematic one after the fact, a bit like the excellent automatic portrait mode for photos.

The iPhone 18 Pro costs from £1,199 (€1,449/$1,199/A$2,099).

For comparison, the iPhone 17 costs £899, the iPhone Air costs £1,099, the iPhone 18 Pro Max costs £1,299, the Google Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,079 and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra costs £1,359.

The iPhone 18 Pro is an iterative upgrade on an already great device from last year. Inside, it has some quite big changes, but their impact is fairly minor on the whole experience.

The new A20 Pro chip is super fast, but you can’t really notice the difference day to day, as previous iPhone chips have already been very quick. The extended battery life is great, but most people will still have to charge it every other day. The smaller camera cutout in the dynamic island now shows three continuing activities instead of two. Even the variable aperture in the main camera makes only a small difference to image quality unless you’re really trying to get creative.

The screen is fantastic and big enough. The aluminium body feels great to hold. The cameras are some of the best on a phone and even Siri is better now.

All of these things add up. The 18 Pro is without doubt the best iPhone ever made and at this size is one of the very best smaller phones available. It’s just not a transformative change unless you’re upgrading from a much older model and it now costs even more thanks to RAMageddon.

Pros: relatively compact, great screen, better dynamic island, longer battery life, great cameras, variable aperture, USB-C, top performance, long software support, Face ID, better AI.

Cons: small upgrade on last year, expensive, heavier than previous model, AI tools still lag behind top competitors.

#3241. USA: Waffenruhe für ukrainische Stadt Oleschky vereinbart

Präsidentengattin Melania Trump meldet sich zu Wort: Sie habe zwischen Russland und der Ukraine vermittelt. Das hatte zuvor schon Papst Leo XIV. getan. Nun sollen Zivilisten die abgeriegelte Stadt verlassen können.

Nach Vermittlung von Papst Leo XIV. und Melania Trump, der Frau des US-Präsidenten Donald Trump, soll am Donnerstag eine lokale Waffenruhe zwischen Russland und der Ukraine für die Stadt Oleschky beginnen. Das Weiße Haus teilte mit, beide Konfliktparteien hätten vereinbart, dort alle Kampfhandlungen einstweilig zu beenden. Dadurch soll humanitäre Hilfe in die seit Monaten abgeriegelte Frontstadt gelangen. Ebenso sollen Zivilisten Oleschky über einen sicheren Korridor verlassen können.

Melania Trump erklärte, die verbliebenen 1700 bis 2000 Einwohner hätten nur eingeschränkt Strom, lebten inmitten verminter Straßen und müssten regelmäßig militärische Angriffe ertragen. Sie habe mit Vertretern beider Kriegsparteien zusammengearbeitet, um die Bedingungen der lokal begrenzten Waffenruhe festzulegen.

Auch Papst Leo hatte sich für die notleidende Zivilbevölkerung eingesetzt. In einem Telefonat mit Kremlchef Wladimir Putin in der vergangenen Woche forderte er ebenfalls eine Waffenruhe für Oleschky und brachte seine "tiefe Besorgnis" über die humanitäre Lage zum Ausdruck. Der Vatikan hatte sich seit Beginn der russischen Großoffensive im Februar 2022 mehrfach um Vermittlung zwischen beiden Seiten bemüht.

Oleschky liegt auf russischem Besatzungsgebiet im Süden der Ukraine am Ufer des Dnipro. Die Stadt, die rundherum vermint wurde, ist von der Versorgung abgeschnitten. Die Gebietshauptstadt Cherson, die sich in ukrainischer Hand befindet, ist nur neun Kilometer entfernt. Dazwischen verläuft die Front.

Der Kreml warf der ukrainischen Armee wiederholt vor, durch Drohnenangriffe die Lieferung von Lebensmitteln nach Oleschky zu verhindern. Hilfsorganisationen beklagen seit langem die humanitäre Lage. Die Angaben der Kriegsparteien lassen sich nicht unabhängig prüfen.

Präsident Trump hatte zuvor erklärt, SpaceX-Gründer Elon Musk habe die Drosselung des Satelliteninternets für die Ukraine wieder aufgehoben. Einen Medienbericht, wonach Musk dies auf Anweisung Trumps getan habe, wollte dieser nicht kommentieren.

"Ob ich angerufen habe oder ob jemand anderes angerufen hat, spielt keine Rolle", sagte der Republikaner in Washington. Wichtig sei, dass Musk die Drosselung des Satelliteninternet-Dienstes Starlink rückgängig gemacht habe. Dieser gehört zu Musks Weltraumfirma SpaceX.

Das "Wall Street Journal" hatte zuvor unter Berufung auf Regierungsbeamte berichtet, Trump habe Musk am Mittwoch aufgefordert, die Verlangsamung des für die ukrainischen Streitkräfte elementar wichtigen Satelliteninternets rückgängig zu machen. Aus der Ukraine kommen allerdings weiter Berichte über eine eingeschränkte Funktion. Präsidentenberater Serhij Beskrestnow schrieb in sozialen Medien: "Derzeit können wir keine Aufhebung der Beschränkungen bei Starlink feststellen."

Vor Trumps jüngsten Äußerungen hatten das Weiße Haus und Musk alle Vorwürfe einer gezielten Drosselung zurückgewiesen - obwohl seit gut einer Woche von ukrainischer Seite über Probleme mit Starlink und der dazugehörigen Variante Starshield berichtet wird.

Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj beklagte, ukrainische Drohnen würden dadurch sowohl bei der Abwehr russischer Jetdrohnen als auch bei eigenen Angriffen behindert. Das ukrainische Militär leidet seit etlichen Tagen darunter, dass Flugobjekte bei einer Geschwindigkeit von mehr als 160 Kilometern in der Stunde ihre Verbindung zu den Starlink-Satelliten verlieren.

Die Spannungen zwischen Selenskyj und Trump hatten zuletzt deutlich zugenommen. Jüngster Auslöser war die Kritik des ukrainischen Präsidenten an einer Vereinbarung Trumps mit Moskau, die die Lieferung von russischem Dieseltreibstoff vorsieht. Spekuliert wurde deshalb, die Drosselung könnte von der Regierung der USA veranlasst worden sein.

Redaktionsschluss 17.50 Uhr (MESZ). Dieser Artikel wird nicht weiter aktualisiert!

#3243. How STEM Challenges Make Math Fun and Engaging at Home

I’m excited to share a fantastic guest post from the online learning platform Brighterly today.

Brighterly has hundreds of expert tutors and is great for helping kids aged 6 to 15 improve their maths and reading skills in a fun, hands-on way.

For many kids, math can feel complicated and overwhelming, all numbers and zero fun. The funny thing is, parents often feel the same way when trying to teach it to their children. Luckily, as parents, we can reshape the experience with a bit of help from STEM challenges. Suddenly, equations turn into experiments, numbers come alive through building and problem-solving, and learning stops feeling like a chore.

STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math) challenges are a fantastic way for busy parents to make math fun and engaging at home. They help kids connect abstract math to real-life scenarios, such as figuring out how to measure ingredients for building a bridge with limited materials. They also boost skills like creativity, logical thinking, and teamwork.

If you’re a parent wondering how to make it all work, digital math lessons are an easy way to implement STEM education into your children’s day-to-day life in the right way. With online platforms like Brighterly, playful problem-solving is just a few clicks away. But more on that later.

STEM challenges blend math with science, engineering, and creativity, transforming math from something kids have to do into something they want to do, helping kids realize that math isn’t just about numbers and homework, it’s an essential tool for solving real world problems.

Research from the National Science Teachers Association (NSTA) shows that hands-on STEM projects that apply math concepts to real-life scenarios help children retain math concepts more easily. Imagine a child who measures angles to design a paper bridge. They will be more likely to see math as useful and exciting, rather than a less interesting paper-based question.

STEM challenges also promote active learning. Children aren’t just memorising formulas, they are testing ideas, making mistakes and learning to try again. Real scientists and engineers use the same approach, but in kids, it builds confidence, a deeper understanding of mathematical thinking, and perseverance. And ultimately, it does make math fun.

Done at home as part of homeschool math, STEM activities also stimulate family connection and strengthen family bonds. For example, you can gather together to build a tower from spaghetti and marshmallows. Parents can ask kids questions like, “What shape do you think will make this tower stronger?” to stimulate curiosity and learning while having fun.

Believe it or not, you don’t have to have a fancy lab or special equipment in your house to spark your kid’s curiosity. There are plenty of home-friendly, engaging math activities you can do together — a few household items and a dash of creativity are more than enough for classic chemistry experiments and fun STEM challenges!

Give your kid spaghetti sticks and marshmallows and challenge them to build the tallest tower possible. Together, you’ll have the time of your lives as well as learning geometry, measurements, and stability!

Do you have popsicle sticks, cardboard, or straws? You can build a bridge! One challenge is to make a bridge so strong it can hold toys or coins. This activity helps your child apply math skills such as calculating weight distribution, estimating length, and experimenting with symmetry.

Cooking is one of the easiest ways to sneak in some math practice. When preparing a meal, invite your kid to double or halve a recipe, measure ingredients, or set timers. You can also time how long it takes for a chemical reaction to occur (like yeast and water or baking soda and vinegar). These activities reinforce fractions, time, and volume, while keeping little ones busy and active.

For older kids, you can introduce basic coding principles by creating color patterns with Lego bricks or paper bricks. Challenging your child to follow, repeat, and predict sequences is an excellent way to boost logic and reasoning, which are core skills in math and computer science.

Brighterly is one of the online maths programs that aims to make math fun and approachable for all students. The Brighterly platform connects US 1st–9th graders to professional math and reading tutors for one-on-one personalized learning. 200K+ parents joined Brighterly last year, giving an average Trustpilot rating of 4.4 stars! Want to explore how Brightelry approaches teaching math and how it leverages STEM challenges? Keep on reading.

The Brighterly tutors know how to make interactive math lessons fun, understandable, and cohesive. The platform only collaborates with experienced tutors who are experts in 1:1 online learning. They create a safe space for kids to learn and explore, without the overwhelm of boring drills and formulas memorisation.

The Brighterly platform emphasises building an adapted curriculum for each student, while staying on track with their strengths, weaknesses, and learning gaps. Additionally, the platform’s learning plan is fully aligned with school requirements, so you don’t have to worry that your child will fall behind the rest of the class.

It can be hard to find learning resources expertly crafted by professional tutors. Luckily, Brighterly is just the place to find them! The platform’s resources are designed by top tutors to provide children with cohesive exercises that help close learning gaps and improve math skills while learning independently.

Additional Brighterly perks to look into:

All in all, STEM challenges are an excellent way for the whole family to bond, help children develop the skills needed for math, and have some serious fun! However, if you’re looking for a platform that can take your child’s learning further, Brighterly offers fun, hands-on, and engaging lessons at an affordable price!

#3244. He wants to clean up the city and banish high prices. But who is ‘London’s Batman’?

The caped crusader is paying for hospital parking fines, giving out fuel to drivers – and sponsoring the return of cut-priced Freddo bars

In the harsh light of day, a caped crusader storms the streets of London to tackle a crime that has long blighted the capital: littering.

“When I said I wanted to save London, I meant it. I will not stop until every single bit of trash is off the streets,” he says in a viral video, narrated in his trademark deep, husky and (suspiciously) American voice, joined by a gang of hooded helpers clearing rubbish-strewn streets in Tower Hamlets.

This was Batman’s first good deed for the capital and, in the month since relocating from Gotham, he has carried out many more: paying parking fines for those visiting loved ones in hospital, giving out “free fuel” to motorists and bringing back £1 chicken and chips to those who once savoured this cheap and filling after-school meal.

But who is he really and what does he stand for? In a recent interview with a BBC reporter, who was only given a time and location before the masked figure emerged in an alleyway, he summed up his mission: “People are struggling and I want to help them.”

As for his identity, Niko Omilana – YouTuber, prankster and fifth-placed London 2021 mayoral candidate, who has pulled off similar stunts – is the most obvious guess, though he has denied it.

When asked by BBC London if he was the city’s masked mystery saviour, Omilana sent the team a voice note saying: “BBC, just to tell you, I’m not Batman.”

Count Binface, who has faced off against some of the nation’s most high-profile politicians in elections across the country, is another name in the mix, though he denied the rumours.

He told the Guardian: “I can see why a human might think that ‘London’s Batman’ is me, but it is actually a bit armour-ist of you. We’re not all the same.

“I’m happy to make the clarification and I would like to take the opportunity to wish London’s Batman well, including with his inevitable battle on the planet Copyright.”

Omilana remains the most likely suspect. His 2021 mayoral manifesto pledges included turning off all power in London once a year to “call it Londoff”, forcing then-prime minister Boris Johnson to “shush” and reducing the price of a Freddo chocolate bar to 5p.

Curiously, in one of his most viral stunts, London’s Batman set up a stall in Oxford Street where a Freddo could be exchanged for a tiny, silver 5p coin. (The frog-shaped chocolate bar was never officially sold for this sum, with 2p in the 1970s and 10p in the 1990s and early 2000s being the lowest retail prices documented.)

Ace Clvrk was in the area buying a guitar when he came across the stall. “I was lucky that day I had exactly 5p. It felt like fate,” said the 32-year-old musician.

He was approached on the street by some “hooded, masked youths” who “seemed really friendly”. They stopped him and asked: “Do you want to buy a Freddo?”

Clvrk was guided to a stall where he saw the caped crusader in the flesh. He told Clvrk he was “trying to bring attention to lowering the cost of Freddos”.

Like Gotham’s caped crusader, his London doppelganger appears to have significant resources behind him. His social media videos are slickly produced and the tasks he has carried out are hardly cheap.

For the “free fuel” stunt, one resident, speaking to the Times, estimated he gave away more than £3,500 to motorists throughout the day. The Guardian contacted several organisations that had benefited from London’s Batman’s good deeds who declined to speak citing confidentiality reasons.

Clvrk said it looked like a well-run stunt. “Everyone that I spoke to was really friendly and the actual content came out looking great too. I don’t remember actually seeing the camera,” he said.

In the video touting his bargain frog-shaped chocolates, London’s Batman featured a clip of Andy Burnham holding a Freddo while declaring it the “most talked about cost of living symbol in the UK” before going on to say he “might not be able to do anything to reduce the price of these”.

The caped crusader’s Freddo policy could suggest he’s vying for real power. “I’d vote for him, 100%,” said Clvrk. “5p Freddo, £1 chicken and chips and paying for fuel. What’s not to love?”

There could be some weight to this, especially if two-time political candidate Omilana, who also ran against Rishi Sunak in his Richmond and Northallerton seat in 2024, is behind the mask.

The message appears to be resonating. On TikTok, he has already amassed 315,000 followers in just over four weeks.

“I think everything he’s doing is amazing,” said Clvrk. “Politics and prime ministers are removed from the everyday Londoner and British person on the streets who used to be able to get a Freddo for 10p or cheap chicken and chips.

“With rising prices, it’s shining a light on things that seem small to those that are removed from it, but not for the everyday person.”

#3245. Zeolite-catalysed olefin carbonylation based on tuning spatial confinement

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Carbonylation is an important process used to produce aldehydes, carboxylic acids and esters1,2,3,4,5 that is usually catalysed by homogeneous metal complexes with ligands and iodide promoters6,7,8,9,10,11,12. Koch has reported that protons of mineral acids can also catalyse carbonylation13. Previous studies have demonstrated that Brønsted acidic zeolites can act as a heterogeneous, Koch-type catalyst for carbonylation of alcohols and olefins, but the products in this case are limited to tertiary carboxylic acids14,15,16,17,18. Here we show that targeted use of spatial confinement in a zeolite together with a high CO/olefin ratio can help break this limitation. We report that, with FER zeolite and a CO/olefin ratio of 360, olefin carbonylation can produce primary and secondary carboxylic acids as the main products; ethylene carbonylation to propanoic acid (PA) is achieved with 80% selectivity over 100 h and propylene carbonylation to isobutyric acid (IBA) is achieved with 95% selectivity over 750 h. The propylene and ethylene carbonylation selectivities decrease to 61% and 57%, respectively, as the CO/olefin ratio decreases to 24 and 90, respectively. Experiments in combination with theoretical calculations suggest that T2-O5 in eight-membered ring (8-MR) cavities of FER zeolite are the primary active sites for ethylene carbonylation and T3-O1 in ten-membered rings (10-MRs) are the primary active sites for propylene carbonylation. Our findings open new directions for olefin carbonylation and provide critical insights into the prerequisites for developing new zeolite-based carbonylation processes.

The proposed catalytic cycle of ethylene and propylene carbonylation in this work over zeolite. For both processes, the reaction proceeds with three steps: protonation of olefins to generate alkyl species, CO attack to alkyl species to form acylium cation species and H2O attack to acylium cation species to generate acids and regenerate H+. Dimerization as representative side processes are also demonstrated, which proceeds by olefins attacking to alkyl species.

The FER structure comprises 10-MR channels along the c-axis and FER cavities with 8-ring pore openings along the b-axis. The T1, T2 and T3 sites are accessible through the 10-ring channels (T1-O1/-O2, T2-O2/-O6, T3-O1) or the FER cavities (T1-O3/-O4, T2-O5, T3-O7/-O8). The T4 site is only accessible through the FER cavities (T4-O5/-O7).

#3246. Brazilian Amazon Sees Sharp Drop in Acres Burned

The Amazon rainforest, near Manaus, Brazil. Neil Palmer / CIAT

Last year, the acreage burned in the Brazilian Amazon reached its lowest level in at least four decades.

A new analysis from the monitoring group MapBiomas finds that 7.7 million acres burned last year, down from a record high of 39 million acres the previous year. The sharp drop in acres burned came as a warming El Niño gave way to a cooling La Niña.

In 2024, El Niño helped fuel the worst drought to hit the Amazon in decades. Fires proliferated on farmland that had recently been cleared and quickly spread to surrounding rainforest. Even as Brazil cracked down on the deliberate destruction of forest, deepening drought gave rise to thousands of fires across the region. In 2025, La Niña brought more rainfall to the Brazilian Amazon, which saw the fewest number of fires in 41 years of record keeping.

Analysts at MapBiomas say that, while the recent drop in acres burned is good news for the Amazon, it would be premature to see the latest figures as a sign of things to come. A powerful El Niño is now taking shape, portending drought in the coming year.

Still, Brazil can take steps, like planting native vegetation, to limit the spread of fires on degraded lands. Since 1985, 64 percent of all land that has burned in Brazil has burned more than once, and most burned areas burn again within four years.

A Missing Piece in Climate Models: Nature’s Own Emissions

#3248. Pixel 11 Pro Fold review: the foldable with the best triple camera

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Big screen folder with slick software and advanced AI is just like a regular Android when closed

Google’s latest folding phone sticks with its tried and tested design of a traditional phone shape when closed and almost square when open, in the face of new competition from Apple’s squat iPhone fold.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is Google’s fourth-generation folder and is still one of the only models with a full water and dust resistance rating similar to standard slab phones. It costs from £1,799 (€1,999/$1,899/A$2,799), which is £50 (€100/$100/A$100) more than last year as the pressure of RAMageddon continues to push up prices.

The 11 Pro Fold looks identical to previous models, but it is 19g lighter and fractionally slimmer in all directions with a slightly larger outside screen. Unlike Samsung’s slender Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra or squat models such as Apple’s iPhone Duo or the Galaxy Z Fold 8, the Pixel has the same ratio screen as Google’s slab phones and so handles precisely like them when shut with a bright and smooth 6.5in display.

Opened up, the internal screen is essentially square, which allows you to run two full-size apps side by side but is less ideal for video. The display is very bright, crisp and smooth, but the crease where it folds is more visible and detectable with your fingers than the best rivals. Like all foldable phones the screen is also delicate compared with standard hardened glass phones.

The back of the phone hides the excellent Qi2 magnetic charging and accessory support from last year, while Google’s gimmicky HiLight notification LED, as seen on the other Pro Pixels, replaces the camera’s flash.

Outside screen: 6.5in FHD+ 120Hz OLED (399ppi)

Camera: 48MP wide, 10.5MP ultrawide, 10.8MP 5x telephoto; two 10MP selfie cameras

Connectivity: 5G, eSim, USB-C, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, UWB, Thread, GNSS

Water resistance: IP68 (1.5 metres for 30 minutes)

The 11 Pro Fold has the same Tensor G6 chip from the other Pixel 11 models with 16GB of memory, which works very well for all kinds of multitasking, remaining snappy and responsive with multiple apps on screen. It handles light gaming, but can’t match rivals for raw performance.

The battery life is a little shorter than last year’s model and rivals, lasting about 36 hours between charges when used on a mix of 5G and wifi with the screens in active use for about 2.5 hours each for browsing, messaging, apps and photos. Most will have to charge it nightly, but even on the heaviest of use days the Pixel managed to end the day without requiring a top-up.

The Fold runs the latest version of Android 17 with all of Google’s AI tools, including Gemini’s proactive system, the new supercharged voice dictation feature and six months of Google AI Pro subscription.

Many of Google’s more creative AI tools, including the Omni video creation tool, Circle to Search and Gemini’s information cards benefit from the larger internal screen. Google has made a number of modifications to Android to better fit the folding form, including a floating taskbar and a split-screen mode that can resize apps beyond the bounds of the physical display introduced last year.

The bubbles system, which was primarily used for messaging apps, has been revamped to allow as many as five apps of any kind to be opened as floating windows on top of a single or split-screen apps and minimised to a little taskbar. But it isn’t as flexible as Samsung’s true desktop-like floating window system that can be resized and placed anywhere on the screen.

The 11 Pro Fold will be supported until August 2033 with operating system and security updates, making it one of the longest supported devices available.

The battery is rated to last in excess of 1,000 full charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is repairable by Google and third-party shops, and self-repair with manuals and parts is due to be available.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold contains 24% recycled materials by weight. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report and will recycle old devices for free.

The Pixel Fold has some of the best cameras on a foldable phone, including three on the back and two very good selfie cameras, one in each screen.

The rear cameras include a new 48MP main camera with a larger sensor, matching that in the regular Pixel 11, which captures better detail and has significantly better lowlight performance than its predecessor. The 10.5MP ultrawide camera is the same as last year and is still as solid this year. The 10.8MP 5x telephoto is also the same and shoots good photos that meaningfully reduce the distance to objects. It has a solid digital zoom that stretches up to 30x magnification, but not the generative AI zoom of the Pixel 11 Pro.

The Fold also has the new software features from the other Pixel 11 phones, including Camera Looks, which allows you to customise the processing of your photos for different styles. Magic Capture shoots video and photos automatically with one button, while the Creator suite helps you storyboard, trim and produce video content for social media.

The camera also has tricks to make use of the folding form, including modes to shoot when propped up and the excellent Made You Look feature that displays an animated character that reacts to your kid’s smiling to help take better photos.

Overall, the 11 Pro Fold has an excellent set of cameras that don’t feel a significant downgrade on top regular smartphones.

The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs from £1,799 (€1,999/$1,899/A$2,799).

For comparison, the Pixel 11 costs £879, Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,079, the Pixel 11 Pro XL costs £1,279, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra costs £1,899, the iPhone Duo costs £1,999 and the Honor Magic V6 costs £1,499.99.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is a fairly minor hardware update for Google’s folding phone line, which makes it slightly lighter, smaller, brighter and faster, while keeping its overall look and feel the same.

It has great AI tools, slick software and some of the very best cameras. The inside screen is super bright and crisp, but the crease down the middle is more noticeable than rivals, the battery life is a bit short and it is thick and heavy compared to the best from rival Samsung.

As with all foldables the inside screen can be permanently marked by a fingernail if you press hard enough, so you must still be careful with it compared with a standard Pixel.

But if you want a folding phone to be exactly the same as a regular one when closed, the Pixel Fold is the one to get.

Pros: just like a regular Pixel when closed, good tablet screen, dust and water resistant, Qi2 magnetic accessory and charging, good performance, great cameras with 5x zoom, great software packed with cutting-edge AI, six months of Google AI Pro included, seven years of software updates.

Cons: very expensive, more fragile and costlier to repair than a regular Pixel, thick and heavy, cameras can’t match regular Pixel 11 Pro, battery life could be better.

#3250. Russlanddeutsche in Kasachstan und der Umgang mit dem Erbe der Sowjetunion

Kasachstan ringt mit dem Erbe der Sowjetdiktatur. Vor 85 Jahren ließ Stalin Hunderttausende Menschen deportieren. Rund 400.000 Russlanddeutsche wurden nach Kasachstan verschleppt.

Sie will Geschichte lebendig halten. Yunna Kinereish ist 22 und studiert Public Relations in der modernen Glitzer-Hauptstadt Astana. Sie bezeichnet sich selbst als "kasachische Deutsche". "Ich bin Deutsche von meiner Nationalität her. Aber ich fühle mich auch als Kasachin, weil ich die Traditionen in meiner Familie lebe und diese Mentalität habe", sagt sie der DW. Yunna Kinereish ist eine von 223.000 Kasachstan-Deutschen, die heute in der zentralasiatischen Republik Kasachstan leben.

Yunna Kinereish engagiert sich bei der "Republikanischen Vereinigung der Deutschen Kasachstans - Wiedergeburt" in der Jugendgruppe "Diamant". Die Studentin hat kürzlich am Jugendtheater als Schauspielerin das Schicksal ihrer Vorfahren auf die Bühne gebracht. Das Schicksal der Russlanddeutschen, die zunächst ins Land gelockt wurden und ab dem 28. August 1941 unter Diktator Josef Stalin aus ihren angestammten Gebieten in der Sowjetunion zu Hunderttausenden gewaltsam nach Sibirien oder Kasachstan deportiert wurden.

Mindestens 200.000 von mehr als einer Million Menschen verloren durch Aussiedlung, Hunger und Zwangsarbeit ihr Leben. Genau vor 85 Jahren begann das Leid mit einem Erlass des Präsidiums des Obersten Sowjets der UdSSR. Eine direkte Reaktion auf den Überfall des nationalsozialistischen Deutschlands auf die Sowjetunion am 22. Juni 1941.

Menschen, die nichts mit dem Terror der Hitler-Truppen zu tun hatten, wurden kollektiv mitverantwortlich gemacht, sie wurden als Spione und Kollaborateure denunziert.

"Meine Familie ist Teil dieser Geschichte, von diesen schweren Zeiten. Sie wurden vertrieben aus dem ukrainischen Dorf Kleinwärter, einer Siedlung von Deutschstämmigen in der Ukraine." Die Schicksale, die sie und ihre Freundinnen auf die Bühne bringen, berührten sie sehr, sagt sie. "Für mich ist das nicht einfach, weil ich das tief im Herzen alles empfinde. Eigentlich möchte ich weinen. Ich muss aber stark sein, wenn ich im Deutschen Haus auf der Bühne stehe."

Das modern ausgestattete "Haus der Wiedergeburt" in der Hauptstadt Astana ist das Zentrum für deutsche Kultur. Es wird überwiegend durch Fördermittel der Bundesregierung in Berlin finanziert. Hier werden Sprachkurse gegeben, wird Sozialarbeit geleistet und Erinnerungskultur gefördert. Im Zentrum stehen dabei die Themen Deportation und Repression in der Sowjetzeit.

Yunna Kinereish steht nicht nur auf der Bühne, sie dokumentierte die Geschichte auch filmisch. Im vergangenen Jahr hat sie einen Film über inhaftierte deutsche Frauen im Lager Alzhir gedreht. Es war eines der berüchtigtsten Lager des sowjetischen Gulag-Systems.

In Kasachstan entstand während der stalinistischen "Säuberungen" ab 1937 das wohl größte Lagersystem der Sowjetunion. Allein das Lager Alzhir durchliefen 18.000 Frauen. Frauen, die dort inhaftiert wurden, nur weil ihre Männer als Volksfeinde oder Verräter verurteilt worden waren. Unter ihnen waren 167 deutschstämmige Frauen, deren Schicksal die Gruppe "Diamant" im Film zeigt.

Die Gedenkstätte für das Frauenlager Alzhir liegt direkt vor den Toren der neuen Hauptstadt Astana. Die 1,7-Millionen-Einwohner-Stadt ist am Reißbrett entstanden und erst seit 1997 Hauptstadt des größten zentralasiatischen Landes geworden. Kasachstan kann man als einen autoritär regierten Präsidialstaat bezeichnen.

Auf den Straßen von Astana herrscht Dauerstau. Fußgänger sind kaum zu sehen, Fahrradfahrer gibt es nicht. Astana wächst. Überall am Stadtrand: Neubauten. Dahinter öde Steppe, bis man nach etwa einer Stunde Autofahrt das Dorf Akmol erreicht.

Bevor man das eigentliche Museum betritt, durchschreitet man den "Bogen der Trauer"; eine riesige Stahlkonstruktion, die an das Leiden der Frauen und die Zwangsarbeit erinnern soll. Im Museum selbst: persönliche Gegenstände der inhaftierten Frauen, Modelle der primitiven Unterkünfte, Originaldokumente und Fotos.

Unter den Fotos ist auch das von Gertrud Platais, einer Frau mit deutschen Wurzeln, die lange in Alzhir inhaftiert war. Platais stammte aus Niederschlesien, das heute zu Polen gehört. Die Druckerin heiratete Karl Eduard Platais und nahm die sowjetische Staatsbürgerschaft an. Während des "Großen Terrors" in der Sowjetunion wurde ihr Ehemann 1938 verhaftet. Auch Gertrud Platais wurde verurteilt; als "Familienangehörige eines Verräters der Heimat".

Sie wurde nach Alzhir überstellt und musste dort bis 1946 als Stickerin Zwangsarbeit leisten, in einer Region, wo im Sommer 40 Grad Hitze herrschen und die Temperaturen im Winter auf minus 40 Grad fallen. Es folgte eine lebenslange Verbannung in das Großlager Karaganda. Erst 1956 wurde Gertrud Platais rehabilitiert. Ein Einzelschicksal, das den Terror des sowjetischen Systems auf kasachischem Boden dokumentiert.

Das weitaus größte Lagersystem war jedoch der sogenannte Karlag (Karagandinsches Besserungslager). Ein Komplex so groß wie das deutsche Bundesland Thüringen. Der Karlag war nicht nur ein Gefangenenlager, sondern ein riesiger Wirtschafts- und Landwirtschaftskomplex, den zwischen 1931 und 1959 fast eine Million Menschen durchliefen.

Allein zwischen 1940 und 1950 sollen hier rund 10.000 Gefangene gestorben sein: durch Hunger, Kälte, Krankheiten und die Folgen der Zwangsarbeit.

Das Museum liegt mitten in der kasachischen Steppe, in der Nähe der Stadt Karaganda, rund 250 Kilometer südöstlich von Astana. Die Gedenkstätte befindet sich im ehemaligen Verwaltungsgebäude des Lagersystems. Deutsche Historiker und Fachleute runzeln ein wenig die Stirn beim Besuch, denn in diesem Gebäude wurde nicht gefoltert oder drangsaliert, hier wurde verwaltet.

Zu sehen sind nachgebaute Verhör- und Folterzellen. Untermalt wird das ganze durch melodramatische Musik, die überall aus den Lautsprechern quillt: Inszenierung statt Authentizität. Wie auch die Alzhir-Gedenkstätte ist das Karlag Museum nicht besonders gut besucht. Selbst akademisch ausgebildete junge Menschen kennen die Gedenkstätte nicht unbedingt.

"Bei vielen Menschen und Teilen der Politik gibt es in Kasachstan kaum Interesse an einer Aufarbeitung der teils grausamen Geschichte des Landes", sagt Katherine M. Erdmann. Seit rund einem Jahrzehnt beschäftigt sich die amerikanische Anthropologin und Archäologin an der Nazarbayev-Universität in Astana mit dem Gulag-System. "Wir wollten herausfinden, wo die Lager genau waren, und wie man sie heute noch erkennen kann."

Erdman und ihre Studentinnen und Studenten setzten auf moderne Technik wie Drohnenüberflüge. Aber auch Befragungen und Recherchen am Boden gehören dazu. "Die Zwangsarbeit hat in großen Landesteilen die Landschaft geformt", sagt Erdman. Neben den primitiven Unterkünften entstanden oft Betriebe. Häuser wurden errichtet, mit Ziegeln, die in Zwangsarbeit hergestellt wurden. Ihre Erkenntnisse teilen die Forscher direkt mit Nachbarn und den lokalen Verwaltungen vor Ort.

"Oft begegnet uns nur Apathie oder bloße Ablehnung", sagt Erdman. Die breite Öffentlichkeit sei an Geschichtsaufarbeitung kaum interessiert. An die unrühmliche Vergangenheit wollen viele nicht erinnert werden in einer Zeit des wirtschaftlichen und gesellschaftlichen Aufstiegs, beklagt Erdmann.

International wolle man demonstrieren, dass man sich mit den dunklen Seiten der Geschichte befasse, aber oft erlebe sie mangelndes Interesse und sogar Ablehnung. Seit einem Jahrzehnt forscht die Wissenschaftlerin in Kasachstan. Für weitere Lehraufträge fehle die staatliche Finanzierung.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yunna Kinereish gehört zu den jungen Menschen in Kasachstan, die nicht wollen, dass die Vergangenheit in Vergessenheit gerät. Die Kasachstan-Deutsche aus Astana gibt der DW zum Abschied dies mit auf den Weg: "Meine Vorfahren haben das Gulag-System in Kasachstan überlebt. Für mich ist es deshalb wichtig, die Wurzeln nicht zu vergessen und das von unseren Vorfahren Erlebte und Erlittene weiterzugeben."

Dieser Text ist im Rahmen einer Studienfahrt der "Bundesstiftung zur Aufarbeitung der SED-Diktatur" entstanden. Die aus Steuergeldern finanzierte Stiftung widmet sich seit 1998 der Auseinandersetzung mit der kommunistischen Diktatur in Deutschland, in der DDR, und in anderen Ländern.
