#3388. Neuer Gebäudetyp E: Schnelles und günstiges Bauen per Gesetz

Deutschland braucht mehr bezahlbaren Wohnraum. Das soll unter anderem mit dem Gebäudetyp E gelingen - das E steht hier für "einfach". Der Gesetzentwurf liegt dem ARD-Hauptstadtstudio exklusiv vor.

Wer Bundesbauministerin Verena Hubertz von der SPD auf den Gebäudetyp E anspricht, bekommt von ihr gerne die Schlagworte "Bauen ohne Schnickschnack" zu hören. Tatsächlich bringt diese griffige Formel die Grundidee auf den Punkt: Bauen soll einfacher, schneller und günstiger werden, indem Bauherrn und Planer auf nicht zwingende Standards verzichten können - sowohl bei Einfamilien- als auch bei Mehrfamilienhäusern.

Beim Gebäudetyp E geht es darum, zwischen wirklich notwendigen Anforderungen und Ausstattungen zu unterscheiden, die zwar Komfort mit sich bringen, aber das Bauen auch teuer machen. Solche Komfortstandards haben sich in den vergangenen Jahren etabliert, als das Bauen dank niedriger Kreditzinsen vergleichsweise günstig war: etwa eine bestimmte Anzahl von Steckdosen im Wohnzimmer, extra hohe Decken oder besonders dicke Fenster und Wände für den Schallschutz.

Das Bauen ist in Deutschland erneut überdurchschnittlich teurer geworden, weil Wohnraum nach wie vor fehlt. mehr

Vieles davon zählt heute zu den "Anerkannten Regeln der Technik". Weicht ein Architekt oder ein Bauunternehmer davon ab, kann ihm nach aktuellem Vertragsrecht eine Klage des Käufers drohen. Künftig sollen die Beteiligten eines Bauprojekts vorab rechtssicher vereinbaren können, dass sie auf gewisse Standards verzichten. Das ist der Gebäudetyp E - E steht für einfach. Fachleute schätzen, dass die Baukosten bei diesem Konzept um etwa zehn Prozent sinken.

Bundesjustizministerin Stefanie Hubig stellt klar: Es werde keine Abstriche bei der Sicherheit beim Bauen geben, die stehe weiter an oberster Stelle. "Der Gebäudetyp E bietet die Chance für einen echten Befreiungsschlag: Bauen ohne teure Extras. Mit dem Gebäudetyp-E-Gesetz ebnen wir dafür den Weg", sagt die SPD-Politikerin. Und Bauministerin Hubertz ergänzt: "Jeder Euro, den wir nicht in überflüssige Standards stecken, ist ein Euro für mehr bezahlbaren Wohnraum. Deswegen bin ich froh, dass wir jetzt einen Entwurf haben."

Geplant war, dass der Gesetzentwurf schon im Sommer vorliegt. So hatten es beide Ministerinnen im Juli angekündigt. Doch daraus wurde nichts. Innerhalb der schwarz-roten Koalition gab es Unstimmigkeiten in Detailfragen. Unter anderem waren die Koalitionspartner uneins, ob der Gebäudetyp E das "neue Normal" beim Bauen oder eine Spezialkategorie im Vertragsrecht werden soll.

Das Bundesbauministerium will zügig für neuen Wohnraum zu sorgen. Wo bleibt der geplante "Gebäudetyp E"? mehr

Der baupolitische Sprecher der Unionsfraktion, Jan-Marco Luczak, sagte vor wenigen Tagen noch: "Statt teurem Goldstandard müssen wir einfaches und kostengünstiges Bauen zum 'neuen Normal' machen - ohne neuen Vertragstyp." Der Kritikpunkt: Sonst könnte eine Art Zwei-Klassen-Bauen entstehen. Auf der einen Seite ein hoher Baustandard - auf der anderen der Gebäudetyp E mit einem möglicherweise schlechteren Image.

Justizministerin Hubig teilt diese Bedenken nicht. Im Gesetzentwurf, der dem ARD-Hauptstadtstudio vorliegt, ist nun vorgesehen, dass der Gebäudetyp E eine eigene Vertragskategorie wird. Die Rede ist von einer freiwilligen Option für die Parteien eines Bauprojekts. Entscheiden sie sich nicht für den Gebäudetyp E, bleibt es bei den bisherigen Regeln des Vertragsrechts. So sei sichergestellt, dass eine einfachere Bauausführung dem Willen beider Parteien entspreche, heißt es. Anschließende Klagen der Käufer hätten damit keine Chance, Planer und Baufirmen gehen kein Risiko ein.

Die Lage am Immobilienmarkt spitzt sich weiter zu. mehr

Der Entwurf geht jetzt an die Bundesländer und an die Verbände. Sie können Kritik äußern. Änderungen im Detail sind im Gesetzentwurf also noch möglich, bevor die Regierung ihn offiziell auf den Weg bringt. Bis das erste Gebäude auf Basis des neuen Gesetzes steht, dürfte es noch etwas dauern: Nach Planung und Bau wäre das Richtfest realistischerweise in frühestens zwei Jahren denkbar.

#3389. Mehrheit in Alberta will weiter zu Kanada gehören

In Kanada haben die Einwohner der wirtschaftsstarken Provinz Alberta über eine mögliche Unabhängigkeit abgestimmt. Die Befürworter fühlen sich von der Regierung in Ottawa benachteiligt. Das Ergebnis fiel deutlich aus.

Die Einwohner der ölreichen Provinz Alberta wollen mehrheitlich Kanadier bleiben. Mehr als 76 Prozent der Wähler stimmten laut vorläufigen Teilergebnissen gegen eine mögliche Abspaltung, wie die Wahlbehörde nach Auszählung von rund 60 Prozent der Wahlkreise bekanntgab.

Bei der Volksabstimmung am Montag ging es darum, ob Alberta ein zweites verbindliches Referendum zur Trennung von Kanada anstreben soll, sowie um neun weitere Fragen zur Einwanderung und zur Verfassung. Die Provinz liegt im Westen des Landes und gilt als besonders konservativ. Viele Unabhängigkeitsbefürworter sind der Ansicht, dass Alberta wirtschaftlich einen großen Beitrag zum Wohlstand Kanadas leistet, von der Regierung in Ottawa aber politisch benachteiligt wird.

Umfragen hatten zuletzt bereits eine große Mehrheit für den Verbleib als Teil Kanadas gesehen - etwa 70 Prozent. Auch die beide großen politischen Parteien des Landes hatten sich immer wieder deutlich gegen eine Abspaltung ausgesprochen. Das endgültige Ergebnis der Abstimmung soll nach Angaben der Wahlbehörde am 29. Oktober veröffentlicht werden.

Aus der US-Regierung von Präsident Donald Trump war im Vorfeld des Referendums Unterstützung für die Unabhängigkeitsbewegung gekommen. Das nun so klare Ergebnis stärkt vor dem Hintergrund von Trumps Annexionsdrohungen und einem Handelskrieg mit Washington das Bestreben von Premierminister Mark Carney, die nationale Einheit zu wahren.

Kanada sei so viel mehr als die Summe seiner Teile, schrieb Carney auf der Online-Plattform X. "Jetzt haben wir die Chance, all das, was uns als Kanadiern gegeben wurde - und uns wurde das großartigste Land der Welt geschenkt - zu nutzen und unser Land für uns alle besser zu machen."

Danielle Smith, die Premierministerin von Alberta, zeigte sich ebenfalls erfreut über die ersten Ergebnisse der Abstimmung. "Die Einwohner Albertas haben für ein stärkeres Alberta in einem vereinten Kanada gestimmt", schrieb sie auf X.

In der Provinzhauptstadt Edmonton herrschte gedrückte Stimmung bei den Befürwortern einer Loslösung von Kanada. Er sei "enttäuscht von seinen Mitbürgern", sagte der Separatist Jour Dain. Er erwäge, in die USA auszuwandern.

Der führende Separatist Keith Wilson sagte laut dem Sender CBC, dass die Sorgen, die sich die Menschen in Alberta hinsichtlich ihres Platzes innerhalb Kanadas machten, nicht mit diesem Referendum enden würden. "Die Debatte über Albertas Zukunft in Kanada - über unseren Platz und unsere Rolle in Kanada - wird weitergehen", so Wilson. Die Separatisten hatten bereits im Voraus angekündigt, auch ein Referendum, das gegen sie ausgeht, nicht als Ende ihrer Bestrebungen zu sehen.

Die Provinz Alberta mit rund fünf Millionen Einwohnern ist das Zentrum der kanadischen Erdöl- und Erdgasindustrie und verfügt über riesige Ölsandvorkommen. Die Klimapolitik der kanadischen Bundesregierung, etwa CO2-Abgaben und Vorgaben für die Energiebranche, wird von Separatisten als Angriff auf die wirtschaftliche Grundlage der Provinz betrachtet.

In Kanada hat es in der Vergangenheit bereits zwei Unabhängigkeits-Referenden gegeben - allerdings beide in der französischsprachigen Provinz Québec. Dort geht es weniger um wirtschaftliche Fragen als um sprachliche und kulturelle Unterschiede. Anfang Oktober ging dort die separatistische Parti Québécois als stärkste Kraft aus der Regionalwahl hervor. Sie strebt ein weiteres Referendum über die Unabhängigkeit der Provinz an. Umfragen zufolge gibt es dafür derzeit allerdings ebenfalls keine Mehrheit in der Bevölkerung.

#3392. In East Africa, a Controversial Oil Project Is Poised for Production

The East African Crude Oil Pipeline being installed in Kikuube, Uganda.  Luke Dray / Bloomberg via Getty Images

An eleventh-hour legal effort is underway to halt the completion of a 900-mile oil pipeline through key African wildlife habitats. The East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP) is weeks from being ready to operate, but the full range of ecological impacts from the pipeline and the two oil fields in Uganda that it will serve are only now becoming clear.

A key concern is the likely threat to Uganda’s Murchison Falls National Park, where the French energy giant TotalEnergies is set to begin producing oil in October. The park is one of Africa’s greatest havens for wildlife, Uganda’s last stronghold for around 240 lions, a critical link in an elephant migration corridor stretching into South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), and home to large populations of giraffes, buffalo, crocodiles, and hippos.

A second oil field is also ready to begin production on the eastern shore of nearby Lake Albert. The oil from both will be delivered to world markets via the pipeline, which stretches from Uganda across neighboring Tanzania to the Indian Ocean.

The project is moving forward despite a years-long campaign that marshaled major banks and insurers against it, and despite revelations of the intimidation, harassment, and abuse of people living in its path.

The world’s oil consumers are keen to see a new source of oil come online that is not dependent on the militarized Strait of Hormuz. But campaigners are planning to make a last legal challenge in courts in London, where EACOP Ltd, the company largely owned by TotalEnergies that is in charge of the pipeline, is registered. Next month, they are expected to claim that its operation will breach the laws and constitution of Uganda.

Murchison Falls National Park was first gazetted as a game reserve by British colonial authorities exactly a century ago, in 1926, and made a national park in 1952. At its heart is one of Africa’s most dramatic waterfalls, where the River Nile bursts through a narrow gorge and creates a spectacular delta wetland before entering Lake Albert, Africa’s seventh largest lake, on the border between Uganda and the DRC.

But since the discovery in 2006 of an estimated 6.5 billion barrels of oil reserves beneath the lake and its vicinity, the biodiversity hotspot has also become a magnet for oil companies. Now, two oil fields are about to begin production, both exporting crude oil via EACOP, which is set to be the world’s longest heated oil pipeline.

The East African Crude Oil Pipeline will stretch 900 miles from Lake Albert in western Uganda to the Tanzanian port of Tanga on the Indian Ocean. Yale Environment 360 / Google Maps

The two production areas are TotalEnergies’ Tilenga oil field, much of it in the national park, and the Kingfisher oil field, run by the China National Offshore Oil Corporation (CNOOC) in a remote marshy area on the southeastern shore of Lake Albert.

Bill Powers, principal of Powers Engineering in San Diego, one of America’s leading energy engineering and environment consultants, reviewed the project design for Yale E360. He says that by not following best practices, the Tilenga project is causing wholly unnecessary destruction of vital ecosystems in the park, which includes headwaters of the River Nile, Africa’s longest river.

Instead of creating nine large, fenced drill pads in the park, Powers says, the company could have concentrated drilling at just one or two pads. And instead of trucking large volumes of drill cuttings to landfills outside the park, it could have injected the cuttings in situ. Such steps “would have avoided hundreds of daily heavy truck movements [along with] the associated road network.” Satellite imagery has revealed almost 24 miles of roads created by TotalEnergies’ contractors within the park.

TotalEnergies did not respond to the technical specifics of the criticisms but said it was limiting development to only a small part of the park and was making the production pads “as compact as possible,” with “minimal visual impact.” Meanwhile, the Kingfisher project, Powers says, could be just as environmentally damaging as the Tilenga operation because of its proximity to the lake, a major fishery on which more than 100,000 locals depend for their livelihoods.

Neighbors of the Kingfisher oil field claim contractors have dumped oil and production waste into the lake, causing fish kills. And after a recent visit to the Murchison Falls National Park, Environmental Defenders, a conservation and human rights group working in Uganda, reported “dramatic changes” to the park.

“Where there were once unbroken vistas of savannah and roaming herds, there are now freshly bulldozed roads, fenced-off well pads, and the faint gleam of an oil rig’s lights on the horizon,” the group says. Villagers outside the park say that elephants and other park wildlife fleeing the noise and disturbance from oil drilling have been trampling their crops and have killed several people.

The Ugandan government sees the oil fields and pipeline as vital to President Yoweri Museveni’s goal of stimulating wider economic activity and job creation to help the nation achieve upper-middle income status by 2040, including doubling GDP every five years. But for now, all the crude oil is set for export, so the local benefits may prove minimal. Work has not yet begun on a long-delayed $4-billion oil refinery intended to supply East African markets.

A Ugandan police officer arrests an activist protesting EACOP in Kampala in August 2024. Badru Katumba / AFP via Getty Images

EACOP Ltd calls the 24-inch pipeline “the world’s most innovative and smart pipeline system,” pressure-tested and monitored along its entire length, and able to detect and isolate any leaks. It says that the pipeline, which must be heated to 50 degrees C (122 degrees F) to prevent the low-sulfur crude from solidifying, will be “underground and invisible, leaving no mark on the landscape.”

But the pipeline will hardly be undetectable: The company will maintain rights to a corridor almost 100 feet wide along the length of the pipeline, where no buildings or other obstructions will be allowed. And the pipeline will be monitored and operated from 80 above-ground control stations along the corridor.

“The pipeline has a far larger footprint than previously estimated,” says Juan Pablo Osornio, engagement and policy director of Earth Insight, a California-based environment and land-rights NGO which in May published a detailed mapping study of that footprint that shows in much greater detail than before the ecological value of the terrain that it will cross.

For instance, the new study found that the pipeline route crosses more than 10,000 subsistence farms, with 84 percent of the route intersecting antelope habitat, 67 percent monkey habitat, 22 percent leopard habitat, and 17 percent giraffe habitat.

It also establishes that EACOP and its feeder pipelines cut through 44 areas registered in a database of protected areas created by the U.N. Environment Programme and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) — apparently contradicting TotalEnergies’ claim that “the pipeline does not cut across any IUCN protected area.”

As Zambia pushes new mining, a legacy of pollution looms. Read more.

And the pipeline could disrupt the ecology of other precious places. It passes through a corridor used by chimpanzees to migrate between the neighboring Wambabya and Bugoma forest reserves in Uganda. And it crosses some 230 rivers that could disperse any leaking oil far and wide.

Osornio singles out the risks where oil-laden pipes tunnel beneath two major rivers. One is the River Nile within the Murchison Falls National Park, where the feeder pipe from Tilenga to EACOP is buried for more than a mile beneath the river and a delta rich in papyrus that is famous for its crocodiles, hippos, and birdlife. The delta is also a vital breeding ground for the fish in Lake Albert.

The second is EACOP’s crossing beneath a wetland, fed by the Kibale and Bukoora rivers, that flows directly into papyrus swamps on the western shore of Lake Victoria, Africa’s largest freshwater lake. The swamps are home to endangered black rhinos, African wild dogs, primates, and pangolins.

A drilling rig in the Kingfisher oil field sits on the shore of Lake Albert in Kikuube, Uganda. Luke Dray / Bloomberg via Getty Images

The company says its technology, which will include robotics devices travelling through the pipeline to inspect its condition, minimizes the risk of leaks. But environmentalists say that is no guarantee against earthquakes. The pipeline passes through two seismically active branches of the East African Rift Valley. An earthquake in 2016, centered along the pipeline route west of Lake Victoria, destroyed almost a thousand buildings.

The pipeline ends on the shores of the Indian Ocean, where some 200 acres of mangrove swamps on the Chongoleani peninsula have been removed to make way for the export terminal. From there, tankers up to a thousand feet long will regularly pass two nearby marine protected areas noted for their coral reefs, as they ship more than 200,000 barrels of oil per day to markets across the world.

That oil will eventually be burned, generating over the project’s 25-year lifespan some 379 million metric tons of CO2 — equivalent to more than 40 years of Uganda’s current domestic emissions, according to the Colorado-based Climate Accountability Institute.

Faced with international environmental opposition to the project, many banks, including Barclays, Deutsche Bank, and Japan’s Sumitomo Mitsui, have backed off funding the pipeline. But others continue to offer support, most notably South Africa’s Standard Bank and the giant state-owned Industrial and Commercial Bank of China.

With its finance underwritten, and production costs likely to be far below the international price of crude oil, installation of the pipeline has rushed ahead this year, with the delivery of 260,000 tons of pipes from China. The EACOP company says the pipeline will be complete by the end of July and delivering oil to the export terminal in October.

While environmental issues have excited international attention, within Uganda and Tanzania concern has mainly focused on the disruption to the lives of 100,000-plus people on the oil fields and along the pipeline, and on the Ugandan government’s treatment of anyone speaking out against the project.

In 2023, after clearing of farms for the pipeline got under way, a panel of U.N. special rapporteurs on human and environmental rights wrote to the Ugandan government criticizing a “pattern of intimidation and harassment” of NGOs raising human-rights concerns about the project.

But rather than taking heed, the government’s crackdown has hardened. Two years ago, Stephen Kwikiriza, a vocal opponent of the project, was abducted in Kampala by military officers in plainclothes, beaten up, knocked unconscious, and dumped five days later on a roadside 150 miles away.

A giraffe on the shore of Lake Albert in Uganda's Murchison Falls National Park. Giulio Origlia / Getty Images

In this hostile environment, most displaced people have taken the compensation proffered by TotalEnergies, whether in cash or new land, despite the sometimes “huge inadequacies” identified by the Africa Institute for Energy Governance (AFIEGO), a Kampala-based energy policy research and advocacy group. The group found TotalEnergies offered poor land to displaced people and insufficient cash compensation to buy new land. Most took the offers “because they were threatened with court action if they refused,” says AFIEGO’s Diana Nabiruma. “The EACOP is not just displacing people from their land — it is displacing them from their dignity and future.”

In May, the government enacted a new Protection of Sovereignty Act, which criminalizes the promotion of “foreign interests” in domestic politics. Local activists say it could result in long prison terms for anyone seen as siding with outsiders in speaking against oil developments. “The law is a huge, huge threat for civil society organizations such as ours,” says Nabiruma.

Opponents have not given up hope, however. Some are seeking redress abroad. In April, Ugandan activists and farmers’ groups and human-rights lawyers at the U.K.-based Leigh Day law firm announced plans to file a legal injunction in London, where the EACOP company is registered, arguing the project should be halted because it breaches Uganda’s national environmental laws and the Ugandan Constitution.

Not all environmentalists have opposed the oil developments outright, however. Some see more to be gained from collaborating with the oil companies to minimize damage and offset it with environmental projects elsewhere.

Local scientists and conservationists at the 117-year-old NGO NatureUganda, along with the U.S.-based Wildlife Conservation Society and the Netherlands-based Wetlands International, have participated in the Independent Biodiversity and Livelihoods Advisory Committee set up by TotalEnergies “to support the company’s efforts to achieve biodiversity net gain” in its project areas. These efforts include funding wildlife monitoring, planting 2,500 acres of forest, a reintroduction program for black rhinos, and a crackdown on poaching.

Baboon raiders: In Cape Town, can big primates and people coexist? Read more.

Meanwhile, the lure of economic development boosted by oil revenues remains strong. The Lake Albert basin is known to hold other oil reserves that are not yet being tapped. But for how much longer? Until now, it has not been feasible to export oil from the remote Lake Albert area. But the pipeline changes that. “Oil blocks across the other side of Lake Albert in the DRC become viable with the completion of EACOP,” says Osornio.

For some in the energy sector, oil is a sunset industry, doomed by the drive to decarbonize global energy systems. Others are continuing to develop new reserves of fossil fuels, increasingly putting many of Africa’s great wilderness areas — the last refuges of the planet’s megafauna — in harm’s way.

Fred Pearce is a freelance author and journalist based in the U.K. He is a contributing writer for Yale Environment 360 and is the author of numerous books, including The Land Grabbers, Earth Then and Now: Amazing Images of Our Changing World, and The Climate Files: The Battle for the Truth About Global Warming. #3395. What are enzymes?

Enzymes are biological catalysts. In simple terms, they speed up chemical reactions.

Living organisms have chemical reactions happening in them all the time. One way enzymes are used is to break down large molecules. For example, enzymes called carbohydrases convert carbohydrates into simple sugars.

This type of reaction needs to be carefully controlled. Reactions outside the body are often sped up by increasing the temperature, but that wouldn’t be very helpful in your body, as all the chemical reactions would speed up, and our bodies need to be at an optimum temperature to work properly. So, living organisms use enzymes to control the speed of chemical reactions.

A catalyst is a substance which increases the speed of a reaction without being changed or used up in the reaction.

Enzymes have an active site which is shaped to fit the molecule ( substrate ) that needs to change in the reaction. This is called the lock and key mechanism. If the substrate doesn’t fit into the active site, the reaction won’t be catalysed.

A slightly adjusted model is the induced fit model, where the active site changes slightly when the substrate binds to it.

Carbohydrases convert carbohydrates into simple sugars. Amylase is an example of a carbohydrase. It breaks down starch into maltose.

Lipases convert lipids into glycerol and fatty acids.

Proteases convert proteins into amino acids.

Enzymes are also used to join molecules together. For example, proteins are made by joining amino acids together.

Enzymes need the right conditions to work properly.

Enzymes have an optimum temperature at which they are the most active, but if the temperature gets too high, the enzymes stop working. This is because bonds holding the enzyme in shape break, which changes the shape of the active site so the substrate no longer fits. When an enzyme changes shape like this, it’s said to be denatured.

As with temperature, enzymes also have an optimum pH. If the pH is too high or too low, it alters the bonds in the enzyme and, consequently, the shape of the active site.

The higher the substrate concentration, the faster the reaction, as the likelihood of an enzyme and substrate making contact is greater the more substrate there is.

There is a maximum substrate concentration, though, as once all enzymes are in use, adding more substrate makes no difference to the rate of reaction.

Amylase is found in saliva and the pancreas. It breaks complex carbohydrates into simple sugars.

Lactase breaks down lactose ( the sugar found in milk ) into glucose and galactose.

DNA Polymerase is involved in DNA replication.

Pepsin breaks down proteins in the stomach into smaller peptides and amino acids.

Trypsin breaks down proteins in the small intestine.

Make a model of the digestive system to learn about digestive enzymes!

Enzymes in fruits such as pineapple, kiwi and papaya break down proteins in jelly, stopping it from setting! This is a great visual way to see enzymes in action!

Find out how to stop polyphenol oxidase from turning fruit brown with a simple kitchen hack.

Use play dough to make a model of an enzyme and substrate.

#3397. Structural basis for protocadherin-1 recognition by New World hantaviruses

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Hantaviruses are rodent-borne pathogens that cause severe human disease for which no approved therapeutics are available. New World hantaviruses, including Andes virus (ANDV), use the cell-surface receptor protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) to enter host cells1. However, the structural basis of this interaction remains unclear. Here we describe the structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV spike at near-atomic resolution. PCDH1 asymmetrically engages a deep central pocket formed by four Gn protomers in the spike, explaining why only intact viral particles or soluble tetramers recognize it. Mutagenesis identified three Gn loops that shape the receptor-binding site and afford the transfer of PCDH1 binding from New World to Old World glycoproteins. Structural and functional analyses of four neutralizing antibodies revealed that they block receptor binding through two distinct mechanisms—occluding access to the PCDH1-binding site or sterically preventing receptor engagement. Together, these findings define the structural determinants of hantavirus–receptor recognition, reveal how a virus can mask its receptor-binding site by recessing it in a surface depression and how antibodies can counter this strategy, and provide a framework for the design of antiviral therapeutics targeting the hantavirus spike.

Hantaviruses are a large and globally distributed family of viruses associated with severe zoonotic disease in humans. The New World hantaviruses (NWHs) ANDV and Sin Nombre virus (SNV) cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) in South and North America, respectively, with high case-fatality rates that can approach 40%. Cardiogenic shock and respiratory failure are hallmarks of HCPS. Old World hantaviruses (OWHs) are endemic in Europe and Asia or globally distributed in some cases (Seoul virus (SEOV)). The OWH Hantaan virus (HTNV), Puumala virus (PUUV) and Dobrava-Belgrade virus (DOBV) are associated with severe zoonotic disease and considerable mortality. Although hantaviruses are typically transmitted to humans through inhalation of aerosolized excreta from infected rodents, ANDV appears uniquely capable of human-to-human transmission2,3, raising its global public health significance and epidemic potential. This risk was underscored by the recent ANDV outbreak on a cruise ship departing Ushuaia, Argentina4. No US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)- or European Medicines Agency (EMA)-approved medical countermeasures are available to prevent or treat hantaviral infections.

Hantavirus glycoprotein spikes are formed by two glycoproteins, Gn and Gc, which are organized into a partial lattice at the surface of the virion. Each spike consists of four Gn molecules that form a central stabilizing core surrounded by four Gc molecules at the periphery. Gc mediates the interspike contacts that stabilize the lattice. Gn consists of a head (GnH) and a base (GnB) domain. GnH is exposed at the viral surface and is thought to participate in receptor binding, whereas GnB is buried within the spike and mediates most of the intraspike interactions. Gc consists of three domains that drive membrane fusion. At neutral pH, GnH interacts with Gc, forming a pre-fusion complex that prevents premature fusion. After exposure to acidic pH, the Gn–Gc complex dissociates, allowing Gc to insert three hydrophobic loops into the host cell membrane and undergo conformational rearrangements that drive fusion of viral and cellular membranes. Structural studies have reported the structures of GnH, GnB, Gc, the GnH–Gc complex and the Gn–Gc spike from several hantaviruses5,6,7,8,9,10.

Understanding how hantaviruses recognize their cellular receptors is a critical step toward the rational development of therapies and vaccines. Previous studies have identified several cell-surface molecules as candidate entry host factors, including integrins β1–3 (refs. 11,12,13,14), decay accelerating factor (DAF, encoded by CD55)15,16, complement factors (gC1qR)17 and the cadherin-superfamily protein PCDH1 (ref. 1). However, only PCDH1 has been shown to directly recognize the ANDV Gn–Gc spike1,18 and to be required for infection of human endothelial cells—major targets of hantavirus infection1,19. Furthermore, PCDH1 is critical for ANDV infection in vivo and for disease pathogenesis in a lethal hamster model of ANDV challenge1,18. PCDH1 is a type I membrane protein expressed in human airway epithelial and endothelial cells. It contains seven extracellular cadherin-repeat (EC) domains that extend into the extracellular space. Binding studies have shown that PCDH1 does not recognize soluble monomeric glycoproteins but instead binds to the tetrameric glycoprotein spikes displayed on the viral surface1,18. Monoclonal antibodies targeting the first EC repeat (EC1) inhibited entry of a recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) pseudotyped with Gn–Gc from multiple NWHs1, and point mutations at the tip of EC1 prevented PCDH1’s interaction with Gn–Gc of rVSVs bearing the glycoproteins of ANDV (rVSV-ANDV)1,18. Together, these findings indicate that NWHs infect host cells by engaging the EC1 domain of PCDH1. However, the structural determinants of this interaction remain unclear. Here we sought to determine the structure of PCDH1 bound to the ANDV Gn–Gc spike.

PCDH1 binds to viral particles but not to the soluble GnH–Gc heterodimer1,18, suggesting that the receptor-binding site is presented only on viral spikes. To elucidate the structural basis for PCDH1 recognition, we designed a soluble version of the ANDV spike tetramer by adding a hetero-octamerization domain at the C-terminal end of the Gn and Gc ectodomains (Fig. 1a). The octamerization sequence was derived from HALC4_136, a de novo tetramerization domain comprising three antiparallel helices per protomer20. We split this scaffold by fusing the first two helices to Gn and the third helix to Gc, so that co-expression of Gn and Gc would reconstitute a hetero-oligomeric assembly with the stoichiometry of the native spike (Extended Data Fig. 1a). We cloned both genes into a bicistronic plasmid, purified the complex from the supernatants of stably transfected Drosophila melanogaster S2 cells using affinity and size-exclusion chromatography and confirmed that it interacts with a truncated PCDH1 construct consisting of wild-type EC domains 1 to 4 (sEC1–4WT) using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA; Fig. 1b). As a negative control, we used a construct containing the substitutions Y81A and F83A (sEC1–4MUT), which are known to abrogate virus binding18. We also confirmed that incubation of the soluble spike with an excess of soluble sEC1WT, but not sEC1MUT, prevented the binding to sEC1–4WT (Fig. 1c). Furthermore, we used biolayer interferometry (BLI) to demonstrate specific spike–EC1 binding. Specifically, sEC1–4WT or sEC1–4MUT were immobilized on sensors, which were then dipped into solutions containing increasing concentrations of soluble spike (Fig. 1d). BLI assays performed in the opposite orientation corroborated these findings (Extended Data Fig. 1b).

a, Schematic of the soluble spike construct (top). The Gn and Gc ectodomains were fused to a C-terminal tetramerization domain (TD). Cysteine residues in the Gn and Gc TD domains were engineered to form a disulfide bond. N-glycosylation sites are shown in green, and the location of the signal peptides (SP) is indicated. Bottom, schematic of the construct used to produce the eVLPs fused to the PCDH1 EC1 domain. b, ELISA binding of soluble spikes to immobilized WT or double-mutant PCDH1 EC1–4 (DM: Y81A/F83A). Data are mean ± s.d. from four independent experiments, two performed in triplicate and two in duplicate (n = 10). c, EC1 competition ELISA. Soluble spike tetramers were preincubated with serial dilutions of WT or DM sEC1 before addition to WT PCDH1 EC1–4-coated plates. Data are mean ± s.d. from two independent experiments performed in triplicate (n = 6). d, BLI analysis of soluble spike tetramer binding to His-tagged WT or DM sEC1–4 immobilized on NTA biosensors. One representative experiment is shown from three independent experiments. e, Cryo-EM maps were obtained after co-expression of the soluble spike tetramers with PCDH1 EC1–4. Left, top view along the four-fold axis. Right, the same map rotated 45° around the y axis. Gn is shown in red, Gc in yellow and PCDH1 EC1 in blue. f, Atomic model of ANDV spike bound to PCDH1 EC1, coloured as in e. g, Contacts of Gn and PCDH1 EC1. Gn is shown in pink and PCDH1 EC1 in light blue; Gn loops AB (violet), CD (dark green) and DE (red) or PCDH1 EC1 loops BC (blue) and FG (light green) are highlighted as indicated in the figure. h, Cryo-EM map obtained by fusing the PCDH1 EC1 domain to the N terminus of the M segment, coloured as in e and as indicated in the bottom schematic of a.

To verify that the soluble spike proteins fold like the spikes observed on the viral surface, we performed cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). We observed a few two-dimensional (2D) classes compatible with Gn–Gc tetramers (Extended Data Fig. 1c). However, a low-resolution three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction obtained from them was not compatible with the known ANDV spike structure5 (Extended Data Fig. 1d), suggesting that, in the absence of lateral contacts between spikes and the transmembrane regions, the intersubunit contacts within the spike are not sufficiently stable to maintain the intact eight-subunit assembly. We next hypothesized that prolonged incubation of the two proteins might help to stabilize the spike in its receptor-binding conformation. To test this hypothesis, we co-transfected S2 cells with the plasmids encoding sEC1–4WT and the soluble spike and purified the complex using double-affinity and size-exclusion chromatography. We performed cryo-EM studies and observed many new 2D classes showing tetramers (Extended Data Fig. 2 and Extended Data Table 1). Using particles from these classes, we reconstructed a map at a resolution of 2.4 Å, and we used the map to build a model of the spike that closely resembles the tetramers observed on viral particles5. The only notable differences between the two models are a slight rotation of the GnH domains relative to GnB and the poorly resolved density for domain III in the soluble spikes (Extended Data Fig. 3).

The cryo-EM map of the complex revealed an additional density at the centre of the spike, consistent in size with a single EC domain of PCDH1. However, as the map was processed using C4 symmetry, and the symmetry axis passes through the centre of the spike, we were unable to model this residual density. We reprocessed the map by combining a masked 3D classification with a non-uniform refinement using a pseudo-C4 symmetry. This approach yielded a new map at a resolution of 2.6 Å (Fig. 1e), in which we modelled PCDH1 EC1 at the centre of the spike (Fig. 1f,g). The final model showed the EC1 domain deeply inserted into a pocket formed by four protomers of Gn, establishing contacts with two neighbouring protomers (660 and 200 Å2, respectively) and sparse contacts with the other two (80 Å2 and 35 Å2). This mode of interaction, whereby one receptor molecule interacts with four viral glycoproteins, represents a binding mode that to our knowledge has not been observed in any enveloped virus, and explains why PCDH1 binds to viral particles but not to soluble GnH–Gc heterodimers. In the model, EC1 loops BCEC1 and FGEC1 interact with the AB and CD loops of GnH and the DE loop of GnB from two neighbouring protomers (Fig. 1g and Extended Data Fig. 4a). Notably, the densities corresponding to the DE and CD loops are weaker in the protomers that do not engage EC1 than in the receptor-contacting protomers (Extended Data Fig. 3b). This suggests that these loops are flexible and that PCDH1 binding stabilizes specific conformations of these regions. Indeed, comparison of the four protomers reveals that EC1 binding induces a conformational change in the CD and DE loops of one protomer, creating asymmetry within the pocket (Extended Data Fig. 3b). Previous studies have identified PCDH1 mutations that inhibit virus binding18, and all are in the BCEC1 loop or nearby regions, probably altering the conformation of the loop. Consistent with the structural data, mutations in the tip of the FG loop had little (D142A, D142R) or no (L143A, V144A, Q145A) effect on virus binding18, probably because none of them introduce steric restrictions (Fig. 1g).

To validate the model with viral particles, we studied the interaction between PCDH1 and virus-like particles (VLPs). We did not attempt to decorate preformed VLPs with soluble receptor because flow cytometry revealed only weak binding of EC1 to ANDV glycoproteins presented on the cell surface. Instead, reasoning that increasing the local concentration of receptor near the spike could enhance binding, we fused EC1 to the N terminus of the M segment through a flexible linker (Fig. 1a). To increase particle production, we introduced an EABR tag21 and the V535K and S1096L mutations, as reported previously5,22, and transfected the construct into FreeStyle293 cells. We analysed the secreted particles using cryo-EM and obtained a reconstruction of the spike at an overall resolution of 3.9 Å (Extended Data Fig. 5). The map revealed clear densities for Gn and Gc and an additional density at the centre of the spike (Fig. 1h). This central density was compatible in size and position with the PCDH1 EC1 domain observed in the soluble spike complex. However, the quality of this density did not allow unambiguous building of the EC1 domain, preventing a detailed comparison of the VLP–receptor interface with that obtained using the soluble spike (Extended Data Fig. 5c). This work nevertheless confirmed that PCDH1 EC1 occupies the central region of the Gn–Gc tetramer in viral particles.

To begin to investigate the roles of the CD and AB loops of GnH and the DE loop of GnB in spike–PCDH1 recognition, we produced rVSV-ANDV and rVSVs bearing the glycoproteins of the PCDH1-independent1,19 OWH HTNV (rVSV-HTNV), as well as rVSV-ANDV variants in which we replaced the GnH CD loop or all three loops in contact with the receptor (Methods and Extended Data Fig. 4a) with those from HTNV. After normalizing the amount of incorporated Gn–Gc in the viral particles (Extended Data Fig. 4b), we measured their interaction with immobilized PCDH1 EC1 on ELISA plates. Consistent with the known receptor specificity of hantaviruses and our structural data, PCDH1 EC1 could capture rVSV-ANDV but not rVSV-HTNV or any of the chimeric variants (Fig. 2a).

a, ELISA binding of PCDH1 EC1–2 to rVSV particles bearing hantavirus envelope glycoproteins. Plates coated with sEC1–2 were incubated with serial dilutions of rVSV expressing ANDV or HTNV glycoproteins, or chimeric ANDV glycoproteins containing the HTNV loop CD or HTNV loops CD, AB and DE, as indicated. The starting dilution of each rVSV chimera was normalized to the parental hantavirus based on its Gn–Gc expression. The ELISA signal was normalized to rVSV-ANDV, and viruses were compared at the 4× viral dilution using two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey’s multiple-comparison test; the reference is shown in bold. Data are mean ± s.d. n = 6 wells per viral particle dilution from three independent experiments (n = 5 wells for the 4× dilution of ANDV). ****P < 0.0001 (ANDV versus ANDVHTNV-all, ANDVHTNV-CDLoop, or HTNV: P = 1.1 × 10−12). b, DMS analysis of PCDH1 binding to an alphavirus-based pseudotyped SHV. SHV particles bearing ANDV glycoproteins were generated from a Gn library containing all amino acid substitutions at each targeted residue. Particles were captured on PCDH1 EC1–2-coated ELISA plates, and the variant abundance in the input and two PCDH1-bound replicates was quantified. Left, Benjamini–Hochberg FDR-corrected significance versus fold change (FC) for each variant in the PCDH1-bound fraction. Right, FC values were mapped onto the ANDV spike. Gc is shown in light yellow, and Gn is coloured according to the largest absolute FC value per residue, as indicated. c, Mapping of high-impact mutations. PCDH1 EC1 is shown as a surface representation, Gn as a cartoon with loops CD and AB and helix α2 coloured green, magenta and pink, respectively. In the right panel, the receptor surface is coloured according to electrostatic potential. Selected residues are shown as sticks, with the corresponding mutations indicated and numbered as in b. An upward arrow indicates that the mutation is enriched in the selection, whereas a downward arrow indicates that it is depleted.

Next, we used a deep-mutational scanning (DMS) approach to more comprehensively survey the sequence landscape of the spike–PCDH1 interaction. We generated two independent Gn libraries, each introducing all possible amino acid substitutions at 427 of 448 positions in the ectodomain (amino acids 24–471; Methods) and used these to create libraries of alphavirus-based vectors pseudotyped with ANDV Gn–Gc (Sem-Hantavirus (SHV)). We captured SHVs bound to PCDH1 EC1 immobilized on ELISA plates and sequenced the PCDH1-bound SHV fractions to identify variants enriched or depleted relative to the input population. We observed strong selective signals for the GnH CD and AB loops and nearby regions in both populations, consistent with roles for these sequences in virus–receptor recognition (Fig. 2b,c and Extended Data Fig. 6). Relatively few variants were recovered from the GnB DE loop, consistent with its higher level of conservation (Extended Data Fig. 4a) and suggesting an important structural role for this sequence in the assembly and/or stability of the spike. Notably, none of the Gn ectodomain substitutions observed in the recent Hondius outbreak isolate of ANDV (LS-CH2016/2016-12-23/Switzerland) mapped to the PCDH1-binding pocket or were selected in the DMS experiments, indicating that this virus probably resembles previous isolates of the virus in its ability to recognize and use PCDH1 (Extended Data Figs. 4 and 6).

PCDH1 is a specific receptor for NWHs, and we wondered whether the structure of the complex could reveal insights into receptor use. We analysed the sequence conservation of the PCDH1-binding pocket across hantaviruses and compared the conformation of the loops using the available crystal structures of HTNV and SNV. We identified two amino acid substitutions: one in the GnH AB loop of SEOV, DOBV and HTNV (L36F) and one in the GnB DE loop of HTNV (G418L) that are predicted to cause steric clashes with PCDH1. By contrast, both the sequence and structure of the GnH CD loop vary substantially across hantaviruses—it is an extended loop in NWHs but a compact helix in OWHs (Fig. 3a and Extended Data Fig. 4). These findings suggest that it is not only the residues directly contacting PCDH1 that are important to the spike–receptor interaction but also nearby residues that influence the overall conformation of the loops, as is also indicated by the DMS data (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 6).

Bottom, alignment of the loop AB from ANDV (red) and HTNV (yellow; PDB: 6Y6P)9. b, ELISA binding of rVSV particles bearing hantavirus glycoproteins to soluble PCDH1-EC1–2-coated plates. The superscript notes indicate loop substitutions: CD, loop CD; All, loops CD, AB and DE. The starting dilutions of the rVSV-chimeras were normalized to their parental hantavirus based on Gn–Gc expression. The ELISA signal was normalized to rVSV-ANDV, and viruses were analysed at the 4× dilution using two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparison test; references are shown in bold.
